questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which three types of muscle tissue are found in the body?
options: Striated, voluntary, and involuntary
Fast, slow, and intermediate
Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth
Skeletal, visceral, and connective
questions.why: Muscle tissue comes in three types, and each is named for where it is found or how it looks: skeletal muscle attaches to the skeleton, cardiac muscle forms the heart wall, and smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels. All three can contract, but they differ in striations, control, and cell shape, and those differences are how you tell them apart on a slide.
notes: Striated, voluntary, and involuntary are words used to describe and compare the tissues, not the names of the tissues. They would fit a question asking how skeletal muscle (striated and voluntary) differs from smooth muscle (nonstriated and involuntary).

Fast, slow, and intermediate describe how quickly individual skeletal muscle fibers contract, so they sort fibers within one tissue rather than naming tissue types. Students choose this when they mix up fiber speed categories with tissue categories.
Correct. Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth are the three muscle tissue types.

Visceral is an older name for smooth muscle in organ walls, but connective tissue is a separate primary tissue, not a muscle. Connective tissue would be the answer if the question asked which tissue forms the sheaths and tendons around a muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which tissue is attached to the skeleton and is described as striated and voluntary?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is the muscle tissue attached to the bones of the skeleton. Its fibers show striations, the light and dark stripes made by lined-up contractile proteins, and it is voluntary, meaning you can contract it on purpose. Those two features, striated and voluntary, are the hallmarks of skeletal muscle.
notes: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but it is involuntary and found only in the heart wall. Pick it if the question describes striated muscle that contracts without conscious control.

Smooth muscle has no striations and is involuntary, and it lines hollow organs and blood vessels rather than attaching to bone. It would be the answer for the muscle layer in the stomach or bladder wall.
Correct. Skeletal muscle is attached to the skeleton and is striated and voluntary.
Dense regular connective tissue does attach to bone, because it forms tendons and ligaments, but it cannot contract and has no striations. Pick it if the question asks what tissue makes up a tendon.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which pair of features describes skeletal muscle tissue?
options: Nonstriated and voluntary
Striated and voluntary
Striated and involuntary
Nonstriated and involuntary
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is striated, meaning its fibers show alternating light and dark bands under the microscope, and it is voluntary, meaning it contracts when you consciously decide to move. Comparing the muscle types by these two features is the fastest way to sort them: skeletal is striated and voluntary, cardiac is striated and involuntary, and smooth is nonstriated and involuntary.
notes: No muscle tissue is both nonstriated and voluntary. Students land on this when they remember that skeletal muscle is voluntary but forget that it is also the most obviously striated tissue.
Correct. Skeletal muscle is striated and under voluntary control.
Striated and involuntary describes cardiac muscle, which has stripes but beats without conscious control. Pick this pair if the question is about the heart wall.
Nonstriated and involuntary describes smooth muscle in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels. Pick this pair if the question asks about the muscle of the stomach or bladder.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which tissue makes up the bulk of the heart wall?
options: Smooth muscle
Elastic connective tissue
Cardiac muscle
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: The thick middle layer of the heart wall, the myocardium, is made of cardiac muscle, and it makes up most of the wall's thickness. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart. It is striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary, so the heart keeps beating without conscious effort.
notes: Smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels, including the coronary arteries that supply the heart, but it does not form the heart wall itself. Pick it for the muscle layer of a blood vessel or the stomach.

Elastic connective tissue is rich in stretchy elastin fibers and is found in the walls of large arteries such as the aorta, where it lets the wall stretch and recoil. It would be the answer for what allows the aorta to stretch, not for the contracting heart wall.
Correct. Cardiac muscle forms the myocardium, the bulk of the heart wall.
Skeletal muscle attaches to the skeleton and is under voluntary control, so it is not found in the heart wall. Pick it if the question asks about the muscles that move the bones of the limbs.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which tissue forms the contracting layer in the walls of hollow organs such as the stomach and urinary bladder, and in the walls of blood vessels?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
questions.why: Smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels, where it squeezes contents along or changes the size of the opening. It is called smooth because it has no striations, and it is involuntary, so it works without conscious control. When you see muscle in the wall of the stomach, bladder, or an artery, think smooth muscle.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue is made of tightly packed parallel collagen fibers and forms tendons and ligaments, but it cannot contract. Pick it if the question asks what tissue attaches a muscle to a bone.
Correct. Smooth muscle forms the contracting layer of hollow organs and blood vessels.
Skeletal muscle attaches to bones and is voluntary, so it does not form the walls of these organs. Pick it for a question about the muscles that move the limbs.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall, not in the stomach, bladder, or blood vessels. Pick it if the question asks about the myocardium.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: What is the characteristic shape of a smooth muscle cell?
options: Long and cylindrical
Flat and scale-like
Short and branched
Spindle shaped
questions.why: A smooth muscle cell is spindle shaped, meaning it is widest in the middle where its single nucleus sits and tapers to a point at each end. These cells pack together in sheets in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels. The spindle shape and the lack of striations are the two features that identify smooth muscle on a slide.
notes: Long and cylindrical describes a skeletal muscle fiber, which can run much of the length of the muscle. Pick this shape for a question about skeletal muscle cells.
Flat and scale-like describes squamous epithelial cells, such as those lining the air sacs of the lungs. Students choose it when they mix up epithelial cell shapes with muscle cell shapes.
Short and branched describes cardiac muscle cells, which branch and join their neighbors at intercalated discs. Pick this shape for a question about the heart wall.
Correct. Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped and taper at both ends.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Under the microscope, which muscle tissue shows no striations?
options: Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
Both skeletal and cardiac muscle
questions.why: Striations are the alternating light and dark bands made when the contractile proteins inside muscle cells line up in repeating units. In smooth muscle those proteins are not arranged in neat rows, so the cells look smooth and even under the microscope. That is where the name smooth muscle comes from.
notes: Correct. Smooth muscle lacks striations.
Skeletal muscle is the most obviously striated tissue, with bold light and dark bands across every fiber. Pick it if the question asks which muscle is striated and voluntary.
Cardiac muscle is striated, even though it is involuntary. Pick it if the question asks which muscle is striated but not under conscious control.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle are the two striated tissues, so this pairing names exactly the muscles that do have stripes. It would be the answer if the question asked which muscle tissues are striated.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: How many nuclei does a smooth muscle cell have, and where do they sit?
options: One nucleus in the center of the cell
Two nuclei, one near each tapered end
Many nuclei pushed to the edge of the cell
One nucleus pushed against the edge of the cell
questions.why: Each smooth muscle cell has a single nucleus located in the center of the cell, in the widest part of the spindle. This sets it apart from a skeletal muscle fiber, which has many nuclei pushed to the edge. Cardiac cells also have one central nucleus, so to separate cardiac from smooth muscle you look for striations and intercalated discs.
notes: Correct. A smooth muscle cell has one nucleus in its center.
No muscle cell places its nuclei at its tips. Students pick this when they picture the tapered spindle shape and guess that something must sit at each end.
Many nuclei pushed to the edge describes a skeletal muscle fiber, which forms when many cells fuse during development. Pick this answer for a question about skeletal muscle nuclei.
One nucleus pushed against the cell edge is how a fat cell (adipocyte) looks, because its large fat droplet pushes the nucleus aside. Pick it for a question about adipose tissue, not smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: One nucleus in the center of the cell

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle property is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus?
options: Contractility
Elasticity
Excitability
Extensibility
questions.why: Excitability, also called responsiveness, is a muscle cell's ability to detect a stimulus, such as a signal from a nerve, and respond to it. It is the first step in every contraction, because a muscle cannot shorten until it has responded to the signal telling it to. Nerve cells share this property, which is why it does not by itself set muscle apart from other tissues.
notes: Contractility is the ability to shorten forcibly when stimulated, which is the step that follows the response to the stimulus. Pick it for a question about the property that sets muscle apart from all other tissues.
Elasticity is the ability to recoil back to resting length after being stretched. Pick it for a question about a muscle springing back after a stretch.
Correct. Excitability is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus.
Extensibility is the ability to be stretched beyond resting length, as when one muscle is pulled long by the contraction of its opposing muscle. Pick it for a question about stretching.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle property is the ability to shorten forcibly when stimulated?
options: Extensibility
Elasticity
Excitability
Contractility
questions.why: Contractility is the ability of a muscle cell to shorten with force once it has been stimulated. This shortening is what pulls on tendons and bones to move the body, squeezes blood out of the heart, and narrows hollow organs. Contractility is the property that makes muscle tissue different from every other tissue.
notes: Extensibility is the ability to be stretched, which is the opposite of shortening. Pick it if the question asks how a muscle can be pulled beyond its resting length.
Elasticity is the ability to recoil to resting length after a stretch. It returns the muscle to its normal length rather than shortening it forcibly, so pick it for a question about springing back.
Excitability is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus, which comes before the shortening. Pick it for a question about how a muscle detects the signal to contract.
Correct. Contractility is the ability to shorten forcibly.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle property is the ability to be stretched beyond resting length?
options: Contractility
Excitability
Elasticity
Extensibility
questions.why: Extensibility is the ability of a muscle to be stretched, or extended, beyond its resting length. This happens every time one muscle contracts and pulls its opposing muscle long, such as the triceps brachii being stretched when the biceps brachii bends the elbow. Extensibility lets muscles in opposing pairs work across a joint without tearing.
notes: Contractility is the ability to shorten forcibly, which is the opposite of being stretched. Pick it for the property that sets muscle apart from all other tissues.
Excitability is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus. Pick it for a question about how a muscle detects the signal to contract.

Elasticity is the ability to recoil to resting length after a stretch, so it describes what happens after the stretch ends. Students mix the two up because both words deal with stretching, so pick elasticity only when the question is about springing back.
Correct. Extensibility is the ability to be stretched.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle property lets a muscle recoil and return to its resting length after being stretched?
options: Contractility
Elasticity
Excitability
Extensibility
questions.why: Elasticity is the ability of a muscle to recoil and resume its resting length once a stretching force is removed, much like a rubber band snapping back. It works as the partner of extensibility: extensibility allows the stretch, and elasticity brings the muscle back. Together they keep muscles from staying overstretched after movement.
notes: Contractility is the ability to shorten forcibly when stimulated. Returning to resting length after a stretch is a passive recoil, not a forceful contraction, so pick contractility only for a question about active shortening.
Correct. Elasticity is the ability to recoil to resting length.
Excitability is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus. Pick it for a question about the first step in starting a contraction.
Extensibility is the ability to be stretched in the first place, so it describes the stretch rather than the return. Pick it for a question about how a muscle can be pulled beyond resting length.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which list names the four functional properties of muscle tissue?
options: Contractility, elasticity, absorption, and secretion
Excitability, conductivity, contractility, and secretion
Excitability, contractility, extensibility, and elasticity
Movement, posture, joint stability, and heat production
questions.why: The four functional properties describe what muscle cells are able to do. Excitability is responding to a stimulus, contractility is shortening forcibly, extensibility is being stretched, and elasticity is recoiling to resting length. Properties describe the abilities of the tissue, while functions describe the jobs muscle does for the body, such as movement and heat production.
notes: Absorption and secretion are functions of epithelial tissue, such as the lining of the small intestine. This list mixes two real muscle properties with two epithelial functions.

Conductivity is a property of neurons, which carry signals along their length, and secretion is a job of glandular epithelium. Students choose this list when they blend the properties of nervous and epithelial tissue into muscle.
Correct. Excitability, contractility, extensibility, and elasticity are the four functional properties.
These are the four functions of muscle tissue, the jobs it performs for the body. Pick this list if the question asks what muscle does for the body rather than what abilities its cells have.
review: gross/histology tagged automatically from wording

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which list names the four general functions of muscle tissue?
options: Movement, absorption, secretion, and filtration
Movement, protection, blood cell formation, and mineral storage
Movement, posture, joint stability, and heat production
Excitability, contractility, extensibility, and elasticity
questions.why: Muscle tissue does four general jobs for the body. It produces movement, maintains posture and body position, stabilizes joints, and generates heat as a byproduct of contraction. These functions all come from muscle's ability to contract and pull, whether that pull moves a bone, holds the body upright, or simply keeps a joint firm.
notes: Absorption, secretion, and filtration are functions of epithelial tissue, such as the lining of the gut and kidney tubules. Students pick this list when they confuse tissue functions across the four primary tissues.
Protection, blood cell formation, and mineral storage are functions of the skeletal system. Pick this list for a question about what bones do for the body.
Correct. Movement, posture, joint stability, and heat production are the four general functions of muscle.

These are the four functional properties of muscle cells, the abilities that make contraction possible. Pick this list if the question asks about properties such as responding to a stimulus or recoiling after a stretch.
questions.answerText: Movement, posture, joint stability, and heat production

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle function keeps the body upright and holds its position, even while you are sitting or standing still?
options: Generation of heat
Maintenance of posture and body position
Production of movement
Stabilization of joints
questions.why: Maintaining posture means muscles are working constantly, making small adjustments that hold the body upright against the pull of gravity. This happens even when you seem to be still, such as when sitting or standing. Muscles of the back, neck, and legs are especially busy with this job.
notes: Generation of heat is a byproduct of muscle contraction that helps keep body temperature normal. Pick it for a question about shivering or warming the body.
Correct. Maintaining posture keeps the body upright and holds its position.
Production of movement is the function used when muscles pull on bones to walk, lift, or reach. Pick it when the question describes visible motion of a body part.

Stabilization of joints is the function where muscles and their tendons hold the bones of a joint firmly together. Pick it if the question describes muscles keeping a particular joint, such as the shoulder, from slipping out of place.
questions.answerText: Maintenance of posture and body position

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle function is a byproduct of contraction that helps keep body temperature near 37 C (98.6 F)?
options: Generation of heat
Stabilization of joints
Maintenance of posture
Production of movement
questions.why: Every time muscle cells contract, they use energy, and much of that energy is released as heat. Because skeletal muscle makes up a large share of body mass, this heat is a major source of warmth that helps keep body temperature near 37 C (98.6 F). Shivering is the body using rapid contractions on purpose to produce extra heat.
notes: Correct. Heat is a byproduct of contraction that helps maintain body temperature.
Stabilization of joints is the function where muscles and tendons hold a joint's bones firmly together. Pick it if the question describes keeping a joint steady during weight bearing.
Maintenance of posture is the steady muscle work that holds the body upright against gravity. Pick it for a question about sitting or standing still.
Production of movement is the main purpose of contraction, such as moving a limb, not a byproduct of it. Pick it when the question describes walking, lifting, or other visible motion.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A tissue is striated, contracts without conscious control, and has cells joined by intercalated discs. Which tissue is it?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Nervous tissue
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Cardiac muscle is the only muscle tissue that is striated but involuntary, and it is the only one with intercalated discs, the junctions that join its branching cells end to end. Any one of those intercalated discs on a slide is enough to identify the tissue as cardiac muscle. It is found only in the heart wall.
notes: Correct. Striated, involuntary, and joined by intercalated discs describes cardiac muscle.
Smooth muscle is involuntary, but it has no striations and no intercalated discs. Pick it if the description says nonstriated cells in the wall of a hollow organ.

Nervous tissue is made of neurons and supporting neuroglia, and it carries signals rather than contracting. Pick it if the description mentions cells with long branching processes such as axons and dendrites.
Skeletal muscle is striated, but it is voluntary and has no intercalated discs. Pick it if the description says striated and under conscious control.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary, and each of their cells has one central nucleus. Which feature does cardiac muscle have that smooth muscle lacks?
options: Striations
Spindle-shaped cells
One central nucleus
Involuntary control
questions.why: Cardiac muscle and smooth muscle share involuntary control and a single central nucleus per cell, so those features cannot tell them apart. Cardiac muscle, however, is striated, with the same light and dark banding seen in skeletal muscle, while smooth muscle has no striations at all. Striations, along with intercalated discs, are how you separate cardiac from smooth muscle on a slide.
notes: Correct. Cardiac muscle is striated, while smooth muscle is not.
Spindle-shaped cells belong to smooth muscle, not cardiac muscle, whose cells are short and branched. Pick this feature if the question asks what smooth muscle has that cardiac muscle lacks.

Both cardiac and smooth muscle cells have one central nucleus, so this feature does not separate them. A single central nucleus would help only if the question asked how either one differs from skeletal muscle, which has many nuclei at the edge.
Both cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary, so this is a shared feature. Pick involuntary control if the question asks how either tissue differs from skeletal muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle tissue type has the longest cells?
options: Cardiac muscle
Skeletal muscle
All three have cells of similar length
Smooth muscle
questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical cells that form when many embryonic cells fuse together, which is also why each fiber has many nuclei. A single fiber can run a long way along the length of a muscle. Cardiac and smooth muscle cells are much shorter, each with a single nucleus.
notes: Cardiac muscle cells are short and branched, joined end to end by intercalated discs. Pick cardiac muscle for a question about branching cells, not long ones.
Correct. Skeletal muscle has the longest cells of the three muscle types.
The three types differ a great deal in cell size and shape, which is one of the ways you tell them apart. Students choose this when they assume all muscle cells look alike because they all contract.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped and short compared with skeletal fibers. Pick smooth muscle for a question about tapered cells with one central nucleus.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares smooth muscle with skeletal muscle?
options: Smooth muscle is nonstriated and involuntary, while skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary
Smooth muscle is striated and involuntary, while skeletal muscle is nonstriated and voluntary
Both are voluntary, but only smooth muscle lacks striations
Both are striated, but only skeletal muscle is under voluntary control
questions.why: Skeletal and smooth muscle differ on both features you use to sort muscle tissue. Skeletal muscle is striated, with bold light and dark bands, and voluntary, so you control it on purpose. Smooth muscle has no striations and is involuntary, working in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels without conscious effort.
notes: Correct. Smooth muscle is nonstriated and involuntary, and skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary.
This reverses the striations. Striated and involuntary actually describes cardiac muscle, so pick that description for a question about the heart wall.

Smooth muscle is not voluntary; you cannot consciously squeeze your stomach or tighten a blood vessel. The part about smooth muscle lacking striations is true, which is what makes this choice tempting.
Smooth muscle is not striated. This statement would be correct if it compared skeletal muscle with cardiac muscle, since both of those are striated and only skeletal is voluntary.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle is nonstriated and involuntary, while skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: The word roots myo and mys, as in myocardium and epimysium, refer to what?
options: Flesh
Muscle
Cell
Fiber
questions.why: Myo and mys both come from the Greek word for muscle. You see them throughout the muscle chapter: myocardium is the muscle layer of the heart, and epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium are the sheaths around and within a muscle. Recognizing the root tells you a term has something to do with muscle before you know its full meaning.
notes: Flesh is the meaning of the prefix sarco, as in sarcolemma and sarcoplasm. Pick flesh for a question about the sarco prefix.
Correct. Myo and mys both mean muscle.
Cell is the meaning of the root cyto, as in cytoplasm. Students pick this because many muscle terms describe parts of a muscle cell.
Fiber is the meaning of the root fibr, as in fibroblast and fibrocartilage. It is tempting because skeletal muscle cells are called muscle fibers, but myo itself means muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Before a muscle can shorten, it must first detect the signal telling it to contract. Which property makes this first step possible?
options: Elasticity
Contractility
Extensibility
Excitability
questions.why: Excitability is the ability to receive and respond to a stimulus, such as a signal arriving from a nerve. It has to come first, because a muscle cell cannot shorten until it has responded to the signal. Contractility, the shortening itself, follows only after excitability has done its job.
notes: Elasticity is the ability to recoil to resting length after a stretch, which happens after the muscle has been stretched. Pick it for a question about springing back.
Contractility is the shortening that follows the stimulus, so it is the second step, not the first. Pick it for a question about the property that sets muscle apart from other tissues.
Extensibility is the ability to be stretched beyond resting length. Pick it for a question about how a muscle lengthens when its opposing muscle contracts.
Correct. Excitability lets the muscle detect and respond to the stimulus.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares extensibility and elasticity?
options: Both terms mean the same ability, the ability to be stretched
Extensibility lets a muscle be stretched, and elasticity lets it recoil to resting length
Extensibility lets a muscle shorten forcibly, and elasticity lets it respond to a stimulus
Elasticity lets a muscle be stretched, and extensibility lets it recoil to resting length
questions.why: Extensibility and elasticity are partners. Extensibility is the ability to be stretched, or extended, beyond resting length, and elasticity is the ability to recoil back to resting length once the stretch is released. A useful memory link is that extensibility sounds like extend, and elasticity works like an elastic band snapping back.
notes: The two terms describe different abilities: one allows the stretch and the other allows the return. Students choose this because both words deal with stretching and sound alike.
Correct. Extensibility allows the stretch, and elasticity allows the recoil.
Shortening forcibly is contractility, and responding to a stimulus is excitability. Pick those terms for questions about the active steps of contraction rather than stretching.
This swaps the two definitions. Linking extensibility with extend helps keep them straight.
questions.answerText: Extensibility lets a muscle be stretched, and elasticity lets it recoil to resting length

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which match of muscle tissue to cell shape is correct?
options: Skeletal muscle: short, branching cells
Cardiac muscle: spindle-shaped cells
Cardiac muscle: short, branching cells
Smooth muscle: long, cylindrical cells
questions.why: Each muscle tissue has its own cell shape. Cardiac muscle cells are short and branched, joined to their neighbors at intercalated discs so they form a connected network in the heart wall. Skeletal muscle fibers are long and cylindrical, and smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped, tapering at both ends.
notes: Skeletal muscle fibers are long and cylindrical with many nuclei at the edge. Short, branching cells belong to cardiac muscle, so pick skeletal muscle only for long cylindrical fibers.
Spindle-shaped cells belong to smooth muscle, not cardiac. Pick this shape for a question about the muscle in the wall of a hollow organ or blood vessel.
Correct. Cardiac muscle cells are short and branched.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped with one central nucleus. Long, cylindrical cells belong to skeletal muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which muscle function makes walking, picking up objects, pumping blood, and pushing food through the gut possible?
options: Generation of heat
Stabilization of joints
Maintenance of posture
Production of movement
questions.why: Production of movement is the main job of all three muscle types. Skeletal muscle moves the body by pulling on bones, cardiac muscle moves blood by pumping it through the heart, and smooth muscle moves contents such as food along the digestive tract. Each example in the question involves something being moved from one place to another.
notes: Generation of heat is a byproduct of contraction that helps maintain body temperature. Pick it for a question about shivering.
Stabilization of joints holds the bones of a joint firmly in place rather than moving anything. Pick it if the question describes muscles keeping a joint steady.
Maintenance of posture is the steady muscle work that holds the body upright. Pick it for a question about sitting or standing still against gravity.
Correct. Producing movement covers locomotion, handling objects, and moving blood and digestive contents.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A muscle is stretched beyond its resting length and then springs back once it is released. Which two properties are at work, in order?
options: Extensibility, then elasticity
Contractility, then extensibility
Excitability, then contractility
Elasticity, then extensibility
questions.why: The stretch comes first, and that depends on extensibility, the ability to be pulled beyond resting length. The return comes second, and that depends on elasticity, the ability to recoil to resting length once the stretching force is gone. These two properties always pair up whenever a muscle is stretched and released.
notes: Correct. Extensibility allows the stretch, then elasticity allows the recoil.
Contractility is active shortening, which is the opposite of being stretched. Students choose this pair when they confuse a muscle being pulled long with a muscle contracting.

Excitability then contractility is the sequence for an active contraction: the muscle responds to a stimulus and then shortens. Pick this pair for a question about what happens when a nerve signal arrives.
This reverses the order. The muscle must be stretched first (extensibility) before it can spring back (elasticity).

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A histology slide shows short, branched, striated cells joined end to end by dark bands, with one central nucleus in each cell. Which tissue is on the slide, and what are the dark bands?
options: Cardiac muscle, and the bands are intercalated discs
Skeletal muscle, and the bands are Z discs
Smooth muscle, and the bands are terminal cisterns
Skeletal muscle, and the bands are intercalated discs
questions.why: Short, branched, striated cells with a single central nucleus describe cardiac muscle. The dark bands crossing the fibers where one cell meets the next are intercalated discs, junctions that hold the cells together with desmosomes and pass the electrical signal through gap junctions. Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle, so they confirm the identification.
notes: Correct. The tissue is cardiac muscle, and the dark end bands are intercalated discs.

Skeletal muscle fibers are long and cylindrical with many nuclei at the edge, not short and branched. Z discs are thin lines inside every sarcomere rather than thick bands where cells meet, so pick them for a question about the borders of a sarcomere.

Smooth muscle has no striations, and terminal cisterns are tiny sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that cannot be seen as bands with a light microscope. Pick smooth muscle for nonstriated spindle-shaped cells.

The dark bands are intercalated discs, but skeletal muscle does not have them, because its fibers are single long cells rather than chains of short cells. Pick skeletal muscle only for long fibers with many nuclei at the edge.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle, and the bands are intercalated discs

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A tissue in the wall of a blood vessel is nonstriated, contracts slowly and steadily, and is not under conscious control. Which tissue is it?
options: Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Elastic connective tissue
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Smooth muscle forms the middle layer of blood vessel walls, where it contracts slowly and can hold that contraction for a long time to narrow or widen the vessel. It has no striations and works involuntarily, so you cannot consciously control it. Every clue in the description points to smooth muscle.
notes: Correct. Nonstriated, slow, involuntary muscle in a vessel wall is smooth muscle.
Cardiac muscle is involuntary but striated, and it is found only in the heart wall. Pick it for striated involuntary muscle with intercalated discs.

Elastic connective tissue is also found in the walls of large arteries, where it lets the wall stretch and recoil, but it cannot contract. Pick it if the question asks what lets the aorta stretch with each heartbeat.
Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, and it attaches to bones rather than forming vessel walls. Pick it for a description of striated muscle you control on purpose.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Nervous tissue can also receive and respond to a stimulus. Which property is unique to muscle tissue and sets it apart from all other tissues?
options: Excitability
Elasticity
Contractility
Extensibility
questions.why: Contractility is the ability to shorten forcibly when stimulated, and no other tissue can do this. Excitability is shared with nervous tissue, and stretching and recoiling are shared with tissues such as elastic connective tissue. Only muscle can actively pull, which is why contractility is the defining property of muscle.
notes: Excitability is shared with neurons, which also receive and respond to stimuli, so it cannot be what sets muscle apart. Pick excitability for a question about the first step before a contraction.

Elasticity, the ability to recoil after a stretch, is also a feature of elastic connective tissue in the skin, lungs, and artery walls. Pick it for a question about a muscle springing back to resting length.
Correct. Contractility is the property found only in muscle tissue.
Extensibility, the ability to be stretched, is shared with other soft tissues such as skin. Pick it for a question about a muscle being pulled long by its opposing muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A hiker caught in the cold begins to shiver, and the shivering warms her body. Which muscle function does shivering show?
options: Maintenance of posture
Production of movement
Generation of heat
Stabilization of joints
questions.why: Muscle contraction always releases heat as a byproduct, because much of the energy used by working muscle cells escapes as warmth. Shivering is rapid, repeated contraction of skeletal muscles that the body uses specifically to produce extra heat. That heat helps bring body temperature back toward 37 C (98.6 F).
notes: Maintenance of posture is the steady muscle work that holds the body upright against gravity. Pick it for a question about sitting or standing still.
Shivering does involve small movements, but their purpose is not to move the body from place to place. Pick production of movement for walking, lifting, or reaching.
Correct. Shivering uses muscle contraction to generate heat.
Stabilization of joints means muscles hold the bones of a joint firmly together. Pick it for a question about keeping a joint such as the shoulder from slipping out of place.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Two striated muscle tissues are compared on slides. Tissue 1 is voluntary, with many nuclei at the edge of each fiber. Tissue 2 is involuntary, with cells joined by intercalated discs. Which identification is correct?
options: Tissue 1 is skeletal muscle, and Tissue 2 is smooth muscle
Tissue 1 is cardiac muscle, and Tissue 2 is skeletal muscle
Tissue 1 is smooth muscle, and Tissue 2 is cardiac muscle
Tissue 1 is skeletal muscle, and Tissue 2 is cardiac muscle
questions.why: Only skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated, so both slides must be one of those two. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and its long fibers carry many nuclei pushed to the edge, which matches Tissue 1. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and its cells are joined by intercalated discs, which matches Tissue 2.
notes: Tissue 1 is skeletal muscle, but smooth muscle has no striations and no intercalated discs, so it cannot be Tissue 2. Pick smooth muscle for nonstriated spindle-shaped cells.
This swaps the two. Cardiac muscle is involuntary with intercalated discs, and skeletal muscle is voluntary with many nuclei at the edge.
Tissue 2 is cardiac muscle, but smooth muscle is neither striated nor voluntary and has one central nucleus, so it cannot be Tissue 1.
Correct. The voluntary tissue with peripheral nuclei is skeletal muscle, and the involuntary tissue with intercalated discs is cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: Tissue 1 is skeletal muscle, and Tissue 2 is cardiac muscle

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: While you carry a heavy bag, the rotator cuff muscles pull the head of the humerus snugly into its socket so the shoulder does not slip out of place. Which muscle function is this?
options: Generation of heat
Production of movement
Stabilization of joints
Maintenance of posture
questions.why: Stabilizing a joint means muscles and their tendons hold the bones of that joint firmly together, often without producing any visible motion. The shoulder joint is very mobile but shallow, so it depends heavily on the rotator cuff muscles to keep the head of the humerus seated in its socket. Here the muscles are working to hold a joint steady, not to move it.
notes: Generation of heat is a byproduct of all contraction, but it is not the purpose described here. Pick it for a question about shivering.
Production of movement means a muscle pulls a bone through a motion. In this example the arm is not being moved; the muscles are holding the joint still.
Correct. Holding the humerus in its socket is stabilization of the joint.

Maintenance of posture is about holding the whole body upright against gravity, mainly with muscles of the back, neck, and legs. Pick it for a question about sitting or standing still rather than securing one joint.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the cells of skeletal muscle and smooth muscle?
options: Skeletal fibers are spindle shaped with one nucleus, while smooth muscle cells are long and cylindrical with many nuclei
Both are long and cylindrical, but only skeletal fibers have many nuclei
Skeletal fibers are long and cylindrical with many nuclei, while smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped with one nucleus
Skeletal fibers are short and branched with one nucleus, while smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped with many nuclei
questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical cells that form when many embryonic cells fuse, which leaves each fiber with many nuclei pushed to its edge. Smooth muscle cells are much smaller and spindle shaped, tapering at both ends, with a single nucleus in the center. Cell shape and number of nuclei together make these two tissues easy to tell apart on a slide.
notes: This swaps the two descriptions. Long and cylindrical with many nuclei belongs to skeletal muscle, and spindle shaped with one nucleus belongs to smooth muscle.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped and tapered, not long cylinders. Only the part about skeletal fibers having many nuclei is accurate.
Correct. Skeletal fibers are long, cylindrical, and multinucleated, and smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped with one nucleus.
Short and branched describes cardiac muscle, not skeletal, and smooth muscle cells have one nucleus, not many. Pick short and branched for a question about heart muscle cells.
questions.answerText: Skeletal fibers are long and cylindrical with many nuclei, while smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped with one nucleus

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A slide shows long, cylindrical, striated cells, each with many nuclei pressed against the edge just under the cell membrane. Which tissue is it?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Long, cylindrical, striated fibers with many nuclei at the edge are the signature of skeletal muscle. Each fiber forms from many fused cells, which explains the many nuclei, and the nuclei sit just under the sarcolemma, the fiber's plasma membrane. No other muscle tissue has more than one or two nuclei per cell.
notes: Cardiac muscle is striated, but its cells are short and branched with one central nucleus, and it has intercalated discs. Pick it for a slide showing branching striated cells.
Smooth muscle has no striations and its spindle-shaped cells each have one central nucleus. Pick it for a slide of nonstriated, tapered cells.

Dense regular connective tissue also shows long parallel strands at low power, but they are collagen fibers with flattened fibroblast nuclei squeezed between them, and there are no striations. Pick it for a slide of a tendon or ligament.
Correct. Long cylindrical striated fibers with many peripheral nuclei are skeletal muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: What is the thick, fleshy middle region of a skeletal muscle called?
options: The belly
The tendon
The origin
The insertion
questions.why: The belly, also called the body, is the thick, fleshy middle portion of a muscle that lies between its two attachments. It is where most of the muscle fibers are and where the muscle bulges when it contracts. The tendons at each end attach the belly to bone.
notes: Correct. The belly is the fleshy middle of the muscle.
The tendon is the cord of dense regular connective tissue at the end of a muscle that attaches it to bone. Pick it for a question about what anchors a muscle to bone, not its fleshy middle.
The origin is the attachment of a muscle to the more stationary bone, at one end of the muscle. Pick it for a question about which attachment stays still during contraction.
The insertion is the attachment of a muscle to the more movable bone, at the other end from the origin. Pick it for a question about which attachment is pulled toward the other.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: In general, what blood and nerve supply serves a single skeletal muscle?
options: Several nerves and one artery, with no veins
One artery and one or more veins, with no nerve
One nerve and one vein, with no artery of its own
One nerve, one artery, and one or more veins
questions.why: As a general rule, each skeletal muscle is served by one nerve, one artery, and one or more veins. The nerve is needed because skeletal muscle is voluntary and contracts only when a nerve signal arrives. The artery and veins are needed because contracting muscle uses large amounts of oxygen and fuel and produces wastes that must be carried away.
notes: Without veins, the blood delivered by the artery would have no way to leave the muscle, so wastes would build up. Students choose this when they forget that every tissue needs blood flowing both in and out.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary, so it contracts only when a nerve signal reaches it. A muscle with no nerve supply could not be moved on purpose, which is what happens when a nerve is cut.
A muscle cannot rely only on a vein, because veins carry blood away from tissues. Without an artery, no fresh oxygen-rich blood would reach the working fibers.
Correct. A typical skeletal muscle has one nerve, one artery, and one or more veins.
questions.answerText: One nerve, one artery, and one or more veins

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which list gives the three connective tissue sheaths of a skeletal muscle in order from outside to inside?
options: Epimysium, endomysium, perimysium
Endomysium, perimysium, epimysium
Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium
Perimysium, epimysium, endomysium
questions.why: The epimysium wraps the whole muscle on the outside, the perimysium wraps each fascicle (bundle of fibers) inside it, and the endomysium wraps each individual muscle fiber at the deepest level. The prefixes help: epi means upon, peri means around, and endo means within. All three are continuous with each other and with the tendon.
notes: The endomysium wraps single fibers, the smallest units, so it must be the deepest layer. This order puts the endomysium in the middle, which mixes up the two inner layers.
This is the correct order read from inside to outside. Pick it if the question asks for the sheaths starting from a single fiber and moving outward.
Correct. From outside to inside, the order is epimysium, perimysium, endomysium.
The perimysium wraps fascicles inside the muscle, so it cannot be outside the epimysium, which wraps the whole muscle. This order mixes up the two outer layers.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which of the three connective tissue sheaths surrounds the whole muscle?
options: The epimysium
The endomysium
The perimysium
The aponeurosis
questions.why: The epimysium is the outermost sheath, a layer of dense irregular connective tissue that wraps the entire muscle. The prefix epi means upon, so it sits upon the outside of the muscle. At the ends of the muscle it blends with the other sheaths to form the tendon.
notes: Correct. The epimysium surrounds the whole muscle.
The endomysium wraps each individual muscle fiber, the deepest level. Pick it for a question about the sheath around a single muscle cell.
The perimysium wraps each fascicle, a bundle of fibers inside the muscle. Pick it for a question about what surrounds a fascicle.

An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet that attaches a muscle to bone or to another muscle, not a sheath wrapping the muscle. Pick it for a question about the sheet-like attachment of a wide muscle such as an abdominal muscle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which tissue makes up the epimysium?
options: Dense irregular connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Adipose tissue
Areolar connective tissue
questions.why: The epimysium is made of dense irregular connective tissue, in which thick collagen fibers run in many different directions. That arrangement lets the epimysium resist pulling from any direction as the muscle contracts and changes shape. The perimysium is made of the same tissue type.
notes: Correct. The epimysium is dense irregular connective tissue.
Dense regular connective tissue has collagen fibers running in parallel, which suits pulling in one direction. Pick it for a question about what makes up a tendon or ligament.
Adipose tissue stores fat, and it is found in the superficial fascia between the skin and the muscles. Pick it for a question about the subcutaneous layer.
Areolar connective tissue is loose and delicate, and it forms the fine endomysium around each individual fiber. Pick it for a question about the endomysium.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which connective tissue sheath surrounds each fascicle?
options: The endomysium
The epimysium
The periosteum
The perimysium
questions.why: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers, and each fascicle is wrapped in perimysium. The prefix peri means around, so the perimysium goes around each bundle. It is the middle of the three sheaths, between the epimysium outside and the endomysium inside.
notes: The endomysium wraps each single muscle fiber inside a fascicle. Pick it for a question about the sheath around one muscle cell.
The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, not individual fascicles. Pick it for a question about the outermost sheath.
The periosteum is the connective tissue membrane covering the outer surface of a bone. Pick it for a question about what a direct muscle attachment fuses to, or what covers a bone.
Correct. The perimysium surrounds each fascicle.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: What is a fascicle?
options: A contractile rod inside a muscle fiber
A single muscle cell wrapped in endomysium
A whole muscle wrapped in epimysium
A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium
questions.why: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers held together by perimysium. Fascicles are the level between the whole muscle and the individual fiber, and they are large enough to see as the grain of a piece of meat. The way fascicles are arranged also gives each muscle its overall shape.
notes: A contractile rod inside a muscle fiber is a myofibril, one level smaller than the fiber. Pick it for a question about the structures that fill most of the sarcoplasm.
A single muscle cell wrapped in endomysium is a muscle fiber. Pick this answer for a question about what the endomysium surrounds.
A whole muscle wrapped in epimysium is the muscle organ itself. Pick it for a question about the highest level of muscle organization.
Correct. A fascicle is a bundle of fibers wrapped in perimysium.
questions.answerText: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which connective tissue sheath surrounds each individual muscle fiber?
options: The sarcolemma
The perimysium
The epimysium
The endomysium
questions.why: The endomysium is the deepest of the three sheaths, a fine layer of areolar connective tissue wrapped around each single muscle fiber. The prefix endo means within, because this sheath lies within the fascicle. It holds the capillaries and nerve branches that reach each fiber.
notes: The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of the muscle fiber itself, part of the cell rather than a connective tissue sheath. The endomysium lies just outside it, so pick the sarcolemma for a question about the fiber's own cell membrane.
The perimysium wraps each fascicle, a bundle of many fibers. Pick it for a question about what surrounds a bundle.
The epimysium wraps the whole muscle on the outside. Pick it for a question about the outermost sheath.
Correct. The endomysium surrounds each individual muscle fiber.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which tissue makes up the endomysium?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Dense irregular connective tissue
Elastic connective tissue
Areolar connective tissue
questions.why: The endomysium is a fine, delicate sheath of areolar connective tissue with reticular fibers around each muscle fiber. Areolar tissue is loose, so it leaves room for the capillaries and nerve endings that must reach every fiber. The outer two sheaths are tougher dense irregular connective tissue.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue, with parallel collagen fibers, forms tendons and ligaments. Pick it for a question about what makes up a tendon.
Dense irregular connective tissue forms the epimysium and perimysium, the two outer sheaths. Pick it for a question about either of those.
Elastic connective tissue is rich in elastin and found in the walls of large arteries and in the lungs. Pick it for a question about the tissue that lets the aorta stretch and recoil.
Correct. The endomysium is a fine layer of areolar connective tissue.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: In a direct (fleshy) attachment, the epimysium of the muscle is fused to which structure?
options: The joint capsule
An aponeurosis
A tendon
The periosteum of the bone
questions.why: In a direct attachment, the muscle has no tendon in between. Its epimysium fuses straight onto the periosteum, the connective tissue membrane covering the bone (or onto the perichondrium if the muscle attaches to cartilage). Direct attachments are less common than indirect ones, which use a tendon or aponeurosis.
notes: The joint capsule is the connective tissue sleeve that encloses a synovial joint. Pick it for a question about the parts of a synovial joint, not about how a muscle attaches to bone.
An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet used in an indirect attachment, not a direct one. Pick it for a question about how a wide flat muscle attaches.
A tendon is used in an indirect attachment, where the connective tissue extends beyond the muscle as a cord. Pick it for a question about indirect attachments.
Correct. In a direct attachment the epimysium fuses to the periosteum.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: In an indirect attachment, what connects the muscle to the bone?
options: The epimysium fused straight to the periosteum
A tendon or an aponeurosis
A ligament
Articular cartilage
questions.why: In an indirect attachment, the connective tissue sheaths of the muscle extend beyond the muscle fibers as a tendon (a cord) or an aponeurosis (a broad flat sheet), and that structure anchors to the bone. Indirect attachments are much more common than direct ones. Most of the muscles you identify in lab attach this way.
notes: The epimysium fusing straight to the periosteum is a direct attachment, also called a fleshy attachment. Pick it for a question about direct attachments.
Correct. An indirect attachment uses a tendon or an aponeurosis.
A ligament connects bone to bone across a joint, not muscle to bone. Pick it for a question about what holds the bones of a joint together.
Articular cartilage is the smooth hyaline cartilage covering bone ends inside a synovial joint. Pick it for a question about the surfaces that glide against each other in a joint.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: What is the rope-like cord that anchors a muscle to bone called?
options: A ligament
A fascia
An aponeurosis
A tendon
questions.why: A tendon is a cord of dense regular connective tissue that forms where the three muscle sheaths merge and extend beyond the muscle. Its collagen fibers run in parallel, which makes it very strong when pulled in one direction. The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon at the back of the ankle is a familiar example.
notes: A ligament is also dense regular connective tissue, but it connects bone to bone across a joint. Pick it for a question about what holds a joint's bones together.

Fascia is a sheet of connective tissue that wraps and separates muscles, but it does not form the cord-like anchor to bone. Pick deep fascia for a question about what groups muscles into compartments.
An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet rather than a cord. Pick it for a question about the sheet-like attachment of a wide muscle.
Correct. A tendon is the cord that anchors muscle to bone.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: What is the broad, sheet-like connective tissue attachment of a muscle called?
options: A tendon
A ligament
A retinaculum
An aponeurosis
questions.why: An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet of tendon-like connective tissue that attaches a muscle where the muscle is wide. It does the same job as a tendon but is spread out like a sheet instead of gathered into a cord. Aponeuroses are prominent in the abdominal wall and on the top of the skull.
notes: A tendon does the same job but is a rope-like cord rather than a flat sheet. Pick it for a question about the cord that anchors a muscle to bone.
A ligament connects bone to bone across a joint rather than attaching a muscle. Pick it for a question about stabilizing a joint.
A retinaculum is a band of connective tissue that holds tendons in place as they cross the wrist or ankle. Pick it for a question about the band that keeps tendons from bowing out at the wrist.
Correct. An aponeurosis is a broad, sheet-like attachment.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Where do the nerve and blood vessels usually enter or leave a skeletal muscle?
options: At the tendon of insertion
Near the central part of the muscle
At the tendon of origin
Evenly along the whole muscle surface
questions.why: The nerve, artery, and veins of a skeletal muscle usually enter or leave near the central part of the muscle. From there they branch extensively through the connective tissue sheaths so that every fiber receives a nerve ending and capillaries. Tendons, by contrast, have a poor blood supply.
notes: The tendon of insertion anchors the muscle to the moving bone and, like other tendons, has a poor blood supply. This is the same mix-up as choosing the origin.
Correct. Nerves and vessels usually enter near the center of the muscle.
The tendon of origin anchors the muscle to the stationary bone, and tendons have relatively few blood vessels. Students choose this because the origin sounds like a starting point for everything.

The vessels and nerve enter at a limited spot and then branch inside the muscle, rather than entering all along its surface. Students choose this when they picture the branching inside the muscle instead of the point of entry.
questions.answerText: Near the central part of the muscle

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Moving from the outside of a whole muscle inward, which sheath is reached immediately after the epimysium?
options: The sarcolemma
The endomysium
The deep fascia
The perimysium
questions.why: The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, and just inside it the muscle is divided into fascicles, each wrapped in perimysium. The perimysium is therefore the next sheath reached after the epimysium. The endomysium comes after that, around each individual fiber.
notes: The sarcolemma is the fiber's own plasma membrane, found inside all three sheaths. Pick it for a question about the membrane of the muscle cell.
The endomysium is the deepest sheath, around individual fibers, so it comes after the perimysium, not right after the epimysium. Pick it if the question asks for the innermost sheath.
Deep fascia lies outside the epimysium, wrapping and separating whole muscles, so you would pass it before reaching the epimysium. Pick it for a question about what binds muscles into compartments.
Correct. The perimysium lies just inside the epimysium.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each connective tissue sheath to what it wraps?
options: The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, the endomysium wraps each fascicle, and the perimysium wraps each fiber
The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, the perimysium wraps each fascicle, and the endomysium wraps each fiber
The endomysium wraps the whole muscle, the perimysium wraps each fascicle, and the epimysium wraps each fiber
The perimysium wraps the whole muscle, the epimysium wraps each fascicle, and the endomysium wraps each fiber
questions.why: The three sheaths wrap the muscle at three scales. The epimysium (epi, upon) wraps the whole muscle, the perimysium (peri, around) wraps each fascicle, and the endomysium (endo, within) wraps each individual fiber. Matching the prefix to the level is the easiest way to keep them straight.
notes: This swaps the two inner sheaths. The perimysium wraps fascicles and the endomysium wraps individual fibers.
Correct. Epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium wrap the muscle, the fascicle, and the fiber.
This swaps the outermost and innermost sheaths. The endomysium is the deepest layer around single fibers, and the epimysium is the outer layer around the whole muscle.
This swaps the two outer sheaths. The epimysium is the outermost layer around the whole muscle, and the perimysium wraps each fascicle inside it.
questions.answerText: The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, the perimysium wraps each fascicle, and the endomysium wraps each fiber

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: When all three connective tissue sheaths merge and continue beyond the muscle as a cord that attaches to bone, what do they form?
options: A tendon
The deep fascia
The periosteum
A ligament
questions.why: The epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium are continuous with each other, and at the ends of the muscle they merge and extend beyond the fibers. When this merged tissue forms a cord, it is a tendon, which anchors the muscle to bone. Because the sheaths are continuous with the tendon, the pull of every fiber is carried all the way to the bone.
notes: Correct. The merged sheaths form a tendon.
Deep fascia is a sheet that wraps and separates whole muscles and groups them by function. Pick it for a question about what binds muscles into compartments.
The periosteum is the membrane covering the bone itself, which a tendon attaches to. Pick it for a question about what the epimysium fuses to in a direct attachment.
A ligament is a cord of dense regular connective tissue too, but it connects bone to bone and is not formed from muscle sheaths. Pick it for a question about what holds the bones of a joint together.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a tendon and a ligament?
options: A tendon connects muscle to bone, and a ligament connects bone to bone
A ligament connects muscle to bone, and a tendon connects bone to bone
A tendon connects muscle to muscle, and a ligament connects muscle to bone
Both connect muscle to bone, but a ligament is a flat sheet
questions.why: Tendons and ligaments are both made of dense regular connective tissue, with parallel collagen fibers that resist pulling. The difference is what they connect. A tendon attaches a muscle to a bone and carries the muscle's pull, while a ligament attaches one bone to another and holds a joint together.
notes: Correct. Tendons connect muscle to bone, and ligaments connect bone to bone.
This swaps the two structures. A tendon carries a muscle's pull to bone, and a ligament joins bone to bone.
Neither statement here is right. A tendon runs from muscle to bone, and a ligament joins bone to bone, so students who pick this have shifted both definitions one step.
A flat sheet that attaches muscle is an aponeurosis, not a ligament. Pick aponeurosis for a question about the broad attachment of a wide muscle.
questions.answerText: A tendon connects muscle to bone, and a ligament connects bone to bone

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Why are indirect attachments by tendons more common than direct (fleshy) attachments?
options: Tendons are made of elastic tissue that stretches with each movement
Tendons are small and durable, so many can cross a joint without taking much space
Tendons have a richer blood supply than muscle fibers
Tendons can contract and add force to the muscle
questions.why: Tendons are made of tough, densely packed collagen, so they hold up well when they rub over bony projections. They are also much narrower than a fleshy muscle belly, so several tendons can pass over a single joint, such as the wrist, without crowding it. Durability and small size are why most muscles attach indirectly.
notes: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue built mainly of collagen, which resists stretching rather than allowing it. Elastic connective tissue, found in large artery walls, is the tissue that stretches and recoils.
Correct. Tendons are durable and compact, so many can cross a joint in a small space.
Tendons have a relatively poor blood supply compared with muscle, which is why tendon injuries heal slowly. This option reverses the real difference between the two tissues.
Tendons cannot contract; only muscle fibers can. Students choose this when they forget that a tendon simply transmits the pull that the muscle fibers produce.
questions.answerText: Tendons are small and durable, so many can cross a joint without taking much space

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which structure is a sheet of dense connective tissue that wraps muscles, separates them, and binds muscles with a common action into functional groups?
options: The epimysium
An aponeurosis
The superficial fascia
The deep fascia
questions.why: Deep fascia is a sheet of dense connective tissue that lies outside the epimysium. It wraps muscles, separates neighboring muscles from each other, and binds muscles that share a common action into groups called compartments. That is why the flexors and extensors of the forearm sit in separate fascial compartments.
notes: The epimysium wraps a single whole muscle rather than binding several muscles into a group. Pick it for a question about the outermost sheath of one muscle.

An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet that attaches a muscle to bone or to another muscle, rather than wrapping muscles into groups. Pick it for a question about the attachment of a wide abdominal muscle.
The superficial fascia is the subcutaneous layer of areolar and adipose tissue between the skin and the muscles. Pick it for a question about the fatty layer just under the skin.
Correct. Deep fascia wraps and separates muscles and binds them into functional groups.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which pair names two functions of a muscle's connective tissue sheaths?
options: They secrete synovial fluid and cushion the joint the muscle crosses
They produce new muscle fibers and generate most of the muscle's heat
They reinforce the muscle and provide routes for its blood vessels and nerves
They contract alongside the fibers and store calcium for them
questions.why: The epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium support and reinforce the muscle so it does not tear apart during strong contractions. They also carry the blood vessels and nerve branches that must reach every fiber. Because they are continuous with the tendon, they also transmit the pull of the fibers to the bone.

When the rings contract they squeeze the opening shut, which is why circular muscles act as sphincters. The orbicularis oris around the mouth and the orbicularis oculi around the eye are the examples to know.
notes: Correct. Ring-shaped fascicles around an opening make a sphincter, like the orbicularis oris.

Parallel fascicles run straight along the long axis of a strap-like muscle such as the sartorius. They would be the answer for a long muscle built for range of motion, not for one that closes an opening.
Convergent fascicles fan out from a broad origin and come together on a single tendon, as in the pectoralis major. Pick this for a triangular, fan-shaped muscle.

questions.q: How are the fascicles arranged in a pennate muscle?

Short fascicles attach at an angle to a central tendon
Fascicles form concentric rings around an opening
Long fascicles run parallel to the long axis

In a pennate muscle, short fascicles attach at an angle to a tendon that runs through the muscle, the way barbs attach to the shaft of a feather. This angled packing lets many fibers fit into the muscle, which is why pennate muscles are built for power.
notes: A broad origin that narrows to one tendon describes a convergent muscle such as the pectoralis major. Pick this for a triangular, fan-shaped muscle.

Concentric rings describe a circular muscle, the sphincter pattern seen in the orbicularis oris. That answers a question about closing an opening.
Long fascicles running along the length of the muscle describe the parallel pattern, as in the sartorius. Choose this if the question asked about a strap-like muscle built for range.

questions.q: A pennate muscle has fascicles attaching to only one side of its tendon. What is this type called?

Multipennate
Bipennate
Fusiform

Bipennate muscles have fascicles on both sides, and multipennate muscles have fascicles on a branched tendon.

A multipennate muscle has fascicles attached to a branched tendon, giving many feather patterns in one muscle. The deltoid is the example to choose for this pattern.
A bipennate muscle has fascicles attaching on both sides of the central tendon, like a full feather. The rectus femoris is the example, so pick this when fascicles come in from two sides.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A muscle is built for power, with many short fascicles packed at an angle around a central tendon. Which fascicle pattern is this?
options: Circular
Convergent
Parallel
Pennate
questions.why: A pennate muscle packs many short fascicles at an angle around a tendon, like the barbs of a feather. Because so many fibers fit into the muscle and all pull on the tendon, the muscle produces more power. The trade-off is a smaller range of motion, because short fascicles cannot shorten very far.

A convergent muscle fans from a broad origin onto a single tendon. Pick it for a triangular muscle such as the pectoralis major.
A parallel muscle has long fascicles running its full length, which gives a large range of motion but less power. Choose it for a strap-like muscle such as the sartorius.

questions.q: A muscle has long fascicles running its full length, giving a large range of motion but less power. Which architecture is this?

Pennate
Bipennate
Multipennate
questions.why: Parallel muscles have long fascicles running the whole length of the muscle. Because a muscle fiber can shorten to about two thirds of its resting length, a long fascicle shortens by a large distance and moves the insertion far. Fewer fibers fit across the muscle, though, so it pulls with less power than a pennate muscle of the same size.

A pennate muscle has short fascicles packed at an angle around a tendon, which gives more power but a smaller range. It is the opposite end of the trade-off.
Bipennate is a pennate muscle with fascicles on both sides of the tendon, such as the rectus femoris. Like all pennate muscles it favors power over range.
Multipennate is a pennate muscle with fascicles on a branched tendon, such as the deltoid. It is built for power, not for a large range of motion.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A surgeon planning a tendon transfer needs a muscle built for power to take over a demanding job. Which fascicle architecture should the surgeon look for?

A circular muscle
A parallel muscle
A fusiform muscle
questions.why: In a tendon transfer, a working muscle is rerouted to take over the job of a muscle that no longer works, so its architecture should match that job. notes: Correct. Many short, angled fascicles give the most power for a demanding job.
A circular muscle forms a sphincter around an opening. It closes a passage rather than pulling a tendon on a bone, so it would fit a job like closing the mouth.
A parallel muscle has long fascicles that give a large range of motion but less power. It would be the choice if the job needed a long, sweeping movement.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A muscle fiber can shorten to about two thirds of its resting length. Why does a muscle with longer fascicles move its insertion farther?

They contain more nuclei
They shorten by a greater distance
They attach at a steeper angle
questions.why: If every fiber shortens by about one third of its length, a long fiber shortens by more centimeters than a short fiber. A muscle with long fascicles therefore pulls its insertion a greater distance toward its origin. That is why parallel muscles, with long fascicles, have a larger range of motion than pennate muscles.
notes: Force depends mainly on how many fibers pull on the tendon, not on how long they are. Pick a force answer for a question about pennate muscles, which pack in more fibers.
Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated, and a long fiber may have many nuclei, but nuclei do not set how far a fiber shortens.
Correct. The same fraction of a longer length is a bigger distance.
A steep angle to the tendon is a feature of pennate muscles, which have short fascicles. Long fascicles in a parallel muscle run along the axis, not at an angle.
questions.answerText: They shorten by a greater distance

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: A strap-like muscle with parallel fascicles shortens a great deal but with modest force. Which explanation accounts for both features?

Long fascicles pull harder but tire before shortening fully
Long fascicles shorten far, but fewer fibers fit across the muscle to pull
Parallel muscles insert far from the joint, so they move bones farther
questions.why: Parallel fascicles run the full length of the muscle, so when each fiber shortens by about a third, the whole muscle shortens a long way and moves its insertion far. Because the fibers run lengthwise, relatively few of them fit across the width of the muscle, so fewer fibers pull on the tendon at once. Long length explains the range, and the smaller number of fibers explains the modest force.
notes: An angled pull on the tendon is a feature of pennate muscles, not parallel ones. Parallel fibers pull in line with the muscle.
Fascicle length does not make a fiber pull harder, and fatigue does not explain range. This choice mixes up length with strength.

Fascicle pattern does not decide where a muscle inserts. An insertion farther from the joint would actually give more force and less speed, the opposite of what is described.

Its fascicles shorten by a greater distance
Its fascicles are longer, so each one pulls harder
Its angled fibers pull straight along the tendon line

Short pennate fascicles shorten by a smaller distance, which is why pennate muscles have less range. A greater shortening distance belongs to long parallel fascicles.
Pennate fascicles are actually shorter than parallel ones, and length does not make a fiber stronger. Longer fascicles explain range of motion in a parallel muscle, not force.

questions.q: The deltoid of the shoulder is a multipennate muscle that lifts the arm against heavy loads. What does this architecture give the deltoid?

Extra shortening distance because short fibers shorten more
High force from many short fibers packed into a compact muscle
A ring of fibers that closes the joint like a sphincter

questions.q: A circular muscle, such as a sphincter, has fascicles arranged in rings around an opening. Why is this ring arrangement suited to controlling a passage?

Contracting the ring pulls a bone toward the origin
Contracting the ring narrows or closes the opening

All of its fibers pull along one straight line
Its parts pull in slightly different directions on one tendon
Its fibers attach at an angle to a tendon running through the muscle

Fibers from the upper, middle, and lower parts of the fan approach the tendon from different angles, so activating different parts pulls the insertion in different directions. With pennate muscles, favoring power over range
With parallel muscles, favoring range over power
With circular muscles, closing an opening

Because its fascicles are long and parallel, it is grouped with parallel muscles, which have a larger range of motion and less power. A muscle cannot be built for maximum range and maximum power at the same time.

questions.topic: Muscle tissue types and muscle organization
questions.q: Which list gives the three connective tissue coverings of a skeletal muscle in order, starting with the whole muscle and moving in to the single fiber?

Epimysium, endomysium, perimysium
Perimysium, epimysium, endomysium
Endomysium, perimysium, epimysium
questions.why: The epimysium wraps the entire muscle, the perimysium wraps each fascicle (a bundle of muscle fibers), and the endomysium wraps each individual muscle fiber. The prefixes help: epi means upon, so it sits on the outside; peri means around, so it surrounds the bundles; endo means within, so it lies deepest, around each cell.
notes: Correct. The order runs from the outside wrapping of the whole organ to the fine sheath around each cell.
This swaps the two inner sheaths. The endomysium wraps single fibers, which sit inside fascicles, so it must come after the perimysium, not before it.
This puts the perimysium outside the epimysium, but the perimysium wraps fascicles inside the muscle. Students choose it when they mix up the prefixes peri (around) and epi (upon).
This is the right three sheaths listed from the inside out, starting at the single fiber. It would be correct if the question asked you to start at the fiber and work outward to the whole muscle.

questions.q: What does the epimysium wrap, and what type of connective tissue is it?

The entire muscle; dense regular connective tissue
The entire muscle; dense irregular connective tissue
Each muscle fiber; areolar connective tissue with reticular fibers

It is dense irregular connective tissue, meaning its collagen fibers run in many directions, which lets it resist pulling from any angle as the muscle changes shape. At the ends of the muscle it blends with the other sheaths into the tendon.
