An elastic spring describes titin, which runs from the Z disc to the M line. It would be the answer for the protein that gives the sarcomere recoil.
questions.answerText: A binding site for a myosin head

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which regulatory protein is rod-shaped and lies end to end along the thin filament?
options: Troponin
Tropomyosin
Titin
Nebulin
questions.why: The thin filament carries two regulatory proteins. Tropomyosin is the rod-shaped one, lying end to end along the groove of the actin strands. In relaxed muscle it covers the myosin-binding sites on actin, and the second regulatory protein, troponin, is bound at intervals along it.
notes: Troponin is the other regulatory protein, but it is a small three-part globular complex bound at intervals to tropomyosin, not a long rod. Pick troponin for the three-subunit complex.
Correct. Tropomyosin rods lie end to end along the actin strands.
Titin is a long structural protein, but it runs from the Z disc to the M line within the sarcomere, not along the thin filament. It would be the answer for elastic recoil.

Nebulin does run along the thin filament, but it is a structural protein that anchors the filament and sets its length, not a regulatory protein. Pick nebulin if the question asked what sets thin filament length.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Troponin is a complex of how many polypeptide subunits?
options: Four
Two
Three
Six
questions.why: Troponin is a small globular complex of three subunits bound at intervals along tropomyosin on the thin filament. Each subunit is named for what it binds: TnI binds actin, TnT binds tropomyosin, and TnC binds calcium ions. Together with tropomyosin, troponin regulates whether myosin heads can reach actin.
notes: Four is the number of light chains in a myosin molecule. It does not describe troponin, which has three subunits.
Two is the number of regulatory proteins on the thin filament (tropomyosin and troponin). Students who mix up that count with the troponin subunits choose this.
Correct. Troponin has three subunits, called TnI, TnT, and TnC.
Six is the total number of polypeptide chains in one myosin molecule (two heavy and four light). It is the wrong protein for this count.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structural protein forms the elastic filament that runs from the Z disc to the M line?
options: Nebulin
Dystrophin
Myomesin
Titin
questions.why: Titin is the largest known protein and forms the elastic filament of the sarcomere. It runs from the Z disc through the core of the thick filament to the M line, holding the thick filament in place. Like a spring, it lets the sarcomere recoil after stretching and keeps it from being overstretched.
notes: Nebulin runs along the thin filament and sets its length. It does not span from the Z disc to the M line or act as a spring.
Dystrophin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma and is faulty in muscular dystrophy. Pick dystrophin for that link to the cell membrane.
Myomesin sits only at the M line, binding thick filaments together. It would be the answer for the protein located at the center of the sarcomere.
Correct. Titin is the giant elastic protein spanning each half sarcomere.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structural protein links the thin filaments to the proteins of the sarcolemma?
options: Myomesin
Dystrophin
Nebulin
Titin
questions.why: Dystrophin is the structural protein that links the thin filaments at the outer edge of the myofibrils to integral proteins of the sarcolemma, the muscle cell membrane. Through this link the force of the sarcomeres is passed out to the connective tissue around the fiber. When the dystrophin gene is faulty, as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, fibers damage themselves with ordinary use.
notes: Myomesin binds thick filaments together at the M line, deep in the center of the sarcomere and far from the membrane.
Correct. Dystrophin connects the myofibrils to the cell membrane.
Nebulin lies along the thin filament and sets its length, but it does not reach the sarcolemma. Pick it for the protein that measures thin filament length.
Titin connects the Z disc to the M line inside the sarcomere. It would be the answer for the elastic filament, not for the link to the sarcolemma.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which region of the sarcomere contains only thin filaments?
options: The zone of overlap
The H zone
The I band
The A band
questions.why: The I band is the region at each end of a sarcomere where thin filaments extend from the Z disc but have not yet reached the thick filaments. Because it contains only thin filaments, it is less dense and appears light. Its mirror image is the H zone in the center, which contains only thick filaments.
notes: The zone of overlap contains both thick and thin filaments interleaved. It would be the answer for the region where cross bridges can form.
The H zone is the mirror image of the I band: it holds thick filaments only. Students swap the two because both are pale regions.
Correct. The I band holds thin filaments only, which is why it is light.
The A band contains the thick filaments across its full width, with thin filaments overlapping at its edges. Pick it for the band as wide as the thick filaments are long.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which region of the sarcomere contains only thick filaments?
options: The I band
The Z disc
The H zone
The zone of overlap
questions.why: The H zone is the central part of the A band where the thin filaments do not reach, so only thick filaments are present. It looks lighter than the edges of the A band, where both filament types overlap. The M line runs through the middle of the H zone and anchors the thick filaments together.
notes: The I band holds thin filaments only, the reverse of this question. Pick it if the question asked for the region of thin filaments alone.
The Z disc is a protein plate at the border of the sarcomere that anchors thin filaments. No thick filaments reach it.
Correct. The center of the A band, where thin filaments do not reach, holds thick filaments only.
The zone of overlap holds both thick and thin filaments interleaved, at each end of the A band. It would be the answer for the region containing both filament types.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which protein anchors the thin filaments and titin to the Z disc?
options: Titin
Myomesin
Desmin
Alpha-actinin
questions.why: Alpha-actinin is a structural protein of the Z disc. It binds the ends of the thin filaments and the ends of titin, holding them firmly at the border of the sarcomere. Its name hints at its partner, actin, which is the main protein of the thin filaments it anchors.
notes: Titin is anchored at the Z disc, but it is the elastic filament being held there, not the anchor itself. It would be the answer for the spring that runs to the M line.
Myomesin is the anchoring protein at the opposite end, the M line, where it binds the thick filaments. Pick it for the protein at the center of the sarcomere.
Desmin wraps around the Z discs to tie neighboring myofibrils together, but it does not anchor the thin filaments within the disc. Pick desmin for the link between adjacent myofibrils.
Correct. Alpha-actinin is the Z disc protein that binds the thin filaments and titin.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which two proteins are the regulatory proteins of the thin filament?
options: Actin and myosin
Titin and nebulin
Tropomyosin and troponin
Myomesin and alpha-actinin
questions.why: The thin filament carries two regulatory proteins that control whether myosin can bind actin. Tropomyosin is a rod lying along the actin strands, covering the myosin-binding sites at rest, and troponin is a three-part complex attached to tropomyosin. Contractile proteins (actin, myosin) and structural proteins (titin, nebulin, myomesin, alpha-actinin, dystrophin) are separate groups.
notes: Actin and myosin are the contractile proteins that make up the thin and thick filaments. Pick this pair if the question asked which proteins form the two main myofilaments.
Titin and nebulin are structural proteins. Titin gives elastic recoil and nebulin sets thin filament length, so they would be the answer for proteins that hold the sarcomere in shape.
Correct. These two proteins sit on the thin filament and control access to actin.
These are anchoring proteins: myomesin at the M line and alpha-actinin at the Z disc. Pick this pair for the proteins at the center and the border of the sarcomere.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A filament sits in the center of the sarcomere, spans the full width of the A band, and is joined to its neighbors at the M line. Which filament is it, and what protein makes it?
options: The thin filament, made of tropomyosin
The thin filament, made of actin
The elastic filament, made of titin
The thick filament, made of myosin
questions.why: The thick filament is built of myosin and lies in the middle of the sarcomere. Its length sets the width of the A band, and the M line at its center ties neighboring thick filaments together. The thin filaments, made of actin, come in from the Z discs at each end and overlap the thick filaments only at the edges of the A band.
notes: Tropomyosin lies along the thin filament as a regulatory protein; it does not form a filament of its own in the A band. This choice mixes a regulatory protein with the wrong filament.
The thin filament is anchored at the Z disc and crosses the I band, so it lies toward the ends of the sarcomere. Pick it for a filament described as anchored at the Z disc.
Titin does reach the M line, but it starts at the Z disc and runs the whole half sarcomere, so it is not confined to the A band. It would be the answer for the filament that gives elastic recoil.
Correct. Central placement, the full A band, and the M line all point to the thick filament.
questions.answerText: The thick filament, made of myosin

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A myosin molecule has a long tail joined to two globular heads. What forms the tail?
options: Four light chains bundled together
Two twisted strands of actin subunits
Two heavy chains wound around each other
A strand of titin running through its core
questions.why: A myosin molecule is built of two heavy chains and four light chains. The two heavy chains wind around each other like a rope to form the long tail, and at one end each heavy chain folds into a globular head. The light chains are small and associated with the heads, so the tail is made of heavy chains alone.
notes: The four light chains are small and sit at the heads, two per head. They do not form the tail; pick them if the question asked what is associated with the myosin heads.
This describes the thin filament, a separate structure. Students choose it because both involve twisted strands, but actin is not part of myosin.
Correct. The two heavy chains intertwine to form the tail, then each ends in a head.
Titin runs through the core of the thick filament, the bundle of many myosin molecules, but it is not part of a single myosin molecule's tail.
questions.answerText: Two heavy chains wound around each other

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches the Z disc and the M line to what each anchors?
options: The Z disc anchors thin filaments; the M line anchors thick filaments
Both anchor the thin filaments, at opposite ends
Both anchor the thick filaments, at opposite ends
The Z disc anchors thick filaments; the M line anchors thin filaments
questions.why: The sarcomere has two anchoring lines. The Z disc, at each border, is where the thin filaments attach, held by the protein alpha-actinin. The M line, at the center, ties the thick filaments together, helped by the protein myomesin. A simple way to keep them apart is that thin filaments start at the edges and thick filaments are centered.
notes: Correct. Thin filaments attach at the border and thick filaments are tied together at the center.
Only the Z disc anchors thin filaments. The M line lies in the H zone, where thin filaments are absent, so it cannot anchor them.
Only the M line anchors thick filaments. The Z disc is at the border, beyond the reach of the thick filaments, and it holds the thin filaments instead.
This reverses the pairs. Thick filaments never reach the Z disc, and thin filaments stop before the M line, so neither attachment is possible.
questions.answerText: The Z disc anchors thin filaments; the M line anchors thick filaments

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What does titin do for the sarcomere?
options: It links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma
It gives elastic recoil and prevents overstretching
It sets the length of the thin filament
It covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
questions.why: Titin is a giant structural protein that runs from the Z disc to the M line. It holds each thick filament centered in the sarcomere, and because it is elastic, it lets a stretched sarcomere spring back to its resting length. It also resists stretching beyond a safe limit, protecting the sarcomere from being pulled apart.
notes: This is the role of dystrophin, the protein faulty in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. It would be the answer for the connection between myofibrils and the cell membrane.
Correct. Titin acts as a molecular spring between the Z disc and the M line.
Setting thin filament length is the job of nebulin, which runs along the thin filament. Pick nebulin if the question asked which protein measures the thin filament.
Covering the binding sites at rest is the role of tropomyosin, a regulatory protein on the thin filament. Titin is structural, not regulatory.
questions.answerText: It gives elastic recoil and prevents overstretching

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structural protein runs along the length of the thin filament, anchoring it and setting its length?
options: Dystrophin
Nebulin
Titin
Tropomyosin
questions.why: Nebulin is a structural protein that runs the full length of the thin filament. It anchors the thin filament and sets how long it is, so every thin filament in the sarcomere is the same length. Along with myomesin at the M line and alpha-actinin at the Z disc, it helps keep the sarcomere in register.
notes: Dystrophin connects the thin filaments to the sarcolemma at the edge of the myofibril. It does not run along the filament to set its length.
Correct. Nebulin lies along the thin filament and acts like a ruler for its length.
Titin is also a long structural protein, but it runs from the Z disc to the M line with the thick filament. Pick titin for the elastic filament.
Tropomyosin lies along the thin filament too, but it is a regulatory protein that covers myosin-binding sites. It would be the answer for the rod-shaped regulatory protein.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Moving from the border of a sarcomere toward its center, which landmark is reached last?
options: The M line
The zone of overlap
The I band
The Z disc
questions.why: A sarcomere is symmetrical around its center. Starting at the Z disc on the border, you cross the light I band, enter the A band at the zone of overlap, pass into the H zone, and reach the M line at the very middle. From the M line the same landmarks repeat in reverse to the next Z disc.
notes: Correct. The M line marks the exact center of the sarcomere.
The zone of overlap is at the edge of the A band, partway in. Past it lie the H zone and finally the M line at the center.
The I band is reached just after the Z disc, near the border. It would be the answer for the region next to the Z disc.
The Z disc is the first landmark, at the border of the sarcomere. Pick it for where the sarcomere begins and ends.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Moving across half a sarcomere, from its border to its center, which sequence of landmarks is correct?
options: Z disc, zone of overlap, I band, H zone, M line
Z disc, I band, zone of overlap, H zone, M line
Z disc, I band, H zone, zone of overlap, M line
M line, H zone, zone of overlap, I band, Z disc
questions.why: The sarcomere is bordered by Z discs and centered on the M line. From the Z disc inward, the thin filaments alone form the I band, then they meet the thick filaments in the zone of overlap at the edge of the A band. Beyond the reach of the thin filaments is the H zone, thick filaments only, and the M line runs through its middle.
notes: This places the zone of overlap before the I band. The I band, with thin filaments only, comes first; overlap begins only where thin filaments reach the thick filaments.
Correct. This follows the sarcomere from its border to its middle.
This swaps the zone of overlap and the H zone. The H zone sits in the center of the A band, so it is reached after the overlap region.
This is the correct order run backward, from center to border. It would be right if the question asked you to move from the M line outward.
questions.answerText: Z disc, I band, zone of overlap, H zone, M line

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: In a relaxed muscle fiber, what does tropomyosin do?
options: It covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
It anchors the thin filament at the Z disc
It forms the heads of the thick filament
It binds calcium ions
questions.why: Tropomyosin is a rod-shaped regulatory protein lying end to end along the groove of the thin filament. In relaxed muscle it sits over the active sites on actin, so the myosin heads cannot attach and form cross bridges. Troponin, bound to tropomyosin, controls when tropomyosin is moved off those sites.
notes: Correct. With the sites covered, myosin heads cannot bind and the muscle stays relaxed.
Anchoring at the Z disc is done by alpha-actinin. It would be the answer for the protein holding thin filaments at the border.
The heads belong to myosin molecules in the thick filament. Tropomyosin is on the thin filament and has no heads.
Binding calcium is the job of TnC, a subunit of troponin. Pick troponin if the question asked which regulatory protein binds calcium.
questions.answerText: It covers the myosin-binding sites on actin

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by a faulty gene for which structural protein?
options: Nebulin
Dystrophin
Myomesin
Titin
questions.why: Muscular dystrophy is a group of inherited diseases of muscle structure. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy the gene for dystrophin is faulty. Dystrophin normally links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma, so without it the fiber tears itself with ordinary use and weakness gets steadily worse. The similar names, dystrophin and dystrophy, make this pairing easy to remember.
notes: Nebulin runs along the thin filament and sets its length. Pick it for the protein that measures thin filament length.
Correct. Dystrophin is the protein missing or faulty in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Myomesin binds thick filaments together at the M line. It is the answer for the protein at the center of the sarcomere.
Titin is the elastic filament from the Z disc to the M line. It would be the answer for the protein that gives the sarcomere recoil, not for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the thick and thin filaments?
options: Thick is myosin anchored at the Z disc; thin is actin joined at the M line
Thick is titin across the I band; thin is actin across the H zone
Thick is actin joined at the M line; thin is myosin anchored at the Z disc
Thick is myosin joined at the M line; thin is actin anchored at the Z disc
questions.why: The two myofilaments differ in protein and position. The thick filament is a bundle of myosin molecules in the center of the sarcomere, spanning the A band and tied together at the M line. The thin filament is two twisted strands of actin, anchored at the Z disc, extending across the I band and partway into the A band.
notes: The proteins are right, but the anchors are swapped. Thick filaments never reach the Z disc, and thin filaments stop before the M line.
Titin is the elastic filament, not the thick filament, and the H zone has no thin filaments. This mixes structural proteins with the regions where they are absent.
The anchors are right, but the proteins are swapped. Myosin forms the thick filament and actin the thin one.
Correct. Each filament's protein and anchor point are matched properly.
questions.answerText: Thick is myosin joined at the M line; thin is actin anchored at the Z disc

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A student needs to tell titin from myomesin. Which statement correctly compares them?
options: Both proteins anchor the thin filaments at the Z disc
Titin links thin filaments to the sarcolemma; myomesin sets thin filament length
Titin spans Z disc to M line for recoil; myomesin binds thick filaments at the M line
Titin sits only at the M line; myomesin spans Z disc to M line
questions.why: Titin and myomesin both attach at the M line, which is why students confuse them. Titin is a giant elastic protein that runs all the way from the Z disc to the M line, holding the thick filament in place and letting the sarcomere spring back after stretching. Myomesin is confined to the M line, where it binds neighboring thick filaments together.
notes: The Z disc anchor for thin filaments is alpha-actinin. Myomesin is at the opposite end, and titin anchors the thick filament, not the thin.
These are the roles of dystrophin and nebulin. Pick those proteins if the question asked about the membrane link or the thin filament ruler.
Correct. Titin is the long spring, and myomesin is the local anchor at the center.
This reverses their locations. Myomesin is the short protein confined to the M line, while titin stretches across the half sarcomere.
questions.answerText: Titin spans Z disc to M line for recoil; myomesin binds thick filaments at the M line

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A filament is built of many molecules shaped like golf clubs, with their tails bundled together and their heads projecting outward. Which filament and protein are described?
options: The thick filament, made of myosin
The elastic filament, made of titin
The thin filament, made of tropomyosin
The thin filament, made of actin
questions.why: The golf club shape belongs to myosin. Each myosin molecule has a long tail of two intertwined heavy chains and two globular heads at one end. Hundreds of these molecules bundle tail to tail to build the thick filament, and their heads stick out to form the cross bridges that grip the thin filament.
notes: Correct. Myosin molecules, with a long tail and paired heads, bundle to form the thick filament.
Titin is a single giant spring running from the Z disc to the M line. It has no projecting heads.
Tropomyosin is a rod lying along the thin filament, not a bundle of headed molecules. It would be the answer for a rod-shaped regulatory protein.
Actin subunits are small and globular, strung like two twisted strands of beads. Pick the thin filament for a description of twisted strands with myosin-binding sites.
questions.answerText: The thick filament, made of myosin

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares titin and desmin?
options: Titin is the sarcomere's elastic filament; desmin links neighboring myofibrils at the Z discs
Both proteins sit at the M line and bind thick filaments
Desmin is the sarcomere's elastic filament; titin links neighboring myofibrils
Titin sets thin filament length; desmin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma
questions.why: Titin and desmin both connect to the Z disc but work at different scales. Titin runs lengthwise inside each sarcomere, from the Z disc to the M line, and acts as the elastic filament that gives recoil. Desmin is an intermediate filament that wraps the Z discs and ties each myofibril to its neighbors, keeping their sarcomeres lined up across the fiber.
notes: Correct. Titin works within a sarcomere, and desmin works between myofibrils.
Binding thick filaments at the M line is the job of myomesin. Pick myomesin for the M line protein.
This reverses the two roles. Titin is the elastic filament from the Z disc to the M line, and desmin is the intermediate filament between myofibrils.
These are the roles of nebulin and dystrophin. They would be the answers for the thin filament ruler and the membrane link.
questions.answerText: Titin is the sarcomere's elastic filament; desmin links neighboring myofibrils at the Z discs

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fiber, which stores calcium ions, called?
options: The triad
The transverse tubule
The sarcolemma
The sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fiber. It forms a network of tubules wrapping each myofibril and stores calcium ions. Its enlarged end sacs, the terminal cisternae, sit on either side of each T tubule.
notes: A triad is one T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It includes part of the reticulum but is not the whole calcium store.
Transverse (T) tubules are tunnels of the sarcolemma that carry the surface signal into the fiber. Pick them for the inward extensions of the membrane.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of the fiber. It would be the answer for the cell's outer membrane.
Correct. The sarcoplasmic reticulum wraps each myofibril and stores calcium ions.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is the structural unit of one T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae called?
options: A fascicle
A myofibril
A triad
A sarcomere
questions.why: A triad is made of three parts: one transverse (T) tubule in the middle and a terminal cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum on each side. It is where the signal traveling in from the cell surface meets the calcium store, and triads repeat along every myofibril.
notes: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium. Pick it for a level of whole-muscle organization.
A myofibril is a long contractile rod made of sarcomeres. It would be the answer for what fills most of the sarcoplasm.
Correct. Tri means three: one T tubule and two terminal cisternae.
A sarcomere is the contractile unit from one Z disc to the next. Pick it for the segment of a myofibril.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which red, oxygen-binding pigment in the sarcoplasm stores oxygen and gives muscle its color?
options: Myoglobin
Hemoglobin
Glycogen
Myosin
questions.why: Myoglobin is a red pigment in the sarcoplasm that binds and stores oxygen inside the muscle fiber. It is related to hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. The amount of myoglobin is a major reason muscle looks red, and muscles rich in it look darker.
notes: Correct. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle fibers.
Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying pigment inside red blood cells. Pick it for oxygen transport in the blood.
Glycogen is stored carbohydrate fuel in the sarcoplasm. It would be the answer for the muscle's energy reserve, not its oxygen store.
Myosin is the protein of the thick filament. Its name starts the same way, but it does not bind oxygen.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which description fits the thick filament?
options: Rod-shaped proteins lying end to end
A giant elastic strand from the Z disc to the M line
Two twisted strands of actin subunits
A bundle of myosin molecules with heads projecting outward
questions.why: The thick filament is built from hundreds of myosin molecules bundled together. Each molecule has a long tail and a pair of heads, and the heads project outward from the filament as cross bridges. Thick filaments lie in the center of the sarcomere, spanning the A band, and are anchored at the M line.
notes: This describes tropomyosin, a regulatory protein along the thin filament. It would be the answer for the protein that covers the myosin-binding sites.
This describes titin, a structural protein. Pick it for the protein that gives the sarcomere elastic recoil.
This describes the thin filament. Pick it for the filament anchored at the Z disc.
Correct. The thick filament is bundled myosin with projecting cross bridges.
questions.answerText: A bundle of myosin molecules with heads projecting outward

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A filament is built of two twisted strands of subunits, and each subunit carries a binding site for myosin. Which protein forms it?
options: Nebulin
Myosin
Titin
Actin
questions.why: The thin filament is made of actin. Small actin subunits string together into two strands that twist around each other, and every subunit carries an active site where a myosin head can attach. Tropomyosin and troponin lie along these strands as regulatory proteins.
notes: Nebulin runs alongside the thin filament and sets its length, but it does not form the twisted strands. Pick it for the thin filament ruler.
Myosin forms the thick filament and carries the heads that bind actin. It would be the answer for the protein with heads, not the one with binding sites.
Titin is a single giant elastic strand from the Z disc to the M line, not twisted strands of subunits. Pick it for the elastic filament.
Correct. Two twisted strands of actin subunits make the thin filament.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structure is made of sarcomeres repeated end to end along its length?
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum
The myofibril
The myofilament
The fascicle
questions.why: A myofibril is a long contractile rod that runs the length of a muscle fiber. It is built of thousands of sarcomeres lined up end to end, each one running from a Z disc to the next. Hundreds to thousands of myofibrils fill each fiber, and their aligned sarcomeres produce the striations.
notes: The sarcoplasmic reticulum wraps around each myofibril and stores calcium ions. It surrounds the sarcomeres rather than being built from them.
Correct. Each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres.
Myofilaments are the thick and thin protein strands inside a sarcomere. They are smaller than a sarcomere, so they cannot be made of sarcomeres.
A fascicle is a bundle of whole muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium. Pick it for the bundle level of organization.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which band contains thick filaments across its full width, with thin filaments overlapping at each edge?
options: The H zone
The I band
The A band
The Z disc
questions.why: The A band is the dark band of the sarcomere, as wide as the thick filaments are long. Thick filaments run across its whole width. At each edge, thin filaments slide in from the Z discs and overlap the thick filaments, forming the zones of overlap, while the center, the H zone, has thick filaments only.
notes: The H zone is the center of the A band, where only thick filaments lie and no thin filaments overlap. It would be the answer for the thick-filaments-only region.
The I band holds thin filaments only, with no thick filaments at all. Pick it for the light band.
Correct. The A band spans the thick filaments, overlapped by thin filaments at its edges.
The Z disc is the protein plate at the sarcomere border that anchors thin filaments. No thick filaments reach it.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What anchors the thin filaments at each end of the sarcomere?
options: The Z disc
The H zone
The A band
The M line
questions.why: The Z disc is a protein plate at each end of the sarcomere. The protein alpha-actinin in the Z disc binds the thin filaments, which then extend inward across the I band toward the center. The thick filaments are anchored separately, at the M line.
notes: Correct. Thin filaments attach to the Z discs at the sarcomere's borders.
The H zone is a region of thick filaments only, so thin filaments are absent there. It would be the answer for where thin filaments do not reach.
The A band is a band defined by the thick filaments, not an anchor. Pick it for the dark band.
The M line anchors the thick filaments, in the center of the sarcomere. Pick it for the thick filament anchor.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A skeletal muscle fiber contains many nuclei pressed against the inner sarcolemma. What is this property called?
options: Anucleate
Multinucleated
Branching
Binucleate
questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated. A single fiber can contain hundreds of nuclei, called myonuclei, flattened against the inner surface of the sarcolemma. This is one of the main ways to tell skeletal muscle from cardiac and smooth muscle, which usually have a single central nucleus.
notes: Anucleate means having no nucleus, as in a mature red blood cell. Pick it for a cell that has lost its nucleus.
Correct. A skeletal muscle fiber has many nuclei.
Branching describes the shape of cardiac muscle cells, not their nuclei. It would be the answer for a feature of heart muscle.
Binucleate means having exactly two nuclei, which some cardiac muscle cells and liver cells have. A skeletal fiber has far more than two.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structure carries the surface signal deep into the interior of a muscle fiber?
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum
The terminal cisternae
The myofibrils
The transverse (T) tubules
questions.why: Transverse (T) tubules are narrow tunnels formed by the sarcolemma that dive inward from the cell surface and wrap around the myofibrils. Because they are continuous with the surface membrane, they carry the signal from the surface deep into the fiber, so the inner myofibrils respond at the same time as the outer ones.
notes: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions around each myofibril; it receives the signal rather than carrying it in from the surface. Pick it for the calcium store.
Terminal cisternae are the end sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum beside each T tubule. They are part of the calcium store, not the inward path from the surface.
Myofibrils are the contractile rods that respond to the signal by shortening. They would be the answer for what fills most of the sarcoplasm.
Correct. T tubules are tunnels of sarcolemma that dive into the fiber.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres, because a Z disc runs through its center?
options: The zone of overlap
The H zone
The I band
The A band
questions.why: The Z disc marks the border between two sarcomeres and runs through the middle of the I band. That means each I band is split in half, with one half belonging to the sarcomere on each side. The A band, by contrast, sits entirely within one sarcomere.
notes: The zone of overlap is at each edge of the A band, inside one sarcomere. Pick it for where thick and thin filaments interleave.
The H zone is in the center of a single sarcomere, bisected by the M line, not the Z disc. It would be the answer for the region of thick filaments only.
Correct. Half of each I band belongs to each of the two sarcomeres meeting at its Z disc.
The A band lies wholly within one sarcomere, centered on the M line. Pick it for the dark band that holds the thick filaments.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: When a muscle fiber shortens, which band keeps the same width?
options: The whole sarcomere
The H zone
The A band
The I band
questions.why: The A band is as wide as the thick filaments are long, and the filaments themselves do not shorten. During contraction the thin filaments slide inward over the thick filaments, so the I band and the H zone narrow and the Z discs move closer together, but the A band stays the same width.
notes: The sarcomere itself shortens as the Z discs are pulled closer together. It is what changes length, not what stays the same.
The H zone also narrows, and can disappear, as the thin filaments slide toward the center. It would be the answer for the central region that shrinks.
Correct. The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not change.
The I band narrows as the thin filaments slide inward over the thick ones. Pick it for a band that gets narrower during contraction.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Where does titin run within the sarcomere?
options: Along the length of the thin filament only
From the Z disc to the M line
At the M line only
From the thin filaments to the sarcolemma
questions.why: Titin is anchored at the Z disc and runs through the core of the thick filament to the M line, spanning half of the sarcomere. Placed there, it holds the thick filament centered and acts like a spring, giving elastic recoil after stretching and keeping the sarcomere from overstretching.
notes: This is the position of nebulin, which sets thin filament length. Pick it for the thin filament ruler.
Correct. Titin spans each half sarcomere.
This is the position of myomesin, which binds thick filaments together. It would be the answer for the M line protein.
This is the position of dystrophin, which links the myofibril to the cell membrane. Pick it for the protein faulty in muscular dystrophy.
questions.answerText: From the Z disc to the M line

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What role does dystrophin play in a muscle fiber?
options: It passes sarcomere force to the sarcolemma
It covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
It gives the sarcomere elastic recoil
It anchors the thick filaments at the M line
questions.why: Dystrophin links the thin filaments at the edge of the myofibrils to proteins in the sarcolemma. Through that link, the pull of the sarcomeres is passed to the cell membrane and from there to the endomysium and the rest of the connective tissue. When dystrophin is faulty, as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the fiber is damaged by its own contractions.
notes: Correct. Dystrophin links the thin filaments to the cell membrane so force reaches the connective tissue.
This is the role of tropomyosin, a regulatory protein. It would be the answer for what keeps relaxed muscle from contracting.
This is the role of titin. Pick titin for the spring between the Z disc and the M line.
This is the role of myomesin. Pick it for the protein at the center of the sarcomere.
questions.answerText: It passes sarcomere force to the sarcolemma

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Where in the sarcomere is myomesin found?
options: At the Z disc
Throughout the I band
At the M line
Along the sarcolemma
questions.why: Myomesin is a structural protein located at the M line, the center of the sarcomere. It binds neighboring thick filaments to one another, keeping them evenly spaced. Remembering that myomesin and the M line share the letter M helps keep it apart from alpha-actinin at the Z disc.
notes: The Z disc holds alpha-actinin, which anchors the thin filaments and titin. Pick it for alpha-actinin.
The I band holds thin filaments only, and its structural protein is nebulin along each thin filament. It would be the answer for nebulin's region.
Correct. Myomesin binds the thick filaments together at the M line.
The sarcolemma is linked to the myofibrils by dystrophin. Pick it for where dystrophin works.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A signal arriving at the surface of a muscle fiber must reach the calcium store throughout the fiber almost at once. Which repeating structure makes this possible?
options: The triad
The myofibril
The Z disc
The sarcomere
questions.why: The triad is one transverse (T) tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The T tubule brings the surface signal deep into the fiber, and right beside it the cisternae hold calcium. Because triads repeat along every myofibril, the signal reaches the calcium store throughout the fiber almost at the same moment.
notes: Correct. Each triad is a meeting point of a T tubule and the calcium store.
The myofibril is the contractile rod made of sarcomeres. It would be the answer for what the sarcoplasmic reticulum wraps around.
The Z disc anchors the thin filaments at the sarcomere border. It has no role in carrying the signal to the calcium store.
The sarcomere is the contractile unit that shortens once calcium is released. It responds to the signal but does not deliver it. Pick it for the unit between two Z discs.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, fibers damage themselves with ordinary use. Which structural link fails?
options: The link between the T tubule and the terminal cisternae
The link between the thick filaments at the M line
The link between the tendon and the bone
The link between the thin filaments and the sarcolemma
questions.why: Dystrophin normally connects the thin filaments at the edge of the myofibrils to the sarcolemma, passing the force of contraction out to the connective tissue. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy the dystrophin gene is faulty, so that link fails. Each contraction then stresses the membrane, the fiber damages itself with ordinary use, and weakness gets worse over time.
notes: This is the triad, where the surface signal meets the calcium store. It would be the answer for the structure that coordinates calcium release.
This link is made by myomesin and is not the defect in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Pick it for the M line connection.
This link fails in a tendon rupture, an injury rather than an inherited disease. Pick it for an injury that separates muscle from bone.
Correct. This is the link made by dystrophin.
questions.answerText: The link between the thin filaments and the sarcolemma

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: At each end of the A band, thick and thin filaments lie interleaved. What is this region called?
options: The H zone
The zone of overlap
The M line
The I band
questions.why: The zone of overlap is at each end of the A band, where thin filaments from the Z disc slide in between the thick filaments. Because both filaments are present, it is the darkest part of the sarcomere, and it is where myosin heads can reach actin to form cross bridges. The center of the A band, beyond the reach of the thin filaments, is the H zone.
notes: The H zone is the center of the A band, with thick filaments only. Pick it for the region thin filaments do not reach.
Correct. Both filament types are present here.
The M line is the protein line in the center of the H zone that anchors thick filaments. It is not where thin filaments are found.
The I band lies outside the A band and holds thin filaments only. It would be the answer for the light band.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Why does a skeletal muscle fiber have many nuclei?
options: The extra nuclei let the fiber contract without nerve input
The extra nuclei store calcium for contraction
It has divided its nucleus repeatedly to prepare for cell division
It forms from many fused embryonic cells, and the nuclei maintain a very long cell
questions.why: A skeletal muscle fiber is unusually long, and it forms during development when many embryonic muscle cells fuse into one. Each of those cells contributes its nucleus, so the mature fiber has hundreds of nuclei flattened along the sarcolemma. Spread along its length, these nuclei direct the protein production needed to maintain such a large cell.
notes: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and contracts only when a motor neuron signals it. The number of nuclei has nothing to do with that control.
Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in nuclei. Pick the sarcoplasmic reticulum for the calcium store.
Mature skeletal muscle fibers do not divide. This misconception treats the many nuclei as a sign of a cell about to split.
Correct. Fusion supplies the nuclei, and a long cell needs many to maintain it.
questions.answerText: It forms from many fused embryonic cells, and the nuclei maintain a very long cell

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A myofibril is built of thousands of sarcomeres lined up end to end. Why does this arrangement produce a large overall shortening?
options: Each sarcomere shortens a little, and the changes add up along the chain
The stripes are pigment and play no role in contraction
Neighboring sarcomeres pull against each other and cancel out
The sarcomeres take turns contracting so motion never stops
questions.why: Each sarcomere shortens only a tiny distance as its Z discs are pulled toward the M line. Because thousands of sarcomeres are joined end to end along a myofibril, all of those tiny shortenings add together. The result is a noticeable shortening of the whole myofibril, the fiber, and finally the muscle.
notes: Correct. Sarcomeres in series sum their shortening.
The stripes are the bands of the sarcomeres themselves, the actual contractile machinery. Pigment in muscle comes from myoglobin, not the striations.

Neighboring sarcomeres are linked end to end through their shared Z discs, so their shortening adds together instead of canceling. If they canceled each other out, the myofibril could not shorten at all.
Sarcomeres along a myofibril shorten together, not in turns. This misconception confuses muscle with a wave-like process.
questions.answerText: Each sarcomere shortens a little, and the changes add up along the chain

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: The sarcoplasmic reticulum forms a network wrapped around each myofibril. Why does placing the calcium store this close to the myofibrils matter?
options: A short distance lets contraction start and stop fast
The location of the store has no effect on response time
Closeness slows calcium down so contraction is gentle
The store must be far away so calcium can build up
questions.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fiber, and it wraps every myofibril like a sleeve. Because the calcium is stored right next to the myofilaments, it reaches them almost instantly when released and can be pulled back just as fast. This short distance lets a muscle fiber contract and relax quickly.
notes: Correct. A close store means fast release and fast reuptake.
A store far from the filaments would delay every contraction. The wrapping arrangement exists precisely because distance matters.
Closeness does the opposite; a short distance speeds the response. This choice reverses the effect of distance.
Calcium builds up inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum itself, wherever it is. Distance from the filaments would only slow release.
questions.answerText: A short distance lets contraction start and stop fast

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: The muscles that move the eye can make very fine adjustments, while large thigh muscles produce strong but coarse movements. How does the number of fibers in each motor unit explain this?
options: Precision depends only on overall muscle size
More fibers per motor neuron always gives finer control
Motor unit size affects muscle color but not control
Fewer fibers per neuron allows finer steps
questions.why: A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it controls. In the eye muscles each neuron controls only a few fibers, so each signal moves a tiny amount of muscle and adjustments can be very fine. In large thigh muscles each neuron controls many fibers, so each signal recruits a large block of muscle, producing strength rather than precision.
notes: Muscle size alone does not set precision. A small muscle with large motor units would still move coarsely.
This reverses the relationship. Large motor units move a lot of muscle at once, which suits power rather than precision.
Muscle color comes mainly from myoglobin. Motor unit size determines how finely a muscle can be controlled.
Correct. Small motor units allow precise control.
questions.answerText: Fewer fibers per neuron allows finer steps

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Muscles used for endurance, such as postural muscles, are rich in mitochondria. Why does an endurance muscle benefit from many mitochondria?
options: Mitochondria store oxygen inside the fiber
Mitochondria store the calcium that triggers contraction
Mitochondria form the striations of the fiber
Mitochondria supply the steady ATP that sustained contraction needs
questions.why: Mitochondria are packed in rows between the myofibrils, where they supply the ATP that contraction demands. They make ATP using oxygen, which provides a steady energy supply over long periods. Muscles that work for hours, like the postural muscles of the back, rely on that steady supply and so contain many mitochondria.
notes: Oxygen is stored by myoglobin, the red pigment in the sarcoplasm. It would be the answer for the fiber's oxygen reserve.
Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Pick the sarcoplasmic reticulum for the calcium store.
The striations come from the A and I bands of the sarcomeres. Mitochondria lie in rows between myofibrils but do not create the stripes.
Correct. Mitochondria produce ATP aerobically for long-lasting work.
questions.answerText: Mitochondria supply the steady ATP that sustained contraction needs

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes myofilaments and how they relate to the sarcomere?
options: They are connective tissue fibers that tie each sarcomere to the tendon
They are membrane tubules that wrap each myofibril and store calcium for the sarcomere
They are the thick and thin protein strands whose ordered overlap forms the sarcomere
They are bundles of myofibrils whose ordered overlap forms the fascicle
questions.why: Myofilaments are the thick filaments (mostly myosin) and thin filaments (mostly actin) packed inside each myofibril. They are arranged in a precise, repeating pattern, and that pattern of overlap is what defines the sarcomere, the segment from one Z disc to the next. The bands you see under the microscope are simply regions where thick filaments, thin filaments, or both are present.
notes: Connective tissue never enters the cell to reach sarcomeres. The link from sarcomere to membrane is made by proteins such as dystrophin, and the link from fiber to tendon is made by the endomysium and other sheaths.
This describes the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the smooth ER that wraps each myofibril and stores calcium ions. Pick it if the question asked which structure stores calcium in a muscle fiber.
Correct. The ordered overlap of thick and thin filaments is the sarcomere.
Myofilaments are smaller than myofibrils, not bundles of them, and a fascicle is a bundle of whole muscle fibers. This choice reverses the size order of the levels.
questions.answerText: They are the thick and thin protein strands whose ordered overlap forms the sarcomere

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is the sarcolemma?
options: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the muscle fiber
The connective tissue sheath around each muscle fiber
The plasma membrane of the muscle fiber
The cytoplasm of the muscle fiber
questions.why: Parts of a muscle fiber carry the prefix sarco, from the Greek for flesh, added to familiar cell terms. The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane that encloses the fiber, and it dives inward at intervals to form the T tubules. On a slide it is the thin boundary of each fiber, with the flattened nuclei lying just beneath it.
notes: This describes the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stores calcium ions. It would be the answer if the question asked about the calcium store of the fiber.

This describes the endomysium, which lies outside the sarcolemma. Choose it if the question asked what connective tissue wraps each fiber; students mix the two up because both form the edge of a fiber on a slide.
Correct. The sarcolemma is the muscle fiber's plasma membrane.
This describes the sarcoplasm, the cytoplasm of the muscle fiber. Pick it if the question asked for the fluid interior that holds the myofibrils, glycogen, and myoglobin.
questions.answerText: The plasma membrane of the muscle fiber

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which description matches the sarcoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fiber?
options: The fluid cytoplasm of the fiber, holding glycogen granules and myoglobin
Rows of organelles between the myofibrils that supply ATP
Inward tunnels of the sarcolemma that carry the surface signal deep into the fiber
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the fiber, which stores calcium ions
questions.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the muscle fiber's version of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a network of tubules wrapping each myofibril. Its job is to store calcium ions and release them when the fiber is signaled. Its enlarged end sacs, the terminal cisternae, sit on either side of each T tubule to form a triad.
notes: This describes the sarcoplasm, the cytoplasm of the fiber. It would be the answer if the question asked where glycogen and myoglobin are held.
This describes the mitochondria, packed in rows between myofibrils. Choose it if the question asked which organelle supplies the ATP that contraction needs.
This describes the transverse (T) tubules, which are extensions of the sarcolemma. Pick it if the question asked which structure carries the signal from the surface into the fiber.
Correct. The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the smooth ER of the fiber and its calcium store.
questions.answerText: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the fiber, which stores calcium ions

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is a triad in a skeletal muscle fiber?
options: One terminal cisterna flanked by two T tubules
One T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae
One A band flanked by two I bands
Three myofibrils bundled together by endomysium
questions.why: A triad is a three-part structural unit: a single transverse (T) tubule in the middle with an enlarged sac of sarcoplasmic reticulum, a terminal cisterna, pressed against it on each side. This is the meeting point where a signal traveling down the T tubule reaches the calcium store. Repeating triads along each myofibril let the whole fiber respond almost at once.
notes: This reverses the arrangement. There is one T tubule in the center, with the sarcoplasmic reticulum sacs on the outside, so students who pick this have the two parts swapped.
Correct. A triad is one T tubule between two terminal cisternae.
The A band and I bands are regions of the sarcomere seen under the microscope, not a triad. Pick the A band and I bands if the question asked which bands produce the striations.
Myofibrils are not wrapped individually by endomysium; the endomysium wraps the whole fiber. This choice comes from guessing that triad means three of something larger.
questions.answerText: One T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What do the transverse (T) tubules of a skeletal muscle fiber do?
options: They store calcium ions in sacs wrapped around each myofibril
They anchor the thick filaments to one another at the center of the sarcomere
They are inward tunnels of the sarcolemma that carry the surface signal deep into the fiber
They are enlarged end sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum beside each tubule
questions.why: T tubules are narrow tunnels of the sarcolemma that dive inward, crossing the fiber at right angles to its length. Because they are continuous with the surface membrane, they carry the signal that starts at the surface down into the middle of a thick fiber. Each one runs between two terminal cisternae, forming a triad, so the signal reaches the calcium store everywhere at once.
notes: This describes the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the calcium store of the fiber. Pick it if the question asked where calcium ions are held.

This describes the M line and its protein myomesin, which bind the thick filaments together in the center of the sarcomere. It would be the answer if the question asked where thick filaments are anchored.
Correct. T tubules extend the sarcolemma inward to carry the signal deep into the fiber.
This describes the terminal cisternae, the end sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that flank each T tubule. Choose them if the question asked what lies on either side of a T tubule in a triad.
questions.answerText: They are inward tunnels of the sarcolemma that carry the surface signal deep into the fiber

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: On a slide of skeletal muscle in longitudinal section, a student sees many flattened nuclei along the edge of a single long fiber. What explains this appearance?
options: Each fiber forms from many fused embryonic cells, so its many nuclei lie against the sarcolemma
Each nucleus belongs to an endomysium cell, while the fiber itself has none
Each nucleus sits inside one sarcomere, spaced along the myofibrils
Each nucleus belongs to a separate short cell, joined end to end by intercalated discs
questions.why: A skeletal muscle fiber develops when many embryonic muscle cells fuse into one long cell, so a single fiber contains many nuclei. The myofibrils fill most of the cell, which pushes these nuclei out to the periphery, where they lie flattened just under the sarcolemma. Peripheral nuclei are one of the features that let you tell skeletal muscle from cardiac and smooth muscle, which have central nuclei.
notes: Correct. Fusion of many cells makes the fiber multinucleated, and the myofibrils push the nuclei to the edge.
The endomysium does contain a few connective tissue cells, but a skeletal muscle fiber is multinucleated in its own right. Students choose this when they assume every cell must have just one nucleus.
Nuclei never sit inside sarcomeres, which are made of filaments within the myofibrils. This choice comes from mistaking the regular spacing of nuclei for part of the striation pattern.
Intercalated discs join separate short cells in cardiac muscle, where each cell has one central nucleus. Pick this description if the slide showed branching cells with dark cross lines between them.
questions.answerText: Each fiber forms from many fused embryonic cells, so its many nuclei lie against the sarcolemma

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which structures mark the two boundaries of a sarcomere?
options: The A bands
The Z discs
The M lines
The H zones
questions.why: A sarcomere is the segment of a myofibril from one Z disc to the next. The Z disc is a protein plate that anchors the thin filaments, and it runs through the center of each I band. Because each Z disc is shared, every sarcomere borders the next one in a continuous chain along the myofibril.
notes: The A band is the dark band in the middle of the sarcomere, as wide as the thick filaments are long. Choose it if the question asked which band never changes length during contraction.
Correct. A sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next.
The M line runs through the center of the sarcomere, not its edges, and it anchors the thick filaments. Pick it if the question asked what marks the middle of a sarcomere.
The H zone is the lighter region in the center of the A band, where only thick filaments are found. It would be the answer for the central zone with thick filaments only.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which filaments are found in the I band of a sarcomere?
options: No filaments, only the Z disc protein
Thick filaments only
Thin filaments only
Thick and thin filaments overlapping
questions.why: The I band is the light band at each end of the sarcomere, the stretch where thin (actin) filaments extend from the Z disc but no thick filaments reach. Having only thin filaments makes it look pale under the microscope. A Z disc runs through the center of each I band, so one I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres.
notes: The Z disc runs through the I band, but the band itself is filled with thin filaments anchored to that disc. Students pick this when they think the light color means the band is empty.
Thick filaments only is the content of the H zone in the center of the A band. Pick it if the question asked about the H zone.
Correct. The I band contains thin filaments only.
Both kinds overlapping is the zone of overlap at each end of the A band. It would be the answer for the region where thick and thin filaments interleave.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which filaments are found in the H zone of a sarcomere?
options: Thick filaments only
Thick and thin filaments overlapping
Thin filaments only
No filaments, only the M line protein
questions.why: The H zone is the lighter region in the center of the A band. Thick (myosin) filaments run through it, but the thin filaments coming in from each Z disc do not reach that far at rest, so only thick filaments are present. The M line runs down the middle of the H zone and holds the thick filaments together.
notes: Correct. The H zone holds thick filaments only.
Overlapping thick and thin filaments make up the zone of overlap at each edge of the A band. It would be the answer for the darkest part of the A band.
Thin filaments only is the content of the I band at the ends of the sarcomere. Pick it if the question asked about the I band.
The M line does run through the H zone, but the zone itself is filled with thick filaments. Students choose this when they mistake the lighter shade of the H zone for an empty space.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which description matches the A band of a sarcomere?
options: The protein line in the center that anchors the thick filaments
The light band with thin filaments only, split down the middle by a Z disc
The lighter central region with thick filaments only
The dark band, as wide as the thick filaments are long, with thin filaments overlapping at each edge
questions.why: The A band is the dark band of the sarcomere, and its width is set by the length of the thick filaments, which run across its full width. Thin filaments slide into each end of it, creating zones of overlap, while its center (the H zone) has thick filaments only. Because its width equals the thick filament length, the A band does not change length when the muscle shortens.
notes: This describes the M line, which runs down the center of the H zone. Choose it if the question asked where the thick filaments are anchored.
This describes the I band, the light band of thin filaments with a Z disc through its center. Pick it if the question asked about the light band.
This describes the H zone, which sits in the middle of the A band. It would be the answer for the central region where only thick filaments are found.
Correct. The A band spans the full length of the thick filaments, with overlap at each edge.
questions.answerText: The dark band, as wide as the thick filaments are long, with thin filaments overlapping at each edge

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Under the microscope, skeletal muscle shows alternating dark and light stripes called striations. Which bands produce them?
options: Dark Z discs alternating with light M lines
Dark A bands alternating with light I bands
Dark I bands alternating with light A bands
Dark intercalated discs alternating with light sarcoplasm
questions.why: Striations are the repeating pattern of thousands of sarcomeres lined up across neighboring myofibrils. The A band, where the thick filaments lie, looks dark, and the I band, which has thin filaments only, looks light. Because the sarcomeres are in register across the whole fiber, these bands line up into visible stripes.
notes: Z discs and M lines are thin lines within the bands, not the broad stripes themselves. Pick the Z disc if the question asked what marks the border of a sarcomere.
Correct. Dark A bands and light I bands repeat to form the striations.
This reverses the shading. The I band is the light band (it has thin filaments only) and the A band is the dark band, so students who pick this have the letters swapped.
Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle, where they appear as dark cross lines joining neighboring cells. Choose them if the question asked what joins cardiac muscle cells end to end.
questions.answerText: Dark A bands alternating with light I bands

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is the main protein of the thick filament, and where is the thick filament anchored?
options: Actin, anchored at the Z disc
Myosin, anchored at the M line
Myosin, anchored at the Z disc
Actin, anchored at the M line
questions.why: The thick filament is a bundle of myosin molecules, each with a long tail and a pair of heads that project outward as cross bridges. Thick filaments sit in the center of the sarcomere and are bound to one another at the M line. Titin then runs from the Z disc to the M line, holding each thick filament in position.
notes: Actin anchored at the Z disc describes the thin filament. Pick it if the question asked about the thin filament.
Correct. The thick filament is made of myosin and anchored at the M line.
Myosin is right, but the Z disc anchors the thin filaments at the ends of the sarcomere. Students pick this when they remember the Z disc as the anchor for every filament.
Actin is the thin filament protein, and the M line holds the thick filaments, not thin ones. This choice pairs each half with the wrong filament.
questions.answerText: Myosin, anchored at the M line

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: What is the main protein of the thin filament, and where is the thin filament anchored?
options: Actin, anchored at the Z disc
Myosin, anchored at the Z disc
Actin, anchored at the M line
Myosin, anchored at the M line
questions.why: The thin filament is made of two twisted strands of actin subunits, each with a binding site for myosin. Thin filaments extend inward from the Z disc at each end of the sarcomere toward the center. The regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin lie along the thin filament as well.
notes: Correct. The thin filament is made of actin and anchored at the Z disc.
Myosin forms the thick filament, and the thick filaments are not attached to the Z disc. This choice pairs the thick filament protein with the thin filament anchor.
Actin is right, but thin filaments come in from the ends of the sarcomere and do not reach the M line at rest. That is why the H zone around the M line has thick filaments only.
Myosin anchored at the M line describes the thick filament. Pick it if the question asked about the thick filament.
questions.answerText: Actin, anchored at the Z disc

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the roles of titin and dystrophin?
options: Titin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma, and dystrophin anchors the thick filament and gives elastic recoil
Titin and dystrophin both lie along the thin filament as regulatory proteins
Titin forms the core of the thin filament, and dystrophin binds the thick filaments together at the M line
Titin anchors the thick filament and gives elastic recoil, and dystrophin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma
questions.why: Titin is a huge elastic protein that spans from the Z disc to the M line, holding the thick filament in place and springing the sarcomere back after it is stretched. Dystrophin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma, passing the force of contraction out to the connective tissue. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy the dystrophin gene is faulty, so the fiber damages itself with ordinary use.
notes: This swaps the two proteins. Titin is the elastic anchor of the thick filament, and dystrophin is the link to the cell membrane.
The regulatory proteins on the thin filament are tropomyosin and troponin. They would be the answer if the question asked which proteins lie along the thin filament.
The core of the thin filament is actin, and the protein that binds thick filaments at the M line is myomesin. Pick actin or myomesin if the question asked about those roles.
Correct. Titin anchors the thick filament and gives recoil, and dystrophin ties the thin filaments to the sarcolemma.
questions.answerText: Titin anchors the thick filament and gives elastic recoil, and dystrophin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: When a skeletal muscle shortens, which region of the sarcomere stays the same length?
options: The A band
The distance between Z discs
The I band
The H zone
questions.why: The width of the A band is set by the length of the thick filaments, and the filaments themselves do not get shorter when a muscle contracts. Instead, the thin filaments slide farther over the thick filaments toward the M line. As a result, the I band and H zone narrow and the Z discs move closer together, while the A band keeps its width.
notes: Correct. The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, so it does not change.
The Z discs move closer together as the muscle shortens, so the sarcomere as a whole gets shorter. Students pick this when they think the sarcomere stays the same and only the filaments move.
The I band narrows during shortening because the thin filaments slide deeper into the A band, leaving less thin-filament-only space. Pick it if the question asked which band gets narrower.
The H zone narrows and can disappear as the thin filaments slide in toward the M line. It would be the answer if the question asked which central region shrinks the most.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A toxin damages only the terminal cisternae in a skeletal muscle fiber. Which organelle are they part of, and which repeating structure that includes them is disrupted?
options: The T tubule; the triad is disrupted.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum; the sarcomere is disrupted.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum; the triad is disrupted.
The sarcolemma; the myofibril is disrupted.
questions.why: Terminal cisternae are the enlarged end sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the fiber's smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions. Two terminal cisternae sit on either side of one T tubule, and that set of three is the triad. Damaging the cisternae breaks the triad, the meeting point between the surface signal and the calcium store.
notes: The triad is the right structure, but terminal cisternae are not part of the T tubule. The T tubule is the narrow tunnel of sarcolemma in the middle of the triad.
The organelle is right, but the sarcomere is the contractile unit from one Z disc to the next, built of myofilaments. Terminal cisternae are part of the triad, not the sarcomere.
Correct. Terminal cisternae belong to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and form two thirds of each triad.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane, and its inward tunnels are the T tubules, not the cisternae. A myofibril is a contractile rod, not a structure that contains terminal cisternae.
questions.answerText: The sarcoplasmic reticulum; the triad is disrupted.

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A cross section cut through one region of a sarcomere shows only thin filaments. Which band was cut, and which structure runs through the center of that band?
options: The H zone, with the M line at its center
The A band, with the H zone at its center
The I band, with a Z disc at its center
The I band, with the M line at its center
questions.why: The I band is the light band and holds thin filaments only. A Z disc runs through its center, which is why one I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres. The H zone, by contrast, holds thick filaments only.
notes: The H zone does have the M line at its center, but it holds thick filaments only, not thin filaments.
The A band holds thick filaments across its full width, with thin filaments only at its edges, so a section through it would not show thin filaments alone.
Correct. Thin filaments alone means the I band, which has a Z disc at its center.
The I band is right, but the M line sits in the center of the H zone, in the middle of the A band. The Z disc runs through the I band.
questions.answerText: The I band, with a Z disc at its center

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A cross section through a sarcomere shows each thick filament surrounded by thin filaments. Which region was cut, and which band is it part of?
options: The H zone, at the center of the A band
The zone of overlap, at the edge of the A band
The zone of overlap, in the middle of the I band
The I band, right beside the Z disc
questions.why: Thick and thin filaments interleave only in the zone of overlap. That region lies at each end of the A band, where thin filaments reaching in from the Z discs overlap the thick filaments. The H zone at the center has thick filaments only, and the I band has thin filaments only.
notes: The H zone is the lighter center of the A band, with thick filaments only. A cut there would show no thin filaments.
Correct. Both filaments together means the zone of overlap, at each end of the A band.
The zone of overlap is right, but it is part of the A band, not the I band. The middle of the I band is the Z disc, where thin filaments are anchored.
The I band, near the Z disc, has thin filaments only. A cut there would show no thick filaments.
questions.answerText: The zone of overlap, at the edge of the A band

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A cut through the exact middle of a sarcomere hits a protein line that binds the thick filaments together. Which line is it, and which region surrounds it?
options: The M line, surrounded by the H zone
The Z disc, surrounded by the I band
The M line, surrounded by the I band
The Z disc, surrounded by the H zone
questions.why: The M line is the protein line in the center of the H zone, and it anchors the thick filaments to one another. The H zone is the lighter region in the center of the A band, where only thick filaments lie. The Z discs sit at the two ends of the sarcomere, not its middle.
notes: Correct. The M line sits at the center of the H zone and binds the thick filaments.
The Z disc does sit in the center of an I band, but it marks the ends of a sarcomere, not its middle, and it anchors thin filaments.
The M line is right, but it sits in the H zone in the middle of the A band. The I band lies at the ends of the sarcomere.
The Z disc anchors thin filaments at the border of the sarcomere. The H zone surrounds the M line, not the Z disc.
questions.answerText: The M line, surrounded by the H zone

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A mutation removes the protein that fastens titin to the Z disc. Which protein is missing, and which filament loses the anchor that titin gives it?
options: Myomesin; the thick filament loses its anchor
Nebulin; the thin filament loses its anchor
Alpha-actinin; the thick filament loses its anchor
Alpha-actinin; the thin filament loses its anchor
questions.why: Alpha-actinin sits at the Z disc and binds both the thin filaments and titin there. Titin spans from the Z disc to the M line and anchors the thick filament. If alpha-actinin is missing, titin comes loose from the Z disc, so the thick filament loses the anchor that titin gives it.
notes: Myomesin is at the M line, where it binds the thick filaments to each other. It does not fasten titin to the Z disc.
Nebulin runs along the thin filament, anchoring it and setting its length. It does not fasten titin, and titin does not anchor the thin filament.
Correct. Alpha-actinin holds titin at the Z disc, and titin anchors the thick filament.
Alpha-actinin is the missing protein, and it also holds the thin filaments at the Z disc. But the anchor titin provides goes to the thick filament, not the thin one.
questions.answerText: Alpha-actinin; the thick filament loses its anchor

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: A filament anchored at the Z disc has nebulin running along its length. Which filament is it, what is its main protein, and which two regulatory proteins lie along it?
options: Thick filament; myosin; tropomyosin and troponin
Thin filament; myosin; titin and myomesin
Thick filament; actin; titin and nebulin
Thin filament; actin; tropomyosin and troponin
questions.why: Nebulin runs the length of the thin filament, anchoring it and setting its length, and thin filaments are anchored at the Z disc. The thin filament is two twisted strands of actin. Tropomyosin lies end to end along it, and troponin is bound at intervals to the tropomyosin.
notes: Thick filaments are made of myosin and anchored at the M line, not the Z disc. Tropomyosin and troponin sit on the thin filament.
The filament is the thin one, but its protein is actin, not myosin. Titin and myomesin are structural proteins tied to the thick filament and the M line, not regulatory proteins.
This mixes up the two filaments. Actin forms the thin filament, and nebulin runs along the thin filament, not the thick one.
Correct. A Z disc anchor and nebulin mark the thin filament, made of actin and carrying tropomyosin and troponin.
questions.answerText: Thin filament; actin; tropomyosin and troponin

questions.topic: Muscle fiber microanatomy and the sarcomere
questions.q: On an electron micrograph, one filament has no nebulin along it, is anchored at the M line, and is tied to the Z disc by a long elastic protein. Which filament is it, what is it made of, and what is the elastic protein?
options: Thin filament of actin, tied by titin
Thick filament of myosin, tied by titin
Thick filament of myosin, tied by dystrophin
Thin filament of actin, tied by nebulin
questions.why: Thick filaments are bundles of myosin anchored at the M line, while thin filaments are actin anchored at the Z disc with nebulin running along them. Titin spans from the Z disc to the M line, anchors the thick filament, and gives the sarcomere its elastic recoil. A filament with no nebulin, anchored at the M line and tied to the Z disc, is the thick filament held by titin.
notes: Titin is the right elastic protein, but the thin filament carries nebulin and is anchored at the Z disc, not the M line. Titin anchors the thick filament.
