Correct. The M line anchor marks the thick filament, made of myosin, and titin ties it to the Z disc.
The filament is right, but dystrophin links the thin filaments to the sarcolemma. The elastic protein that runs from the Z disc to the M line is titin.
Nebulin runs along the thin filament and sets its length, but this filament has no nebulin and is anchored at the M line, which rules out the thin filament.
questions.answerText: Thick filament of myosin, tied by titin

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The origin of a muscle is its attachment to which bone?
options: The more stationary bone
The more movable bone
The more distal bone
The larger bone
questions.why: A muscle crosses a joint and attaches to the bones on either side. When it contracts, one bone stays relatively still and the other moves. The attachment to the stationary bone is the origin, and the attachment to the moving bone is the insertion, which is pulled toward the origin.
notes: Correct. The origin is the attachment to the more stationary bone.
The attachment to the more movable bone is the insertion. Pick this answer for a question about the insertion.
In the limbs the origin is usually proximal, not distal, so this reverses the usual rule of thumb. The more distal attachment is usually the insertion.
Bone size does not decide which attachment is the origin. What matters is which bone stays still during the movement, so students who pick this are guessing from size rather than function.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The insertion of a muscle is its attachment to which bone?
options: The larger bone
The more movable bone
The more proximal bone
The more stationary bone
questions.why: The insertion is where a muscle attaches to the bone that moves when the muscle contracts. During contraction, the muscle pulls the insertion toward the origin, which stays relatively still. For example, the biceps brachii inserts on the radius, so when it contracts the forearm moves up toward the shoulder.
notes: Bone size does not decide which attachment is the insertion. What matters is which bone moves during the action.
Correct. The insertion is the attachment to the more movable bone.
In the limbs the more proximal attachment is usually the origin, not the insertion. The insertion is usually the more distal attachment, so this reverses the rule of thumb.
The attachment to the more stationary bone is the origin. Pick this answer for a question about the origin.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: As a general rule of thumb for limb muscles, which pairing of origin and insertion is usual?
options: Origin proximal, insertion distal
Origin medial, insertion lateral
Origin superficial, insertion deep
Origin distal, insertion proximal
questions.why: In the limbs, the origin is usually the proximal attachment, closer to the trunk, and the insertion is usually the distal attachment, farther from the trunk. That fits how limbs work: the proximal bone usually stays steady while the distal bone moves. The biceps brachii follows this rule, with its origin on the scapula and its insertion on the radius.
notes: Correct. The origin is usually proximal and the insertion usually distal.
Medial and lateral describe position relative to the midline, and they do not determine which attachment is the origin. Students pick this when they mix up directional term pairs.
Superficial and deep describe depth from the body surface, not which bone moves. This pairing has nothing to do with defining origin and insertion.
This reverses the rule of thumb. The distal bone is usually the one that moves, so it usually carries the insertion.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is the movement a muscle produces when it contracts called?
options: The lever
The action
The origin
The insertion
questions.why: A muscle's action is the movement it produces when it contracts and pulls its insertion toward its origin. Actions are named with movement terms such as flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction. For example, the action of the biceps brachii is flexion of the elbow.
notes: In a lever system the lever is the rigid bar that moves, which in the body is a bone. Pick it for a question about what plays the role of the bar in a body lever.
Correct. The movement produced by a contracting muscle is its action.
The origin is the attachment to the more stationary bone, not a movement. Pick it for a question about which attachment stays still.
The insertion is the attachment to the more movable bone, the point that gets pulled. Pick it for a question about which end moves toward the other.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The brachialis attaches to the distal humerus and to the ulna, and it flexes the elbow. During elbow flexion the forearm moves while the arm stays steady. Which attachment is its origin?
options: Its attachment on the scapula
Its attachment on the radius
Its attachment on the ulna
Its attachment on the humerus
questions.why: The origin is the attachment on the bone that stays relatively still, and in the limbs it is usually the proximal one. When the brachialis flexes the elbow, the humerus stays steady and the ulna moves up toward it. That makes the humerus attachment the origin and the ulna attachment the insertion.
notes: The brachialis does not reach the scapula. The scapula carries the origins of the biceps brachii and the long head of the triceps brachii, so pick it for questions about those muscles.
The brachialis does not attach to the radius. The radius carries the insertion of the biceps brachii, so pick it for a question about where the biceps inserts.
The ulna is the bone that moves during elbow flexion, so the brachialis attachment there is its insertion. Pick the ulna if the question asks for the insertion of the brachialis.
Correct. The humerus stays steady, so the brachialis attachment there is the origin.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When a muscle contracts, which statement describes the usual movement of its attachments?
options: The insertion is pulled toward the origin
Both attachments are pushed apart
The origin is pulled toward the insertion
The belly lengthens while both attachments stay still
questions.why: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls on both of its attachments, but the bone carrying the origin is held steady. As a result, the insertion on the more movable bone is pulled toward the origin. This is why the insertion is defined as the attachment that moves.
notes: Correct. The insertion is pulled toward the origin.
Muscles can only pull; they never push. Students choose this when they picture a muscle bulging outward and assume it pushes the bones apart.
In a usual movement the origin stays steady and the insertion moves. The origin moves only in a reversed action, such as a pull-up, where the limb is fixed and the trunk is pulled toward it.

A belly that lengthens while being pulled describes a muscle being stretched, as the antagonist is during a movement. Pick this idea for a question about what happens to the triceps brachii when the elbow bends.
questions.answerText: The insertion is pulled toward the origin

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The biceps brachii runs from the scapula to the radius. When it flexes the elbow, the forearm rises while the scapula stays steady. Which bone carries its insertion?
options: The humerus
The scapula
The radius
The ulna
questions.why: The insertion is the attachment on the bone that moves, which is pulled toward the origin. During elbow flexion the forearm rises while the scapula stays steady, so the attachment on the radius (at the radial tuberosity) is the insertion. The scapula attachments are the origins of its two heads.
notes: The biceps brachii crosses the humerus but does not attach to it. The humerus carries the origin of the brachialis, so pick it for a question about that muscle.
The scapula stays steady during elbow flexion, so it carries the origins of the biceps brachii, not its insertion. Pick the scapula if the question asks for the origin.
Correct. The radius moves, so it carries the insertion of the biceps brachii.
The ulna is a forearm bone that moves during elbow flexion, but the biceps brachii does not insert on it. The brachialis inserts on the ulna, so pick the ulna for a question about the brachialis.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which list contains only criteria used to name skeletal muscles?
options: Direction of fibers, nerve supply, blood supply, and color
Direction of fibers, relative size, shape, and number of origins
Action, location, contraction speed, and fiber color
Relative size, number of nuclei, shape, and striation pattern
questions.why: Skeletal muscles are named for features you can see or describe: the direction of their fibers, their relative size, their shape, their action, their number of origins, their location, and their origin and insertion. Most names combine two or more of these, such as rectus femoris, which gives direction and location. Learning the criteria lets the name tell you something about the muscle.
notes: Direction of fibers is a real naming criterion, but nerve supply, blood supply, and color are not used to name muscles. Students pick this list when they mix up how muscles are described with how they are named.
Correct. Direction of fibers, relative size, shape, and number of origins are all naming criteria.
Action and location are real naming criteria, but contraction speed and fiber color describe fiber types inside a muscle. This list mixes two real criteria with two fiber characteristics.
Number of nuclei and striation pattern describe muscle tissue under the microscope, which is the same for every skeletal muscle. They help identify the tissue type, not name individual muscles.
questions.answerText: Direction of fibers, relative size, shape, and number of origins

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a muscle name, what does the direction term rectus tell you about the fascicles?
options: They run perpendicular to the midline
They run parallel to the midline
They run in rings around an opening
They run diagonal to the midline
questions.why: Rectus means straight, and in a muscle name it tells you the fascicles run straight up and down, parallel to the midline of the body or to the long axis of a limb. The rectus abdominis, which runs vertically down the front of the abdomen, is a clear example. Direction terms describe how the fascicles run relative to the midline.
notes: Fascicles running perpendicular to the midline are described as transversus, as in the transversus abdominis. Pick perpendicular for a question about that term.
Correct. Rectus means the fascicles run parallel to the midline.
Fascicles arranged in rings around an opening describe a circular muscle such as the orbicularis oris, which is named for its shape. Pick rings for a question about the term orbicularis.
Fascicles running diagonally are described as oblique, as in the external and internal oblique muscles. Pick diagonal for a question about the term oblique.
questions.answerText: They run parallel to the midline

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a muscle name, what does the direction term oblique tell you about the fascicles?
options: They run parallel to the midline
They run perpendicular to the midline
They run in rings around an opening
They run diagonal to the midline
questions.why: Oblique means slanted, and in a muscle name it tells you the fascicles run at an angle, diagonal to the midline. The external and internal obliques of the abdominal wall are named for this slanted fiber direction. Comparing them with the rectus abdominis, whose fibers run straight, shows how direction terms work.
notes: Fascicles running parallel to the midline are described as rectus, as in the rectus abdominis. Pick parallel for a question about the term rectus.
Fascicles running perpendicular to the midline are described as transversus, as in the transversus abdominis. Pick perpendicular for a question about that term.
Fascicles in rings around an opening describe a circular muscle such as the orbicularis oculi. Pick rings for a question about the term orbicularis.
Correct. Oblique means the fascicles run diagonal to the midline.
questions.answerText: They run diagonal to the midline

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In muscle names, what do the size terms maximus and minimus mean?
options: Maximus means most superficial, and minimus means deepest
Maximus means strongest, and minimus means weakest
Maximus means longest, and minimus means shortest
Maximus means largest, and minimus means smallest
questions.why: Maximus and minimus describe relative size, meaning how big a muscle is compared with its neighbors. Maximus means largest and minimus means smallest, as in the gluteus maximus and gluteus minimus. The gluteus medius, named with medius, is the middle-sized muscle between them.
notes: The gluteus maximus does happen to be superficial and the gluteus minimus deep, which makes this tempting, but the terms themselves describe size. Depth is described with words such as superficialis and profundus.

Size terms do not describe strength. A muscle's power depends on many things, including how its fascicles are arranged, so students who pick this are reading meaning into the name that it does not carry.
Longest and shortest are expressed by longus and brevis, as in the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Correct. Maximus means largest and minimus means smallest.
questions.answerText: Maximus means largest, and minimus means smallest

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In muscle names, what do the size terms longus and brevis mean?
options: Longus means lateral, and brevis means medial
Longus means superficial, and brevis means deep
Longus means large, and brevis means small
Longus means long, and brevis means short
questions.why: Longus and brevis are relative size terms that describe length. Longus means long and brevis means short, so the fibularis longus is the longer of the two fibularis muscles and the fibularis brevis is the shorter one. The word brief comes from the same root as brevis.
notes: Lateral and medial describe position relative to the midline, and they appear in names as lateralis and medialis, as in the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Depth is expressed by superficialis and profundus, as in the flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Large and small are expressed by maximus and minimus, as in the gluteus maximus and minimus. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Correct. Longus means long and brevis means short.
questions.answerText: Longus means long, and brevis means short

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The shape term deltoid describes which shape?
options: Circular
Triangular
Trapezoid
Diamond shaped
questions.why: Deltoid means triangular, from the Greek letter delta, which is shaped like a triangle. The deltoid muscle caps the shoulder with a broad base along the clavicle and scapula and narrows to a point on the lateral humerus. Shape terms let a muscle name describe its outline.
notes: Circular is described by orbicularis, as in the orbicularis oris around the mouth. Pick circular for a question about the term orbicularis.
Correct. Deltoid means triangular.
Trapezoid is the shape described by trapezius, the large muscle of the upper back. Pick trapezoid for a question about the trapezius.
Diamond shaped is described by rhomboid, as in the rhomboid major and minor between the scapulae. Pick diamond shaped for a question about the rhomboids.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The shape term orbicularis describes which shape?
options: Saw-toothed
Triangular
Diamond shaped
Circular
questions.why: Orbicularis means circular, from the Latin word for a small circle or disc. The orbicularis oris surrounds the mouth and the orbicularis oculi surrounds the eye, and both have fascicles arranged in rings that close the opening like a sphincter. The name tells you the muscle encircles something.
notes: Saw-toothed is described by serratus, as in the serratus anterior on the side of the chest. Pick saw-toothed for a question about the term serratus.
Triangular is described by deltoid. Pick it for a question about the muscle that caps the shoulder.
Diamond shaped is described by rhomboid. Pick it for a question about the rhomboid muscles between the scapulae.
Correct. Orbicularis means circular.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When a muscle is named for its action, what does the term flexor tell you?
options: It moves a bone toward the midline
It increases the angle of a joint
It decreases the angle of a joint
It moves a bone away from the midline
questions.why: Flexion is a movement that decreases the angle between two bones at a joint, such as bending the elbow or the fingers. A muscle named flexor performs flexion. The flexor carpi radialis, for example, flexes the wrist.
notes: Moving a bone toward the midline is adduction, done by muscles named adductor. Pick this for a question about the term adductor.
Increasing a joint angle is extension, done by muscles named extensor. Pick this for a question about the term extensor.
Correct. A flexor decreases a joint angle.
Moving a bone away from the midline is abduction, done by muscles named abductor. Pick this for a question about the term abductor.
questions.answerText: It decreases the angle of a joint

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When muscles are named for their action, which statement correctly describes an abductor and an adductor?
options: An abductor raises a body part, and an adductor lowers it
An abductor decreases a joint angle, and an adductor increases it
An abductor moves a bone away from the midline, and an adductor moves it toward the midline
An abductor moves a bone toward the midline, and an adductor moves it away from the midline
questions.why: Abduction moves a bone away from the midline of the body, and adduction moves it back toward the midline. A helpful memory link is that to abduct means to take away, while adduction adds the limb back to the body. Muscles named abductor and adductor perform these actions, such as the adductor muscles on the medial thigh.
notes: Raising and lowering a body part are done by muscles named levator and depressor, such as the levator scapulae. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Decreasing and increasing a joint angle are flexion and extension, performed by flexors and extensors. Pick this pairing for a question about those terms.
Correct. Abductors move a bone away from the midline, and adductors move it toward the midline.
This swaps the two terms. Abduction takes the limb away from the midline, and adduction brings it back.
questions.answerText: An abductor moves a bone away from the midline, and an adductor moves it toward the midline

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The names biceps, triceps, and quadriceps are based on which naming criterion?
options: Number of origins
Location
Shape
Relative size
questions.why: The ending ceps comes from the Latin word for head, so these names count how many heads, or origins, a muscle has. Biceps has two, triceps has three, and quadriceps has four. Each head starts from its own origin and they join to share a common insertion.
notes: Correct. Biceps, triceps, and quadriceps name the number of origins.
Location is shown by terms that name a bone or region, such as temporalis or tibialis anterior. Pick it for a question about a muscle named for where it lies.
Shape is shown by terms such as deltoid, trapezius, and rhomboid. Pick it for a question about a muscle named for its outline.
Relative size is shown by terms such as maximus, minimus, longus, and brevis. Pick it for a question about the gluteus maximus or fibularis longus.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The muscle name temporalis is based on which naming criterion?
options: Location
Shape
Number of origins
Action
questions.why: The temporalis is named for its location, because it lies over the temporal bone on the side of the skull. Many muscles are named this way, such as the frontalis over the frontal bone and the tibialis anterior along the front of the tibia. The name points you to where the muscle sits.
notes: Correct. Temporalis is named for its location over the temporal bone.
Shape names describe a muscle's outline, such as deltoid (triangular) or trapezius (trapezoid). Pick shape for a question about one of those muscles.
Number of origins is shown by names like biceps and triceps. Pick it for a question about how many heads a muscle has.
Action names describe the movement a muscle produces, such as flexor or adductor. Pick action for a question about a muscle like the adductor longus.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a lever system in the body, what does the effort represent?
options: The resistance being moved
The rigid bar that moves
The force applied to move the lever
The fixed pivot point
questions.why: A lever has four parts: the lever itself, the fulcrum, the effort, and the load. The effort is the force applied to move the lever, and in the body it is the pull of a contracting muscle on a bone. The effort acts at the point where the muscle inserts on the bone.
notes: The resistance being moved is the load, such as the weight of the forearm plus anything held in the hand. Pick it for a question about the load.
The rigid bar that moves is the lever itself, which in the body is a bone. Pick it for a question about what acts as the lever.
Correct. The effort is the force applied to move the lever, the pull of a muscle.
The fixed pivot point is the fulcrum, which in the body is a joint. Pick it for a question about the fulcrum.
questions.answerText: The force applied to move the lever

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a lever system in the body, what does the load represent?
options: The force applied by the contracting muscle
The rigid bar that moves
The fixed point the lever turns around
The resistance moved by the lever
questions.why: The load, also called the resistance, is what the lever moves or works against. In the body it is the weight of the body part being moved plus anything that part is carrying, such as a book held in the hand. The muscle's effort must overcome the load to produce movement.
notes: The force applied by the contracting muscle is the effort. Pick it for a question about the effort.
The rigid bar that moves is the lever, which in the body is a bone. Pick it for a question about what acts as the lever.
The fixed point the lever turns around is the fulcrum, which in the body is a joint. Pick it for a question about the fulcrum.
Correct. The load is the resistance the lever moves.
questions.answerText: The resistance moved by the lever

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a body lever system, which structure acts as the fulcrum?
options: A tendon
A joint
A muscle
A bone
questions.why: The fulcrum is the fixed point that a lever turns around. In the body, bones pivot at joints, so the joint acts as the fulcrum. For example, the elbow joint is the fulcrum when the biceps brachii lifts the forearm.
notes: A tendon transmits the muscle's pull to the bone at the point where the effort is applied. It is part of how the effort reaches the lever, not the pivot point.
Correct. A joint acts as the fulcrum.
A contracting muscle supplies the effort, the force that moves the lever. Pick a muscle for a question about the source of the effort.
A bone is the rigid bar that moves, so it acts as the lever, not the fulcrum. Pick a bone for a question about what acts as the lever.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a body lever system, which structure acts as the lever?
options: A tendon
A bone
A joint
A ligament
questions.why: A lever is a rigid bar that moves around a fixed point. In the body, bones are the rigid bars, so a bone acts as the lever. When a muscle pulls on a bone, the bone pivots at a joint and moves the body part.
notes: A tendon carries the muscle's pull to the bone where the effort is applied. It delivers the effort to the lever rather than acting as the lever itself.
Correct. A bone acts as the lever.
A joint is the fixed point the bone pivots around, so it acts as the fulcrum. Pick a joint for a question about the fulcrum.
A ligament connects bone to bone and holds a joint together, but it is not the rigid bar that moves. Pick it for a question about what stabilizes a joint.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a first-class lever, how are the parts arranged along the lever?
options: The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load
The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort
The effort and the load act at the fulcrum itself
The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load
questions.why: Lever classes are sorted by which part sits in the middle. In a first-class lever the fulcrum is in the middle, with the effort on one side and the load on the other, like a seesaw. In the body, nodding the head works this way, with the atlanto-occipital joint between the posterior neck muscles and the weight of the face.
notes: An effort in the middle describes a third-class lever, like tweezers or flexing the elbow. Pick this arrangement for a third-class lever question.
A load in the middle describes a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow or standing on tiptoe. Pick this arrangement for a second-class lever question.
If the effort and load acted right at the fulcrum, the lever could not turn, because force at the pivot point produces no rotation. Students choose this when they are unsure what the fulcrum does.
Correct. In a first-class lever the fulcrum is in the middle.
questions.answerText: The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a second-class lever, how are the parts arranged along the lever?
options: The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load
The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort
The effort and the load act at the fulcrum itself
The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load
questions.why: In a second-class lever the load sits in the middle, with the fulcrum at one end and the effort at the other, like a wheelbarrow. In the body, standing on tiptoe is the classic example: the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, the body's weight is the load, and the calf muscles pull up on the heel as the effort.
notes: An effort in the middle describes a third-class lever, like tweezers or flexing the elbow. Pick this arrangement for a third-class lever question.
Correct. In a second-class lever the load is in the middle.
Force applied right at the pivot point cannot turn a lever. Students choose this when they are unsure what the fulcrum does.
A fulcrum in the middle describes a first-class lever, like a seesaw or nodding the head. Pick this arrangement for a first-class lever question.
questions.answerText: The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a third-class lever, how are the parts arranged along the lever?
options: The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load
The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load
The effort and the load act at the fulcrum itself
The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort
questions.why: In a third-class lever the effort sits in the middle, between the fulcrum and the load, like a pair of tweezers. This is the most common lever in the body. Flexing the elbow is the classic example: the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps brachii pulls on the forearm just below the elbow, and the load is the weight held in the hand.
notes: Correct. In a third-class lever the effort is in the middle.
A fulcrum in the middle describes a first-class lever, like a seesaw or nodding the head. Pick this arrangement for a first-class lever question.
Force applied right at the pivot point cannot turn a lever. Students choose this when they are unsure what the fulcrum does.
A load in the middle describes a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow or standing on tiptoe. Pick this arrangement for a second-class lever question.
questions.answerText: The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which muscle role is the prime mover, the muscle chiefly responsible for producing a movement?
options: The agonist
The synergist
The antagonist
The fixator
questions.why: The agonist, also called the prime mover, is the muscle that contracts to produce a given movement and does most of the work. For example, the biceps brachii is the agonist during elbow flexion. Other muscles help or oppose it, but the agonist is the one chiefly responsible for the action.
notes: Correct. The agonist is the prime mover.
A synergist assists the prime mover by adding force or preventing unwanted movement, but it is not the main muscle doing the job. Pick it for the brachialis helping the biceps brachii flex the elbow.
The antagonist opposes the prime mover, relaxing and stretching as the agonist contracts. Pick it for the triceps brachii during elbow flexion.
A fixator holds the origin bone steady so the prime mover can work efficiently. Pick it for muscles steadying the scapula during arm movements.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which muscle role opposes the prime mover, relaxing and stretching as the prime mover contracts?
options: The agonist
The synergist
The antagonist
The fixator
questions.why: The antagonist sits on the opposite side of the joint from the prime mover and produces the opposite action. When the prime mover contracts, the antagonist relaxes and lengthens so the movement can happen, and it can also slow or reverse the movement. The triceps brachii is the antagonist when the biceps brachii flexes the elbow.
notes: The agonist is the prime mover itself, the muscle doing the contracting. Pick it for the biceps brachii during elbow flexion.
A synergist works with the prime mover rather than against it, adding force or preventing unwanted movement. Pick it for the brachialis assisting elbow flexion.
Correct. The antagonist opposes and yields to the prime mover.
A fixator holds the origin bone steady so the prime mover acts efficiently. Pick it for muscles stabilizing the scapula during arm movements.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which muscle role assists the prime mover by adding force to the same movement?
options: The agonist
The synergist
The fixator
The antagonist
questions.why: A synergist works together with the prime mover. It can add its own pull to the same movement, or it can prevent unwanted movements that would waste the prime mover's effort. A fixator is a special kind of synergist whose job is to hold the origin bone steady rather than add force.
notes: The agonist is the prime mover itself, the muscle chiefly responsible for the movement. Pick it if the question asked which muscle does most of the work.
Correct. A muscle that adds force to the prime mover's action is a synergist.
A fixator is a synergist that holds the origin bone steady rather than adding force to the movement. Pick it for muscles steadying the scapula during arm movements.

The antagonist opposes the movement, relaxing and lengthening as the prime mover contracts, as the triceps brachii does during elbow flexion. Pick it if the question asked which muscle works against the movement.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Some synergists have a special job: they hold the origin bone steady so the prime mover can act efficiently on the insertion. What are these muscles called?
options: Agonists
Flexors
Fixators
Antagonists
questions.why: A fixator is a synergist that stabilizes the origin of the prime mover. If the origin bone wobbled, part of the prime mover's pull would be wasted moving it, so fixators hold it firm. Muscles that steady the scapula while the arm moves are a common example.
notes: Agonists are the prime movers themselves, the muscles that produce the movement. Pick agonists for a question about the muscle chiefly responsible for an action.
Flexor is an action term in a muscle's name, meaning it decreases a joint angle. It describes a movement, not the stabilizing role in this question.
Correct. Muscles that hold the origin bone steady for the prime mover are fixators.
Antagonists oppose the prime mover and stretch as it contracts. Pick antagonists for a question about the muscle on the opposite side of the joint.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is a muscle compartment?
options: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium
A single muscle wrapped in its epimysium
A group of muscles with a shared function, vessels, and nerves
A pair of muscles with opposite actions at a joint
questions.why: A compartment is a group of skeletal muscles, along with the blood vessels and nerves that serve them, bound together by deep fascia and sharing a common function. The limbs are divided into compartments such as the anterior flexor compartment and posterior extensor compartment of the forearm. Knowing a muscle's compartment tells you a lot about its likely action.
notes: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium is a fascicle, which is a part of one muscle. Pick it for a question about what the perimysium surrounds.
A single muscle wrapped in epimysium is one whole muscle organ, not a group. Pick it for a question about the outermost sheath.
Correct. A compartment is a functional group of muscles with their vessels and nerves.
A pair of muscles producing opposite actions describes an agonist and its antagonist, which usually sit in opposite compartments. Pick this idea for a question about opposing muscle pairs.
questions.answerText: A group of muscles with a shared function, vessels, and nerves

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In the name gluteus maximus, which naming criterion does the word maximus use?
options: Action
Shape
Relative size
Direction of fibers
questions.why: Maximus means largest, so it describes the muscle's relative size compared with its neighbors. The gluteus maximus is the largest of the three gluteal muscles, with the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus being smaller. The other word, gluteus, names the location in the buttock region.
notes: Action is described by terms such as flexor, extensor, and adductor. Pick action for a muscle like the adductor longus.
Shape is described by terms such as deltoid, trapezius, and rhomboid. Pick shape for a question about one of those names.
Correct. Maximus describes relative size.
Direction of fibers is described by terms such as rectus, oblique, and transversus. Pick direction for a muscle like the rectus abdominis.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which naming criterion does the name sternocleidomastoid use?
options: Shape
Action
Direction of fibers
Origin and insertion
questions.why: Sternocleidomastoid is built from the names of the muscle's attachments. Sterno refers to the sternum and cleido to the clavicle, where the muscle originates, and mastoid refers to the mastoid process of the temporal bone, where it inserts. Reading the name tells you exactly where the muscle runs on the side of the neck.
notes: Shape names describe a muscle's outline, such as deltoid or trapezius. Nothing in sternocleidomastoid describes a shape.
Action names describe the movement a muscle produces, such as flexor or levator. Sternocleidomastoid names bones, not a movement.
Direction names describe how fibers run, such as rectus or oblique. Pick direction for a question about the rectus abdominis or external oblique.
Correct. Sternocleidomastoid names its origin and insertion.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In the name rectus abdominis, what does each word tell you?
options: Rectus gives the fiber direction, and abdominis gives the location
Rectus gives the shape, and abdominis gives the action
Rectus gives the relative size, and abdominis gives the number of origins
Rectus gives the location, and abdominis gives the fiber direction
questions.why: Rectus means straight, so it tells you the fibers run parallel to the midline. Abdominis tells you the muscle is located in the abdomen. Put together, the name describes a muscle with straight vertical fibers on the front of the abdomen.
notes: Correct. Rectus is direction and abdominis is location.
Rectus describes the direction of fibers, not an outline, and abdominis names a region, not a movement. Pick shape for a name like deltoid and action for a name like flexor.
Size is described by terms such as maximus or longus, and number of origins by terms such as biceps. Neither word in rectus abdominis carries that information.
This swaps the two words. Rectus is the direction term and abdominis is the location term.
questions.answerText: Rectus gives the fiber direction, and abdominis gives the location

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The term transversus in a muscle name tells you the fascicles run in which direction?
options: Perpendicular to the midline
Parallel to the midline
In rings around an opening
Diagonal to the midline
questions.why: Transversus means across, so its fascicles run horizontally, at a right angle to the midline. The transversus abdominis, the deepest of the flat abdominal muscles, wraps around the abdomen like a belt with fibers running side to side. Direction terms always describe the fibers relative to the midline.
notes: Correct. Transversus means the fascicles run perpendicular to the midline.
Fibers parallel to the midline are described as rectus, as in the rectus abdominis. Pick parallel for a question about the term rectus.
Fibers in rings around an opening belong to circular muscles such as the orbicularis oris. Pick rings for a question about the term orbicularis.
Fibers running diagonally are described as oblique, as in the external and internal obliques. Pick diagonal for a question about the term oblique.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The shape term serratus describes what appearance?
options: Slender
Trapezoid
Square
Saw-toothed
questions.why: Serratus means saw-toothed, from the Latin word for a saw. The serratus anterior on the side of the chest attaches to the ribs by a row of finger-like slips, which gives its edge a jagged, saw-like look. The name describes that outline.
notes: Slender is described by gracilis, as in the gracilis of the medial thigh. Pick slender for a question about the gracilis.
Trapezoid is described by trapezius, the large muscle of the upper back. Pick trapezoid for a question about the trapezius.
Square or four-sided is described by quadratus, as in the quadratus lumborum. Pick square for a question about that term.
Correct. Serratus means saw-toothed.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When you stand on tiptoe, the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, the body's weight is the load, and the calf muscles pull up on the heel as the effort. Which lever class is this?
options: A third-class lever
A second-class lever
A fourth-class lever
A first-class lever
questions.why: To classify a lever, find which part is in the middle. On tiptoe, the fulcrum is at the ball of the foot in front, the effort is at the heel in back, and the body's weight passes down through the ankle in between. With the load in the middle, this is a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow.
notes: A third-class lever has the effort in the middle, like tweezers. Pick it for flexing the elbow, where the biceps brachii pulls between the elbow and the hand.
Correct. With the load between the fulcrum and the effort, standing on tiptoe is a second-class lever.
There is no fourth class of lever. Only three arrangements are possible, depending on whether the fulcrum, the load, or the effort sits in the middle.
A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw. Pick it for nodding the head, where the joint sits between the neck muscles and the face.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Nodding the head uses the atlanto-occipital joint, the posterior neck muscles, and the weight of the face. Which lever class is this?
options: A first-class lever
A third-class lever
It is not a lever system
A second-class lever
questions.why: In head nodding, the atlanto-occipital joint between the skull and the atlas is the fulcrum. The weight of the face sits in front of the joint as the load, and the posterior neck muscles pull from behind as the effort. With the fulcrum in the middle, this is a first-class lever, like a seesaw.
notes: Correct. The joint sits between the effort and the load, making it a first-class lever.
A third-class lever has the effort in the middle. Pick it for flexing the elbow.
Any time a muscle pulls a bone around a joint, a lever system is at work. Students choose this when they think levers apply only to the limbs.
A second-class lever has the load in the middle. Pick it for standing on tiptoe.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When the biceps brachii flexes the elbow to lift a weight in the hand, which lever class is at work?
options: A fourth-class lever
A second-class lever
A first-class lever
A third-class lever
questions.why: In elbow flexion, the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the weight in the hand is the load at the far end, and the biceps brachii pulls on the radius just below the elbow as the effort. With the effort in the middle, this is a third-class lever. Third-class levers are the most common in the body.
notes: There is no fourth class of lever. Only three arrangements are possible, depending on which part sits in the middle.
A second-class lever has the load in the middle. Pick it for standing on tiptoe.
A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle. Pick it for nodding the head.
Correct. With the effort between the fulcrum and the load, elbow flexion is a third-class lever.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: During elbow flexion, the biceps brachii contracts while the triceps brachii relaxes and stretches. What role is the triceps brachii playing?
options: Antagonist
Fixator
Synergist
Agonist
questions.why: The triceps brachii lies on the opposite side of the elbow from the biceps brachii and produces the opposite action, elbow extension. During flexion it relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement, which is the job of an antagonist. If the movement reversed to extension, the triceps would become the agonist.
notes: Correct. The triceps brachii is the antagonist during elbow flexion.
A fixator holds the origin bone steady for the prime mover. Pick it for muscles steadying the scapula during arm movements.
A synergist helps the prime mover, as the brachialis does in elbow flexion. The triceps works against flexion, not with it.
The agonist in elbow flexion is the biceps brachii, the muscle doing the contracting. The triceps would be the agonist only during elbow extension.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The biceps brachii lifts a book held in the hand. Which statement correctly identifies the parts of this lever?
options: The fulcrum is the shoulder joint, the effort is the triceps brachii, and the load is the forearm
The fulcrum is the elbow joint, the effort is the biceps pulling on the radius, and the load is the forearm plus the book
The fulcrum is the biceps brachii, the effort is the elbow joint, and the load is the book
The fulcrum is the hand, the effort is the book, and the load is the biceps brachii
questions.why: In a body lever, a joint is the fulcrum, a muscle's pull is the effort, and the weight being moved is the load. Here the forearm pivots at the elbow joint, the biceps brachii pulls on the radius to supply the effort, and the load is the weight of the forearm plus the book. Because the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load, this is a third-class lever.
notes: The forearm pivots at the elbow, not the shoulder, and the triceps brachii is the antagonist during this movement rather than the source of the effort.
Correct. The elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps pull is the effort, and the forearm plus book is the load.
This swaps the fulcrum and the effort. A muscle supplies the force, and a joint is the pivot point.
This scrambles all three parts. The book is part of the load being lifted, and the biceps brachii supplies the effort.
questions.answerText: The fulcrum is the elbow joint, the effort is the biceps pulling on the radius, and the load is the forearm plus the book

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Whether a lever works at a mechanical advantage or a mechanical disadvantage depends on what?
options: The length of the muscle's tendon
The size of the muscle supplying the effort
How far the effort and the load each act from the fulcrum
The number of origins the muscle has
questions.why: Mechanical advantage comes from comparing distances. When the effort acts farther from the fulcrum than the load, a small effort can move a large load, which is a mechanical advantage. When the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load, a larger effort is needed, which is a mechanical disadvantage, but the load moves faster and farther.
notes: Tendon length does not decide advantage. What matters is where the effort is applied relative to the fulcrum and the load, which depends on where the tendon inserts, not how long it is.
A larger muscle can pull harder, but that changes how much force is available, not whether the lever arrangement gives an advantage. Students pick this when they mix up strength with leverage.
Correct. Advantage or disadvantage depends on the distances of the effort and load from the fulcrum.
The number of origins is a naming criterion, as in biceps and triceps, and has nothing to do with leverage. Pick it for a question about muscle names.
questions.answerText: How far the effort and the load each act from the fulcrum

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The forearm muscles are grouped into two main compartments by position and function. Which pair names them correctly?
options: An anterior extensor compartment and a posterior flexor compartment
A medial adductor compartment and a lateral abductor compartment
A superficial flexor layer and a deep flexor layer
An anterior flexor compartment and a posterior extensor compartment
questions.why: The forearm is divided into an anterior compartment, whose muscles mainly flex the wrist and fingers, and a posterior compartment, whose muscles mainly extend them. Each compartment holds its own muscles, vessels, and nerves wrapped by deep fascia. Knowing which compartment a muscle sits in tells you its likely action.
notes: This swaps the two compartments. The flexors sit on the anterior side of the forearm and the extensors on the posterior side.
A medial adductor compartment exists in the thigh, where the adductor muscles pull the thigh toward the midline. Pick it for a question about the medial thigh.

Superficial and deep layers are subdivisions inside the anterior flexor compartment, not the two main compartments. Pick these layers for a question about how the anterior forearm muscles are stacked.
Correct. The forearm has an anterior flexor compartment and a posterior extensor compartment.
questions.answerText: An anterior flexor compartment and a posterior extensor compartment

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: A muscle is named flexor carpi radialis. Reading only the name, which three kinds of information does it give, in order?
options: Origin, insertion, and action
Shape, number of origins, and size
Action, region, and position
Direction of fibers, shape, and size
questions.why: Each word in flexor carpi radialis carries a clue. Flexor is the action, meaning it decreases a joint angle; carpi is the region, the wrist; and radialis is the position, the radial (thumb) side of the forearm. Before you ever see the muscle, the name tells you it flexes the wrist from the radial side.
notes: Flexor is an action, but carpi and radialis name a region and a side rather than specific origin and insertion points. Pick origin and insertion for a name like sternocleidomastoid.
None of the three words describes a shape, a count of heads, or a size. Those would be terms such as deltoid, biceps, or longus.
Correct. Flexor is the action, carpi the region, and radialis the position.
Direction, shape, and size terms such as rectus, deltoid, and maximus do not appear in this name. Students choose this when they recognize a muscle name but not the meaning of its parts.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: It is easier to crack a hard nut with the back teeth than with the front teeth. Using lever principles, which explanation is correct?
options: Biting with the back teeth moves the fulcrum forward
The back teeth sit farther from the fulcrum, giving more leverage
The back teeth sit closer to the fulcrum, so less effort is needed
The back teeth are harder, so less muscle force is needed
questions.why: When you bite, the jaw joint is the fulcrum, the jaw-closing muscles supply the effort, and the nut is the load. The back teeth sit much closer to the jaw joint than the front teeth, so the load acts over a shorter distance from the fulcrum. A load closer to the fulcrum needs less effort to move, which is why the back teeth crack hard foods more easily.
notes: The fulcrum is always the jaw joint, no matter which teeth do the biting. Only the position of the load changes.
The back teeth are closer to the jaw joint, not farther from it. A load placed farther from the fulcrum would take more effort, which is why biting with the front teeth is harder.
Correct. A load closer to the fulcrum requires less effort.
Tooth hardness is not the reason; the explanation is about where the load sits along the lever. Students choose this when they look for a reason in the teeth rather than in the lever.
questions.answerText: The back teeth sit closer to the fulcrum, so less effort is needed

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The biceps brachii is the prime mover during elbow flexion but acts as an antagonist during elbow extension. What does this show about muscle roles?
options: Each muscle has one fixed role for life
Only flexor muscles can be prime movers
Its role depends on which movement is happening
A muscle changes roles only after an injury
questions.why: Agonist, antagonist, synergist, and fixator are job titles for a specific movement, not permanent labels. The biceps brachii is the prime mover when the elbow bends, but when the triceps brachii straightens the elbow, the biceps relaxes and stretches as the antagonist. The same muscle can even act as a synergist or fixator in other movements.
notes: Muscle roles are assigned movement by movement, so they change whenever the movement changes. The biceps example in the question shows one muscle in two different roles.
Extensors, abductors, and other muscles serve as prime movers for their own actions. The triceps brachii, for example, is the prime mover during elbow extension.
Correct. A muscle's role depends on the movement being performed.
Roles change with normal movement, not with injury. Every time you bend and straighten your arm, the biceps and triceps trade roles.
questions.answerText: Its role depends on which movement is happening

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When the deltoid abducts the arm, muscles attached to the scapula contract to hold the scapula steady so the deltoid can pull efficiently on the humerus. What role are the scapular muscles playing?
options: Fixator
Agonist
Abductor
Antagonist
questions.why: The deltoid originates on the scapula and clavicle and inserts on the humerus. If the scapula were free to slide around, some of the deltoid's pull would be wasted moving it. Muscles that hold the origin bone steady so the prime mover can act efficiently are fixators.
notes: Correct. Muscles that steady the origin bone of the prime mover are fixators.
The agonist in this movement is the deltoid, the muscle producing abduction. The scapular muscles are not moving the arm; they are holding the origin bone still.
Abductor is an action term that describes the deltoid's job of moving the arm away from the body. The scapular muscles are stabilizing the scapula, not abducting the arm.
An antagonist would oppose abduction by pulling the arm back toward the body, and it relaxes during the movement. The scapular muscles here are contracting to stabilize, not opposing the action.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: A muscle is named biceps femoris. Which statement correctly breaks the name into its two criteria?
options: Biceps gives the relative size, and femoris gives the action
Biceps gives the number of origins, and femoris gives the location
Biceps gives the number of origins, and femoris gives the fiber direction
Biceps gives the shape, and femoris gives the origin and insertion
questions.why: Biceps means two heads, so it tells you the number of origins. Femoris refers to the femur, so it tells you the muscle's location in the thigh. Together the name describes a two-headed muscle of the thigh, which is one of the hamstrings on the posterior thigh.
notes: Biceps counts heads rather than describing size, and femoris names a region rather than a movement. Size would be a term like maximus, and action a term like flexor.
Correct. Biceps is the number of origins and femoris is the location.
Biceps is correctly the number of origins, but femoris names the thigh region rather than how the fibers run. Direction would be a term like rectus or oblique.
Biceps does not describe a shape, and femoris names a region, not two attachment points. Pick origin and insertion for a name like sternocleidomastoid.
questions.answerText: Biceps gives the number of origins, and femoris gives the location

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a lever, the effort acts farther from the fulcrum than the load does, so a small effort can move a large load. What is this condition called?
options: Mechanical disadvantage
Increased range of motion
A third-class lever
Mechanical advantage
questions.why: A lever works at a mechanical advantage when the effort is applied farther from the fulcrum than the load. The longer distance lets a small effort balance or move a large load. The trade-off is that the load moves only a short distance and fairly slowly.
notes: Mechanical disadvantage is the opposite case, when the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load, so a large effort is needed. Pick it for most limb movements, such as elbow flexion.
Increased range of motion is the benefit of a mechanical disadvantage, where the load moves fast and far. It is the opposite of what this arrangement provides.

A third-class lever places the effort between the fulcrum and the load, so the effort is always closer to the fulcrum and the lever works at a mechanical disadvantage. Pick third-class for a question about elbow flexion.
Correct. When the effort is farther from the fulcrum than the load, the lever works at a mechanical advantage.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Match these three movements to their lever classes: nodding the head, standing on tiptoe, and flexing the elbow.
options: Nodding is first class, tiptoe is third class, and elbow flexion is second class
Nodding is third class, tiptoe is second class, and elbow flexion is first class
Nodding is second class, tiptoe is first class, and elbow flexion is third class
Nodding is first class, tiptoe is second class, and elbow flexion is third class
questions.why: Each class is defined by the part in the middle. In nodding, the joint (fulcrum) lies between the face and the neck muscles, so it is first class. On tiptoe, the body's weight (load) lies between the ball of the foot and the calf's pull, so it is second class. In elbow flexion, the biceps pull (effort) lies between the elbow and the hand, so it is third class.
notes: Nodding is correctly first class, but this swaps tiptoe and elbow flexion. On tiptoe the load is in the middle, and in elbow flexion the effort is in the middle.
This swaps nodding and elbow flexion. Nodding has the fulcrum in the middle, and elbow flexion has the effort in the middle.
This swaps nodding and tiptoe. Nodding has the fulcrum in the middle, which is first class, and tiptoe has the load in the middle, which is second class.
Correct. Nodding is first class, tiptoe is second class, and elbow flexion is third class.
questions.answerText: Nodding is first class, tiptoe is second class, and elbow flexion is third class

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: A group of anterior forearm muscles is wrapped together by deep fascia, shares its blood vessels and nerves, and has the common function of flexion. What is this grouping called?
options: A fascicle
An aponeurosis
A retinaculum
A compartment
questions.why: A compartment is a group of muscles, together with their blood vessels and nerves, bound by deep fascia and sharing a common function. The anterior forearm muscles form the flexor compartment, and the posterior forearm muscles form the extensor compartment. Grouping by compartment is how the limb muscles are organized in lab.
notes: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers inside a single muscle, wrapped in perimysium. Pick it for a question about what the perimysium surrounds.
An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet that attaches a wide muscle, not a group of muscles. Pick it for a question about the attachment of a flat abdominal muscle.
A retinaculum is a band of connective tissue that holds tendons in place where they cross the wrist or ankle. Pick it for a question about what keeps the forearm tendons from bowing out at the wrist.
Correct. A functional group of muscles with shared vessels and nerves is a compartment.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is the attachment of a muscle to the more stationary bone called?
options: The belly
The action
The origin
The insertion
questions.why: A skeletal muscle crosses at least one joint and attaches to bone at both ends. The origin is the attachment to the more stationary bone, usually the proximal one, and the insertion is the attachment to the more movable bone, usually the distal one. When the muscle contracts, the insertion is pulled toward the origin.
notes: The belly is the thick, fleshy middle region of the muscle, between its attachments. It would be the answer for the part that bulges when the muscle contracts.
The action is the movement the muscle produces, not an attachment. Pick it for what happens when the muscle contracts.
Correct. The origin is the attachment that stays put during the action.
The insertion is the attachment to the more movable bone, the one pulled toward the origin. Pick it for the bone that moves.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a lever system, what is the fixed point that the lever turns around called?
options: The fulcrum
The lever
The load
The effort
questions.why: Every lever has four parts: the lever itself, the fulcrum, the effort, and the load. The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point the lever rotates around. In the body, a joint serves as the fulcrum, a bone serves as the lever, a contracting muscle supplies the effort, and the body part being moved is the load.
notes: Correct. The fulcrum is the pivot, and in the body that pivot is a joint.
The lever is the rigid bar that moves around the fulcrum. In the body a bone plays this role, so it fits a question about the rigid bar rather than the pivot.
The load is the resistance the lever moves, such as the weight of the forearm and anything held in the hand. Pick it when the question asks what is being moved.
The effort is the force applied to move the lever. In the body it is the pull of a contracting muscle, so choose it when the question asks what supplies the force.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a body lever system, what serves as the effort that moves the lever?
options: The joint where the bones meet
The bone that the muscle pulls on
The weight of the body part being moved
The pull of a contracting muscle
questions.why: The effort is the force that moves a lever. In the body, that force comes from a skeletal muscle that contracts and pulls on its insertion. The muscle pull is applied to a bone (the lever), which pivots at a joint (the fulcrum) to move a body part (the load).
notes: The joint is the fulcrum, the fixed point the bone pivots around. Choose it for a question about the pivot point.
The bone is the lever, the rigid bar that moves. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure acts as the bar.
The weight of the body part, plus anything it carries, is the load. It is the answer when the question asks what resistance the lever moves.
Correct. Muscle contraction supplies the force, so it is the effort.
questions.answerText: The pull of a contracting muscle

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a body lever system, which structure acts as the rigid bar that moves around a fixed point?
options: A muscle
A tendon
A joint
A bone
questions.why: A lever is a rigid bar that rotates around a fixed point. In the body, bones are the rigid bars, joints are the fixed points, and muscles supply the pulling force. When the biceps brachii flexes the elbow, for example, the forearm bones act as the lever pivoting at the elbow joint.
notes: A muscle supplies the effort, the pulling force that moves the lever. Pick it if the question asked what provides the force.
A tendon is the cord of dense connective tissue that transmits the muscle pull to the bone. It carries the effort but is flexible, so it is not the rigid bar.
A joint is the fulcrum, the fixed pivot point. It fits a question about where the lever turns.
Correct. Bones are rigid enough to act as the lever bar.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: In a first-class lever, where does the fulcrum lie?
options: At one end, with the effort between it and the load
Between the effort and the load
At one end, with the load between it and the effort
At the point where the muscle attaches to the bone
questions.why: Levers are classified by which part sits in the middle. In a first-class lever, the fulcrum sits in the middle, with the effort on one side and the load on the other, like a seesaw. Nodding the head is the body example: the atlanto-occipital joint is the fulcrum between the posterior neck muscles and the weight of the face.
notes: This arrangement puts the effort in the middle, which is a third-class lever, like tweezers. It is the answer for flexing the elbow.
Correct. A fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw, defines a first-class lever.
This arrangement puts the load in the middle, which is a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow. Choose it for standing on tiptoe.
The point where a muscle attaches is where the effort is applied, not the fulcrum. Students who pick this are mixing up the insertion with the pivot, which is always the joint.
questions.answerText: Between the effort and the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which lever class is the most common in the body, and what lies in the middle of it?
options: Third class, with the load in the middle
First class, with the fulcrum in the middle
Second class, with the load in the middle
Third class, with the effort in the middle
questions.why: In a third-class lever the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load, like a pair of tweezers. Most skeletal muscles insert close to the joint they move, which places their pull between the joint and the load. That makes the third-class lever the most common lever in the body, with flexing the elbow as the standard example.
notes: Third class is the right class, but the load does not sit in the middle. A load in the middle describes a second-class lever, so this mixes the two definitions.
A fulcrum in the middle is a first-class lever, the seesaw arrangement seen when nodding the head. It occurs in the body but is not the most common.
A load in the middle is a second-class lever, the wheelbarrow arrangement seen when standing on tiptoe. It is uncommon in the body.
Correct. Most muscles insert near the joint, so the effort sits between the fulcrum and the load.
questions.answerText: Third class, with the effort in the middle

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is the agonist in a movement?
options: The muscle that assists by adding force
The muscle that opposes the movement and relaxes
The muscle that holds the origin bone steady
The prime mover, chiefly responsible for the movement
questions.why: Muscles work in teams, and each muscle in the team plays a role. The agonist, also called the prime mover, is the muscle chiefly responsible for producing a given movement. During elbow flexion, for example, the biceps brachii is the agonist, while other muscles assist, oppose, or steady the movement.
notes: A muscle that assists the agonist by adding force or preventing unwanted movement is a synergist, such as the brachialis during elbow flexion.
A muscle that opposes the agonist and relaxes as it contracts is the antagonist, such as the triceps brachii during elbow flexion.
A muscle that steadies the origin bone so the agonist can work efficiently is a fixator, such as the scapular muscles during arm movements.
Correct. Agonist and prime mover are two names for the same role.
questions.answerText: The prime mover, chiefly responsible for the movement

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which muscle role opposes the agonist, relaxing and lengthening as the agonist contracts?
options: The synergist
The antagonist
The prime mover
The fixator
questions.why: The antagonist works on the opposite side of the joint from the agonist. As the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes and lengthens, and it can slow the movement or reverse it. During elbow flexion the biceps brachii is the agonist and the triceps brachii is the antagonist.
notes: A synergist assists the agonist by adding force or preventing an unwanted movement. Pick it for a helper muscle such as the brachialis during elbow flexion.
Correct. The antagonist opposes the agonist and lengthens while it contracts.
The prime mover is another name for the agonist, the muscle chiefly responsible for the movement. It is the muscle the antagonist works against, not the antagonist itself.
A fixator is a synergist that holds the origin bone steady. It fits a question about scapular muscles stabilizing the scapula during arm movements.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What does the term 'biceps' in a muscle name tell you about the muscle?
options: It produces flexion of a joint
It is the largest muscle in its region
It has two heads, or origins
It is located on the arm
questions.why: One of the naming criteria for muscles is the number of origins, meaning the number of heads or origin tendons. Bi means two, so the biceps brachii has two heads. Triceps means three heads and quadriceps means four, so the name alone tells you how many origin tendons to look for.
notes: Action is shown by terms such as flexor, extensor, and abductor. The biceps does flex the elbow, but the name biceps itself describes its heads, not its action.
Relative size is shown by terms such as maximus, minimus, longus, and brevis. Pick this if the name contained one of those size words.
Correct. Biceps names the number of origins, two heads.
Location is shown by terms such as brachii, which means arm. In biceps brachii, the word brachii tells you the location, not the word biceps.
questions.answerText: It has two heads, or origins

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What does the naming term 'maximus' describe about a muscle?
options: Its action
Its shape
Its relative size
Its number of origins
questions.why: Relative size compares a muscle with its neighbors. Maximus means largest, so the gluteus maximus is the largest of the gluteal muscles, while the gluteus minimus is the smallest. Longus and brevis are size terms too, meaning long and short.
notes: Action is shown by terms such as flexor, extensor, adductor, and levator. Choose action when the name tells you the movement the muscle produces.
Shape is shown by terms such as deltoid (triangular), trapezius (trapezoid), and rhomboid. Choose shape when the name describes a geometric form.
Correct. Maximus, minimus, longus, and brevis all describe size compared with neighboring muscles.
The number of origins is shown by biceps, triceps, and quadriceps. Choose this when the name counts heads.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is meant by the action of a muscle?
options: The fixed point the bone turns around
Its attachment to the more movable bone
Its attachment to the more stationary bone
The movement it produces when it contracts
questions.why: When a muscle contracts it pulls its two attachments toward each other. The insertion, on the more movable bone, is pulled toward the origin, on the more stationary bone. The movement that results, such as flexion of the elbow, is called the action of the muscle.
notes: The fixed point a bone turns around is the fulcrum, which in the body is a joint. That is a lever term rather than a property of the muscle.
The attachment to the more movable bone is the insertion. Pick it when the question asks which end is pulled toward the other.
The attachment to the more stationary bone is the origin. Pick it when the question asks which end of the muscle stays relatively fixed.
Correct. The action is the movement that results from that pull.
questions.answerText: The movement it produces when it contracts

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: During elbow flexion the biceps brachii is the agonist. What role does the triceps brachii play in this movement?
options: Fixator
Synergist
Antagonist
Agonist
questions.why: The triceps brachii lies on the posterior side of the arm, opposite the biceps brachii. During elbow flexion it relaxes and lengthens while the biceps contracts, so it is the antagonist. If the triceps contracts instead, the elbow extends, and the roles switch, which shows that a muscle role depends on the movement.
notes: A fixator holds the origin bone steady. Scapular muscles that stabilize the scapula during arm movements are fixators.
A synergist assists the agonist. The brachialis plays this role during elbow flexion, so pick synergist for a muscle that helps rather than opposes.
Correct. The triceps opposes the biceps and lengthens during elbow flexion.
The agonist is the prime mover. During elbow flexion that is the biceps brachii, while the triceps would be the agonist for elbow extension.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which example shows muscles acting as fixators?
options: The brachialis adding force to elbow flexion
Scapular muscles steadying the scapula
The triceps brachii relaxing during elbow flexion
The biceps brachii producing elbow flexion
questions.why: A fixator is a special kind of synergist that holds the origin bone steady so the agonist can act efficiently on the insertion bone. Many arm muscles originate on the scapula, so scapular muscles contract to anchor the scapula while those arm muscles move the humerus. Without that stable base, the pull of the arm muscles would partly move the scapula instead.
notes: The brachialis adding force to elbow flexion is acting as a synergist. Choose this example when the question asks for a muscle that assists the prime mover.
Correct. Steadying the origin bone is exactly what a fixator does.
The triceps relaxing and lengthening while the biceps flexes the elbow is acting as the antagonist. Pick this example for the opposing role.
The biceps producing elbow flexion is the agonist, the prime mover. Pick this example for the muscle chiefly responsible for the movement.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The name 'sternocleidomastoid' is built from which naming criterion?
options: Shape
Origin and insertion
Direction of fascicles
Relative size
questions.why: Sternocleidomastoid combines three attachment sites: sterno for the sternum, cleido for the clavicle, and mastoid for the mastoid process of the temporal bone. The muscle runs from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process, so its name lists its origin and insertion. Reading the name tells you where to find both ends of the muscle.
notes: Shape names describe a geometric form, such as deltoid (triangular), trapezius, or rhomboid. Pick shape when the name sounds like a geometry word.
Correct. The name lists the sternum, clavicle, and mastoid process, the attachments of the muscle.
Direction of fascicles names describe how the fibers run, such as rectus (straight), oblique (at an angle), or transversus (across).
Relative size names compare a muscle with its neighbors, such as maximus, minimus, longus, or brevis.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Nodding the head uses the posterior neck muscles, the atlanto-occipital joint, and the weight of the face. Which lever class is this, and why?
options: First class, because the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load
First class, because the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load
Second class, because the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort
Third class, because the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load
questions.why: In head nodding, the atlanto-occipital joint (between the skull and the first cervical vertebra) is the fulcrum. The weight of the face sits in front of that joint and the posterior neck muscles pull behind it. With the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw, this is a first-class lever.
notes: Correct. The joint sits between the neck muscle pull and the weight of the face.
The class is right but the reason describes a third-class lever. A first-class lever is defined by the fulcrum, not the effort, sitting in the middle.
A load in the middle is a second-class lever, like standing on tiptoe. In nodding, the face is in front of the joint, not between the joint and the muscles.
An effort in the middle is a third-class lever, like flexing the elbow. The neck muscles pull behind the joint, so they are not between the joint and the face.
questions.answerText: First class, because the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Standing on tiptoe places the body weight between the ball of the foot and the pull of the calf muscles on the heel. Which lever class is this?
options: First class
Third class
Second class
Fourth class
questions.why: When you rise on tiptoe, the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, the calf muscles pull up on the heel as the effort, and the body weight is the load in between. A load in the middle defines a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow. This arrangement always works at a mechanical advantage, but it is uncommon in the body.
notes: A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw. Nodding the head is the body example.
A third-class lever has the effort in the middle, like tweezers. Flexing the elbow is the body example, and it is the most common class.
Correct. The load sits between the fulcrum and the effort, like a wheelbarrow.
There is no fourth class of lever. Levers are sorted into only three classes, by whether the fulcrum, the load, or the effort is in the middle.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Flexing the elbow places the pull of the biceps between the elbow joint and the weight held in the hand. Which lever class is this?
options: First class
Fourth class
Third class
Second class
questions.why: In elbow flexion the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the weight in the hand is the load at the far end, and the biceps pulls on the radius just below the elbow. The effort therefore lies between the fulcrum and the load, which defines a third-class lever, like tweezers. This is the most common lever class in the body.
notes: A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw. It fits nodding the head, not elbow flexion.
There is no fourth lever class. Students sometimes invent one when a body example does not look like a textbook drawing, but all body levers fit one of the three classes.
Correct. The effort sits between the fulcrum and the load.
A second-class lever has the load in the middle, like a wheelbarrow. It fits standing on tiptoe.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which statement defines mechanical advantage in a lever system?
options: The effort acts farther from the fulcrum than the load does
The muscle pulls with more force than the load weighs
The effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load does
The fulcrum lies exactly between the effort and the load
questions.why: Mechanical advantage depends on distances from the fulcrum. When the effort acts farther from the fulcrum than the load, a small effort can move a large load. The reverse, where the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load, is mechanical disadvantage, which needs a large effort but moves the load fast and far.
notes: Correct. A longer distance for the effort lets a small force move a large load.
A muscle pulling harder than the load it lifts is a sign of mechanical disadvantage, not advantage. Students who choose this confuse a strong pull with an efficient lever.
This is the definition of mechanical disadvantage. It describes most body levers, where a muscle inserts near the joint and must pull hard to move the load.
This describes a first-class lever, which can work at an advantage or a disadvantage depending on the distances. It is a lever class, not the definition of advantage.
questions.answerText: The effort acts farther from the fulcrum than the load does

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which naming criterion produces the term 'rectus', meaning straight?
options: Action of the muscle
Shape of the muscle
Direction of fascicles
Location of the muscle
