questions.why: The direction of fascicles criterion describes how the fibers run relative to the body midline. Rectus means the fibers run straight, parallel to the midline, oblique means they run at an angle, and transversus means they run across. The rectus abdominis, external oblique, and transversus abdominis are named this way.
notes: Action names describe the movement produced, such as flexor, extensor, or levator. Choose action when the name tells you what the muscle does.
Shape names describe a geometric form, such as deltoid, trapezius, or rhomboid. Choose shape when the name sounds like a geometric figure.
Correct. Rectus, oblique, and transversus all describe fiber direction.
Location names describe the bone or region the muscle is near, such as tibialis anterior, frontalis, or intercostals.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: A clinician reads the name 'flexor carpi radialis' and learns a lot about the muscle before seeing it. What does the word 'flexor' tell the clinician?
options: The region the muscle acts on
The number of origins
The action the muscle produces
The shape of the muscle
questions.why: Muscle names usually combine several naming criteria. In flexor carpi radialis, flexor names the action, carpi names the region (the wrist), and radialis names the position (the radial, or thumb, side). Reading the name piece by piece tells you the muscle flexes the wrist and lies on the radial side of the forearm.
notes: The region is named by carpi, meaning the wrist. Pick region if the question asked about the word carpi instead of flexor.
The number of origins is shown by names such as biceps, triceps, or quadriceps. Flexor does not count heads.
Correct. Flexor names the movement, flexion.
Shape is shown by names such as deltoid or rhomboid. None of the words in flexor carpi radialis describes a geometric shape.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Most body movements run on third-class levers, which work at a mechanical disadvantage. What does the body gain in return?
options: A smaller force needed from the muscle
A greater load the limb can lift
Speed and a wide range of motion
A more stable joint
questions.why: In a third-class lever the muscle inserts close to the joint, so the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load. That is a mechanical disadvantage, meaning the muscle must pull much harder than the weight it lifts. In exchange, a small shortening of the muscle swings the far end of the bone through a large arc quickly, so the body gains speed and range of motion.
notes: This is the reverse of what happens. At a mechanical disadvantage the muscle must generate more force than the load, not less.
Lifting heavy loads with little effort is the benefit of mechanical advantage, as in a second-class lever. A third-class lever gives that up.
Correct. A short muscle pull near the joint moves the far end of the limb fast and far.
Joint stability comes from the shape of the bones, the ligaments, and muscle tone around the joint. It is not what a lever trades force for.
questions.answerText: Speed and a wide range of motion

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: During a movement, one muscle does most of the work while a second muscle crossing the same joint adds its own pull to the same action. Which role is the second muscle playing?
options: Agonist
Synergist
Antagonist
Fixator
questions.why: A synergist assists the agonist, either by adding force to the same movement or by preventing an unwanted movement. Here the first muscle is the agonist, doing most of the work, and the second muscle adds its own pull to the same action. That helping role is what makes the second muscle a synergist.
notes: The agonist is the prime mover, the muscle doing most of the work. In this question that is the first muscle, not the one helping it.
Correct. A muscle that adds force to the agonist's action is a synergist.
An antagonist opposes the movement, relaxing and lengthening while the agonist contracts, as the triceps brachii does during elbow flexion. Pick it if the second muscle worked against the action.
A fixator is a synergist that holds the origin bone steady, like the scapular muscles during arm movements. Pick it if the second muscle stabilized a bone rather than adding force to the action.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The biceps brachii shortens only a little, yet the hand moves through a large arc. Why does a small muscle shortening create a large movement at the end of the limb?
options: The muscle shortens farther than the hand moves
It inserts close to the elbow, the pivot
The forearm works as a second-class lever
It inserts near the wrist, far from the elbow
questions.why: The forearm is a lever that pivots at the elbow, and the biceps inserts on the radius close to that pivot. A small shortening close to the fulcrum rotates the whole forearm, and the hand at the far end travels a much longer distance. This is the speed and range that a third-class lever gains in exchange for its mechanical disadvantage.
notes: This reverses what happens. The hand moves much farther than the muscle shortens, which is the point of the question.
Correct. A small movement near the fulcrum becomes a large arc at the hand.
In elbow flexion the effort is between the joint and the load, which is a third-class lever. A second-class lever has the load in the middle, as in standing on tiptoe.
The biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity, just below the elbow, not near the wrist. An insertion far from the joint would give more force and less range.
questions.answerText: It inserts close to the elbow, the pivot

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Muscles usually work in antagonistic pairs, such as the biceps brachii and triceps brachii at the elbow. Why can one muscle not both bend and straighten a joint by itself?
options: A muscle with two heads can bend and straighten a joint alone
A muscle pushes the bone back by actively lengthening
The opposing muscle only steadies the joint and does not move it
A muscle can only pull, so an opposing muscle must move the joint back
questions.why: Muscle tissue produces force only by shortening, which pulls its insertion toward its origin. It cannot actively lengthen to push the bone back. So bending the elbow takes the biceps on the anterior side, and straightening it takes the triceps on the posterior side, with one relaxing while the other contracts.
notes: Having two heads, as the biceps does, gives two origins, not two directions of pull. Both heads pull the same insertion, so the biceps still only flexes the elbow.
Muscles do not push. A muscle lengthens only passively, when the opposing muscle contracts and stretches it.
Steadying a bone is the job of a fixator. In an antagonistic pair the opposing muscle can actively move the joint the other way, as the triceps extends the elbow.
Correct. Contraction only shortens a muscle, so reversing a movement takes a muscle on the other side.
questions.answerText: A muscle can only pull, so an opposing muscle must move the joint back

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which description fits the agonist, also called the prime mover, in a movement?
options: The muscle that assists the movement by adding force or preventing unwanted motion
The muscle chiefly responsible for producing the movement
The muscle that opposes the movement, relaxing and lengthening as it happens
The muscle that holds the origin bone steady during the movement
questions.why: The agonist, or prime mover, is the muscle that does most of the work for a given movement. For example, during elbow flexion the biceps brachii acts as an agonist. The other roles, antagonist, synergist, and fixator, are defined by how they relate to the agonist.
notes: This describes a synergist, such as the brachialis assisting elbow flexion. It would be the answer if the question asked which muscle helps the prime mover.
Correct. The agonist is the main muscle producing the movement.
This describes the antagonist, such as the triceps brachii during elbow flexion. Pick it if the question asked which muscle opposes the prime mover.
This describes a fixator, a synergist that steadies the origin bone, such as the scapular muscles during arm movements. Choose it if the question asked which muscle stabilizes the origin.
questions.answerText: The muscle chiefly responsible for producing the movement

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: During elbow flexion, the triceps brachii relaxes and lengthens while the biceps brachii contracts. What role is the triceps playing?
options: Agonist
Antagonist
Synergist
Fixator
questions.why: An antagonist is the muscle on the opposite side of the joint from the agonist, and it relaxes and lengthens as the agonist contracts. The triceps extends the elbow, so during elbow flexion it gives way to the biceps. The antagonist can also slow the movement or reverse it, which is how the triceps controls and then undoes elbow flexion.
notes: The agonist in elbow flexion is the muscle producing the movement, here the biceps. The triceps would be the agonist if the movement were elbow extension.
Correct. The triceps opposes elbow flexion and lengthens as the biceps contracts.
A synergist helps the agonist, as the brachialis helps the biceps flex the elbow. Pick synergist if the question described a muscle adding force to the same movement.
A fixator holds the origin bone steady so the agonist can pull efficiently. Choose it if the question described a muscle stabilizing the scapula or another origin bone.

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: What is a fixator?
options: A muscle that opposes the agonist by relaxing as the agonist contracts
A muscle that holds the origin bone steady so the agonist can act efficiently
The muscle chiefly responsible for producing a movement
A muscle that crosses the same joint and adds force in the same direction as the agonist
questions.why: A fixator is a special kind of synergist whose job is stabilization. It holds the bone where the agonist originates still, so the agonist's pull moves the insertion bone instead of wasting force by shifting the origin. A common example is the group of scapular muscles that steady the scapula while arm muscles move the humerus.
notes: This describes the antagonist, which yields to the agonist on the opposite side of the joint. Pick it if the question asked about the triceps during elbow flexion.
Correct. A fixator stabilizes the origin bone for the agonist.
This describes the agonist, or prime mover. It would be the answer if the question asked which muscle does most of the work in a movement.

This describes a synergist that adds force, such as the brachialis helping the biceps flex the elbow. A fixator is also a synergist, but its job is to steady the origin, not to add force to the movement.
questions.answerText: A muscle that holds the origin bone steady so the agonist can act efficiently

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a synergist from a fixator?
options: A synergist assists the agonist or prevents unwanted movement, and a fixator is a synergist that steadies the origin bone
A fixator adds force to the agonist, and a synergist holds the insertion bone steady
A synergist works only at the elbow, and a fixator works only at the shoulder
A synergist opposes the agonist, and a fixator assists the agonist
questions.why: A synergist is any muscle that helps the agonist, either by adding force to the movement or by preventing an unwanted movement at the same time. A fixator is one particular kind of synergist that holds the origin bone steady, so the agonist pulls efficiently on the insertion. Every fixator is a synergist, but not every synergist is a fixator.
notes: Correct. Synergists help in general, and fixators help by stabilizing the origin.
This reverses the two roles and also names the wrong bone. Fixators steady the origin, the more stationary attachment, while the insertion is the bone that moves.
Muscle roles are not tied to a particular joint. Any muscle can act as a synergist or fixator depending on the movement, so this is a made-up rule.
Opposing the agonist is the job of the antagonist, not a synergist. Students pick this when they mix up synergist (working together) with antagonist (working against).
questions.answerText: A synergist assists the agonist or prevents unwanted movement, and a fixator is a synergist that steadies the origin bone

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The name flexor carpi radialis tells you three things about the muscle. Which choice reads the name correctly?
options: Action (flexor), region (carpi, the wrist), and position (radialis, the radial side)
Action (flexor), origin (carpi, the carpal bones), and insertion (radialis, the radius)
Fiber direction (flexor), region (carpi, the wrist), and origin (radialis, the radius)
Action (flexor), number of heads (carpi), and size (radialis)
questions.why: Flexor names the action, so the muscle bends a joint. Carpi refers to the carpus, the wrist, which is the joint it flexes, and radialis tells you it lies on the radial (thumb) side of the forearm. Reading the name this way predicts that the muscle flexes the wrist and sits laterally in the anterior forearm.
notes: Correct. The name gives the action, the region, and the side of the forearm.

Flexor carpi radialis actually arises from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and inserts on the bases of metacarpals 2 and 3, so carpi and radialis are not its attachments. A name built on origin and insertion looks like sternocleidomastoid.

Flexor is an action, not a fiber direction; direction words are rectus, oblique, and transversus. Radialis also does not mean the muscle arises from the radius, since this muscle starts at the medial epicondyle.
Number of heads is shown by words like biceps and triceps, and size by words like longus and brevis. Neither carpi nor radialis carries that meaning.
questions.answerText: Action (flexor), region (carpi, the wrist), and position (radialis, the radial side)

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: When a muscle moves a body part, which choice correctly matches each part of the lever?
options: The bone is the lever, the joint is the fulcrum, the body part is the effort, and the muscle pull is the load
The joint is the lever, the bone is the fulcrum, the muscle pull is the effort, and the body part is the load
The muscle is the lever, the tendon is the fulcrum, the joint is the effort, and the bone is the load
The bone is the lever, the joint is the fulcrum, the muscle pull is the effort, and the body part is the load
questions.why: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a fixed point. In the body the bone is the rigid bar, the joint is the fixed point (fulcrum) it turns around, the pull of the contracting muscle is the effort, and the weight of the body part plus anything it holds is the load. Once these four are identified, you can sort any movement into a lever class.
notes: This swaps the effort and the load. The muscle supplies the force (effort), and the body part is the weight being moved (load).
This swaps the lever and the fulcrum. The bone is the rigid bar that moves, and the joint is the pivot point it turns on.

A muscle is soft tissue that pulls, so it supplies the effort rather than acting as the rigid bar, and a tendon only transmits that pull. Students pick this when they mix up the parts that move with the parts that pull.
Correct. Bone, joint, muscle pull, and body part weight are the lever, fulcrum, effort, and load.
questions.answerText: The bone is the lever, the joint is the fulcrum, the muscle pull is the effort, and the body part is the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: Which lever class is the most common in the body, and how are its parts arranged?
options: Second class, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort
Third class, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort
Third class, with the effort between the fulcrum and the load
First class, with the fulcrum between the effort and the load
questions.why: Most body movements use third class levers, in which the muscle attaches between the joint and the load, as the biceps does between the elbow and the hand. Because the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the load, these levers work at a mechanical disadvantage, meaning the muscle must pull much harder than the weight it lifts. In return, the load moves fast and through a wide range.
notes: A second class lever has the load in the middle, like a wheelbarrow. It would be the answer if the question asked about standing on tiptoe.
Third class is the right class, but load in the middle is the arrangement of a second class lever. In a third class lever the effort is in the middle.
Correct. Third class levers, with the effort in the middle, are the most common in the body.
A first class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw. Pick it if the question asked about nodding the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
questions.answerText: Third class, with the effort between the fulcrum and the load

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The biceps brachii flexes the elbow to lift a weight held in the hand. Which lever class is this, and why?
options: Second class, because the weight sits between the elbow and the biceps
First class, because the triceps pulls on the olecranon behind the elbow
Third class, because the biceps pulls between the elbow and the weight
First class, because the elbow joint sits between the biceps and the weight
questions.why: In elbow flexion the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the weight in the hand is the load at the far end, and the biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity just below the elbow. That puts the effort between the fulcrum and the load, which defines a third class lever. This is the standard example of a third class lever in the body.
notes: The weight is held in the hand at the far end of the forearm, not between the elbow and the biceps. A second class lever puts the load in the middle, as in standing on tiptoe.
The triceps pulling on the olecranon does form a first class lever, but that movement is elbow extension, not flexion. Pick this if the question asked about straightening the elbow.
Correct. The biceps pulls between the fulcrum (elbow) and the load (weight in the hand).
The elbow is the fulcrum here, but it sits at one end of the forearm, not between the biceps and the weight. A first class lever needs the pivot in the middle, as in nodding the head.
questions.answerText: Third class, because the biceps pulls between the elbow and the weight

questions.topic: Muscle roles, naming and lever systems
questions.q: The first words of rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis come from the same naming criterion. Which criterion is it, and what does each word tell you about the fascicles?
options: Direction of fascicles; rectus runs straight and transversus runs across.
Shape; rectus is a narrow strap and transversus is a broad flat sheet.
Direction of fascicles; rectus runs at an angle and transversus runs straight.
Location; rectus lies near the midline and transversus lies to the side.
questions.why: Rectus, oblique, and transversus are direction terms that describe how the fascicles run relative to the midline of the body. Rectus means straight, so the rectus abdominis fascicles run vertically, and transversus means across, so the transversus abdominis fascicles run horizontally. The word the two names share, abdominis, is a location term that places both on the abdomen.
notes: Correct. Rectus and transversus are both direction terms, straight and across.
Shape terms describe a muscle's overall outline, such as deltoid or trapezius. Rectus and transversus describe the direction the fascicles run.
The criterion is right, but the meanings are wrong. Rectus means straight, and the direction term for at an angle is oblique.
Location is the criterion behind abdominis, the word both names share. The first words, rectus and transversus, describe fascicle direction.
questions.answerText: Direction of fascicles; rectus runs straight and transversus runs across.

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which large, fan-shaped chest muscle flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm?
options: Serratus anterior
Pectoralis minor
Pectoralis major
Subclavius
questions.why: Pectoralis major arises from the medial clavicle, the sternum, and costal cartilages 1 to 6, and its fibers converge onto the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Because it inserts on the humerus, it moves the arm, flexing, adducting, and medially rotating it. Its broad origin and single tendon make it the classic convergent muscle.
notes: Serratus anterior runs from the ribs to the medial border of the scapula, so it acts on the scapula. It would be the answer for the muscle that protracts the scapula and holds it against the chest wall.

Pectoralis minor lies deep to pectoralis major and inserts on the coracoid process, so it moves the scapula, not the arm. Pick it if the question asked which chest muscle depresses and protracts the scapula.
Correct. Pectoralis major inserts on the humerus and flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
Subclavius is a small muscle from rib 1 to the underside of the clavicle that depresses and steadies the clavicle. Choose it if the question asked which muscle anchors the clavicle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which muscle runs from the upper eight or nine ribs to the medial border of the scapula, protracts the scapula as in throwing a punch, and holds it flat against the chest wall?
options: Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
Rhomboid major
Serratus posterior superior
questions.why: Serratus anterior arises by finger-like slips from ribs 1 to 8 or 9 on the lateral chest wall and inserts on the anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula. It pulls the scapula forward (protraction), which is why it is called the boxer's muscle, and it rotates the glenoid upward. Its pull also keeps the scapula pressed flat against the ribs; when it fails, the scapula lifts off the back as a winged scapula.
notes: Pectoralis minor also protracts the scapula, but it runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process, not to the medial border. Pick it if the question asked which chest muscle depresses the scapula from the coracoid process.
Correct. Serratus anterior protracts the scapula and holds it against the chest wall.
Rhomboid major attaches to the medial border of the scapula but pulls it toward the spine, retracting it. It would be the answer for the muscle that squeezes the shoulder blades together.
Serratus posterior superior runs from the C7 to T3 spinous processes to ribs 2 to 5 and elevates the ribs. It does not reach the scapula; students pick it because of the shared name serratus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which list names the four rotator cuff muscles (SITS)?
options: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres major, and subscapularis
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subclavius
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and deltoid
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
questions.why: The rotator cuff is made of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, remembered as SITS. All four run from the scapula to the head of the humerus and hold it in the shallow glenoid cavity. Three insert on the greater tubercle, and only subscapularis reaches the lesser tubercle.
notes: Teres major runs from the inferior angle of the scapula to the intertubercular sulcus and extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm, but it is not part of the cuff. Students pick it because its name looks almost the same as teres minor.
Subclavius is a small muscle under the clavicle that steadies the clavicle. Students choose it because its name starts like subscapularis, the S that belongs in SITS.

The deltoid covers the shoulder and abducts the arm, but it sits superficial to the cuff and does not wrap the humeral head. Pick the deltoid if the question asked which muscle forms the rounded contour of the shoulder.
Correct. These are the four SITS muscles of the rotator cuff.
questions.answerText: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which broad superficial back muscle, arising from the lower spine, thoracolumbar fascia, and iliac crest, extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm?
options: Latissimus dorsi
Rhomboid major
Trapezius
Teres major
questions.why: Latissimus dorsi arises from the spinous processes of T7 to L5, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest, and the lower ribs, and it inserts in the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Pulling the humerus down and back, it extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm. That powerful downward pull is why it is called the swimmer's muscle.
notes: Correct. Latissimus dorsi arises from the lower back and pelvis and extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
Rhomboid major runs from the T2 to T5 spinous processes to the medial border of the scapula and retracts the scapula. Choose it if the question asked which muscle pulls the scapula toward the spine.

Trapezius is a broad superficial back muscle, but it inserts on the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula, so it moves the scapula rather than the arm. Pick it if the question asked which muscle elevates, retracts, and depresses the scapula.

Teres major has the same actions on the arm, but it arises from the inferior angle of the scapula, not from the spine and iliac crest. It would be the answer if the question named the inferior angle of the scapula as the origin.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm, the first 15 degrees?
options: Supraspinatus
Subscapularis
Teres minor
Infraspinatus
questions.why: Supraspinatus arises from the supraspinous fossa above the spine of the scapula, passes under the acromion, and inserts on the greater tubercle. From that position on top of the joint it starts lifting the arm out to the side. The middle fibers of the deltoid then take over to carry abduction further.
notes: Correct. Supraspinatus initiates abduction of the arm.

Subscapularis lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, inserts on the lesser tubercle, and is the only cuff muscle that medially rotates the arm. It would be the answer for the cuff muscle reaching the lesser tubercle.

Teres minor runs from the lateral border of the scapula to the greater tubercle and laterally rotates the arm. Choose it if the question asked which small cuff muscle below infraspinatus rotates the arm outward.

Infraspinatus arises from the infraspinous fossa below the spine of the scapula and laterally rotates the arm. Pick it if the question asked which cuff muscle in the infraspinous fossa turns the arm outward.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: What job do all four rotator cuff muscles share?
options: They flex the elbow and supinate the forearm
They hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity, stabilizing the shoulder
They produce all of the abduction of the arm above shoulder height
They hold the scapula flat against the posterior chest wall
questions.why: The glenoid cavity of the scapula is shallow, so the shoulder relies on muscles rather than a deep socket to stay together. The four cuff muscles run from the scapula to the humeral head and wrap it on the top, front, and back, pulling it snugly into the glenoid cavity. This gives the shoulder its wide range of motion but also explains why it dislocates more than any other joint.
notes: Elbow flexion and supination are the actions of biceps brachii, which crosses the elbow. The cuff muscles end on the humeral head and do not reach the forearm.
Correct. The cuff muscles together keep the humeral head seated in the glenoid cavity.

Among the cuff muscles only supraspinatus abducts, and its main job is starting the movement; the deltoid and the upward rotation of the scapula carry the arm higher. This choice gives the whole cuff the job of the deltoid.
Holding the scapula flat against the chest wall is the job of serratus anterior. Pick this if the question asked what goes wrong in a winged scapula.
questions.answerText: They hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity, stabilizing the shoulder
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: A house painter who works overhead every day develops shoulder pain from a cuff tendon pinched between the head of the humerus and the acromion. Which tendon is most likely affected?
options: The infraspinatus tendon
The subscapularis tendon
The teres minor tendon
The supraspinatus tendon
questions.why: The supraspinatus tendon runs from the supraspinous fossa across the top of the shoulder, passing under the acromion to reach the greater tubercle. The acromion is a bony roof with no give, so repeated overhead arm raising pinches the tendon against it. This is why impingement and rotator cuff tears are concentrated in the supraspinatus.
notes: Infraspinatus passes behind the shoulder from the infraspinous fossa, below the spine of the scapula, so it is not trapped under the acromion. Choose it if the question asked which cuff muscle covers most of the back of the scapula.
Subscapularis crosses the front of the shoulder to the lesser tubercle, not under the acromion. Pick it if the question asked which cuff muscle medially rotates the arm.

Teres minor runs from the lateral border of the scapula to the lowest part of the greater tubercle, passing behind the joint rather than under the acromion. It would be the answer for a small cuff muscle that laterally rotates the arm.
Correct. Only the supraspinatus tendon runs under the acromion, where overhead work pinches it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which broad muscle of the upper back and neck elevates the scapula with its upper fibers and retracts it with its middle fibers?
options: Latissimus dorsi
Trapezius
Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
questions.why: The trapezius is a large, flat, diamond-shaped muscle that runs from the occipital bone, the ligamentum nuchae, and the spinous processes of C7 to T12 out to the lateral clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula. Its fibers run in different directions, so different parts do different jobs: upper fibers elevate the scapula, middle fibers retract it, and lower fibers depress it. Upper and lower fibers together rotate the glenoid upward.
notes: The latissimus dorsi covers the lower back and inserts on the humerus, so it moves the arm, extending, adducting, and medially rotating it. Pick it for a question about pulling the arm down and back, as in a swimming stroke.
Correct. The trapezius elevates, retracts, and depresses the scapula with different fiber groups.
The pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process and depresses and protracts the scapula. Choose it for a question about pulling the scapula down and forward.

The serratus anterior lies on the lateral chest wall and protracts the scapula, pulling it forward around the ribs, the opposite of retraction. It would be the answer for the muscle that holds the scapula flat, whose loss causes a winged scapula.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Where does the trapezius insert?
options: The floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
The coracoid process on the front of the scapula
The lateral clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula
The medial border of the scapula, from the spine down
questions.why: The trapezius is the large diamond-shaped muscle covering the upper back and neck. It arises from the occipital bone, the ligamentum nuchae, and the spinous processes of C7 to T12, and its fibers converge laterally onto one continuous bony line: the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula. Because it inserts on the pectoral girdle and not the humerus, all of its actions move the scapula.
notes: The intertubercular sulcus is the groove between the two tubercles of the humerus where the latissimus dorsi inserts. It would be the answer for the latissimus dorsi, the other large superficial back muscle.

The coracoid process is the hook on the front of the scapula where the pectoralis minor inserts and the short head of the biceps and the coracobrachialis arise. It would fit a question about the pectoralis minor.
Correct. The trapezius converges on the lateral clavicle, acromion, and scapular spine, the same line the deltoid arises from.
The medial border of the scapula is where the rhomboid major and minor insert, with the levator scapulae at its upper end. Pick it if the question asked where the rhomboids attach.
questions.answerText: The lateral clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which broad sheet of connective tissue in the lower back is a major origin of the latissimus dorsi?
options: The thoracolumbar fascia
The ligamentum nuchae
The bicipital aponeurosis
The clavipectoral fascia
questions.why: The latissimus dorsi arises from the spinous processes of T7 to L5, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest, and the lower ribs. The thoracolumbar fascia is a tough diamond-shaped sheet of deep fascia covering the lower back, and it gives the latissimus its wide, flat lower origin. From there the muscle sweeps up and laterally to a narrow tendon in the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
notes: Correct. The thoracolumbar fascia anchors the lower origin of the latissimus dorsi across the lumbar region.
The ligamentum nuchae is the midline ligament on the back of the neck that gives origin to the upper trapezius and the splenius capitis. Pick it for a question about the neck origin of those muscles.
The bicipital aponeurosis is a flat band from the biceps tendon that fans into the fascia of the medial forearm. It belongs at the elbow, not the back, and fits a question about the biceps insertion.
The clavipectoral fascia is a sheet on the front of the chest that encloses the subclavius and pectoralis minor. It would be the answer for a question about the fascia deep to the pectoralis major.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: The ligamentum nuchae gives origin to which pair of back muscles?
options: Levator scapulae and rhomboid major
Trapezius and splenius capitis
Iliocostalis and longissimus
Latissimus dorsi and quadratus lumborum
questions.why: The ligamentum nuchae is a thick midline ligament running from the occipital bone down the back of the neck along the cervical spinous processes. It gives the neck muscles a midline anchor where the cervical spinous processes are short. The upper fibers of the trapezius arise from it superficially, and the splenius capitis arises from it in a deeper layer before wrapping up to the mastoid process and occipital bone.
notes: The levator scapulae arises from the transverse processes of C1 to C4, and the rhomboid major from the spinous processes of T2 to T5. They would fit a question about muscles that insert on the medial border of the scapula.
Correct. Both the trapezius and the splenius capitis take part of their origin from the ligamentum nuchae.

The iliocostalis and longissimus are columns of the erector spinae that run along the ribs and transverse processes. They would be the answer for a question about the lateral and intermediate erector spinae columns.

The latissimus dorsi and quadratus lumborum are lower back muscles that arise from the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lumbar region. Pick them for a question about origins in the lower back, not the neck.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which set of actions does the latissimus dorsi produce at the shoulder?
options: Elevates and retracts the scapula
Flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm
Extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm
Abducts and laterally rotates the arm
questions.why: The latissimus dorsi runs from the lower back up to the intertubercular sulcus on the front of the humerus. Because it pulls the humerus down and back from that anterior attachment, it extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm. This is the movement of a swimming stroke or of pushing yourself up out of a chair.
notes: Elevating and retracting the scapula describes scapular muscles such as the upper trapezius and the rhomboids. The latissimus dorsi inserts on the humerus, so its actions are arm actions.
Flexion, adduction, and medial rotation are the actions of the pectoralis major, which lies on the front of the chest and pulls the arm forward. Pick this set for the pectoralis major.
Correct. The latissimus dorsi brings the arm down and back while turning it inward.

Abduction with lateral rotation does not describe the latissimus dorsi, which pulls the arm down and turns it inward. Abduction belongs mainly to the middle deltoid and supraspinatus, and lateral rotation to the infraspinatus and teres minor.
questions.answerText: Extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Where does the levator scapulae take its origin?
options: The spinous processes of C7 to T1
The outer surfaces of ribs 1 to 8
The transverse processes of C1 to C4
The spinous processes of T2 to T5
questions.why: The levator scapulae is a strap-like muscle on the side and back of the neck. It arises from the transverse processes of the first four cervical vertebrae and descends to the superior part of the medial border of the scapula. As its name says, it lifts (levates) the scapula, and it also rotates the glenoid downward.
notes: The spinous processes of C7 to T1 are the origin of the rhomboid minor, which inserts on the medial border at the level of the scapular spine. Pick this for the rhomboid minor.
The outer surfaces of the upper ribs on the lateral chest wall are the origin of the serratus anterior. Pick this for the muscle that protracts the scapula.
Correct. The levator scapulae comes off the transverse processes of C1 to C4.
The spinous processes of T2 to T5 are the origin of the rhomboid major. It would be the answer for the larger rhomboid, which inserts on the medial border below the spine.
questions.answerText: The transverse processes of C1 to C4
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which muscle arises from the spinous processes of T2 to T5 and inserts on the medial border of the scapula below the spine?
options: Serratus anterior
Levator scapulae
Rhomboid major
Rhomboid minor
questions.why: The rhomboid major is the larger of the two rhomboids and lies just below the rhomboid minor, deep to the trapezius. It runs from the spinous processes of T2 to T5 down and laterally to the medial border of the scapula below the spine. It retracts the scapula toward the spine and rotates the glenoid downward.
notes: The serratus anterior also inserts along the medial border of the scapula, but on its anterior surface, and it arises from the ribs on the lateral chest wall. Pick it for the muscle that protracts the scapula.
The levator scapulae arises from the transverse processes of C1 to C4 and reaches only the upper medial border. It would be the answer for the muscle that elevates the scapula from the neck.
Correct. The rhomboid major spans T2 to T5 and the medial border below the spine.
The rhomboid minor arises higher, from the spinous processes of C7 and T1, and inserts on the medial border at the level of the scapular spine. Pick it if the origin were C7 to T1.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which muscle or muscle part depresses the scapula?
options: Levator scapulae
Upper fibers of the trapezius
Lower fibers of the trapezius
Rhomboid minor
questions.why: The trapezius has three sets of fibers that pull in different directions. The upper fibers elevate the scapula, the middle fibers retract it, and the lower fibers, which run upward from the lower thoracic spinous processes to the scapular spine, pull it down. That downward pull is depression of the scapula.
notes: The levator scapulae runs from the upper cervical vertebrae to the top of the medial border, so it elevates the scapula. It would be the answer for a shrugging muscle, not a depressing one.
The upper fibers of the trapezius run down from the skull and neck to the clavicle and acromion, so they elevate the scapula, as in a shrug. Pick them for elevation.
Correct. The lower fibers of the trapezius pull the scapula down.
The rhomboid minor runs from C7 and T1 to the medial border and retracts the scapula. Pick it for pulling the shoulder blades together, not down.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the trapezius and the rhomboids?
options: The trapezius protracts the scapula, while the rhomboids retract it
Both retract the scapula, and both rotate the glenoid upward
Both retract the scapula, but they rotate the glenoid in opposite directions
Both elevate the scapula, but only the trapezius retracts it
questions.why: The middle trapezius and the rhomboids both pull the scapula toward the spine, so they agree on retraction. They disagree on rotation: the upper and lower trapezius fibers together turn the glenoid cavity upward, while the rhomboids pull the medial border up and in, which turns the glenoid downward. That makes them synergists for retraction and antagonists for rotation.
notes: The trapezius does not protract the scapula. Protraction, pulling the scapula forward around the chest, is the job of the serratus anterior and pectoralis minor.
The first half is right, since both retract, but the rhomboids rotate the glenoid downward, not upward. The upward rotators are the trapezius and the serratus anterior.
Correct. They share retraction, but the trapezius turns the glenoid up and the rhomboids turn it down.
This is wrong because the rhomboids are retractors, and retraction is the action they share with the middle trapezius. Elevation is mainly the job of the upper trapezius and the levator scapulae.
questions.answerText: Both retract the scapula, but they rotate the glenoid in opposite directions
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: On a cadaver, you reflect the trapezius from the upper back. At the level of T2 to T5, which muscle lies directly deep to it, between the medial border of the scapula and the spine?
options: Latissimus dorsi
Serratus anterior
Rhomboid major
Longissimus
questions.why: The back muscles are dissected in layers. The trapezius is the most superficial muscle of the upper back, and once it is lifted away the next layer between the scapula and the spine is the rhomboids and the levator scapulae. At T2 to T5 the muscle exposed is the rhomboid major, which runs from those spinous processes to the medial border of the scapula.
notes: The latissimus dorsi is superficial too, but it arises from T7 downward and covers the lower back, not the T2 to T5 region. Pick it for the superficial muscle of the lower back.

The serratus anterior runs from the lateral ribs to the anterior surface of the medial border, so it lies between the scapula and the chest wall, not between the scapula and the spine. Pick it for the muscle deep to the scapula on the side of the chest.
Correct. The rhomboid major sits immediately deep to the trapezius between the scapula and T2 to T5.
The longissimus is a column of the erector spinae, which lies in a deeper layer beneath the rhomboids. It would be the answer only after the rhomboids are also reflected.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Three muscles attach in or beside the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Which arrangement is correct?
options: Pectoralis major on the lateral lip, teres major in the floor, latissimus dorsi on the medial lip
Teres major on the lateral lip, latissimus dorsi in the floor, pectoralis major on the medial lip
Latissimus dorsi on the lateral lip, pectoralis major in the floor, teres major on the medial lip
Pectoralis major on the lateral lip, latissimus dorsi in the floor, teres major on the medial lip
questions.why: The intertubercular sulcus is the groove between the greater and lesser tubercles on the front of the humerus. The pectoralis major inserts on its lateral lip, the latissimus dorsi inserts in its floor, and the teres major inserts on its medial lip. Students often remember this as a lady (latissimus) lying between two majors.
notes: This swaps the latissimus dorsi and the teres major. The teres major is on the medial lip, and the latissimus dorsi lies in the floor between the two majors.
This reverses the two lips. The teres major attaches to the medial lip and the pectoralis major to the lateral lip.
This swaps the latissimus dorsi and the pectoralis major. The latissimus tendon lies in the floor of the groove, and the pectoralis major reaches the lateral lip.
Correct. Pectoralis major lateral, latissimus dorsi in the floor, teres major medial.
questions.answerText: Pectoralis major on the lateral lip, latissimus dorsi in the floor, teres major on the medial lip
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: During a chin-up, the arms are pulled down and back from an overhead position to lift the body. Which back muscle is the prime mover of that arm movement?
options: Trapezius
Serratus anterior
Latissimus dorsi
Levator scapulae
questions.why: A chin-up brings the humerus from overhead down toward the side of the body, which is adduction and extension of the arm. The latissimus dorsi is the large back muscle that runs from the lower back to the humerus and produces exactly those movements. Because the hands are fixed on the bar, its pull lifts the trunk up toward the arms instead of moving the arms.
notes: The trapezius inserts on the clavicle and scapula, not the humerus, so it moves the scapula rather than pulling the arm down. Pick it for elevating, retracting, or depressing the scapula.
The serratus anterior pulls the scapula forward around the chest wall. It would fit a pushing or punching movement, not a pull.
Correct. The latissimus dorsi adducts and extends the arm, which is the main work of a chin-up.
The levator scapulae runs from the neck to the top of the scapula and elevates it. It would be the answer for a shrug, not a pull-up.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which column of the erector spinae is the most lateral?
options: Multifidus
Spinalis
Iliocostalis
Longissimus
questions.why: The erector spinae is made of three vertical columns on each side of the spine. From lateral to medial they are the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis, remembered as I Love Spaghetti. The iliocostalis is the most lateral column, and as its name suggests (ilio for the ilium, costalis for the ribs), it attaches to the ribs.
notes: The multifidus is not part of the erector spinae. It is a deeper muscle beneath it that spans two to four vertebral segments.
The spinalis is the most medial column, running right along the spinous processes. Pick it for the column closest to the midline.
Correct. The iliocostalis is the lateral column and attaches to the ribs.
The longissimus is the intermediate column between the other two. It would be the answer for the middle column or for the column that reaches the mastoid process.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which column of the erector spinae is the most medial, running along the spinous processes?
options: Spinalis
Iliocostalis
Semispinalis
Longissimus
questions.why: The spinalis is the smallest and most medial of the three erector spinae columns. It lies right next to the spinous processes, which is where its name comes from. Going outward from it are the longissimus and then the iliocostalis.
notes: Correct. The spinalis sits closest to the spinous processes.
The iliocostalis is the most lateral column, attaching to the ribs. Pick it for the column farthest from the midline.

The semispinalis is a deeper back muscle that runs from transverse processes up to the occipital bone and spinous processes above. It is not one of the three erector spinae columns, even though its name looks similar to spinalis.
The longissimus is the intermediate column and the longest of the three. Pick it for the middle column.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which sequence lists the erector spinae columns from medial to lateral?
options: Iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis
Spinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis
Spinalis, iliocostalis, longissimus
Longissimus, spinalis, iliocostalis
questions.why: The usual mnemonic, I Love Spaghetti, lists the columns from lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis. This question asks for the opposite direction, starting at the midline. Starting next to the spinous processes you meet the spinalis, then the intermediate longissimus, then the lateral iliocostalis.
notes: This is the correct order, but from lateral to medial. It would be the answer if the question asked for lateral to medial, the direction of the I Love Spaghetti mnemonic.
Correct. Spinalis is medial, longissimus is intermediate, and iliocostalis is lateral.
This order starts correctly with the spinalis but then jumps to the lateral column. The longissimus always sits between the other two.
This puts the longissimus at the midline, but the longissimus is the intermediate column. The spinalis is the one next to the spinous processes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: What does the erector spinae do when the columns on both sides contract together, and when only one side contracts?
options: Both sides extend the spine; one side bends it to that side
Both sides bend the spine sideways; one side extends it
Both sides flex the spine; one side bends it to that side
Both sides retract the scapulae; one side elevates the scapula
questions.why: The erector spinae columns run vertically behind the axis of the vertebral column. When both sides pull together, they straighten and arch the back, which is extension. When only one side pulls, the spine bends toward that side, which is lateral flexion. This is the main muscle mass that keeps the trunk upright.
notes: Correct. Bilateral contraction extends the spine, and one-sided contraction bends it laterally.
This reverses the two situations. Lateral bending needs one side pulling alone, and extension needs both sides pulling together.
Flexion of the trunk, bending forward, is done by muscles in front of the spine such as the rectus abdominis. The erector spinae lies behind the spine, so it does the opposite.
Retracting and elevating the scapulae are actions of the rhomboids, trapezius, and levator scapulae. The erector spinae attaches to vertebrae, ribs, and skull, not the scapula.
questions.answerText: Both sides extend the spine; one side bends it to that side
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which deep back muscle wraps up the side of the neck from the ligamentum nuchae to the mastoid process and occipital bone?
options: Levator scapulae
Splenius cervicis
Semispinalis
Splenius capitis
questions.why: The splenius capitis arises from the ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 to T3 and runs up and laterally to the mastoid process and the occipital bone. Splenius means bandage, which describes how it wraps around the deeper neck muscles, and capitis means head. Acting together, the two sides extend the head, and acting alone, one side turns the head toward the same side.
notes: The levator scapulae also lies on the side of the neck, but it runs from the transverse processes of C1 to C4 down to the scapula. Pick it for the muscle that elevates the scapula.

The splenius cervicis is its lower partner. It arises from the spinous processes of T3 to T6 and stops at the transverse processes of C1 to C3, so it never reaches the skull. Pick it for the splenius that moves the neck.

The semispinalis runs from transverse processes up to the occipital bone and spinous processes above, in a layer deep to the splenius. It would be the answer for a muscle arising from transverse processes C7 to T12.
Correct. The splenius capitis runs from the ligamentum nuchae to the mastoid process and occipital bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the splenius capitis and the splenius cervicis?
options: The capitis reaches the skull, while the cervicis stops at the upper cervical transverse processes
The cervicis reaches the skull, while the capitis stops at the upper cervical transverse processes
Both insert on the mastoid process, and only their origins differ
Both arise from the lumbar spine and insert on the occipital bone
questions.why: The two splenius muscles are named for where they end. Capitis means head: the splenius capitis inserts on the mastoid process and occipital bone, so it moves the head. Cervicis means neck: the splenius cervicis arises lower, from T3 to T6, and inserts on the transverse processes of C1 to C3, so it extends and rotates the neck.
notes: Correct. The capitis inserts on the skull and the cervicis on the transverse processes of C1 to C3.
This reverses the two names. The word capitis always signals a head attachment, and cervicis a neck attachment.
Only the splenius capitis reaches the mastoid process. The splenius cervicis inserts on cervical transverse processes, so their insertions differ, not just their origins.
Neither splenius arises from the lumbar spine. Both come from the upper thoracic and lower cervical spinous processes, and the capitis also from the ligamentum nuchae.
questions.answerText: The capitis reaches the skull, while the cervicis stops at the upper cervical transverse processes
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which deep back muscle runs from the transverse processes of C7 to T12 up to the occipital bone and the spinous processes above?
options: Multifidus
Spinalis
Splenius capitis
Semispinalis
questions.why: The semispinalis belongs to the deep layer of back muscles that run from transverse processes up toward spinous processes. Its fibers start on the transverse processes of C7 to T12 and climb several segments to reach the spinous processes above, with its uppermost part inserting on the occipital bone. It extends the head and the vertebral column.
notes: The multifidus also runs from lower attachments up to spinous processes, but it starts on the sacrum, ilium, and transverse processes and spans only two to four segments. Pick it for the short segmental stabilizer of the spine.
The spinalis is the medial erector spinae column, running along the spinous processes themselves rather than from transverse processes. Pick it for the most medial erector spinae column.
The splenius capitis reaches the occipital bone too, but it arises from the ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T3, not from transverse processes.
Correct. The semispinalis runs from transverse processes of C7 to T12 to the occipital bone and spinous processes above.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which deep back muscle spans two to four vertebral segments from the sacrum, ilium, and transverse processes to the spinous processes above, stabilizing the spine segment by segment?
options: Quadratus lumborum
Longissimus
Multifidus
Interspinales
questions.why: The multifidus lies deep to the erector spinae, packed into the groove beside the spinous processes. Its many bundles each run from the sacrum, ilium, or a transverse process up to a spinous process two to four segments higher. That short span lets it extend and rotate the spine while holding each vertebra steady on the one below.
notes: The quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to rib 12 and the lumbar transverse processes, and it laterally flexes the trunk. It would be the answer for the muscle of the posterior abdominal wall.
The longissimus is the intermediate erector spinae column, a long vertical muscle that reaches up to the mastoid process. Pick it for the long middle column, not a short segmental one.
Correct. The multifidus is the short, deep, segmental stabilizer of the vertebral column.
The interspinales are tiny muscles linking each spinous process to the next one only. Pick them for a muscle spanning a single segment between spinous processes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which small deep back muscles connect the spinous process of one vertebra to the spinous process of the next?
options: Interspinales
Rotatores
Intertransversarii
Multifidus
questions.why: The interspinales are among the smallest and deepest muscles of the back. Their name is a direct description: inter means between, and spinales refers to the spinous processes, so each one runs between two neighboring spinous processes. They help steady and extend the spine one segment at a time.
notes: Correct. The interspinales link adjacent spinous processes.
The rotatores are small deep muscles that run from a transverse process up and medially to the base of the spinous process above. Pick them for the deepest muscles that help rotate the vertebrae.
The intertransversarii run between neighboring transverse processes, not spinous processes. Pick them if the muscle bridged one transverse process to the next.
The multifidus is larger and spans two to four segments from transverse processes, sacrum, and ilium to spinous processes. It would be the answer for a multi-segment stabilizer.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: A lab tag sits on a tiny muscle bridging the transverse process of one lumbar vertebra to the transverse process of the next. Which muscle is tagged?
options: Rotatores
Intertransversarii
Interspinales
Quadratus lumborum
questions.why: The intertransversarii take their name from their position: between (inter) the transverse processes. Each short slip spans one segment from one transverse process to the next, so a muscle bridging two neighboring transverse processes is an intertransversarius. They help bend the spine to the side and steady it.
notes: The rotatores run from a transverse process to the spinous process of the vertebra above, so they cross from a lateral point toward the midline. Pick them for a muscle linking a transverse process to the spinous process above.
Correct. The intertransversarii link adjacent transverse processes.
The interspinales connect neighboring spinous processes in the midline, not transverse processes. Pick them if the tag were between two spinous processes.

The quadratus lumborum does attach to the lumbar transverse processes, but it is a large muscle that runs from the iliac crest to rib 12, not a tiny single-segment slip. Pick it for the deep muscle between the iliac crest and the last rib.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: A patient has pain when bending the trunk to one side. The tender muscle lies deep to the erector spinae and runs from the iliac crest only as far as rib 12 and the transverse processes of L1 to L4. Which muscle is it?
options: Quadratus lumborum
Latissimus dorsi
Iliocostalis
Serratus posterior inferior
questions.why: The quadratus lumborum is a four-sided muscle in the posterior abdominal wall, deep to the erector spinae. It arises from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament and inserts on rib 12 and the transverse processes of L1 to L4. When one side contracts it bends the trunk laterally, which is why side-bending hurts when it is strained.
notes: Correct. The quadratus lumborum connects the iliac crest to rib 12 and the lumbar transverse processes and bends the trunk to the side.
The latissimus dorsi is a superficial muscle that runs from the lower back and iliac crest up to the humerus. Pick it for the muscle that extends and adducts the arm.

The iliocostalis is the lateral column of the erector spinae, so it lies superficial to the tender muscle, and it continues up the back along the angles of many ribs. Pick it for the most lateral erector spinae column.
The serratus posterior inferior runs from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 to ribs 9 to 12 and depresses those ribs. Pick it for the thin muscle deep to the latissimus dorsi on the lower ribs.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Of these back muscles, which lies deepest, closest to the vertebrae?
options: Rhomboid major
Longissimus
Trapezius
Multifidus
questions.why: The back is built in layers. The trapezius is superficial, the rhomboids lie just under it, the erector spinae columns such as the longissimus lie deeper along the spine, and the multifidus is deeper still, tucked against the laminae and spinous processes. Only the tiny rotatores, interspinales, and intertransversarii lie closer to the bone.
notes: The rhomboid major lies just deep to the trapezius but is still a superficial back muscle that attaches to the scapula. Pick it for the second layer of the upper back.
The longissimus is an erector spinae column, deep to the scapular muscles but superficial to the multifidus. Pick it for the intermediate column of the erector spinae.
The trapezius is the most superficial muscle of the upper back, lying just under the skin and fascia. Pick it for the outermost layer.
Correct. The multifidus lies beneath the erector spinae, directly against the vertebrae.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: In which direction do the fibers of the external intercostals run?
options: Horizontally along the rib
Downward and backward
Straight up and down
Downward and forward
questions.why: The external intercostals run from the inferior border of one rib to the superior border of the rib below. Their fibers slant downward and forward, toward the front of the body, the same direction your fingers point when you slide your hands into your front pockets. That slant lets them lift the ribs during inspiration.
notes: A horizontal course would follow the rib rather than cross the space between ribs, so it could not connect one rib to the next. This is a misreading of how the intercostal space is spanned.
Downward and backward is the direction of the internal intercostals, which lie just deep and run at right angles to the external layer. Pick it for the internal intercostals.
No intercostal layer runs straight vertically. Students sometimes guess this because the muscle simply connects one rib to the next, but the fibers slant.
Correct. External intercostal fibers run downward and forward, the hands-in-pockets direction.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: In which direction do the fibers of the internal intercostals run?
options: Downward and backward
Straight up and down
Horizontally along the rib
Downward and forward
questions.why: The internal intercostals lie just deep to the external layer and run from the superior border of the rib below to the inferior border of the rib above. Their fibers run at right angles to the external intercostals, so they slant downward and backward. Crossing the external layer this way, like the plies of plywood, also strengthens the wall of each intercostal space.
notes: Correct. Internal intercostal fibers run downward and backward, perpendicular to the external layer.
No intercostal layer runs straight vertically. The fibers of each layer slant across the intercostal space.
A horizontal course would follow the rib instead of spanning the gap between two ribs. Intercostal fibers always cross the space at a slant.
Downward and forward is the hands-in-pockets direction of the external intercostals. Pick it for the superficial layer of the intercostal space.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: During a forceful exhalation, such as blowing out birthday candles, which muscle layer pulls the ribs down?
options: Diaphragm
Internal intercostals
Serratus posterior superior
External intercostals
questions.why: Quiet exhalation is mostly passive, but a forceful exhalation needs muscles that pull the ribs down and shrink the chest. The internal intercostals depress the ribs, and their downward and backward fibers suit that job. The innermost intercostals and the transversus thoracis act with them.
notes: The diaphragm is the chief muscle of inspiration. When it contracts it flattens and enlarges the chest, so it would be the answer for quiet breathing in.
Correct. The internal intercostals depress the ribs during forced exhalation.
The serratus posterior superior elevates ribs 2 to 5, which helps inspiration. It would be the answer for a thin upper back muscle that lifts the upper ribs.
The external intercostals elevate the ribs, so they work during inspiration. Pick them for the layer that helps you breathe in.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which intercostal layer is separated from the internal intercostals by the neurovascular bundle?
options: External intercostals
Innermost intercostals
Transversus thoracis
Serratus posterior inferior
questions.why: Each intercostal space has three muscle layers: external, internal, and innermost. The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve travel in the costal groove between the internal and innermost layers. The innermost intercostals act with the internal intercostals but are separated from them by this neurovascular bundle.
notes: The external intercostals are the most superficial layer, outside the internal intercostals. The neurovascular bundle does not run beneath them, so they would be the answer for the outer layer that elevates the ribs.
Correct. The innermost intercostals lie deep to the neurovascular bundle.

The transversus thoracis also lies on the inner surface of the chest wall, but it is on the back of the sternum, fanning to costal cartilages 2 to 6. Pick it for the deep muscle of the anterior chest wall.
The serratus posterior inferior is a thin back muscle on the outside of the lower ribs, deep to the latissimus dorsi. Pick it for the muscle that depresses ribs 9 to 12.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: When placing a needle through an intercostal space to drain fluid from the chest, clinicians insert it just above the upper border of the rib below. Why?
options: The neurovascular bundle runs along the lower border of each rib
The external intercostals are missing along the lower border of each rib
The innermost intercostals block the needle near the upper border of each rib
The pleura is absent just above the upper border of each rib
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve travel together in the costal groove, a shallow channel on the inner lower edge of each rib. A needle passed just under the rib above would run right into that bundle. Passing just over the top of the rib below keeps the needle as far as possible from the main vessels and nerve of that space.
notes: Correct. The neurovascular bundle lies in the costal groove on the lower border of each rib, so clinicians stay near the top of the rib below.

The external intercostals attach along the inferior border of the rib above, so they are present there. This choice is a misconception, and the muscle layers are not what clinicians are trying to avoid anyway.
The innermost intercostals are a thin layer that does not block a needle. The real concern is the vessels and nerve, not the muscle layer.
The pleura lines the whole inner chest wall, so a needle entering the pleural cavity always passes through it. Thinking the pleura has gaps leads students to this choice.
questions.answerText: The neurovascular bundle runs along the lower border of each rib
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which sequence lists the muscle layers of an intercostal space from superficial to deep?
options: External, internal, innermost intercostals
Innermost, internal, external intercostals
Internal, external, innermost intercostals
External, innermost, internal intercostals
questions.why: The intercostal space between two ribs is filled by three sheets of muscle. The external intercostals lie outermost, the internal intercostals lie just deep to them with fibers at right angles, and the innermost intercostals form the deepest layer, separated from the internal layer by the neurovascular bundle. Their names match their order from the outside in.
notes: Correct. External, then internal, then innermost, from the skin inward.
This is the correct list read from deep to superficial. It would be the answer if the question asked for the order from the inside of the chest outward.
This places the internal layer outside the external layer. The external intercostals are always the most superficial, as their name says.
This swaps the two deeper layers. The innermost intercostals are the deepest, and the neurovascular bundle runs between them and the internal layer.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: As you take a deep breath in, which intercostal layer helps lift the ribs, and which way do its fibers run?
options: Internal intercostals, fibers downward and backward
External intercostals, fibers downward and backward
External intercostals, fibers downward and forward
Internal intercostals, fibers downward and forward
questions.why: The external intercostals elevate the ribs, which widens the chest and helps draw air in. Their fibers run downward and forward, the hands-in-pockets direction. The internal intercostals, whose fibers run at right angles downward and backward, do the opposite and depress the ribs in forced exhalation.
notes: This pairing is accurate for the internal intercostals, but they depress the ribs during forced exhalation. Pick it for the layer that helps you breathe out hard.
The muscle is right but the direction is not. Downward and backward is the fiber direction of the internal intercostals.
Correct. The external intercostals lift the ribs, and their fibers run downward and forward.
The internal intercostals do not lift the ribs, and their fibers do not run downward and forward. This mixes the internal layer with the external fiber direction.
questions.answerText: External intercostals, fibers downward and forward
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which thoracic wall muscle lies on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall, fanning from the back of the lower sternum to costal cartilages 2 to 6?
options: Innermost intercostals
Subclavius
Pectoralis minor
Transversus thoracis
questions.why: The transversus thoracis is a thin muscle you only see from inside the chest. It arises from the posterior surface of the lower sternum and fans upward and laterally to the costal cartilages of ribs 2 to 6. It depresses the ribs, so it works with the internal and innermost intercostals during forced exhalation.
notes: The innermost intercostals are also deep, but they run between the internal surfaces of neighboring ribs within each intercostal space, not from the sternum. Pick them for the deepest layer of an intercostal space.
The subclavius is a small muscle under the clavicle that runs from rib 1 to the clavicle. Pick it for the muscle that steadies the clavicle.

The pectoralis minor lies on the outside of the chest wall, deep to the pectoralis major, running from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process. Pick it for the muscle that depresses and protracts the scapula.
Correct. The transversus thoracis fans from the back of the sternum to costal cartilages 2 to 6.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the serratus posterior superior and the serratus posterior inferior?
options: The superior depresses ribs 2 to 5, while the inferior elevates ribs 9 to 12
The superior elevates ribs 2 to 5, while the inferior depresses ribs 9 to 12
Both elevate the ribs, the superior on ribs 2 to 5 and the inferior on ribs 9 to 12
Both depress the ribs, the superior on ribs 2 to 5 and the inferior on ribs 9 to 12
questions.why: Both serratus posterior muscles are thin sheets on the back of the rib cage, named for their sawtooth slips. The superior one runs from the spinous processes of C7 to T3 down and laterally to ribs 2 to 5, so it pulls those ribs up. The inferior one runs from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 up and laterally to ribs 9 to 12, so it pulls those ribs down. Their actions follow the direction each muscle pulls.
notes: This reverses both actions. The superior muscle pulls upward on the upper ribs, and the inferior muscle pulls downward on the lower ribs.
Correct. The superior elevates the upper ribs, and the inferior depresses the lower ribs.
The superior muscle does elevate ribs 2 to 5, but the inferior muscle pulls ribs 9 to 12 down toward its lower origin.
The inferior muscle does depress ribs 9 to 12, but the superior muscle pulls ribs 2 to 5 up toward its higher origin.
questions.answerText: The superior elevates ribs 2 to 5, while the inferior depresses ribs 9 to 12
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: A lab tag sits on a thin muscle deep to the latissimus dorsi, where the thoracic and lumbar regions meet. Its slips run up and laterally from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 to the lowest four ribs. Which muscle is tagged?
options: Quadratus lumborum
Serratus posterior superior
Serratus posterior inferior
External oblique
questions.why: The serratus posterior inferior lies just deep to the latissimus dorsi in the lower thoracic region. It arises from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 and its slips angle upward and laterally to ribs 9 to 12. Its position at the thoracolumbar junction and its attachment to the lowest four ribs identify it.
notes: The quadratus lumborum lies deeper, in the posterior abdominal wall, and runs from the iliac crest to rib 12 and the lumbar transverse processes. Pick it for the muscle that bends the trunk to the side.
The serratus posterior superior has the same thin, slipped shape, but it lies high on the back, deep to the rhomboids, running from C7 to T3 to ribs 2 to 5. Pick it for the upper partner.
Correct. The serratus posterior inferior runs from T11 to L2 to ribs 9 to 12, deep to the latissimus dorsi.

The external oblique is an abdominal wall muscle on the lateral side of the trunk, arising from the outer surfaces of the lower ribs. Pick it for the most superficial lateral abdominal muscle, not a muscle arising from spinous processes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which structure passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm at vertebral level T8?
options: The inferior vena cava
The aorta
The thoracic duct
The esophagus
questions.why: The diaphragm has three main openings at the even levels T8, T10, and T12. The caval opening at T8 is the highest, and its name tells you what passes through it: the inferior vena cava, the large vein returning blood from the lower body to the right atrium. The right phrenic nerve also passes through or near this opening.
notes: Correct. The caval opening at T8 transmits the inferior vena cava.
The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, the lowest opening. Pick it for T12.
The thoracic duct travels with the aorta through the aortic hiatus at T12. Pick it if the question asked about the lowest opening.
The esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus at T10, with the vagus nerves. Pick it for the middle opening.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: At which vertebral level does the esophageal hiatus pass through the diaphragm?
options: T8
L1
questions.why: The esophageal hiatus is the middle of the three main diaphragm openings, at T10. It transmits the esophagus along with the vagus nerves on their way to the stomach. The openings follow a simple count: vena cava at 8, esophagus at 10, aorta at 12.
notes: T8 is the level of the caval opening for the inferior vena cava. Pick it for the highest opening.
T12 is the level of the aortic hiatus, which transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. Pick it for the lowest opening.
Correct. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at T10.
L1 lies below all three main openings. Students may choose it because the crura anchor to the upper lumbar vertebrae, but no main opening sits there.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which set of structures passes through the aortic hiatus at T12?
options: The esophagus and the vagus nerves
The trachea, aorta, and pulmonary trunk
The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein
The inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve
questions.why: The aortic hiatus is the lowest of the three main openings, at T12, set behind the diaphragm between the two crura. The descending aorta passes through it into the abdomen.
