Two structures heading up into the thorax travel with it: the thoracic duct carrying lymph, and the azygos vein.
notes: The esophagus and vagus nerves pass through the esophageal hiatus at T10. Pick them for the middle opening.
The trachea and pulmonary trunk stay in the thorax and never cross the diaphragm. Students sometimes pick this because the aorta is listed, but the other two do not belong.
Correct. The aortic hiatus transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct, and the azygos vein.
The inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve pass through the caval opening at T8. Pick them for the highest opening.
questions.answerText: The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: What is the central tendon of the diaphragm?
options: The pair of tendons anchored to the lumbar vertebrae
The muscle slip that arises from the xiphoid process
The opening at T12 that transmits the aorta
The aponeurosis where the muscle fibers insert
questions.why: The diaphragm's muscle fibers arise around the margin of the lower opening of the rib cage, from the xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of ribs 7 to 12, and the lumbar vertebrae. All of them converge on the central tendon, a flat sheet of dense connective tissue (an aponeurosis) at the top of the dome. When the fibers contract, they pull the central tendon down and flatten the dome.
notes: The tendons anchored to the upper lumbar vertebrae are the right and left crura, the lumbar origin of the diaphragm. Pick them for the posterior attachments.
The slip from the xiphoid process is the sternal part of the diaphragm, one of its origins. Pick it if the question asked which part arises from the sternum.
The opening at T12 for the aorta is the aortic hiatus, which lies between the crura. Pick it for a question about what the aorta passes through.
Correct. The central tendon is the aponeurosis that receives all the diaphragm's muscle fibers.
questions.answerText: The aponeurosis where the muscle fibers insert
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Where do the right and left crura anchor the diaphragm?
options: To the central tendon
To the inner surfaces of ribs 7 to 12
To the upper lumbar vertebrae
To the xiphoid process
questions.why: The diaphragm has three origins: sternal (the xiphoid process), costal (the inner surfaces of the lower ribs), and lumbar. The lumbar origin is formed by the right and left crura, two tendinous legs (crus means leg) that anchor to the bodies of the upper lumbar vertebrae. The right crus is the larger of the two.
notes: The central tendon is where the muscle fibers insert, not where they anchor to bone. Pick it for the insertion of the diaphragm.
The inner surfaces of ribs 7 to 12 are the origin of the costal part, the largest muscular part of the diaphragm. Pick it for the costal part.
Correct. The crura anchor the diaphragm to the upper lumbar vertebrae.
The xiphoid process is the origin of the sternal part of the diaphragm, at the front. Pick it for the sternal part.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm and the thoracic cavity when the diaphragm contracts?
options: It pulls the ribs inward and narrows the cavity
It domes upward and shortens the thoracic cavity
It flattens and lengthens the thoracic cavity
It relaxes and pushes air out of the lungs
questions.why: At rest the diaphragm is a dome bulging up into the thorax. When its fibers contract they pull the central tendon down, so the dome flattens and moves inferiorly. That increases the height of the thoracic cavity, the lungs expand with it, and air flows in, which is why the diaphragm is the chief muscle of quiet inspiration.
notes: Pulling the ribs inward and down is the job of muscles of forced exhalation such as the internal intercostals. The diaphragm acts vertically, not by squeezing the ribs.
Doming upward is what happens when the diaphragm relaxes, which shortens the cavity during exhalation. Pick this for relaxation, not contraction.
Correct. Contraction flattens the dome and makes the thoracic cavity taller.
A contracting muscle is not relaxing. Relaxation of the diaphragm does help push air out, but that describes exhalation, not contraction.
questions.answerText: It flattens and lengthens the thoracic cavity
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: A mass presses on the opening of the diaphragm at vertebral level T10. Which structure passing through that opening is most directly compressed, causing trouble swallowing?
options: The thoracic duct
The inferior vena cava
The esophagus
The aorta
questions.why: The opening at T10 is the esophageal hiatus, which transmits the esophagus and the vagus nerves. A mass narrowing this opening squeezes the esophagus as food passes from the thorax to the stomach, which makes swallowing difficult. Linking the vertebral level to the opening, and the opening to its contents, solves this kind of question.
notes: The thoracic duct also passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, with the aorta. It would be the answer for a lymph flow problem at T12.
The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening at T8, higher than this mass. Compression there would affect venous return from the lower body, not swallowing.
Correct. The esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus at T10.
The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, below this level. Pick it for a mass at T12.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: In a hiatal hernia, part of the stomach slides up into the thorax through an opening in the diaphragm. Which opening is it?
options: An intercostal space
The esophageal hiatus
The caval opening
The aortic hiatus
questions.why: The stomach lies just below the diaphragm, connected to the esophagus where the esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus at T10. Because the stomach already sits at this opening, a widened hiatus lets part of the stomach push up alongside the esophagus into the thorax. The word hiatal in hiatal hernia points to this esophageal hiatus.
notes: An intercostal space is the gap between two ribs, filled by the intercostal muscles. It is not an opening in the diaphragm, so pick it only for a question about where a chest needle is inserted.
Correct. A hiatal hernia pushes the stomach up through the esophageal hiatus.
The caval opening at T8 lies in the central tendon and transmits the inferior vena cava. The stomach does not sit beside it, so it would be the answer only for the vein's passage.
The aortic hiatus at T12 lies behind the diaphragm between the crura and transmits the aorta. Pick it for the opening used by the aorta and thoracic duct.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the pectoralis major and the pectoralis minor?
options: The major inserts on the humerus and moves the arm; the minor inserts on the coracoid and moves the scapula
Both insert on the coracoid, and the major simply lies superficial to the minor
The major inserts on the coracoid and moves the scapula; the minor inserts on the humerus and moves the arm
Both insert on the humerus, and the minor simply lies deep to the major
questions.why: The pectoralis major arises from the medial clavicle, sternum, and costal cartilages 1 to 6, and inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus, so it flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm. The pectoralis minor lies deep to it, running from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process. Because it attaches to the scapula, it depresses and protracts the scapula rather than moving the arm.
notes: Correct. The major reaches the humerus and moves the arm, and the minor reaches the coracoid process and moves the scapula.
The major does lie superficial to the minor, but it does not insert on the coracoid process. It reaches the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
This swaps the two insertions. The larger muscle reaches the humerus, and the smaller, deeper muscle stops at the coracoid process.
The minor does lie deep to the major, but it does not reach the humerus. It inserts on the coracoid process.
questions.answerText: The major inserts on the humerus and moves the arm; the minor inserts on the coracoid and moves the scapula
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Where does the pectoralis minor insert?
options: The inferior surface of the clavicle
The lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus
The coracoid process of the scapula
The anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula
questions.why: The pectoralis minor is a thin triangular muscle hidden deep to the pectoralis major. It arises from ribs 3 to 5 and converges upward on the coracoid process, the hook-shaped projection on the front of the scapula. Pulling on the coracoid, it depresses and protracts the scapula.
notes: The inferior surface of the clavicle is the insertion of the subclavius. Pick it for the small muscle running from rib 1 to the clavicle.
The lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus is the insertion of the pectoralis major. Pick it for the large superficial chest muscle.
Correct. The pectoralis minor inserts on the coracoid process.
The anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula is the insertion of the serratus anterior. Pick it for the muscle that holds the scapula against the chest wall.
questions.answerText: The coracoid process of the scapula
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which actions does the pectoralis minor produce?
options: Depresses and protracts the scapula
Depresses and steadies the clavicle
Retracts the scapula and rotates the glenoid down
Flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm
questions.why: The pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 up to the coracoid process. Pulling the coracoid down and forward, it depresses the scapula and draws it forward around the chest wall, which is protraction. When the scapula is held still, the same pull works in reverse and lifts the ribs, which is why it can assist forced inspiration.
notes: Correct. The pectoralis minor depresses and protracts the scapula.
Depressing and steadying the clavicle is the job of the subclavius, the small muscle under the clavicle. Pick it for the subclavius.
Retraction with downward rotation of the glenoid is the action of the rhomboids on the back. The pectoralis minor pulls the scapula forward, the opposite of retraction.
Flexion, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm belong to the pectoralis major, which inserts on the humerus. Pick this set for the larger chest muscle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: When a patient pushes against a wall, the medial border of one scapula lifts away from the ribs like a wing. Which muscle is not doing its job?
options: Pectoralis major
Serratus anterior
Latissimus dorsi
Pectoralis minor
questions.why: The serratus anterior runs from the outer surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs to the anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula. That position lets it pull the scapula forward and hold it flat against the chest wall. When it fails, pushing forward makes the medial border lift off the back, a sign called a winged scapula.
notes: The pectoralis major moves the humerus, not the scapula, so weakness would affect flexing and adducting the arm. Pick it for a weak bench press or hug.
Correct. Loss of the serratus anterior lets the medial border of the scapula wing away from the chest wall.
The latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm. Weakness would make pulling down hard, not cause the scapula to wing.

The pectoralis minor pulls the coracoid process down and forward, but it does not hold the medial border against the ribs. Pick it for the muscle that depresses and protracts the scapula from the coracoid.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which small muscle runs from rib 1 to the inferior surface of the clavicle and depresses and steadies the clavicle?
options: Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
Subclavius
Levator scapulae
questions.why: The subclavius is named for its position under (sub) the clavicle. It arises from rib 1 near its costal cartilage and inserts on the inferior surface of the clavicle. It pulls the clavicle down and steadies it at the sternoclavicular joint during shoulder movement.
notes: The pectoralis minor also lies deep to the pectoralis major, but it runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process. Pick it for the muscle that depresses and protracts the scapula.
The serratus anterior runs from the lateral ribs to the medial border of the scapula. Pick it for the muscle that holds the scapula against the chest wall.
Correct. The subclavius runs from rib 1 to the underside of the clavicle.
The levator scapulae runs from the cervical transverse processes to the scapula and elevates it. It moves the scapula upward, the opposite direction from this muscle's pull on the clavicle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: Which sheet of deep fascia encloses the subclavius and the pectoralis minor, lying deep to the pectoralis major?
options: Ligamentum nuchae
Bicipital aponeurosis
Clavipectoral fascia
Thoracolumbar fascia
questions.why: The clavipectoral fascia hangs down from the clavicle, wrapping the subclavius and then the pectoralis minor. Its name describes its span from the clavicle (clavi) down over the chest (pectoral). It lies in the layer just deep to the pectoralis major, so it is exposed when the pectoralis major is reflected.
notes: The ligamentum nuchae is the midline ligament on the back of the neck that gives origin to the trapezius and splenius capitis. Pick it for the neck ligament.
The bicipital aponeurosis is a flat band from the biceps tendon that fans into the fascia of the medial forearm. Pick it for the structure at the front of the elbow.
Correct. The clavipectoral fascia encloses the subclavius and the pectoralis minor.
The thoracolumbar fascia covers the deep muscles of the lower back and gives origin to the latissimus dorsi. Pick it for the large fascia of the lumbar region.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: On the lateral chest wall, the lower slips of the serratus anterior interlock with the upper slips of which muscle?
options: Internal intercostals
External oblique
Pectoralis minor
Latissimus dorsi
questions.why: The external oblique, the most superficial lateral abdominal muscle, arises by fleshy slips from the outer surfaces of the lower ribs. Its upper slips alternate with the lower slips of the serratus anterior along the lateral chest wall, like interlocking fingers. That zigzag line is a useful landmark for telling the two muscles apart on a model or cadaver.
notes: The internal intercostals lie deep within the intercostal spaces, between the ribs, not on the outer surface where the serratus slips attach. Pick them for the muscles of forced exhalation.
Correct. The upper slips of the external oblique interlock with the lower slips of the serratus anterior.

The pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3 to 5 on the front of the chest, deep to the pectoralis major. It does not form a zigzag with the serratus anterior, so pick it for the muscle inserting on the coracoid process.
The latissimus dorsi covers the lower back and sweeps toward the axilla over the inferior angle of the scapula. Pick it for the large superficial muscle of the lower back.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: After reflecting the pectoralis major on a cadaver, you find a thin triangular muscle running from ribs 3 to 5 up to a hook-like process on the front of the scapula. Which muscle is it?
options: Serratus anterior
Subclavius
Pectoralis minor
Coracobrachialis
questions.why: The pectoralis minor lies immediately deep to the pectoralis major. It arises from ribs 3 to 5 and its fibers converge upward on the coracoid process, the hook-like projection on the front of the scapula. Its triangular shape and coracoid insertion identify it.
notes: The serratus anterior arises from the ribs on the lateral chest wall and inserts on the medial border of the scapula, not the coracoid process. Pick it for the sawtooth muscle on the side of the chest.
The subclavius also lies deep to the pectoralis major, but it is a small cylinder under the clavicle running from rib 1. Pick it for the muscle attached to the underside of the clavicle.
Correct. The pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process.
The coracobrachialis also attaches to the coracoid process, but it arises there and runs down to the medial shaft of the humerus. Pick it for the arm muscle that flexes and adducts the arm.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the back, thorax and shoulder
questions.q: To reach high overhead, the scapula must rotate so the glenoid cavity turns upward. Which pair of muscles produces this upward rotation?
options: Rhomboid major and levator scapulae
Trapezius and serratus anterior
Latissimus dorsi and teres major
Pectoralis minor and subclavius
questions.why: Raising the arm fully overhead needs the scapula to swing so the glenoid cavity faces upward. The upper and lower fibers of the trapezius pull the scapula from above and from the spine, while the serratus anterior pulls its inferior angle forward around the chest wall. Working together, they rotate the glenoid upward.
notes: The rhomboids and levator scapulae rotate the glenoid downward, so they are the antagonists here. Pick this pair for lowering the arm back down against resistance.
Correct. The trapezius and the serratus anterior rotate the glenoid upward together.
The latissimus dorsi and teres major act on the humerus, extending, adducting, and medially rotating the arm. Pick them for pulling the arm down from overhead.
The pectoralis minor pulls the scapula down and forward, and the subclavius steadies the clavicle. Neither produces upward rotation, so pick them for depression of the shoulder girdle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which anterior arm muscle flexes the elbow and also supinates the forearm?
options: Brachialis
Biceps brachii
Triceps brachii
Coracobrachialis
questions.why: Biceps brachii has a long head from the supraglenoid tubercle and a short head from the coracoid process, and it inserts on the radial tuberosity and the bicipital aponeurosis. Because it attaches to the radius, it can rotate the forearm into the palm-up position (supination) as well as flex the elbow. This is why the biceps is strongest at elbow flexion when the palm faces up.
notes: Brachialis flexes the elbow but inserts on the ulna, which cannot rotate, so it has no role in supination. Pick it if the question asked for the pure elbow flexor that lies deep to the biceps.
Correct. Biceps brachii inserts on the radius, so it flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.
Triceps brachii is in the posterior compartment and extends the elbow, the opposite movement. Choose it if the question asked which arm muscle extends the elbow.

Coracobrachialis runs from the coracoid process to the humeral shaft and flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder. It does not cross the elbow, so it would be the answer only for a shoulder movement.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which anterior arm muscle lies deep to the biceps brachii, inserts on the ulna, and acts only to flex the elbow?
options: Brachialis
Pronator teres
Coracobrachialis
Anconeus
questions.why: Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus, lies directly under the biceps, and inserts on the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Since the ulna does not rotate, the brachialis cannot supinate or pronate; it only flexes the elbow. That is why it flexes the elbow with the same strength whether the palm faces up or down.
notes: Correct. Brachialis lies under the biceps, inserts on the ulna, and is a pure elbow flexor.

Pronator teres is in the anterior forearm and inserts on the radius, so it pronates the forearm and only assists elbow flexion. Choose it if the question asked which forearm muscle turns the palm down.

Coracobrachialis lies in the anterior arm, but it runs from the coracoid process to the humeral shaft and acts at the shoulder. Pick it if the question asked which anterior arm muscle flexes and adducts the arm.
Anconeus is a small posterior muscle near the olecranon that assists elbow extension. It would be the answer if the question asked which small muscle helps the triceps.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student lifts a grocery bag by bending the elbow, palm up. Which two anterior arm muscles work together to flex the elbow?
options: Coracobrachialis and anconeus
Biceps brachii and brachialis
Brachialis and triceps brachii
Biceps brachii and coracobrachialis
questions.why: The anterior compartment of the arm holds the elbow flexors. Biceps brachii and brachialis both cross the front of the elbow and pull the forearm toward the arm, so they work together when lifting a bag. Coracobrachialis also lies in the anterior arm, but it ends on the humerus and acts only at the shoulder.
notes: Neither of these flexes the elbow. Coracobrachialis acts at the shoulder, and anconeus is a small posterior muscle that assists elbow extension.
Correct. Biceps brachii and brachialis are the elbow flexors of the anterior arm.

Brachialis is correct, but triceps brachii is the posterior arm muscle that extends the elbow, so it acts as the antagonist here. Choose the triceps if the question asked which muscle opposes elbow flexion.

Biceps brachii is correct, but coracobrachialis inserts on the humeral shaft and never crosses the elbow. Pick coracobrachialis if the question asked which anterior arm muscle flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle fills the fossa above the spine of the scapula?
options: Subscapularis
Infraspinatus
Supraspinatus
Teres minor
questions.why: The supraspinatus is named for its position: supra means above, and spinatus refers to the spine of the scapula. It arises from the supraspinous fossa, passes under the acromion, and inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus. It starts the movement of abduction, lifting the arm out to the side.
notes: The subscapularis lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, in the subscapular fossa against the ribs. Pick it for the only cuff muscle on the front of the scapula.
The infraspinatus fills the fossa below (infra) the scapular spine. Pick it for the muscle in the infraspinous fossa.
Correct. The supraspinatus arises from the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine.
The teres minor arises from the lateral border of the scapula, not a fossa. Pick it for the small cuff muscle along the lateral border.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus?
options: Teres minor
Infraspinatus
Supraspinatus
Subscapularis
questions.why: Three of the four rotator cuff muscles insert on the greater tubercle, the large lateral bump on the proximal humerus. Only the subscapularis, which lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, reaches the lesser tubercle on the front of the humerus. Pulling from the front, it medially rotates the arm.
notes: The teres minor inserts on the greater tubercle, at its lowest part. Pick it for the lateral rotator from the lateral border of the scapula.
The infraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle, just below the supraspinatus. Pick it for a lateral rotator from the infraspinous fossa.
The supraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle, at its highest part. Pick it for the cuff muscle that starts abduction.
Correct. The subscapularis is the only cuff muscle that inserts on the lesser tubercle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main action of the infraspinatus?
options: Extends the elbow
Initiates abduction of the arm
Laterally rotates the arm
Medially rotates the arm
questions.why: The infraspinatus arises from the infraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula and inserts on the greater tubercle. Because it wraps around the back of the humeral head, its pull turns the arm outward, which is lateral rotation. It shares this action with the teres minor just below it.
notes: Extending the elbow is the action of the triceps brachii, which crosses the elbow to the olecranon. The infraspinatus does not cross the elbow, so pick this for the triceps.
Initiating abduction is the job of the supraspinatus, which sits above the scapular spine. Pick it for the supraspinatus.
Correct. The infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm.
Medial rotation is the action of the subscapularis, the cuff muscle that pulls from the front of the humerus. Pick it for the subscapularis.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the teres minor take its origin?
options: The inferior angle of the scapula
The lateral border of the scapula
The coracoid process
The infraspinous fossa
questions.why: The teres minor is a small, round (teres) rotator cuff muscle that arises from the lateral border of the scapula, just below the infraspinatus. It runs up and laterally behind the shoulder joint to the lowest part of the greater tubercle. Like the infraspinatus, it laterally rotates the arm.
notes: The inferior angle of the scapula is the origin of the teres major, the larger muscle just below the teres minor. Pick it for the teres major.
Correct. The teres minor arises from the lateral border of the scapula.
The coracoid process is the origin of the short head of the biceps and the coracobrachialis. Pick it for those anterior arm muscles.
The infraspinous fossa is the origin of the infraspinatus, which lies just above the teres minor. Pick it for the infraspinatus.
questions.answerText: The lateral border of the scapula
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Moving from superior to inferior, in what order do the rotator cuff tendons attach to the greater tubercle?
options: Teres minor, infraspinatus, supraspinatus
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor
Supraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
Infraspinatus, supraspinatus, teres minor
questions.why: Three cuff tendons land on the greater tubercle, and they stack in the same order as their origins on the back of the scapula. The supraspinatus, from above the spine, takes the highest spot. The infraspinatus, from below the spine, attaches in the middle, and the teres minor, from the lateral border, attaches lowest.
notes: This is the right list in reverse. It would be the answer if the question asked for the order from inferior to superior.
Correct. Supraspinatus, then infraspinatus, then teres minor, from top to bottom.
The subscapularis does not attach to the greater tubercle at all. It is the one cuff muscle that inserts on the lesser tubercle.
This puts the infraspinatus on top, but the supraspinatus comes from above the scapular spine and inserts highest.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how the subscapularis differs from the other three rotator cuff muscles?
options: It lies on the anterior scapula, inserts on the lesser tubercle, and medially rotates the arm
It lies on the posterior scapula, inserts on the lesser tubercle, and laterally rotates the arm
It lies on the anterior scapula, inserts on the greater tubercle, and abducts the arm
It lies on the posterior scapula, inserts on the greater tubercle, and medially rotates the arm
questions.why: The subscapularis is the odd one out in every way. It is the only cuff muscle on the anterior surface of the scapula, the only one that reaches the lesser tubercle, and the only one that medially rotates the arm. The other three lie on the back of the scapula, insert on the greater tubercle, and either start abduction or rotate the arm laterally.
notes: Correct. Anterior surface, lesser tubercle, and medial rotation all set the subscapularis apart.

The subscapularis does insert on the lesser tubercle, but it lies on the anterior surface and rotates the arm medially. Posterior position and lateral rotation describe the infraspinatus and teres minor.
Anterior position is right, but the greater tubercle and abduction belong to the supraspinatus.
Posterior position and the greater tubercle describe the other three cuff muscles, and none of them rotates the arm medially.
questions.answerText: It lies on the anterior scapula, inserts on the lesser tubercle, and medially rotates the arm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement is true of all four rotator cuff muscles?
options: Each laterally rotates the arm at the shoulder
Each arises from the scapula and inserts on a tubercle of the humerus
Each arises from the posterior surface of the scapula
Each inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus
questions.why: The four cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis) all run from the scapula to the greater or lesser tubercle of the humerus. Their tendons blend around the head of the humerus like a cuff, holding it in the shallow glenoid cavity. That shared layout is what defines the group, while their individual actions differ.
notes: Only the infraspinatus and teres minor are lateral rotators. The subscapularis rotates medially, and the supraspinatus starts abduction.
Correct. All four run from the scapula to a tubercle of the humerus.
Three arise from the posterior scapula, but the subscapularis arises from the anterior surface, in the subscapular fossa.
Three insert on the greater tubercle, but the subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle.
questions.answerText: Each arises from the scapula and inserts on a tubercle of the humerus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient has weak lateral rotation of the arm, and imaging shows wasting of the muscle that fills the fossa below the scapular spine. Which muscle is affected?
options: Supraspinatus
Subscapularis
Teres minor
Infraspinatus
questions.why: Two clues point to the same muscle. The fossa below the scapular spine is the infraspinous fossa, which is filled by the infraspinatus. The infraspinatus is also a lateral rotator of the arm, so its wasting would weaken that movement.
notes: The supraspinatus fills the fossa above the spine and starts abduction. Pick it if the weakness were in lifting the arm out to the side.
The subscapularis lies on the front of the scapula and rotates the arm medially. Pick it if the patient had trouble turning the arm inward.
The teres minor also laterally rotates the arm, but it arises from the lateral border of the scapula, not the fossa below the spine. Pick it for the smaller lateral rotator along the lateral border.
Correct. The infraspinatus fills the infraspinous fossa and laterally rotates the arm.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient cannot turn the arm inward against resistance. Imaging shows a tear in the one rotator cuff tendon that crosses in front of the shoulder joint. Which muscle is torn?
options: Subscapularis
Supraspinatus
Infraspinatus
Teres minor
questions.why: Turning the arm inward is medial rotation. The subscapularis is the only cuff muscle on the anterior surface of the scapula, and its tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint to reach the lesser tubercle. A tear here weakens medial rotation while the other cuff muscles still work.
notes: Correct. The subscapularis crosses the front of the joint and medially rotates the arm.
The supraspinatus tendon crosses the top of the joint under the acromion and starts abduction. Pick it for trouble starting to lift the arm sideways.
The infraspinatus crosses the back of the joint and rotates the arm laterally, outward rather than inward. Pick it for weak lateral rotation.
The teres minor also crosses the back of the joint and rotates the arm laterally. Pick it for weak outward rotation with a problem along the lateral border of the scapula.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the deltoid insert?
options: The medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus
The deltoid tuberosity of the humerus
The radial tuberosity
The greater tubercle of the humerus
questions.why: The deltoid is the thick triangular muscle that rounds the shoulder. Its anterior, middle, and posterior fibers arise from the lateral clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula, then converge on one roughened area on the lateral side of the humeral shaft, the deltoid tuberosity. That single insertion lets each set of fibers swing the arm in a different direction.
notes: The medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus is the insertion of the teres major. Pick it for the teres major.
Correct. All three parts of the deltoid converge on the deltoid tuberosity.
The radial tuberosity is on the proximal radius and receives the biceps brachii tendon. Pick it for the biceps insertion.
The greater tubercle receives the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor. Pick it for those rotator cuff muscles.
questions.answerText: The deltoid tuberosity of the humerus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The deltoid arises from the lateral clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula. Which muscle inserts along this same bony line?
options: Pectoralis minor
Trapezius
Rhomboid major
Levator scapulae
questions.why: The trapezius inserts on the lateral clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula, and the deltoid arises from exactly the same line. The two muscles meet on either side of this bony ridge, the trapezius coming in from the neck and back and the deltoid continuing down to the humerus. Remembering one attachment gives you the other.
notes: The pectoralis minor inserts on the coracoid process. Pick it for the muscle deep to the pectoralis major that depresses the scapula.
Correct. The trapezius inserts on the same line from which the deltoid arises.
The rhomboid major inserts on the medial border of the scapula below the spine. Pick it for a muscle that retracts the scapula.
The levator scapulae inserts on the superior part of the medial border of the scapula. Pick it for the muscle that elevates the scapula from the neck.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: From which bony landmark do the middle fibers of the deltoid arise?
options: The lateral clavicle
The spine of the scapula
The coracoid process
The acromion
questions.why: The deltoid arises from a continuous bony line: the lateral clavicle in front, the acromion at the tip of the shoulder, and the spine of the scapula behind. The middle fibers come from the acromion, directly above the shoulder joint, and run straight down to the deltoid tuberosity. Pulling from directly above, they abduct the arm.
notes: The lateral clavicle is the origin of the anterior fibers of the deltoid, which flex and medially rotate the arm. Pick it for the front part of the deltoid.
The spine of the scapula is the origin of the posterior fibers, which extend and laterally rotate the arm. Pick it for the back part of the deltoid.
The coracoid process is not a deltoid attachment. It is the origin of the short head of the biceps and the coracobrachialis and the insertion of the pectoralis minor, so pick it for those muscles.
Correct. The middle deltoid fibers arise from the acromion.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What do the posterior fibers of the deltoid do?
options: Flex and medially rotate the arm
Extend and laterally rotate the arm
Abduct the arm
Adduct and medially rotate the arm
questions.why: The posterior fibers of the deltoid arise from the spine of the scapula and pass behind the shoulder joint to the deltoid tuberosity. Pulling from behind, they swing the arm backward (extension) and turn it outward (lateral rotation). They are the mirror image of the anterior fibers.
notes: Flexion with medial rotation is the action of the anterior deltoid fibers, which pass in front of the joint. Pick it for the anterior fibers.
Correct. The posterior deltoid extends and laterally rotates the arm.
Abduction is the action of the middle fibers, which pull from directly above the joint. Pick it for the middle fibers.
Adduction with medial rotation is not a deltoid action. It describes muscles such as the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi that pull the arm toward the body.
questions.answerText: Extend and laterally rotate the arm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: In which pairs of movements are the anterior and posterior fibers of the deltoid antagonists?
options: Elevation versus depression of the scapula
Flexion versus extension, and medial versus lateral rotation
Pronation versus supination of the forearm
Abduction versus adduction of the arm
questions.why: The anterior deltoid passes in front of the shoulder joint and flexes and medially rotates the arm. The posterior deltoid passes behind the joint and extends and laterally rotates it. Because they sit on opposite sides of the joint, they oppose each other in both the flexion and extension pair and the rotation pair, even though they belong to the same muscle.
notes: Elevation and depression of the scapula are done by scapular muscles such as the trapezius and levator scapulae. The deltoid inserts on the humerus, so it moves the arm.
Correct. The front and back fibers oppose each other in flexion and extension and in rotation.
Pronation and supination happen at the forearm. The deltoid does not cross the elbow, so pick this for muscles such as the biceps brachii and pronator teres.
Abduction is done by the middle fibers, and neither the anterior nor posterior fibers are the main adductors. This pair does not describe how the front and back fibers oppose each other.
questions.answerText: Flexion versus extension, and medial versus lateral rotation
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A person lifts the arm out to the side up to shoulder height. Once the movement is under way, which muscle becomes the prime mover of the abduction?
options: Middle fibers of the deltoid
Supraspinatus
Anterior fibers of the deltoid
Infraspinatus
questions.why: Abduction is shared between two muscles. The supraspinatus initiates the movement from the resting position, and then the middle fibers of the deltoid take over as the prime mover as the arm rises. This hand-off is why a supraspinatus tear causes trouble starting abduction while the deltoid can still raise the arm once it is partly lifted.
notes: Correct. The middle deltoid is the prime mover once abduction is under way.
The supraspinatus initiates abduction, so it would be the answer if the question asked which muscle starts the movement from the resting position.
The anterior deltoid flexes and medially rotates the arm, lifting it forward rather than out to the side. Pick it for raising the arm in front of the body.
The infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm and does not drive abduction. Pick it for turning the arm outward.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a model, a tag sits on deltoid fibers that arise from the lateral clavicle and pass in front of the shoulder joint. What movement do these fibers produce?
options: Flex and medially rotate the arm
Extend and laterally rotate the arm
Adduct and extend the arm
Abduct the arm
questions.why: Fibers arising from the lateral clavicle are the anterior fibers of the deltoid. Because they pass in front of the shoulder joint to the deltoid tuberosity, they swing the arm forward (flexion) and turn it inward (medial rotation). Working out where fibers start and which side of the joint they cross lets you predict the action.
notes: Correct. The anterior deltoid fibers flex and medially rotate the arm.
Extension with lateral rotation is the action of the posterior fibers, which arise from the scapular spine and pass behind the joint. Pick it for a tag on the posterior fibers.
Adduction with extension describes muscles such as the latissimus dorsi and teres major that pull the arm down and back. No part of the deltoid adducts as its main action.
Abduction is the action of the middle fibers, which arise from the acromion directly above the joint. Pick it for a tag on the middle fibers.
questions.answerText: Flex and medially rotate the arm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What are the origin and insertion of the teres major?
options: From the inferior angle of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus
From the coracoid process to the medial surface of the humeral shaft
From the lateral border of the scapula to the greater tubercle of the humerus
From the subscapular fossa to the lesser tubercle of the humerus
questions.why: The teres major is a thick, round muscle that arises from the inferior angle of the scapula. It runs up and laterally, passing in front of the humerus, to insert on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus. Because it follows the same path as the latissimus dorsi, it shares the latissimus dorsi's actions.
notes: Correct. The teres major runs from the inferior angle to the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus.
The coracoid process to the medial humeral shaft is the coracobrachialis. Pick it for the arm muscle that flexes and adducts the arm.
The lateral border to the greater tubercle is the teres minor, the smaller cuff muscle just above the teres major. Pick it for the teres minor.
The subscapular fossa to the lesser tubercle is the subscapularis. Pick it for the cuff muscle on the front of the scapula.
questions.answerText: From the inferior angle of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle shares all three of the latissimus dorsi's actions at the shoulder: extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm?
options: Infraspinatus
Pectoralis major
Teres minor
Teres major
questions.why: The teres major runs from the inferior angle of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus, right beside the latissimus dorsi tendon. Because the two muscles pull on the front of the humerus from below and behind, they produce the same movements: extension, adduction, and medial rotation. The teres major is often called the latissimus dorsi's little helper.
notes: The infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm. Pick it for turning the arm outward.
The pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the arm, but it flexes rather than extends, since it pulls from the front of the chest. Pick it for raising the arm forward and across the body.
The teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle that laterally rotates the arm, the opposite rotation. Pick it for a lateral rotator from the lateral border of the scapula.
Correct. The teres major extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm, just like the latissimus dorsi.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The teres major arises from the scapula, yet it is not part of the rotator cuff. Which fact explains this?
options: It laterally rotates the arm
It lies on the anterior surface of the scapula
It arises from the clavicle rather than the scapula
It inserts on the shaft of the humerus, not on a tubercle
questions.why: The rotator cuff muscles all insert on the greater or lesser tubercle, where their tendons blend with the joint capsule around the humeral head. The teres major instead inserts lower, on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus on the humeral shaft. Without that cuff of tendon around the head, it does not help hold the humerus in the glenoid cavity the way the SITS muscles do.
notes: The teres major medially rotates the arm, and even if it did rotate laterally, that would not exclude it, since cuff muscles rotate in both directions.
The teres major lies on the posterior side, at the inferior angle. The subscapularis is the muscle on the anterior surface, and it is a cuff muscle.
The teres major arises from the inferior angle of the scapula, not the clavicle. The deltoid is the shoulder muscle with a clavicular origin.
Correct. Its insertion on the shaft rather than a tubercle keeps it out of the cuff.
questions.answerText: It inserts on the shaft of the humerus, not on a tubercle
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Two muscles run from the lateral part of the scapula toward the humerus. A tag is on the smaller, upper one, whose tendon passes behind the humerus to the greater tubercle. Which muscle is tagged?
options: Triceps brachii, long head
Infraspinatus
Teres minor
Teres major
questions.why: The teres minor and teres major lie one above the other along the lateral side of the scapula. The teres minor is the smaller, upper muscle; it arises from the lateral border and passes behind the humerus to the lowest part of the greater tubercle, which makes it a rotator cuff muscle. The teres major is larger, arises lower from the inferior angle, and passes in front of the humerus to the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus.
notes: The long head of the triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle and runs down between the two teres muscles to the elbow. Pick it for the vertical muscle crossing between them.
The infraspinatus also reaches the greater tubercle, but it fills the infraspinous fossa rather than running along the lateral border. Pick it for the broad muscle below the scapular spine.
Correct. The teres minor is the smaller upper muscle that reaches the greater tubercle.
The teres major is the larger, lower muscle from the inferior angle, and it passes in front of the humerus to the intertubercular sulcus. Pick it for the lower muscle of the pair.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle runs from the coracoid process to the medial surface of the humeral shaft and flexes and adducts the arm?
options: Teres major
Pectoralis minor
Brachialis
Coracobrachialis
questions.why: The coracobrachialis is named for its two attachments: coraco for the coracoid process and brachialis for the arm. It arises from the coracoid process alongside the short head of the biceps and inserts on the medial surface of the humeral shaft. It lies in the anterior compartment of the arm, where it flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
notes: The teres major inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus but arises from the inferior angle of the scapula. Pick it for the muscle that extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
The pectoralis minor inserts on the coracoid process, but it comes from ribs 3 to 5 and moves the scapula. Pick it for the chest muscle deep to the pectoralis major.
The brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus and inserts on the ulna, so it crosses the elbow and flexes the forearm. Pick it for the muscle deep to the biceps.
Correct. The coracobrachialis runs from the coracoid process to the medial humeral shaft.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which two arm muscles arise from the coracoid process of the scapula?
options: Short head of the biceps brachii and brachialis
Long head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis
Short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis
Long head of the triceps brachii and brachialis
questions.why: The coracoid process is the hook on the front of the scapula. Two arm muscles take origin there side by side: the short head of the biceps brachii and the coracobrachialis. The long head of the biceps arises separately, from the supraglenoid tubercle above the glenoid cavity.
notes: The short head of the biceps is right, but the brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. Pick the brachialis for a muscle starting on the lower humerus.
The coracobrachialis is right, but the long head of the biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle, not the coracoid process. Pick the long head for the supraglenoid tubercle.
Correct. The short head of the biceps and the coracobrachialis share the coracoid process.
The long head of the triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle, and the brachialis from the distal humerus. Neither touches the coracoid process.
questions.answerText: Short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the long head of the biceps brachii arise?
options: The coracoid process
The supraglenoid tubercle
The radial tuberosity
The infraglenoid tubercle
questions.why: The biceps brachii has two heads (bi means two). The long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle, a small bump just above (supra) the glenoid cavity, and its tendon travels over the head of the humerus and down the intertubercular sulcus. The short head arises from the coracoid process, and the two heads join into one belly in the anterior arm.
notes: The coracoid process is the origin of the short head of the biceps. Pick it for the short head.
Correct. The long head of the biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle.
The radial tuberosity is where the biceps inserts, on the proximal radius, not where it arises. Pick it for the biceps insertion.
The infraglenoid tubercle, just below the glenoid cavity, is the origin of the long head of the triceps. Pick it for the triceps long head.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii runs down the front of the humerus in which landmark?
options: The olecranon fossa
The intertubercular sulcus
The radial groove
The deltoid tuberosity
questions.why: After arising from the supraglenoid tubercle, the tendon of the long head passes over the head of the humerus and drops into the intertubercular sulcus, the groove between the greater and lesser tubercles. The groove guides the tendon down the front of the arm. This is also called the bicipital groove for that reason.
notes: The olecranon fossa is the deep pit on the posterior distal humerus that receives the olecranon when the elbow straightens. Pick it for that elbow landmark.
Correct. The long head tendon runs in the intertubercular sulcus.

The radial groove spirals across the posterior humeral shaft and carries the radial nerve and deep brachial artery. Pick it for the landmark between the origins of the lateral and medial triceps heads.
The deltoid tuberosity is the roughened area on the lateral humeral shaft where the deltoid inserts. Pick it for the deltoid insertion.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the biceps brachii insert?
options: The olecranon of the ulna
The styloid process of the radius
The radial tuberosity
The coronoid process of the ulna
questions.why: The biceps brachii ends in a strong tendon that crosses the front of the elbow and attaches to the radial tuberosity, a bump on the medial side of the proximal radius. A flat band from the tendon, the bicipital aponeurosis, also fans into the deep fascia of the medial forearm. Pulling on the radius lets the biceps both flex the elbow and supinate the forearm.
notes: The olecranon is the insertion of the triceps brachii on the back of the elbow. Pick it for the elbow extensor.
The styloid process of the radius is the insertion of the brachioradialis, near the wrist. Pick it for that muscle.
Correct. The biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity.
The coronoid process of the ulna, with the ulnar tuberosity, is the insertion of the brachialis. Pick it for the muscle deep to the biceps.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which pair of actions does the biceps brachii produce at the elbow and forearm?
options: Flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm
Extends the elbow and pronates the forearm
Extends the elbow and supinates the forearm
Flexes the elbow and pronates the forearm
questions.why: The biceps crosses the front of the elbow, so it flexes it. Because its tendon wraps around the radius to reach the radial tuberosity, contracting it also spins the radius so the palm turns up, which is supination. It is strongest at supination when the elbow is bent, and it also helps flex the arm at the shoulder.
notes: Correct. The biceps flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.
Both halves are reversed. Extension of the elbow belongs to the triceps, and pronation belongs to the pronator teres and pronator quadratus.
Supination is right, but the biceps lies in front of the elbow and flexes it. Elbow extension belongs to the triceps and anconeus.
Elbow flexion is right, but pronation is the opposite rotation. Flexing the elbow while pronating describes the pronator teres.
questions.answerText: Flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the bicipital aponeurosis go after leaving the biceps tendon?
options: Down to the coronoid process of the ulna
Laterally to the styloid process of the radius
Up to the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula
Medially into the deep fascia over the forearm flexors
questions.why: The bicipital aponeurosis is a flat sheet of tendon (an aponeurosis) that splits off the biceps tendon at the front of the elbow. Instead of reaching bone, it angles medially and blends into the deep fascia covering the flexor muscles of the medial forearm. It forms part of the roof over the cubital fossa and adds a second, soft-tissue insertion to the biceps.
notes: The coronoid process of the ulna is the insertion of the brachialis. Pick it for the deep elbow flexor beneath the biceps.
The styloid process of the radius is the insertion of the brachioradialis, on the lateral side near the wrist. The aponeurosis runs medially, not laterally.
The supraglenoid tubercle is the origin of the long head of the biceps, at the opposite end of the muscle. Pick it for where the long head starts.
Correct. The aponeurosis fans medially into the fascia over the forearm flexors.
questions.answerText: Medially into the deep fascia over the forearm flexors
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle lies deep to the biceps, arising from the distal anterior humerus and inserting on the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna?
options: Anconeus
Coracobrachialis
Brachioradialis
Brachialis
questions.why: The brachialis lies directly under the biceps brachii on the lower half of the anterior humerus. It arises from the distal anterior humerus and inserts on the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Since it crosses only the elbow and attaches to the ulna, its only action is flexing the elbow.
notes: The anconeus is a small muscle on the back of the elbow, running from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon and posterior ulna. Pick it for the muscle that assists elbow extension.
The coracobrachialis lies higher in the arm, running from the coracoid process to the medial humeral shaft. Pick it for the muscle that flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
The brachioradialis arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the styloid process of the radius. Pick it for the elbow flexor along the thumb side of the forearm.
Correct. The brachialis lies deep to the biceps and inserts on the ulna.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which elbow flexor works just as well whether the palm faces up or down?
options: Brachialis
Coracobrachialis
Triceps brachii
Biceps brachii
questions.why: When the forearm pronates and supinates, the radius rotates around the ulna while the ulna stays put. The brachialis inserts on the ulna, so its line of pull is the same in any forearm position, and it flexes the elbow equally well with the palm up or down. The biceps pulls on the radius, so turning the palm down twists its tendon and lessens its flexing power.
notes: Correct. The brachialis pulls on the ulna, so forearm rotation does not change its flexion.
The coracobrachialis does not cross the elbow at all. It flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
The triceps brachii extends the elbow rather than flexing it. It is the antagonist of the elbow flexors.
The biceps flexes the elbow, but it inserts on the radius, so its flexing power changes as the forearm rotates. It is strongest with the palm up.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A weightlifter ruptures the distal biceps tendon at the radial tuberosity, yet can still bend the elbow fairly well. Which muscle, lying deep to the biceps, is mainly responsible?
options: Coracobrachialis
Triceps brachii, medial head
Brachialis
Anconeus
questions.why: The brachialis lies directly beneath the biceps and inserts separately on the ulna. When the biceps tendon tears away from the radius, the brachialis is untouched and still flexes the elbow. What the patient loses most is the biceps' contribution, especially strong supination.
notes: The coracobrachialis lies in the anterior arm too, but it ends on the humeral shaft and never crosses the elbow. It cannot flex the elbow.
The medial head of the triceps lies deep in the posterior arm and extends the elbow. It works against elbow flexion, not for it.
Correct. The brachialis, deep to the biceps, keeps flexing the elbow after the biceps tendon ruptures.
The anconeus is a small muscle at the back of the elbow that assists extension. It cannot replace an elbow flexor.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A right-handed person tightens a screw by twisting a screwdriver clockwise with the elbow bent, turning the palm from down to up. Which arm muscle provides most of the power?
options: Triceps brachii
Coracobrachialis
Brachialis
Biceps brachii
questions.why: Turning the palm from down to up is supination. The biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity, so when it contracts it spins the radius and supinates the forearm, and it does this most powerfully when the elbow is bent. That is why tightening a screw with the right hand feels strong.
notes: The triceps brachii extends the elbow and does not rotate the forearm. Pick it for straightening the elbow.
The coracobrachialis acts at the shoulder, flexing and adducting the arm, and does not reach the forearm. Pick it for moving the arm forward and toward the body.
The brachialis inserts on the ulna, which does not rotate, so it cannot supinate. Pick it for pure elbow flexion.
Correct. The biceps is the most powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What divides the arm into anterior and posterior compartments?
options: The flexor retinaculum
The interosseous membrane
The medial and lateral intermuscular septa
The bicipital aponeurosis
questions.why: The arm has two compartments wrapped in deep fascia. Sheets of fascia called the medial and lateral intermuscular septa run inward from the fascia to the humerus, splitting the arm into an anterior (flexor) compartment and a posterior (extensor) compartment. Muscles in the same compartment tend to share an action.
notes: The flexor retinaculum is a band across the front of the wrist that forms the roof of the carpal tunnel. Pick it for the wrist.
The interosseous membrane joins the radius and ulna in the forearm and helps separate the forearm compartments. Pick it for the forearm, not the arm.
Correct. The intermuscular septa separate the anterior and posterior compartments of the arm.
The bicipital aponeurosis is a flat band from the biceps tendon into the forearm fascia. It does not divide compartments.
questions.answerText: The medial and lateral intermuscular septa
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the long head of the triceps brachii arise?
options: The supraglenoid tubercle
The posterior humerus above the radial groove
The posterior humerus below the radial groove
The infraglenoid tubercle
questions.why: The triceps brachii has three heads (tri means three). The long head arises from the infraglenoid tubercle, a small bump just below (infra) the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The lateral and medial heads arise from the posterior humerus, above and below the radial groove.
notes: The supraglenoid tubercle, just above the glenoid cavity, is the origin of the long head of the biceps. Pick it for the biceps long head.
The posterior humerus above the radial groove is the origin of the lateral head of the triceps. Pick it for the lateral head.
The posterior humerus below the radial groove is the origin of the medial head of the triceps. Pick it for the medial head.
Correct. The long head of the triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where do all three heads of the triceps brachii insert?
options: The radial tuberosity
The lateral epicondyle of the humerus
The olecranon of the ulna
The coronoid process of the ulna
questions.why: The three heads of the triceps join into one tendon that crosses the back of the elbow. That tendon attaches to the olecranon, the point of the elbow on the proximal ulna. Pulling on the olecranon straightens the elbow, so the triceps is the main extensor of the forearm.
notes: The radial tuberosity is the insertion of the biceps brachii on the front of the forearm. Pick it for the biceps.
The lateral epicondyle is an origin, not an insertion here. It is where the anconeus and several forearm extensors arise.
Correct. The triceps inserts on the olecranon.
The coronoid process of the ulna is on the front of the elbow and receives the brachialis. Pick it for the brachialis.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which part of the triceps brachii can also extend the arm at the shoulder?
options: Lateral head of the triceps
Long head of the triceps
Medial head of the triceps
Anconeus
questions.why: A muscle can only move a joint it crosses. The long head of the triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, so it crosses both the shoulder and the elbow, and it extends both. The lateral and medial heads arise from the humerus itself, so they cross only the elbow.
notes: The lateral head arises from the posterior humerus above the radial groove, so it also crosses only the elbow. Pick it for the head on the lateral side of the arm.
Correct. The long head crosses the shoulder and can extend the arm.
The medial head arises from the posterior humerus below the radial groove, so it crosses only the elbow. Pick it for the deep head that only extends the forearm.
The anconeus runs from the lateral epicondyle to the ulna and only assists elbow extension. It does not reach the shoulder.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which humeral landmark spirals across the posterior shaft between the origins of the lateral and medial heads of the triceps?
options: The deltoid tuberosity
The olecranon fossa
The radial groove
The intertubercular sulcus
questions.why: The radial groove is a shallow channel that winds diagonally across the back of the humeral shaft. The lateral head of the triceps arises above it and the medial head below it. The groove is named for the radial nerve, which runs in it together with the deep brachial artery.
notes: The deltoid tuberosity is the roughened area on the lateral shaft where the deltoid inserts. Pick it for the deltoid.
The olecranon fossa is the deep pit on the posterior distal humerus that receives the olecranon. Pick it for the landmark at the back of the elbow.
Correct. The radial groove separates the origins of the lateral and medial heads.
The intertubercular sulcus is on the front of the proximal humerus, between the two tubercles, and holds the biceps long head tendon. Pick it for that tendon.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which head of the triceps brachii lies deepest, largely covered by the other two heads?
options: Medial head
Long head
Short head
Lateral head
questions.why: The medial head arises from the posterior humerus below the radial groove, right on the bone. The long head and lateral head lie over it, so in a posterior view the medial head is mostly hidden, showing only near the elbow. Its name refers to its position on the medial side of the posterior humerus, not to being superficial.
notes: Correct. The medial head lies deep, covered by the long and lateral heads.
The long head is superficial, running down the medial side of the back of the arm from the infraglenoid tubercle. Pick it for the head that crosses the shoulder.
The triceps has no short head. Short head is a part of the biceps brachii, which arises from the coracoid process, so choosing it mixes up the two muscles.
The lateral head is also superficial, forming the bulge on the lateral side of the back of the arm. Pick it for the head that arises above the radial groove.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which small muscle at the back of the elbow runs from the lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon and posterior ulna and assists elbow extension?
options: Anconeus
Supinator
Brachialis
Brachioradialis
questions.why: The anconeus is a small triangular muscle on the posterolateral side of the elbow, almost continuous with the lower triceps. It arises from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus and inserts on the lateral olecranon and posterior ulna. It helps the triceps extend the elbow.
notes: Correct. The anconeus runs from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon and assists extension.
The supinator also arises from the lateral epicondyle and ulna, but it wraps around the proximal radius and supinates the forearm. Pick it for turning the palm up.
The brachialis lies on the front of the elbow and flexes it, inserting on the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Pick it for the deep elbow flexor.
The brachioradialis arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge but runs down to the styloid process of the radius and flexes the elbow. Pick it for the muscle along the thumb side of the forearm.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A fracture through the middle of the humeral shaft damages the structures that lie in a groove on its posterior surface. Which structures are at risk?
options: The ulnar nerve and the basilic vein
The median nerve and the brachial artery
The axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery
The radial nerve and the deep brachial artery
questions.why: The groove on the posterior surface of the mid humeral shaft is the radial groove. The radial nerve and the deep brachial artery travel in it, pressed against the bone between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps. A mid-shaft fracture can stretch or cut them because they lie right on the bone at this level.
notes: The ulnar nerve runs down the medial side of the arm and passes behind the medial epicondyle, and the basilic vein is a superficial vein on the medial arm. Pick them for an injury near the medial epicondyle.
The median nerve and brachial artery run down the medial side of the anterior arm, beside the biceps. Pick them for an injury on the front of the arm or at the cubital fossa.
The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery wrap around the surgical neck of the humerus. Pick them for a fracture just below the humeral head.
Correct. The radial nerve and deep brachial artery run in the radial groove.
questions.answerText: The radial nerve and the deep brachial artery
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A muscle you have not studied lies in the posterior compartment of the arm. Based on the compartment, what is its most likely action at the elbow?
options: Supination of the forearm
Flexion of the elbow
Pronation of the forearm
Extension of the elbow
questions.why: The arm's compartments sort muscles by action. The posterior compartment holds the triceps brachii, which crosses the back of the elbow to the olecranon and extends it, so a muscle in that compartment most likely extends the elbow. The anterior compartment holds the biceps, brachialis, and coracobrachialis, the flexors.
notes: Supination is done by the biceps from the anterior arm and the supinator in the forearm. It is not the shared action of the posterior arm compartment.
Flexion of the elbow is the shared action of the anterior compartment, where the biceps and brachialis lie. Pick it for a muscle on the front of the arm.
Pronation is done mainly by forearm muscles such as the pronator teres and pronator quadratus. Pick it for a muscle in the anterior forearm.
Correct. Posterior arm muscles extend the elbow.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the general action of the muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm?
options: Extending the wrist and fingers and supinating the forearm
Flexing the wrist and fingers and pronating the forearm
Flexing the elbow and supinating the forearm
Extending the elbow and abducting the arm
questions.why: The anterior forearm compartment holds the flexors and pronators. Most of its superficial muscles share a common origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus and flex the wrist and fingers, while pronator teres and pronator quadratus turn the palm down. Knowing the compartment lets you predict the action of a muscle before you have learned it individually.
notes: Extending the wrist and fingers and supinating the forearm is the job of the posterior forearm compartment. It would be the answer for the muscles that share the lateral epicondyle origin.
Correct. The anterior forearm flexes the wrist and fingers and pronates the forearm.
Flexing the elbow and supinating the forearm is the job of biceps brachii in the anterior arm, not the anterior forearm. Pick this if the question asked about the anterior compartment of the arm.
Extending the elbow is the job of the posterior arm (triceps brachii), and abducting the arm is done at the shoulder by the deltoid and supraspinatus. Neither belongs to the forearm compartments.
questions.answerText: Flexing the wrist and fingers and pronating the forearm
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares where flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus insert on the fingers?
options: The superficialis inserts on the distal phalanges, and the profundus inserts on the middle phalanges
Both insert on the distal phalanges, with the profundus lying deeper
The superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges, and the profundus inserts on the distal phalanges
Both insert on the proximal phalanges, with the superficialis lying more superficial
questions.why: Flexor digitorum superficialis lies in a more superficial layer and stops at the middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5, so it flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum profundus lies deep to it, and its tendons pass through split tendons of the superficialis to reach the distal phalanges, so it flexes the distal interphalangeal joints. Clinicians test them separately by asking the patient to bend one finger joint at a time.
notes: This swaps the two insertions. The deeper muscle, profundus, actually travels farther out to the fingertips.
Only the profundus reaches the distal phalanges; the superficialis stops one bone short at the middle phalanges. This is why the profundus alone can bend the fingertip joint.
Correct. Superficialis reaches the middle phalanges and profundus continues on to the distal phalanges.
Neither muscle inserts on the proximal phalanges. Students pick this when they assume the names superficialis and profundus describe depth only and say nothing about how far each tendon travels.
questions.answerText: The superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges, and the profundus inserts on the distal phalanges
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Most of the superficial muscles of the anterior forearm share one common flexor origin. Which bony landmark is it?
options: Coronoid process of the ulna
Medial epicondyle of the humerus
Radial tuberosity
Lateral epicondyle of the humerus
questions.why: The medial epicondyle is the knob on the medial side of the distal humerus, and it serves as the common flexor origin. Pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris all arise from it through a shared tendon, which is why the anterior forearm muscles fan out from the medial side of the elbow. Irritation of this tendon is called golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis).
notes: The coronoid process is the anterior lip of the ulna's trochlear notch. It gives a small second head to pronator teres, but it is better known as the insertion of brachialis, so choose it if the question asked where brachialis attaches.
Correct. The medial epicondyle is the common flexor origin for the superficial anterior forearm muscles.
The radial tuberosity is a bump on the proximal radius where the biceps brachii tendon inserts. Pick it if the question asked for the insertion of biceps brachii.

The lateral epicondyle is the knob on the opposite side of the distal humerus. It is the common extensor origin for the superficial posterior forearm muscles, so pick it if the question asked where the wrist and finger extensors begin.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which anterior forearm muscle inserts on the palmar aponeurosis, the sheet of deep fascia in the palm?
options: Pronator teres
Flexor carpi radialis
Palmaris longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.why: Palmaris longus is a small, slender muscle of the superficial layer that arises from the medial epicondyle. Its long, thin tendon passes in front of the flexor retinaculum and spreads out into the palmar aponeurosis, so when it contracts it tightens that sheet and weakly assists wrist flexion. The name says the same thing: palmaris means palm and longus means long.
notes: Pronator teres runs from the medial epicondyle to the lateral mid-shaft of the radius and never reaches the hand. It would be right if the question asked which round muscle pronates the forearm near the elbow.
Flexor carpi radialis inserts on the bases of metacarpals 2 and 3 on the palmar side. Choose it if the question asked which superficial flexor bends the wrist and pulls it toward the thumb side.
Correct. The palmaris longus tendon continues into the palmar aponeurosis.

Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts on the pisiform, hamate and metacarpal 5 on the medial side of the wrist. Pick it if the question asked which flexor bends the wrist and pulls it toward the little finger side.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle runs straight across the front of the distal forearm, from the ulna to the radius, and is the prime mover of pronation?
options: Supinator
Pronator teres
Brachioradialis
Pronator quadratus
questions.why: Pronator quadratus is a flat, four-sided muscle in the deep layer of the anterior forearm, lying right on the bones just above the wrist. Its fibers run from the distal anterior ulna across to the distal anterior radius, so when it shortens it pulls the radius across the front of the ulna and turns the palm to face posteriorly. The course notes name it the prime mover of pronation, with pronator teres assisting.
notes: Supinator wraps around the proximal radius in the deep posterior forearm and does the opposite movement, turning the palm to face anteriorly. Choose it if the question asked which forearm muscle supinates.

Pronator teres also pronates, but it lies in the proximal forearm and runs diagonally from the medial epicondyle to the lateral mid-shaft of the radius. Pick it if the question described the round pronator near the elbow.

Brachioradialis runs from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the styloid process of the radius along the thumb side of the forearm. Pick it if the question asked which muscle flexes the elbow most strongly with the forearm in mid-position.
Correct. Pronator quadratus runs horizontally between the distal ulna and radius and is the prime mover of pronation.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does pronator teres insert?
options: Styloid process of the radius
Radial tuberosity
Coronoid process of the ulna
Lateral mid-shaft of the radius
questions.why: Pronator teres arises from the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process of the ulna, then crosses the front of the forearm diagonally to insert on the lateral surface of the radius about halfway down its shaft. Because it pulls the lateral radius toward the medial elbow, it rolls the radius over the ulna and pronates the forearm. Crossing the front of the elbow also lets it assist elbow flexion.
notes: The styloid process of the radius is the pointed tip of the radius at the wrist, where brachioradialis inserts. Pick it if the question asked for the insertion of brachioradialis.
The radial tuberosity is the bump on the proximal radius where biceps brachii inserts. Choose it if the question asked where the biceps tendon attaches.

The coronoid process is one of the two origins of pronator teres, not its insertion, so this choice reverses the muscle's attachments. It is also where brachialis inserts, so pick it if the question asked for the insertion of brachialis.
Correct. Pronator teres inserts on the lateral surface of the radius at mid-shaft.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does flexor digitorum superficialis insert?
options: Middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5
Proximal phalanges of digits 2 to 5
Bases of metacarpals 2 and 3
Distal phalanges of digits 2 to 5
questions.why: Flexor digitorum superficialis sends four tendons through the carpal tunnel, one to each finger from the index to the little finger. Each tendon splits near the base of the finger and attaches to the sides of the middle phalanx, so the muscle bends the fingers at the proximal interphalangeal joints (the middle knuckles). It cannot bend the fingertips because it stops before the distal phalanx.
notes: Correct. Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5.

No long forearm flexor ends on the proximal phalanges of the fingers, so this choice usually comes from guessing that the superficial muscle stops at the first bone. The long finger flexors pass the proximal phalanx and insert farther out on the middle and distal phalanges.
The bases of metacarpals 2 and 3 receive the tendon of flexor carpi radialis. Choose them if the question asked where the radial wrist flexor inserts.
The distal phalanges of digits 2 to 5 are where flexor digitorum profundus inserts. Pick this if the question asked about the deep finger flexor that bends the fingertips.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does flexor digitorum profundus insert?
options: Middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5
Distal phalanx of the thumb
Pisiform, hamate and metacarpal 5
Distal phalanges of digits 2 to 5
questions.why: Flexor digitorum profundus is the deep finger flexor.
