notes: The adductor group on the medial thigh pulls the thighs toward the midline. It would be the answer for squeezing the knees together, not controlling knee bend.
The gastrocnemius and soleus are calf muscles that plantarflex the foot. They are the answer for rising onto your toes, not for controlling the knee as you sit.

The hamstrings flex the knee, which is the movement gravity is already producing as you sit. They would be the answer if the question asked which group actively bends the knee against resistance, as in a leg curl.
Correct. The quadriceps resist knee flexion and control the descent.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle is the largest of the gluteal group and the most powerful extensor of the hip?
options: Gluteus medius
Gluteus maximus
Tensor fasciae latae
Gluteus minimus
questions.why: The gluteus maximus forms most of the bulk of the buttock. It runs from the back of the ilium, sacrum, and coccyx to the gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial (IT) band, so when it contracts it pulls the thigh backward. That makes it the main extensor of the hip, the muscle you rely on to climb stairs or rise from a chair.
notes: The gluteus medius lies partly under the gluteus maximus on the upper outer buttock and inserts on the greater trochanter. It is smaller, and its main action is abduction, not extension.
Correct. The gluteus maximus is the largest gluteal muscle and the main extensor of the hip.
The tensor fasciae latae is a small muscle on the lateral hip that tightens the IT band. It flexes the thigh, the opposite of extension.
The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the three gluteal muscles, lying under the gluteus medius. It helps abduct the thigh rather than extend it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main action of the gluteus medius?
options: Flexion of the knee
Extension of the thigh
Adduction of the thigh
Abduction of the thigh
questions.why: The gluteus medius runs from the outer surface of the ilium down to the greater trochanter on the lateral side of the femur. Because it sits on the outside of the hip joint, it pulls the thigh away from the midline, which is abduction. It also medially rotates the thigh and steadies the pelvis each time you stand on one leg.
notes: Flexion of the knee is done mainly by the hamstrings on the back of the thigh. The gluteus medius ends at the greater trochanter and never crosses the knee, so it cannot move that joint.

Extension of the thigh is the main job of the gluteus maximus, helped by the hamstrings. Pick extension if the question named the gluteus maximus or asked what happens when you push your leg backward.
Adduction pulls the thigh toward the midline and belongs to the medial thigh muscles, such as the adductor longus, brevis, and magnus. It is the opposite of what the gluteus medius does.
Correct. The gluteus medius is the main abductor of the thigh.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient stands on her right leg only, and the left side of her pelvis drops instead of staying level. Weakness of which muscle best explains this?
options: Left gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius
Right adductor longus
Right gluteus maximus
questions.why: When you stand on one leg, the gluteus medius on the standing side pulls on the pelvis from its attachment at the greater trochanter and keeps the opposite side from sagging. If that muscle is weak, the unsupported side of the pelvis drops. Here she is standing on the right leg, so the right gluteus medius is the muscle failing to hold the pelvis level. Clinicians call this a positive Trendelenburg sign.
notes: The left gluteus medius belongs to the leg that is lifted off the ground, so it is not holding up the pelvis at that moment. It would be the weak muscle if she stood on her left leg and the right side of her pelvis dropped.
Correct. The stance-side gluteus medius holds the pelvis level, so a drop on the left points to weakness on the right.

The right adductor longus pulls the thigh toward the midline from the medial side. It does not act as the lateral support that keeps the pelvis level, so its weakness would not cause the opposite side to drop.

The right gluteus maximus is the main extensor of the hip, used to push the thigh backward when climbing or rising from a chair. Weakness there shows up as trouble with those movements, not as a pelvis that tilts while standing on one leg.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which gluteal muscle is the smallest and lies deepest, under the gluteus medius?
options: Gluteus maximus
Gluteus minimus
Tensor fasciae latae
Gluteus medius
questions.why: The three gluteal muscles stack from superficial to deep: gluteus maximus on the surface, gluteus medius beneath it, and gluteus minimus deepest of all. The names follow size as well, since minimus means smallest. The gluteus minimus runs from the ilium to the greater trochanter and works with the gluteus medius to abduct and medially rotate the thigh.
notes: The gluteus maximus is the largest and most superficial gluteal muscle, the one that gives the buttock its shape. It lies on top of the other two, not under them.
Correct. The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the gluteal muscles.
The tensor fasciae latae is not deep in the buttock at all. It sits on the front of the lateral hip and pulls on the IT band.
The gluteus medius is the middle layer, directly under the gluteus maximus. The muscle under the gluteus medius is a different, smaller one.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The iliopsoas is formed by which two muscles?
options: Psoas major and sartorius
Iliacus and psoas major
Iliacus and pectineus
Pectineus and sartorius
questions.why: The iliopsoas is a combined muscle. The iliacus fills the iliac fossa on the inner surface of the ilium, and the psoas major arises from the bodies and transverse processes of vertebrae T12 to L5. The two pass together under the inguinal ligament and insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur.
notes: The sartorius is the long strap muscle that crosses the front of the thigh from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia. It helps flex the hip, but it is a separate muscle, not part of the iliopsoas.
Correct. The iliacus and the psoas major join to form the iliopsoas.
The pectineus is a flat muscle of the medial compartment that lies right beside the iliopsoas at the top of the thigh. That closeness makes it easy to mix up, but it is not part of the iliopsoas.
Neither of these is part of the iliopsoas. The pectineus is in the medial compartment, and the sartorius is the strap muscle crossing the front of the thigh.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the iliopsoas insert on the femur?
options: Lesser trochanter
Linea aspera
Gluteal tuberosity
Greater trochanter
questions.why: The iliopsoas comes down from vertebrae T12 to L5 and the iliac fossa, passes in front of the hip joint, and ends on the lesser trochanter, the small projection on the medial side of the upper femur. Pulling on this point from above and in front swings the thigh forward, so the iliopsoas flexes the thigh at the hip.
notes: Correct. The iliopsoas tendon attaches to the lesser trochanter.
The linea aspera is the rough ridge running down the back of the femoral shaft. It would be the answer for where most of the adductor muscles insert.
The gluteal tuberosity is a roughened area on the upper posterior femur. Choose it for part of the insertion of the gluteus maximus.
The greater trochanter is the large projection on the lateral side of the upper femur. Pick it for the insertion of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The iliopsoas runs from vertebrae T12 to L5 and the iliac fossa, passes in front of the hip joint, and inserts on the lesser trochanter. What action does this arrangement produce?
options: Abduction of the thigh
Extension of the thigh
Extension of the knee
Flexion of the thigh
questions.why: A muscle that crosses the front of a joint usually flexes it. The iliopsoas crosses the front of the hip and pulls the lesser trochanter upward and forward, lifting the thigh toward the trunk. It is the prime mover of hip flexion, the movement used when you raise your knee to march or climb.
notes: Abduction moves the thigh out to the side and is the job of muscles on the lateral hip, such as the gluteus medius. The iliopsoas lies in front of the joint, not beside it.
Extension of the thigh moves it backward and is done by muscles that cross the back of the hip, mainly the gluteus maximus and the hamstrings. That is the opposite action of the iliopsoas.
Extension of the knee is done by the quadriceps, which reach the tibia. The iliopsoas stops at the lesser trochanter of the femur and never crosses the knee.
Correct. Crossing the front of the hip, the iliopsoas flexes the thigh.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which part of the quadriceps femoris lies deep to the rectus femoris, between the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis?
options: Vastus intermedius
Vastus lateralis
Sartorius
Vastus medialis
questions.why: The quadriceps femoris has four parts. The rectus femoris runs down the middle of the front of the thigh, the vastus lateralis lies on the outer side, the vastus medialis on the inner side, and the vastus intermedius lies hidden beneath the rectus femoris, directly on the femur. The name intermedius tells you it sits between the other two vasti.
notes: Correct. The vastus intermedius lies under the rectus femoris, between the other two vasti.
The vastus lateralis is the large quadriceps muscle on the outer side of the thigh. Pick it for the lateral part of the quadriceps or for the thigh muscle often used for injections in infants.

The sartorius is a long strap muscle crossing the front of the thigh diagonally, and it is not part of the quadriceps. Pick it for the longest muscle in the body or the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
The vastus medialis is the quadriceps muscle on the inner side of the thigh, forming the bulge just above and medial to the knee. It would be the answer for the medial part of the group.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which quadriceps muscle arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine rather than from the femur?
options: Vastus medialis
Rectus femoris
Vastus intermedius
Vastus lateralis
questions.why: Three parts of the quadriceps, the three vasti, arise from the shaft of the femur. The rectus femoris is different because it starts higher, on the anterior inferior iliac spine of the hip bone. Since it begins above the hip joint, it crosses both the hip and the knee, so it can flex the hip as well as extend the knee.
notes: The vastus medialis arises from the medial side of the femur along the linea aspera. Pick it for the inner quadriceps muscle that bulges above the medial knee.
Correct. The rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine.
The vastus intermedius arises from the front and side of the femoral shaft, under the rectus femoris. Pick it for the deep quadriceps muscle lying directly on the femur.
The vastus lateralis arises from the upper lateral femur, including near the greater trochanter and the linea aspera. Choose it for the outer quadriceps muscle, which crosses only the knee.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The four parts of the quadriceps femoris share a common insertion. Where is it?
options: Lesser trochanter
Tibial tuberosity
Head of the fibula
Medial condyle of the tibia
questions.why: All four quadriceps muscles join into the quadriceps tendon, which wraps around the patella. Below the patella the same line of pull continues as the patellar ligament and anchors to the tibial tuberosity on the front of the tibia. Pulling on that point straightens the knee.
notes: The lesser trochanter is on the upper medial femur, far above the knee. Pick it for the insertion of the iliopsoas.
Correct. The quadriceps inserts on the tibial tuberosity by way of the patella and patellar ligament.
The head of the fibula is the knob at the top of the lateral leg bone. Pick it for the insertion of the biceps femoris, the lateral hamstring.
The medial condyle of the tibia is on the inner side of the top of the tibia. It would be the answer for where the semimembranosus inserts on the back of the medial knee.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main action shared by all four parts of the quadriceps femoris?
options: Flexion of the knee
Adduction of the thigh
Extension of the knee
Plantar flexion of the foot
questions.why: Every part of the quadriceps ends on the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament, on the front of the knee. Pulling on the front of the tibia straightens the leg at the knee, so knee extension is the action all four share. Only the rectus femoris adds a second action, flexion of the hip.
notes: Flexion of the knee bends it and is the job of the hamstrings on the back of the thigh. The hamstrings are the antagonists of the quadriceps.
Adduction of the thigh pulls it toward the midline and belongs to the medial thigh group, such as the adductor longus and adductor magnus.
Correct. The quadriceps extends the knee.
Plantar flexion points the foot downward and is done by the calf muscles, mainly the gastrocnemius and soleus. The quadriceps does not cross the ankle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The patella is a sesamoid bone, meaning it forms inside a tendon. Inside the tendon of which muscle group does it sit?
options: Adductor group
Hamstrings
Quadriceps femoris
Gluteal group
questions.why: The patella develops within the quadriceps tendon at the front of the knee. It lets that tendon glide smoothly over the knee joint and improves the leverage of the quadriceps as it extends the knee. Below the patella, the tendon continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
notes: The adductor group sits on the medial thigh and inserts mainly on the linea aspera of the femur, well above the knee. It has no tendon crossing the front of the knee.
The hamstrings run down the back of the thigh and insert behind and beside the knee, on the tibia and fibula. They have no sesamoid bone at the front of the knee.
Correct. The patella lies within the quadriceps tendon.
The gluteal group acts at the hip and inserts on the upper femur and the IT band. It has no tendon at the front of the knee.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle is the longest in the body, running diagonally across the front of the thigh?
options: Gracilis
Sartorius
Rectus femoris
Biceps femoris
questions.why: The sartorius is a long, narrow strap muscle that starts at the anterior superior iliac spine, crosses the front of the thigh at an angle, and ends on the medial side of the upper tibia. Its length and diagonal course make it the longest muscle in the body. It also forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
notes: The gracilis is also long and strap-like, but it runs down the medial side of the thigh from the pubis. Choose it for the medial thigh muscle that crosses the knee.
Correct. The sartorius is the longest muscle in the body.
The rectus femoris runs straight down the middle of the front of the thigh, not diagonally. Pick it for the quadriceps muscle that arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine.
The biceps femoris is on the back of the thigh, running to the head of the fibula. It would be the answer for the lateral hamstring.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A tailor sits on the floor with legs crossed, each ankle resting on the opposite knee. The muscle named for this posture flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh while also flexing the knee. Which muscle is it?
options: Tensor fasciae latae
Gracilis
Semitendinosus
Sartorius
questions.why: The name sartorius comes from the Latin word for tailor. Because it runs from the anterior superior iliac spine, across the front of the thigh, to the medial tibia, it crosses both the hip and the knee. Its pull flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh and also bends the knee, which together place the leg in the cross-legged position.
notes: The tensor fasciae latae flexes and abducts the thigh, but it medially rotates it and ends in the IT band on the lateral side. It does not flex the knee or rotate the thigh outward the way this posture needs.
The gracilis also crosses the hip and knee and ends near the sartorius on the medial tibia, but it adducts the thigh rather than abducting it.
The semitendinosus is a hamstring that extends the thigh and flexes the knee. Thigh extension is the opposite of what the cross-legged position needs.
Correct. The sartorius produces the cross-legged position it is named for.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which small muscle on the lateral side of the hip pulls on the iliotibial (IT) band?
options: Gluteus minimus
Tensor fasciae latae
Vastus lateralis
Biceps femoris
questions.why: The tensor fasciae latae arises from the anterior iliac crest and the anterior superior iliac spine and ends in the iliotibial (IT) band, which runs to the lateral condyle of the tibia. Its name describes its job: tensor means tightener, and fasciae latae refers to the wide fascia of the thigh. It also flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the thigh, and tightening the IT band steadies the knee.
notes: The gluteus minimus is a deep gluteal muscle that inserts on the greater trochanter, not into the IT band.
Correct. The tensor fasciae latae tightens the IT band.
The vastus lateralis lies under the IT band on the outer thigh, but it is a quadriceps muscle that inserts on the tibial tuberosity, not into the band.
The biceps femoris is on the back of the thigh and inserts on the head of the fibula, not into the IT band.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the thick band of fascia that runs down the lateral thigh from the iliac crest to the lateral side of the tibia?
options: Calcaneal tendon
Patellar ligament
Iliotibial (IT) band
Inguinal ligament
questions.why: The iliotibial (IT) band is not a muscle. It is a thick band of fascia that runs from the iliac crest down the outer thigh to the lateral condyle of the tibia, just below the knee. The tensor fasciae latae and the gluteus maximus pull on it, which helps steady the knee.
notes: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon attaches the calf muscles to the heel bone at the back of the ankle, not the thigh.
The patellar ligament runs from the patella to the tibial tuberosity on the front of the knee. It is short and anterior, not a long band down the lateral thigh.
Correct. The IT band runs down the lateral thigh from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia.
The inguinal ligament stretches across the groin from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It does not run down the thigh.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A distance runner has pain along the outside of the thigh and knee where a tight band rubs over the lateral femoral epicondyle. Which structure is most likely irritated?
options: Iliotibial (IT) band
Adductor longus tendon
Patellar ligament
Semitendinosus tendon
questions.why: The iliotibial (IT) band runs down the lateral thigh and crosses the outer side of the knee near the lateral femoral epicondyle. With repeated bending and straightening of the knee during running, a tight band can rub over this bony bump and become painful. Pain on the outer thigh and knee points to this band.
notes: Correct. The IT band crosses the lateral femoral epicondyle and can be irritated there.
The adductor longus tendon is high on the inner thigh near the pubis. Pain there would be in the groin, not the outer knee.
The patellar ligament is on the front of the knee, below the kneecap, not on the outer side.
The semitendinosus tendon passes along the back and inner side of the knee to the medial tibia. It is on the medial side, not the lateral side.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main action shared by the muscles of the medial thigh compartment?
options: Flexion of the knee
Adduction of the thigh
Extension of the knee
Abduction of the thigh
questions.why: The medial compartment holds the adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, pectineus, and gracilis. They arise from the pubis and ischium and insert on the femur or medial tibia, so they pull the thigh toward the midline. That movement, adduction, is the shared job of the group.
notes: Flexion of the knee is mainly done by the hamstrings in the posterior compartment. Only the gracilis of the medial group crosses the knee, so knee flexion is not the shared action.
Correct. The medial thigh muscles adduct the thigh.
Extension of the knee is the job of the quadriceps in the anterior compartment. The medial muscles mostly stop on the femur and do not straighten the knee.
Abduction moves the thigh away from the midline and is done by the gluteus medius and minimus on the lateral hip. It is the opposite of the medial group's action.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which medial thigh muscle is a long, thin strap that runs from the pubis to the medial tibia and is the only member of its group to cross the knee?
options: Adductor magnus
Adductor longus
Pectineus
Gracilis
questions.why: Most medial thigh muscles end on the femur, along the linea aspera or near the adductor tubercle. The gracilis is the exception. It is a slender strap that runs down the inner thigh from the pubis and inserts on the medial side of the upper tibia, so it crosses the knee and can help flex it as well as adduct the thigh.
notes: The adductor magnus is the largest adductor and inserts on the linea aspera and adductor tubercle of the femur, above the knee. Choose it for the biggest muscle of the medial group.
The adductor longus is a triangular muscle of the upper medial thigh that inserts on the linea aspera. Pick it for the medial border of the femoral triangle.

The pectineus is a short, flat muscle at the top of the medial thigh that inserts on the upper femur. It would be the answer for the medial muscle lying in the floor of the femoral triangle beside the iliopsoas.
Correct. The gracilis is the long medial strap muscle that crosses the knee.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which is the largest muscle of the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh?
options: Adductor magnus
Adductor longus
Gracilis
Adductor brevis
questions.why: Magnus means large, and the adductor magnus is the biggest and deepest muscle of the medial thigh. It arises from the pubis and the ischium, including the ischial tuberosity, and fans out to insert along the linea aspera and on the adductor tubercle of the femur. Its broad shape makes it a powerful adductor.
notes: Correct. The adductor magnus is the largest adductor.
The adductor longus is long but narrow, a triangular muscle near the surface of the upper medial thigh. Pick it for the medial border of the femoral triangle.
The gracilis is a long, thin strap, not a large muscle. Choose it for the medial thigh muscle that crosses the knee to reach the tibia.
The adductor brevis is short, as brevis means, and lies between the adductor longus and adductor magnus. It would be the answer for the short middle adductor.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Most of the adductor muscles insert along which ridge on the back of the femur?
options: Linea aspera
Lateral epicondyle
Intertrochanteric line
Gluteal tuberosity
questions.why: The linea aspera is a long, rough ridge running down the middle of the posterior femoral shaft. Rough bone markings like this anchor muscles, and the adductor longus, adductor brevis, and adductor magnus all insert along it. From there they pull the femur toward the midline.
notes: Correct. The adductor longus, brevis, and magnus insert along the linea aspera.
The lateral epicondyle is a bump on the outer side of the femur just above the knee, not a ridge on the back of the shaft. The IT band passes over it.
The intertrochanteric line runs across the front of the upper femur between the two trochanters. It is where the vastus medialis begins, not where the adductors insert.
The gluteal tuberosity is a rough area high on the back of the femur where part of the gluteus maximus inserts, not the adductors.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which flat muscle lies in the floor of the femoral triangle, between the iliopsoas laterally and the adductor longus medially?
options: Sartorius
Pectineus
Gracilis
Adductor magnus
questions.why: The floor of the femoral triangle is formed, from lateral to medial, by the iliopsoas, the pectineus, and the adductor longus. The pectineus runs from the superior ramus of the pubis to the pectineal line of the femur, just below the lesser trochanter, and it adducts and flexes the thigh. Because it lies right next to the iliopsoas, it is often mistaken for part of it.
notes: The sartorius forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle, not its floor. Choose it when the question asks which muscle runs along the lateral edge of the triangle.
Correct. The pectineus forms the medial part of the floor of the femoral triangle.
The gracilis runs down the medial edge of the thigh to the tibia and is not part of the triangle's floor. Pick it for the long strap of the medial thigh that crosses the knee.
The adductor magnus is a large, deep muscle lower and further back in the medial thigh. It would be the answer for the largest adductor.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A soccer player feels a sudden pull high on the inner thigh while sweeping the leg across the body to kick. Which muscle group was most likely strained?
options: Gluteal group
Hamstring group
Quadriceps group
Adductor group
questions.why: Sweeping the leg across the front of the body pulls the thigh toward and past the midline, which is adduction. The adductors on the medial thigh produce that movement and attach high on the pubis, right at the groin. A sudden forceful contraction or stretch there is the classic groin pull, an adductor strain.
notes: The gluteal muscles lie in the buttock and act mainly to extend and abduct the hip. A strain there would be felt in the buttock rather than on the inner thigh.
The hamstrings are on the back of the thigh and are usually strained during sprinting, when they work hard to slow the swinging leg. Pick them for pain in the back of the thigh.
The quadriceps fill the front of the thigh and extend the knee. They would be the answer for a strain felt on the front of the thigh, such as during a hard kick that straightens the knee.
Correct. A groin pull during a cross-body kick is an adductor strain.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which set names the three hamstring muscles?
options: Biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus
Rectus femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus
Semitendinosus, adductor magnus, gracilis
Biceps femoris, gracilis, sartorius
questions.why: The hamstrings are the three muscles of the posterior thigh: the biceps femoris on the lateral side and the semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the medial side. All three arise mainly from the ischial tuberosity and run down the back of the thigh to the leg, so they extend the hip and flex the knee.
notes: Correct. These are the three hamstrings.
The rectus femoris is a quadriceps muscle on the front of the thigh. Swapping it in for the biceps femoris mixes the anterior compartment with the posterior one.
The adductor magnus and gracilis belong to the medial compartment. Part of the adductor magnus arises from the ischial tuberosity, which causes confusion, but it is classed with the adductors.

The gracilis and sartorius are not hamstrings. The gracilis is in the medial compartment and the sartorius in the anterior compartment, though both share an insertion on the medial tibia with the semitendinosus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: From which bone marking do the hamstrings mainly arise?
options: Greater trochanter
Ischial tuberosity
Pubic crest
Anterior superior iliac spine
questions.why: The hamstrings share a common origin on the ischial tuberosity, the rough knob of the hip bone that you sit on. From there they run down the back of the thigh. Because they start behind the hip and end below the knee, they extend the hip and flex the knee.
notes: The greater trochanter is a large projection on the lateral upper femur. It is where the gluteus medius inserts, not where the hamstrings arise.
Correct. The hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity.
The pubic crest is on the front of the pubis, near where medial thigh muscles such as the adductor longus arise. The hamstrings start farther back, on the ischium.
The anterior superior iliac spine is the bony point at the front of the iliac crest. The sartorius and tensor fasciae latae arise there, not the hamstrings.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The hamstrings run from the ischial tuberosity, behind the hip, down to the tibia and fibula below the knee. Which pair of actions does this course produce?
options: Hip flexion and knee extension
Hip extension and knee extension
Hip extension and knee flexion
Hip flexion and knee flexion
questions.why: A muscle acts on every joint it crosses. The hamstrings cross the back of the hip, so they pull the thigh backward, which is hip extension. They also cross the back of the knee, so they bend it, which is knee flexion. This makes them the antagonists of the quadriceps at the knee.
notes: This is the reverse combination, produced by the rectus femoris on the front of the thigh, which flexes the hip and extends the knee. Pick it for the one quadriceps muscle that crosses both joints.
No muscle of the posterior thigh extends both joints. Extension at the hip comes from the back of the thigh, but extension at the knee comes from the quadriceps on the front.
Correct. The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee.
Flexing both the hip and the knee together is what the sartorius does as it crosses the front of the hip and the medial knee. The hamstrings lie behind the hip, so they cannot flex it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which hamstring lies on the lateral side of the posterior thigh and inserts on the head of the fibula?
options: Semitendinosus
Semimembranosus
Gracilis
Biceps femoris
questions.why: The biceps femoris has a long head from the ischial tuberosity and a short head from the linea aspera. The two heads join and run down the outer side of the back of the thigh to insert on the head of the fibula. That makes it the lateral hamstring, while the other two hamstrings lie medially.
notes: The semitendinosus is a medial hamstring with a long cord-like tendon that inserts on the medial surface of the upper tibia. Pick it for the superficial medial hamstring.
The semimembranosus is the other medial hamstring, lying deep to the semitendinosus and inserting on the medial condyle of the tibia. Choose it for the deep medial hamstring.
The gracilis is a medial thigh muscle, not a hamstring, and it inserts on the medial tibia. It would be the answer for the adductor that crosses the knee.
Correct. The biceps femoris is the lateral hamstring and inserts on the fibular head.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus?
options: Both lie on the lateral side of the posterior thigh
Semimembranosus is superficial, semitendinosus lies deep to it
Both insert on the head of the fibula
Semitendinosus is superficial, semimembranosus lies deep to it
questions.why: The two medial hamstrings are stacked. The semitendinosus is on top, and its name points to its long, rope-like tendon in the lower thigh. The semimembranosus lies under it, named for its flat, membrane-like tendon of origin. Both run along the medial side of the back of the thigh and insert on the medial tibia.
notes: The lateral side of the posterior thigh belongs to the biceps femoris. The semitendinosus and semimembranosus both lie on the medial side, which is why they are called the medial hamstrings.
This reverses their layers. Remember that the semitendinosus, with its long tendon, rests on top of the broader semimembranosus.
The head of the fibula receives the biceps femoris, the lateral hamstring. The two semi muscles insert on the medial side of the tibia instead.
Correct. The semitendinosus is superficial and the semimembranosus lies deep to it.
questions.answerText: Semitendinosus is superficial, semimembranosus lies deep to it
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which part of the hamstring group crosses only the knee, so it can flex the knee but cannot extend the hip?
options: Semimembranosus
Long head of biceps femoris
Short head of biceps femoris
Semitendinosus
questions.why: A muscle can only move a joint it crosses. The long head of the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus, and the semimembranosus all start on the ischial tuberosity, above the hip, so they act at both the hip and knee. The short head of the biceps femoris starts lower, on the linea aspera of the femur, so it crosses only the knee and acts only as a knee flexor.
notes: The semimembranosus also arises from the ischial tuberosity and crosses both joints. Choose it for the deep medial hamstring.
The long head of the biceps femoris arises from the ischial tuberosity and crosses the hip, so it does extend the hip. Pick it for the part of the biceps femoris that acts at two joints.
Correct. The short head of the biceps femoris arises from the femur and crosses only the knee.
The semitendinosus arises from the ischial tuberosity and crosses both the hip and knee. It would be the answer for a superficial medial hamstring that acts at both joints.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A sprinter feels a sharp pain in the back of the thigh during a race and cannot continue. Which muscle group was most likely strained?
options: Hamstrings
Quadriceps
Iliopsoas
Adductors
questions.why: The back of the thigh is occupied by the hamstrings. During sprinting they work hard both to drive the hip into extension and to slow the swinging leg before the foot lands, which puts them under heavy load while they are being stretched. That is why hamstring strains are so common in sprinters and why the pain is felt behind the thigh.
notes: Correct. Pain in the back of the thigh during sprinting points to a hamstring strain.
The quadriceps lie on the front of the thigh. A strain there would cause pain on the anterior thigh, not the back.

The iliopsoas runs from vertebrae T12 to L5 and the iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter, deep in the front of the hip. A strain there would be felt in the groin or front of the hip, not the back of the thigh.
The adductors lie on the inner thigh near the groin. A strain there is a groin pull, felt high on the medial thigh, not the back of the thigh.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What forms the superior border of the femoral triangle?
options: Adductor longus
Inguinal ligament
Sartorius
Iliac crest
questions.why: The femoral triangle is a hollow on the upper front of the thigh, just below the groin. Its upper border is the inguinal ligament, which stretches from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The sartorius forms the lateral border and the adductor longus forms the medial border.
notes: The adductor longus forms the medial border of the triangle. Choose it for the medial side.
Correct. The inguinal ligament is the superior border of the femoral triangle.
The sartorius forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle as it angles down and inward across the thigh. Pick it for the lateral side.
The iliac crest is the upper rim of the ilium, well above the groin. It is a landmark of the hip bone, not a border of the femoral triangle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which pair correctly gives the lateral and medial borders of the femoral triangle?
options: Sartorius lateral, adductor longus medial
Iliopsoas lateral, pectineus medial
Rectus femoris lateral, gracilis medial
Adductor longus lateral, sartorius medial
questions.why: The femoral triangle has three borders: the inguinal ligament above, the sartorius on the lateral side, and the adductor longus on the medial side. The sartorius runs down and inward from the anterior superior iliac spine, while the adductor longus comes down and outward from the pubis, so the two meet at the lower point of the triangle.
notes: Correct. The sartorius is the lateral border and the adductor longus is the medial border.
The iliopsoas and pectineus are real parts of the femoral triangle, but they form its floor, not its borders. Pick this pair if the question asked which muscles lie in the floor of the triangle.
The rectus femoris lies in the middle of the front of the thigh and the gracilis on the far medial side. Neither one outlines the femoral triangle.
These are the right two muscles placed on the wrong sides. The sartorius starts at the anterior superior iliac spine on the outside, so it must be the lateral border.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle belongs to the anterior compartment of the thigh?
options: Vastus medialis
Semimembranosus
Gracilis
Adductor brevis
questions.why: The thigh is divided into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. The anterior compartment holds the quadriceps femoris and the sartorius. The vastus medialis is one of the four parts of the quadriceps, so it belongs to the anterior compartment even though its name includes the word medial.
notes: Correct. The vastus medialis is part of the quadriceps in the anterior compartment.
The semimembranosus is a hamstring in the posterior compartment, on the back of the thigh.
The gracilis is in the medial compartment with the adductors, on the inner thigh. Do not let the word medial in vastus medialis pull you toward the medial group.
The adductor brevis is in the medial compartment and adducts the thigh. It is not an anterior muscle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A thigh muscle arises from the pubis and inserts along the linea aspera of the femur. Which compartment does it belong to?
options: Anterior compartment
Medial compartment
Posterior compartment
Lateral compartment
questions.why: Muscles that start on the pubis and attach along the back of the femur lie on the inner thigh and pull the femur toward the midline. That pattern fits the adductors, such as the adductor longus and adductor brevis, which make up the medial compartment.
notes: The anterior compartment muscles, the quadriceps and sartorius, arise from the ilium or the femur and insert on the tibia, at or below the knee. None of them runs from the pubis to the linea aspera.
Correct. A muscle from the pubis to the linea aspera is an adductor in the medial compartment.
The posterior compartment muscles, the hamstrings, arise mainly from the ischial tuberosity and insert below the knee on the tibia or fibula. None of them arises from the pubis.
The thigh is divided into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. A lateral compartment belongs to the leg, where it holds the fibularis muscles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: After a thigh injury, a patient can bend his knee but cannot straighten it against resistance or rise from a chair without using his arms. Which muscle group is most likely damaged?
options: Adductors
Quadriceps femoris
Gluteus medius and minimus
Hamstrings
questions.why: Straightening the knee is knee extension, and the muscle group that extends the knee is the quadriceps femoris on the front of the thigh. Rising from a chair also depends heavily on the quadriceps. Since knee bending still works, the hamstrings are intact and the problem lies on the front of the thigh.
notes: The adductors pull the thigh toward the midline. Damage to them would weaken squeezing the knees together, not straightening the knee.
Correct. Loss of knee extension points to the quadriceps.
The gluteus medius and minimus abduct the thigh and keep the pelvis level when walking. Weakness there causes a tilting gait, not loss of knee extension.
The hamstrings flex the knee, and this patient can still bend it. Pick the hamstrings if the patient could straighten the knee but not bend it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Climbing a steep flight of stairs, a hiker drives the body upward by forcefully pulling the thigh backward at the hip. Which muscle provides most of this power?
options: Iliopsoas
Gluteus medius
Rectus femoris
Gluteus maximus
questions.why: Pulling the thigh backward at the hip is extension of the thigh. The gluteus maximus is the largest gluteal muscle and the main extensor of the thigh, the muscle used most for climbing stairs and rising from a chair. It runs from the back of the pelvis to the posterior femur and the IT band, behind the hip, which is why it pulls the thigh backward.
notes: The iliopsoas is the prime mover of hip flexion, lifting the knee to place the foot on the next step. That is the opposite movement from the push that drives the body upward.
The gluteus medius abducts the thigh and keeps the pelvis level on the stance leg. It helps you stay balanced on each step but is not the main source of upward drive.
The rectus femoris flexes the hip and extends the knee. It helps straighten the knee during the climb but works against hip extension, not for it.
Correct. The gluteus maximus powers hip extension when climbing.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which two muscles pull on the iliotibial (IT) band?
options: Sartorius and rectus femoris
Biceps femoris and semitendinosus
Gluteus medius and gracilis
Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae
questions.why: The iliotibial (IT) band is a thick band of fascia on the lateral thigh, running from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia. The tensor fasciae latae inserts into it from the front of the hip, and the gluteus maximus inserts into it from behind. The tensor fasciae latae tightens the band to steady the knee.
notes: The sartorius ends on the medial tibia, and the rectus femoris ends on the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament. Neither attaches to the IT band.
These are two hamstrings. The biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula and the semitendinosus on the medial tibia, not into the IT band.
The gluteus medius inserts on the greater trochanter and the gracilis on the medial tibia. Neither attaches to the IT band.
Correct. The gluteus maximus and the tensor fasciae latae both insert into the IT band.
questions.answerText: Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Three muscles from three different thigh compartments insert together on the medial side of the upper tibia. Which set is it?
options: Sartorius, adductor longus, semimembranosus
Biceps femoris, semimembranosus, adductor magnus
Rectus femoris, vastus medialis, gracilis
Sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus
questions.why: The sartorius from the anterior compartment, the gracilis from the medial compartment, and the semitendinosus from the posterior compartment all end side by side on the medial surface of the upper tibia. Their joined tendons are called the pes anserinus, meaning goose's foot, because of the way they spread out. Each comes from a different compartment, which makes this a useful landmark.
notes: The sartorius belongs, but the adductor longus inserts on the linea aspera of the femur, and the semimembranosus inserts on the medial condyle of the tibia rather than joining the other two.
The biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula on the lateral side, and the adductor magnus stops on the femur above the knee. Neither belongs to this medial tibial group.
The rectus femoris and vastus medialis insert on the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament, on the front of the tibia, not its medial side. Both are also from the same compartment.
Correct. The sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus share an insertion on the medial tibia.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which quadriceps muscle, on the outer side of the thigh, is a common site for intramuscular injections, especially in infants?
options: Gracilis
Rectus femoris
Vastus lateralis
Vastus medialis
questions.why: The vastus lateralis is the large quadriceps muscle on the lateral side of the thigh, running from the greater trochanter and the lateral lip of the linea aspera to the tibial tuberosity. It is thick and well developed even in infants, so it is a standard injection site, especially for babies whose gluteal muscles are still small.
notes: The gracilis is a thin strap on the inner thigh, far too narrow for injections. It would be the answer for the medial thigh muscle that crosses the knee.

The rectus femoris runs down the middle of the front of the thigh. It is sometimes used as an alternative site, but the outer thigh muscle is the standard choice. Choose rectus femoris for the quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip.
Correct. The vastus lateralis is a common injection site, especially in infants.
The vastus medialis is on the inner side of the thigh near the knee. Major vessels run along the medial thigh, which makes it a poor injection site. Pick it for the medial part of the quadriceps.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient lies face down and bends the knee to pull the heel toward the buttock while the examiner pushes against the ankle. Which muscle group is being tested?
options: Hamstrings
Quadriceps
Adductors
Gluteal group
questions.why: Bringing the heel toward the buttock is flexion of the knee. The muscles that flex the knee against resistance are the hamstrings on the back of the thigh, which run from the ischial tuberosity to the tibia and fibula. Testing in the face-down position isolates this movement.
notes: Correct. Knee flexion against resistance tests the hamstrings.
The quadriceps extend the knee, straightening it. They would be tested by asking the patient to kick the leg straight while sitting.
The adductors pull the thigh toward the midline. To test them, an examiner would ask the patient to squeeze the knees together.
The gluteal group acts at the hip, mainly extending and abducting the thigh. They do not cross the knee, so they cannot bring the heel toward the buttock.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A doctor taps the patellar ligament just below the kneecap and the lower leg kicks forward. Which muscle group contracted to produce the kick?
options: Quadriceps femoris
Hamstrings
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Adductors
questions.why: The patellar ligament is the lower continuation of the quadriceps tendon. Tapping it briefly stretches the quadriceps, which contracts in response and extends the knee, so the lower leg kicks forward. This is the knee jerk, or patellar, reflex.
notes: Correct. The quadriceps contracts to extend the knee in the knee jerk.
The hamstrings flex the knee, which would pull the leg backward rather than forward. They are the antagonists of the muscle tested here.
The gastrocnemius and soleus attach to the heel through the calcaneal tendon. Pick them for the ankle reflex, tested by tapping the calcaneal tendon.
The adductors pull the thigh toward the midline and do not attach to the patellar ligament. Their contraction would not kick the leg forward.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the gluteus maximus and the gluteus medius?
options: Both insert on the lesser trochanter and adduct the thigh
Medius is superficial and extends; maximus is deeper and abducts
Maximus is superficial and extends; medius is deeper and abducts
Both lie deep to the gluteus minimus and flex the hip
questions.why: The gluteus maximus is the largest, most superficial gluteal muscle and the main hip extensor. The gluteus medius lies on the upper outer buttock, partly covered by the gluteus maximus, and inserts on the greater trochanter, where it abducts the thigh and keeps the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.
notes: The lesser trochanter receives the iliopsoas, and adduction is done by the medial thigh muscles. The gluteus maximus and medius insert on the gluteal tuberosity, the IT band, and the greater trochanter instead.
This swaps the two muscles. The gluteus maximus is the large surface muscle that extends, and the gluteus medius is the abductor partly beneath it.
Correct. The maximus is superficial and extends; the medius is deeper and abducts.
The gluteus minimus is the deepest of the three, so the other two lie on top of it, not beneath it. The gluteus maximus and medius also extend and abduct rather than flex the hip.
questions.answerText: Maximus is superficial and extends; medius is deeper and abducts
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which two muscles form the bulk of the calf and share the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon?
options: Gastrocnemius and soleus
Tibialis anterior and soleus
Tibialis posterior and gastrocnemius
Fibularis longus and brevis
questions.why: The gastrocnemius is the superficial two-headed calf muscle, and the soleus is the broad, flat muscle just deep to it. Both are in the posterior compartment of the leg, and both insert on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. Pulling on the heel bone, they plantarflex the foot, pointing the toes down.
notes: Correct. The gastrocnemius and soleus share the calcaneal tendon.
The tibialis anterior lies on the front of the leg beside the shin and dorsiflexes the foot. The soleus is right, but this pair mixes a front muscle with a calf muscle.
The tibialis posterior is a deep posterior muscle whose tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the bones of the foot. Only the gastrocnemius in this pair uses the calcaneal tendon.
The fibularis longus and brevis lie on the lateral side of the leg and evert the foot. Their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus rather than into the calcaneal tendon.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle of the anterior leg compartment is the main dorsiflexor of the foot?
options: Soleus
Tibialis posterior
Fibularis longus
Tibialis anterior
questions.why: The tibialis anterior lies along the lateral side of the shin in the anterior compartment. It runs from the tibia down across the front of the ankle to the medial side of the foot, so it pulls the top of the foot up toward the shin, which is dorsiflexion. It also inverts the foot.
notes: The soleus is a calf muscle of the posterior compartment that plantarflexes the foot. It does the opposite of dorsiflexion and is the answer for pointing the toes.
The tibialis posterior is a deep muscle of the posterior compartment, behind the tibia. It plantarflexes and inverts the foot, so it fits a question about inversion from the back of the leg.
The fibularis longus lies in the lateral compartment and everts the foot. It would be the answer for turning the sole outward.
Correct. The tibialis anterior is the main dorsiflexor of the foot.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscles of the lateral leg compartment evert the foot?
options: Tibialis anterior and posterior
Flexor digitorum and hallucis longus
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Fibularis longus and brevis
questions.why: The fibularis longus and fibularis brevis run down the lateral side of the leg along the fibula, and their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus into the foot. From that lateral path they pull the sole of the foot outward, which is eversion. Some texts call them the peroneus longus and brevis.
notes: The tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior both invert the foot, turning the sole inward. Pick this pair for a question about inversion, the opposite of eversion.
The flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus are deep posterior muscles that flex the toes. They would be the answer for curling the toes, including the big toe.
The gastrocnemius and soleus are the calf muscles that plantarflex the foot through the calcaneal tendon. They are the answer for standing on tiptoe.
Correct. The fibularis longus and brevis are the lateral compartment evertors.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the actions of the anterior and posterior leg compartments?
options: Anterior flexes the knee; posterior extends it
Anterior dorsiflexes the foot; posterior plantarflexes it
Anterior everts the foot; posterior inverts it
Anterior plantarflexes the foot; posterior dorsiflexes it
questions.why: Muscles in front of the ankle, in the anterior compartment, pull the top of the foot up toward the shin, which is dorsiflexion. Muscles behind the ankle, in the posterior compartment, pull the heel up and point the toes down, which is plantarflexion. The two compartments are antagonists across the ankle, much as the quadriceps and hamstrings are across the knee.
notes: Flexing and extending the knee are thigh actions, done by the hamstrings and quadriceps. The leg compartments act mainly at the ankle and toes.
Correct. The anterior compartment dorsiflexes and the posterior compartment plantarflexes.
Eversion is the job of the lateral compartment, the fibularis muscles. This option skips the lateral compartment, which is the answer for turning the sole outward.
This reverses the two compartments. A muscle in front of the ankle lifts the top of the foot, so the anterior compartment must be the dorsiflexor group.
questions.answerText: Anterior dorsiflexes the foot; posterior plantarflexes it
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Standing on tiptoe lifts the heel off the ground. Which tendon carries the pull of the calf muscles to the heel bone?
options: Calcaneal tendon
Patellar ligament
Iliotibial (IT) band
Tibialis posterior tendon
questions.why: Rising onto your toes is plantarflexion, done mainly by the gastrocnemius and soleus in the posterior compartment of the leg. Both muscles end in the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, the thickest tendon in the body, which attaches to the calcaneus, the heel bone. When the calf contracts, this tendon pulls the heel up.
notes: Correct. The gastrocnemius and soleus lift the heel through the calcaneal tendon.
The patellar ligament runs from the patella to the tibial tuberosity and carries the pull of the quadriceps. It is the answer for a question about straightening the knee, not lifting the heel.

The iliotibial (IT) band is a thick band of fascia on the lateral thigh, running from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia. It is pulled on by the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus and does not reach the heel.

The tibialis posterior tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the bones of the foot and helps invert the foot. It does not attach to the heel bone, so it fits a question about the deep posterior muscles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle runs along the lateral side of the tibial shaft and is the most superficial muscle of the anterior leg?
options: Tibialis posterior
Extensor digitorum longus
Tibialis anterior
Fibularis longus
questions.why: The tibialis anterior lies right against the lateral surface of the tibia, the shin bone, and you can feel it tighten just outside the sharp anterior border of the tibia when you lift your toes. It arises from the upper lateral tibia and its tendon crosses the front of the ankle to the medial side of the foot.
notes: The tibialis posterior is the deepest muscle on the back of the leg, lying on the interosseous membrane. Pick it for the deepest muscle of the posterior compartment.
The extensor digitorum longus is also in the anterior compartment, but it lies lateral to the tibialis anterior, closer to the fibula. Choose it for the muscle that extends the four lateral toes.
Correct. The tibialis anterior lies along the lateral side of the tibia on the front of the leg.
The fibularis longus lies on the lateral side of the leg along the fibula. It would be the answer for the larger muscle of the lateral compartment.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What two actions does the tibialis anterior perform at the foot?
options: Dorsiflexion and inversion
Plantar flexion and inversion
Plantar flexion and eversion
Dorsiflexion and eversion
questions.why: The tibialis anterior runs down the front of the leg, so it lifts the top of the foot toward the shin, which is dorsiflexion. Its tendon then crosses to the medial side of the foot and attaches to the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal, so it also pulls the sole to face inward, which is inversion.
notes: Correct. The tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
Plantar flexion with inversion describes the tibialis posterior in the deep posterior compartment. The tibialis anterior is on the front of the leg, so it dorsiflexes rather than plantar flexes.
Plantar flexion with eversion is the work of the fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment. Pick this pair for those muscles.

Dorsiflexion with eversion describes the fibularis tertius, the small anterior compartment muscle that inserts on the lateral side of the foot. The tibialis anterior pulls on the medial side, so it inverts.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main shared action of the muscles in the anterior compartment of the leg?
options: Knee flexion
Dorsiflexion
Plantar flexion
Eversion
questions.why: The anterior compartment holds the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. All of their tendons cross the front of the ankle, so they lift the top of the foot toward the shin, which is dorsiflexion. The two long extensors also straighten the toes.
notes: Knee flexion is done by the hamstrings and the gastrocnemius. The anterior leg muscles arise below the knee and do not cross it.
Correct. The anterior compartment muscles dorsiflex the foot.
Plantar flexion points the foot downward and is done by the posterior compartment, especially the gastrocnemius and soleus. It is the opposite of the anterior group's action.
Eversion turns the sole outward and is the main job of the lateral compartment, the fibularis longus and brevis. Only the small fibularis tertius in the anterior group helps with it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle extends the great toe and helps dorsiflex the foot?
options: Extensor hallucis longus
Fibularis tertius
Flexor hallucis longus
Extensor digitorum longus
questions.why: Hallux is the anatomical name for the great toe, so a muscle with hallucis in its name acts on the great toe. The extensor hallucis longus lies in the anterior compartment, between the tibialis anterior and the extensor digitorum longus, and its tendon runs over the top of the foot to the great toe. Because it crosses the front of the ankle, it also helps dorsiflex the foot.
notes: Correct. The extensor hallucis longus extends the great toe.
The fibularis tertius is a small anterior compartment muscle that inserts on the fifth metatarsal. It dorsiflexes and everts the foot but does not move any toe.
The flexor hallucis longus also acts on the great toe, but it lies in the deep posterior compartment and flexes the toe, curling it down. It is the antagonist of the correct answer.
The extensor digitorum longus extends the other four toes, numbers two through five. Pick it if the question asked about the lateral four toes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle extends toes two through five and helps dorsiflex the foot?
options: Flexor digitorum longus
Extensor hallucis longus
Tibialis anterior
Extensor digitorum longus
questions.why: Digitorum refers to the digits, here the four lateral toes. The extensor digitorum longus lies in the anterior compartment along the fibula, and its tendon splits on the top of the foot into four slips, one for each of toes two through five. Pulling on them straightens those toes, and because the muscle crosses the front of the ankle it also dorsiflexes the foot.
notes: The flexor digitorum longus reaches the same four toes but from the deep posterior compartment, so it curls them down. It is the antagonist of the correct answer.
The extensor hallucis longus extends only the great toe. Pick it when the question names the hallux or big toe.
The tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot but ends on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal. It does not move the toes.
Correct. The extensor digitorum longus extends the four lateral toes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle carries the fibularis name but belongs to the anterior compartment of the leg?
options: Tibialis anterior
Fibularis longus
Fibularis tertius
Fibularis brevis
questions.why: The fibularis tertius is a small muscle that looks like a fifth slip of the extensor digitorum longus. It lies in the anterior compartment and inserts on the top of the base of the fifth metatarsal, so it dorsiflexes and everts the foot. The other two fibularis muscles sit in the lateral compartment.
notes: The tibialis anterior is in the anterior compartment, but it does not carry the fibularis name. It would be the answer for the main dorsiflexor and invertor.
The fibularis longus is the larger, more superficial muscle of the lateral compartment. Pick it for the lateral muscle whose tendon crosses the sole of the foot.
Correct. The fibularis tertius lies in the anterior compartment despite its name.
The fibularis brevis is the smaller, deeper muscle of the lateral compartment and inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal. Choose it for the short fibularis muscle in the lateral group.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscles make up the lateral compartment of the leg?
options: Gastrocnemius and soleus
Tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis anterior and fibularis tertius
Fibularis longus and brevis
questions.why: The lateral compartment lies along the outer surface of the fibula and holds just two muscles, the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis. These muscles may also be called the peroneus longus and brevis. Their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus and they evert the foot.
notes: The gastrocnemius and soleus form the superficial posterior compartment, the calf. Choose them for the muscles that join the calcaneal tendon.
The tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus are in the deep posterior compartment. They would be the answer for muscles whose tendons pass behind the medial malleolus.
The tibialis anterior and fibularis tertius are in the anterior compartment and dorsiflex the foot. Pick this pair for front-of-leg muscles.
Correct. The fibularis longus and brevis form the lateral compartment.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the main action of the lateral compartment muscles of the leg?
options: Toe flexion
Dorsiflexion
Eversion
Inversion
questions.why: The fibularis longus and brevis run down the outer side of the leg and their tendons hook behind the lateral malleolus before reaching the foot. Pulling from the lateral side, they turn the sole of the foot outward, which is eversion. Because the tendons pass behind the ankle, they also help plantar flex.
notes: Toe flexion is done by the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus in the deep posterior compartment. The fibularis muscles end on the metatarsals and cuneiform, not on the toes.
Dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot and is the job of the anterior compartment. The fibularis tendons pass behind the ankle, so they plantar flex instead.
Correct. The lateral compartment everts the foot.
Inversion turns the sole inward and is done by the tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior, which pull on the medial side of the foot. It is the opposite of the lateral group's action.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The tendons of which two muscles curve behind the lateral malleolus?
options: Tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
Fibularis longus and brevis
questions.why: The lateral malleolus is the bump at the lower end of the fibula on the outside of the ankle. The tendons of the lateral compartment, the fibularis longus and brevis, run down the fibula and turn forward just behind this bump, held in place by the fibular retinacula. Using the malleolus as a pulley lets them evert the foot.
notes: The tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus tendons curve behind the medial malleolus on the inner side of the ankle. Pick them for the medial side.
The gastrocnemius and soleus end in the calcaneal tendon, which attaches to the back of the heel. They pass between the two malleoli rather than around either one.
The tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus tendons cross the front of the ankle under the extensor retinacula. Choose them for tendons on the top of the ankle.
Correct. The fibularis tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where does the fibularis brevis insert?
options: Base of the fifth metatarsal
Navicular bone
Calcaneus
Base of the first metatarsal
questions.why: The fibularis brevis arises from the lower lateral fibula, passes behind the lateral malleolus, and runs forward along the outer edge of the foot. It ends on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal, the bump you can feel halfway along the lateral border of the foot. Pulling there everts the foot.
notes: Correct. The fibularis brevis inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal.
The navicular bone receives the main insertion of the tibialis posterior on the medial side of the foot. Choose it for the deepest posterior muscle.
The calcaneus is the heel bone and receives the calcaneal tendon of the gastrocnemius and soleus. It would be the answer for the calf muscles.
The base of the first metatarsal, together with the medial cuneiform, receives the fibularis longus and the tibialis anterior. Pick it for the fibularis longus, whose tendon crosses the sole.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which leg muscle has a tendon that runs under the sole from lateral to medial and inserts near the same bones as the tibialis anterior?
options: Fibularis brevis
Flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior
Fibularis longus
questions.why: The fibularis longus tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, turns under the cuboid bone, and crosses the sole to the medial side, where it inserts on the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. The tibialis anterior reaches the same bones from above. Together the two tendons form a sling under the foot that helps support its arches.
notes: The fibularis brevis stays on the lateral side and inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal. Pick it for the lateral muscle that does not cross the sole.
The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs along the sole to the great toe, but it enters from behind the medial malleolus and ends on the toe, not on the cuneiform and metatarsal base.
The tibialis posterior enters the foot on the medial side, behind the medial malleolus, and inserts mainly on the navicular. It does not cross the sole from the lateral side.
Correct. The fibularis longus tendon crosses the sole to the medial side.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The two heads of the gastrocnemius arise from which structures?
options: Head of fibula and soleal line
Ischial tuberosity and linea aspera
Medial and lateral tibial condyles
Medial and lateral femoral condyles
questions.why: The gastrocnemius has a medial head and a lateral head that begin on the back of the medial and lateral condyles of the femur, just above the knee joint. The two bellies form the bulge of the calf and join into the calcaneal tendon. Because they start on the femur, the gastrocnemius crosses the knee as well as the ankle.
notes: The head of the fibula and the soleal line of the tibia are where the soleus arises. Pick them for the muscle lying deep to the gastrocnemius.
The ischial tuberosity and linea aspera are origins for the hamstrings, including the long and short heads of the biceps femoris. Choose them for posterior thigh muscles.
The tibial condyles lie just below the knee joint. If the gastrocnemius started there it would not cross the knee, so this is the mistake of placing it one bone too low.
Correct. The gastrocnemius heads arise from the femoral condyles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Because the gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and the ankle, which pair of actions can it perform?
options: Knee flexion and dorsiflexion
Knee extension and dorsiflexion
Knee flexion and plantar flexion
Knee extension and plantar flexion
questions.why: The gastrocnemius starts on the back of the femoral condyles and ends on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. Crossing the back of the knee, it helps bend the knee. Crossing the back of the ankle, it pulls the heel up and points the foot down, which is plantar flexion.
notes: Dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot and is the job of the anterior leg muscles, such as the tibialis anterior. The gastrocnemius pulls on the heel, which points the foot down.
This pair describes front-of-limb actions. Extending the knee and dorsiflexing the ankle come from the quadriceps and the anterior leg compartment, not from the calf.
Correct. The gastrocnemius flexes the knee and plantar flexes the foot.
Knee extension is done by the quadriceps on the front of the thigh. The gastrocnemius lies behind the knee, so it bends the knee rather than straightening it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which calf muscle lies directly deep to the gastrocnemius?
options: Plantaris
Soleus
Tibialis posterior
Fibularis longus
questions.why: The soleus is a broad, flat muscle that lies just under the gastrocnemius. It arises from the upper fibula and the soleal line of the tibia and joins the gastrocnemius in the calcaneal tendon. Its flat shape is where the name comes from, since it resembles the sole fish.
notes: The plantaris is a small muscle with a long, thin tendon. Its tendon runs between the gastrocnemius and soleus, but the muscle itself is not the broad layer under the gastrocnemius.
Correct. The soleus lies directly deep to the gastrocnemius.
The tibialis posterior is in the deep posterior compartment, beneath the soleus, lying on the interosseous membrane. Pick it for the deepest muscle on the back of the leg.
The fibularis longus is on the lateral side of the leg, not in the calf. Choose it for the lateral compartment muscle that everts the foot.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the soleus and the gastrocnemius?
options: Both cross only the ankle and dorsiflex the foot
Both cross the knee and insert on the tibial tuberosity
Gastrocnemius crosses only the ankle; soleus crosses knee and ankle
Soleus crosses only the ankle; gastrocnemius crosses knee and ankle
questions.why: Both muscles join the calcaneal tendon and plantar flex the foot. The difference is where they begin. The gastrocnemius starts on the femoral condyles, above the knee, so it also flexes the knee. The soleus starts on the tibia and fibula, below the knee, so it acts only at the ankle.
notes: Both calf muscles plantar flex, pointing the foot down. Dorsiflexion is the job of the anterior compartment, and the gastrocnemius also crosses the knee.
The tibial tuberosity receives the patellar ligament from the quadriceps. Both calf muscles insert on the calcaneus, and only the gastrocnemius crosses the knee.
This reverses the two muscles. The gastrocnemius is the one that reaches up to the femur, and the soleus starts on the leg bones.
Correct. The soleus crosses only the ankle, while the gastrocnemius crosses both.
questions.answerText: Soleus crosses only the ankle; gastrocnemius crosses knee and ankle
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A gym-goer does calf raises while seated with the knees bent at 90 degrees. Which muscle does most of the work of plantar flexion in this position?
options: Fibularis tertius
Tibialis anterior
Soleus
Gastrocnemius
questions.why: With the knee bent, the gastrocnemius is already shortened across the back of the knee because it arises from the femur. A shortened muscle cannot pull as hard, so it adds little force at the ankle. The soleus starts below the knee on the tibia and fibula, so knee position does not affect it, and it carries most of the load in a seated calf raise.
notes: The fibularis tertius dorsiflexes and everts the foot from the anterior compartment. It cannot raise the heel.
The tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the foot, lifting the toes. It works against a calf raise rather than producing it.
Correct. With the knee flexed, the soleus is the main plantar flexor.
The gastrocnemius is the main calf muscle in a standing calf raise with straight knees. With the knees bent it is slack across the knee, so it contributes less here.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon attaches which muscles to which bone?
options: Gastrocnemius and soleus to the talus
Tibialis posterior and soleus to the calcaneus
Quadriceps to the tibial tuberosity
Gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus
questions.why: The calcaneal tendon is the thick tendon at the back of the ankle, the strongest tendon in the body. It forms where the gastrocnemius and the soleus merge in the lower calf, and it anchors to the back of the calcaneus, the heel bone. Pulling on the heel lifts it and points the foot down.
notes: The talus sits above the calcaneus and forms the ankle joint with the tibia and fibula. No muscle tendon anchors to it, so it is the wrong bone for the calcaneal tendon.
The tibialis posterior is a deep muscle whose tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the navicular. It does not join the calcaneal tendon.
The quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament attach to the tibial tuberosity at the front of the knee. That is the knee's tendon system, not the heel's.
Correct. The calcaneal tendon joins the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus.
questions.answerText: Gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: During a basketball game a player feels a snap at the back of the heel and afterward cannot rise onto the toes on that side. Which structure was most likely torn?
options: Patellar ligament
Extensor retinaculum
Calcaneal tendon
Iliotibial (IT) band
questions.why: Rising onto the toes is plantar flexion, and the strongest plantar flexors, the gastrocnemius and soleus, act through the calcaneal tendon at the back of the heel. When that tendon ruptures, the calf can no longer pull on the calcaneus, so the heel cannot be lifted against body weight. The location of the snap fits as well.
notes: The patellar ligament is at the front of the knee and carries the pull of the quadriceps. A tear there would stop the person from straightening the knee, not rising onto the toes.
The extensor retinaculum is a band across the front of the ankle that holds down the dorsiflexor tendons. Damage there would not stop plantar flexion.
Correct. A snap at the back of the heel with loss of tiptoe rising points to the calcaneal tendon.
The IT band runs down the lateral thigh to the lateral condyle of the tibia. It is nowhere near the heel and does not raise it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which small posterior leg muscle has a short belly behind the knee and a very long, thin tendon running down between the gastrocnemius and soleus?
options: Plantaris
Soleus
Fibularis brevis
Flexor hallucis longus
questions.why: The plantaris arises just above the lateral femoral condyle, has a small belly behind the knee, and then becomes one of the longest, thinnest tendons in the body. The tendon runs down between the gastrocnemius and soleus to reach the calcaneus. It is a weak helper in plantar flexion and knee flexion, and it is sometimes absent.
notes: Correct. The plantaris has a small belly and a very long, thin tendon.
The soleus is a broad, flat muscle with a large belly in the lower calf. Pick it for the muscle lying directly under the gastrocnemius.
The fibularis brevis is in the lateral compartment along the lower fibula. It would be the answer for the muscle that inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal.
The flexor hallucis longus is a deep posterior muscle that arises from the fibula and ends on the great toe. Choose it for the muscle that flexes the hallux.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which three deep posterior leg muscles send their tendons behind the medial malleolus into the foot?
options: Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris
Fibularis longus, fibularis brevis, fibularis tertius
Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus
questions.why: The posterior leg has two layers. The superficial layer holds the gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris, which end on the calcaneus. Beneath them, the deep layer holds the tibialis posterior and the two long toe flexors, the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus. The tendons of these three pass behind the medial malleolus into the foot.
notes: The gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris form the superficial posterior compartment, the calf. Their tendons end on the calcaneus rather than passing behind the medial malleolus, so pick them for the muscles that act through or beside the calcaneal tendon.
This mixes compartments. The fibularis longus and brevis are lateral, but the fibularis tertius is anterior. None of the three is in the posterior compartment.
Correct. These three deep posterior muscles send their tendons behind the medial malleolus into the foot.
These are the main anterior compartment muscles, which dorsiflex the foot and extend the toes. They are the toe extensors, not the flexors.
questions.answerText: Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle is the deepest muscle on the back of the leg and both inverts and plantar flexes the foot?
options: Soleus
Fibularis longus
Tibialis anterior
Tibialis posterior
questions.why: The tibialis posterior lies on the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula, deeper than any other posterior leg muscle. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and attaches mainly to the navicular on the medial side of the foot. Pulling from behind the ankle and from the medial side, it plantar flexes and inverts the foot, and it helps support the medial arch.
notes: The soleus plantar flexes but is in the superficial posterior layer, under the gastrocnemius, and does not invert. Choose it for the flat calf muscle deep to the gastrocnemius.
