The fibularis longus plantar flexes but everts the foot and lies in the lateral compartment. It is the antagonist of the correct answer for inversion.
The tibialis anterior also inverts the foot, but it lies on the front of the leg and dorsiflexes. Pick it for the superficial muscle beside the shin.
Correct. The tibialis posterior is the deepest posterior muscle and inverts and plantar flexes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle flexes the great toe?
options: Flexor hallucis longus
Flexor digitorum longus
Extensor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior
questions.why: The flexor hallucis longus arises from the back of the fibula in the deep posterior compartment. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and runs along the sole to the distal phalanx of the great toe, so it curls the hallux down. This gives the strong push-off from the great toe in walking and running.
notes: Correct. The flexor hallucis longus flexes the great toe.
The flexor digitorum longus flexes the other four toes, numbers two through five. Pick it when the question asks about the lateral toes.
The extensor hallucis longus acts on the same toe from the front of the leg and lifts it rather than curling it. It is the antagonist of the correct answer.
The tibialis posterior is in the same deep compartment but ends on the navicular and other tarsal bones. It inverts and plantar flexes the foot without moving the toes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle flexes toes two through five?
options: Flexor digitorum longus
Extensor digitorum longus
Flexor hallucis longus
Fibularis brevis
questions.why: The flexor digitorum longus arises from the back of the tibia in the deep posterior compartment. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus, enters the sole, and splits into four tendons that reach the distal phalanges of toes two through five. Pulling on them curls those toes downward.
notes: Correct. The flexor digitorum longus flexes the four lateral toes.
The extensor digitorum longus reaches the same four toes from the anterior compartment and straightens them. It is the antagonist of the correct answer.
The flexor hallucis longus flexes only the great toe. Pick it when the question names the hallux.
The fibularis brevis is a lateral compartment muscle that inserts on the fifth metatarsal and everts the foot. It does not reach the toes.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Several tendons pass behind the medial malleolus. Which tendon lies closest to the malleolus, in front of the others?
options: Tibialis posterior
Flexor digitorum longus
Flexor hallucis longus
Fibularis longus
questions.why: Behind the medial malleolus, the structures line up in a set order from front to back: the tibialis posterior tendon, the flexor digitorum longus tendon, the posterior tibial artery and veins, the tibial nerve, and finally the flexor hallucis longus tendon. Students often remember this as Tom, Dick, And Very Nervous Harry. The tibialis posterior tendon sits in a groove right against the malleolus.
notes: Correct. The tibialis posterior tendon lies closest to the medial malleolus.
The flexor digitorum longus tendon is second in line, just behind the tibialis posterior. It would be the answer if the question asked which tendon comes next.
The flexor hallucis longus tendon is last in line, behind the artery, veins, and tibial nerve. Pick it for the most posterior structure behind the medial malleolus.
The fibularis longus tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus on the outer side of the ankle. It does not travel on the medial side at all.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle acts as the antagonist of the fibularis longus for movement of the sole inward and outward?
options: Fibularis tertius
Extensor digitorum longus
Fibularis brevis
Tibialis anterior
questions.why: The fibularis longus everts the foot, turning the sole outward. An antagonist produces the opposite movement, so the answer must invert the foot, turning the sole inward. The tibialis anterior inserts on the medial side of the foot and inverts it, making it the antagonist for this movement.
notes: The fibularis tertius dorsiflexes and everts the foot, so it also helps with eversion. Pick it for the fibularis muscle in the anterior compartment.
The extensor digitorum longus extends the lateral four toes and dorsiflexes the foot. It does not invert the foot, so it cannot oppose eversion.
The fibularis brevis also everts the foot, so it works with the fibularis longus as a synergist rather than against it.
Correct. The tibialis anterior inverts the foot and opposes the eversion of the fibularis longus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which structure separates the anterior compartment of the leg from the deep posterior compartment?
options: Interosseous membrane
Calcaneal tendon
Plantar aponeurosis
Extensor retinaculum
questions.why: The interosseous membrane is a sheet of dense connective tissue stretched between the tibia and fibula along their length. Together with the two bones, it forms a wall between the front and back of the leg. Muscles of the anterior compartment arise from its front surface and the tibialis posterior arises from its back surface.
notes: Correct. The interosseous membrane divides the anterior and posterior compartments.
The calcaneal tendon attaches the calf muscles to the heel. It lies at the back of the ankle and does not divide compartments.
The plantar aponeurosis is a thick sheet of fascia on the sole of the foot. Choose it for the structure that supports the longitudinal arch.
The extensor retinaculum is a band across the front of the ankle that holds the anterior tendons in place. Pick it for the structure that keeps those tendons from bowing out.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What holds the tendons of the anterior leg muscles against the front of the ankle so they do not bow outward when the foot dorsiflexes?
options: Fibular retinacula
Plantar aponeurosis
Flexor retinaculum
Extensor retinacula
questions.why: A retinaculum is a band of thickened deep fascia that holds tendons in place where they cross a joint. At the front of the ankle, the superior and inferior extensor retinacula strap down the tendons of the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and fibularis tertius. Without them, the tendons would lift away from the ankle like a bowstring.
notes: The fibular retinacula hold the fibularis longus and brevis tendons behind the lateral malleolus. Pick them for the band on the outside of the ankle.
The plantar aponeurosis is the thick fascia on the sole of the foot. It supports the arches rather than holding tendons at the front of the ankle.
The flexor retinaculum spans the medial side of the ankle from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus. Choose it for the band that roofs the tarsal tunnel.
Correct. The extensor retinacula hold the anterior tendons at the ankle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which bands hold the fibularis longus and brevis tendons in place behind the lateral malleolus?
options: Fibular retinacula
Flexor retinaculum
Extensor retinacula
Interosseous membrane
questions.why: The fibularis tendons curve behind the lateral malleolus, using it as a pulley. The superior and inferior fibular retinacula, also called the peroneal retinacula, hold these tendons in their groove on the outside of the ankle so they stay in place as the foot moves.
notes: Correct. The fibular retinacula hold the fibularis tendons.
The flexor retinaculum lies on the medial side of the ankle and covers the tendons of the deep posterior muscles. It is the mirror image of the correct answer on the opposite side.
The extensor retinacula cross the front of the ankle and hold the anterior compartment tendons. Pick them for the tendons of the tibialis anterior and the toe extensors.
The interosseous membrane joins the tibia and fibula along the leg. It separates compartments rather than holding tendons at the ankle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On the medial side of the ankle, which band forms the roof of a tunnel that carries the deep posterior tendons, the posterior tibial vessels, and the tibial nerve?
options: Flexor retinaculum
Superior extensor retinaculum
Superior fibular retinaculum
Plantar aponeurosis
questions.why: The flexor retinaculum stretches from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus. It covers the passage called the tarsal tunnel, through which the tendons of the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus travel into the sole, along with the posterior tibial artery and veins and the tibial nerve.
notes: Correct. The flexor retinaculum roofs the tarsal tunnel on the medial ankle.
The superior extensor retinaculum lies across the front of the leg just above the ankle. Pick it for the band holding down the dorsiflexor tendons.
The superior fibular retinaculum lies on the lateral ankle behind the lateral malleolus. It holds the fibularis tendons, not the deep posterior ones.
The plantar aponeurosis spreads across the sole from the calcaneus toward the toes. It supports the arch but does not form a tunnel at the medial ankle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient's toes drag on the ground when he walks, so he lifts the knee high with each step. Weakness of which group of leg muscles best explains this?
options: Anterior compartment
Deep posterior compartment
Lateral compartment
Superficial posterior compartment
questions.why: To clear the ground while the leg swings forward, the foot must be held in dorsiflexion, with the toes lifted. The anterior compartment muscles, led by the tibialis anterior, do this. When they are weak the foot hangs down, a problem called foot drop, and the person lifts the knee unusually high so the toes do not catch.
notes: Correct. Weak dorsiflexors in the anterior compartment cause the toes to drag.
The deep posterior compartment inverts the foot and flexes the toes. Weakness there would affect push-off and the medial arch rather than lifting of the toes.
The lateral compartment everts the foot. Weakness there makes the ankle prone to rolling inward but does not stop the toes from lifting.
The superficial posterior compartment, the calf, plantar flexes the foot. Weakness there would make it hard to push off or rise onto the toes, not cause the toes to drag.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dancer has weak lateral compartment muscles and keeps rolling her ankle so the sole turns inward. Which movement are the weak muscles failing to produce?
options: Inversion
Knee flexion
Eversion
Dorsiflexion
questions.why: Rolling the ankle with the sole turning inward is excessive inversion. The muscles that resist it are the evertors, which turn the sole outward. The fibularis longus and brevis of the lateral compartment are the main evertors, so when they are weak, nothing pulls back against a sudden inward roll.
notes: Inversion is the movement that is happening too much. It is produced by the tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior, not by the weak lateral muscles.
Knee flexion is done by the hamstrings and gastrocnemius. The lateral compartment muscles arise from the fibula below the knee and do not cross it.
Correct. The lateral compartment muscles evert the foot and resist inward rolling.
Dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot and is the job of the anterior compartment. The fibularis muscles pass behind the ankle and plantar flex instead.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: To screen a patient's leg muscles, an examiner asks her to walk on her heels with her toes lifted off the floor. Which muscle group is mainly being tested?
options: Superficial posterior compartment
Deep posterior compartment
Anterior compartment
Lateral compartment
questions.why: Walking on the heels requires holding the foot in dorsiflexion so the front of the foot stays off the floor. That is the job of the anterior compartment muscles, especially the tibialis anterior. Walking on the toes would instead test the plantar flexors of the calf.
notes: The superficial posterior compartment, the gastrocnemius and soleus, would be tested by walking on the toes, which needs strong plantar flexion.
The deep posterior compartment inverts the foot and flexes the toes. It is not what keeps the forefoot lifted during heel walking.
Correct. Heel walking tests the dorsiflexors of the anterior compartment.
The lateral compartment everts the foot. Heel walking does not depend on turning the sole outward.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A muscle arises from the interosseous membrane and the backs of the tibia and fibula, and its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the navicular. Which compartment holds this muscle?
options: Anterior compartment
Deep posterior compartment
Superficial posterior compartment
Lateral compartment
questions.why: A muscle that arises from the back of the interosseous membrane lies in the deepest layer of the posterior leg. A tendon passing behind the medial malleolus to the navicular describes the tibialis posterior, the deepest muscle of the deep posterior compartment.
notes: Anterior compartment muscles arise from the front of the interosseous membrane and their tendons cross the front of the ankle, not behind the medial malleolus.
Correct. This is the tibialis posterior in the deep posterior compartment.
The superficial posterior compartment holds the gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris, which reach the calcaneus through or beside the calcaneal tendon, not the navicular.
Lateral compartment muscles arise from the outer fibula and their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus. They are the mirror image of this muscle on the other side of the ankle.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Pressing down on a car's gas pedal points the foot downward. Which movement is this, and which group mainly produces it?
options: Plantar flexion by the anterior leg muscles
Dorsiflexion by the anterior leg muscles
Plantar flexion by the calf muscles
Dorsiflexion by the calf muscles
questions.why: Pointing the foot downward is plantar flexion. It is produced mainly by the gastrocnemius and soleus, which pull up on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon and so tip the front of the foot down. The anterior leg muscles do the reverse, lifting the foot in dorsiflexion as you ease off the pedal.
notes: The movement is named correctly, but the anterior leg muscles lie in front of the ankle and lift the foot. They are the antagonists of plantar flexion.
Dorsiflexion by the anterior leg muscles is a correct pairing, but it describes lifting the foot off the pedal. Pick it for the movement of releasing the gas.
Correct. Pressing the pedal is plantar flexion by the calf muscles.
Dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot, which is easing off the pedal, and the calf muscles cannot produce it because they pull on the heel.
questions.answerText: Plantar flexion by the calf muscles
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which muscle forms most of the visible bulge of the calf?
options: Soleus
Plantaris
Tibialis posterior
Gastrocnemius
questions.why: The gastrocnemius is the most superficial muscle on the back of the leg. Its two heads form the rounded, diamond-shaped bulge of the upper calf just below the knee. The soleus lies beneath it and shows mainly at the sides of the lower calf.
notes: The soleus is large but lies deep to the gastrocnemius and is mostly hidden by it. Pick it for the broad flat muscle under the gastrocnemius.
The plantaris is a small muscle with a thin tendon and adds almost nothing to the shape of the calf. Choose it for the muscle with a very long, slender tendon.
The tibialis posterior is the deepest posterior leg muscle, lying on the interosseous membrane. It cannot be seen or felt as part of the calf bulge.
Correct. The gastrocnemius forms the main bulge of the calf.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis?
options: Brevis arises higher and crosses the sole; longus ends on the fifth metatarsal
Both lie in the anterior compartment and dorsiflex the foot
Longus arises higher and crosses the sole; brevis ends on the fifth metatarsal
Both pass behind the medial malleolus and invert the foot
questions.why: The fibularis longus starts on the head and upper shaft of the fibula and is the more superficial of the two. Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, turns under the cuboid, and crosses the sole to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal. The fibularis brevis lies under it on the lower fibula and ends on the base of the fifth metatarsal. Both evert the foot.
notes: This swaps the two muscles. Longus means long, so the fibularis longus has the longer course, starting higher and crossing the whole sole.
The anterior compartment holds the fibularis tertius, not these two. The fibularis longus and brevis are in the lateral compartment and evert rather than dorsiflex.
Correct. The longus is higher and crosses the sole; the brevis ends on the fifth metatarsal.
The medial malleolus is passed by the deep posterior tendons, which invert the foot. The fibularis tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus and evert.
questions.answerText: Longus arises higher and crosses the sole; brevis ends on the fifth metatarsal
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: How do most muscles of facial expression differ from typical skeletal muscles of the limbs?
options: They contract without any nerve signal reaching them
They insert into the skin instead of onto a bone
They lack an origin and attach only at an insertion
They are made of smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle
questions.why: Most muscles of facial expression arise from bones of the skull but insert into the skin of the face or into other facial muscles rather than onto a bone. When they contract, they pull on the skin, which is how they produce smiles, frowns, and raised eyebrows. Limb muscles, in contrast, usually cross a joint and insert on a bone to move it.
notes: Like all skeletal muscle, facial muscles contract only when a motor nerve signals them, which is why nerve damage can paralyze one side of the face. This choice confuses skeletal muscle with cardiac muscle, which has its own pacemaker.
Correct. Pulling on skin rather than bone is what lets these muscles change facial expression.

Every skeletal muscle has an origin and an insertion; for most facial muscles the origin is on a skull bone. This choice comes from noticing the unusual insertion and assuming the origin is missing too.

Facial muscles are skeletal muscle under voluntary control, with striated fibers like any limb muscle. Smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs and vessels, which would be the answer for involuntary muscle in the digestive tract.
questions.answerText: They insert into the skin instead of onto a bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle closes the eyelids, as in blinking?
options: Orbicularis oculi
Levator palpebrae superioris
Frontalis
Orbicularis oris
questions.why: The orbicularis oculi is a ring of muscle around the eye. Its fascicles are arranged in a circle, so contracting it squeezes the eyelids closed like a sphincter, for blinking or squinting tightly. Its name tells you this: orbicularis means small circle, and oculi means of the eye.
notes: Correct. The orbicularis oculi is the circular muscle that closes the eyelids.
The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid, the opposite of blinking. It would be the answer for which muscle opens the eye.
The frontalis raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. Choose it if the question asked which muscle produces a look of surprise.
The orbicularis oris is the matching ring of muscle around the mouth, which closes and purses the lips. Pick it if the question asked which muscle you use to whistle or kiss.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle closes and purses the lips?
options: Buccinator
Orbicularis oculi
Orbicularis oris
Zygomaticus major
questions.why: The orbicularis oris encircles the mouth, with fascicles arranged in rings that act like a sphincter. Contracting it closes the lips and pushes them forward, as when whistling or kissing. Its name means small circle of the mouth.
notes: The buccinator is the cheek muscle that presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food between the teeth while chewing and helping blow out air. It would be the answer for the trumpeter's muscle.
The orbicularis oculi is the ring of muscle around the eye that closes the eyelids. Pick it if the question asked about blinking or squinting.
Correct. The orbicularis oris is the circular muscle around the mouth.
The zygomaticus major pulls the corner of the mouth up and back to smile. Choose it for a question about which muscle raises the corners of the mouth.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead?
options: Orbicularis oculi
Occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis
Procerus
Frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis
questions.why: The occipitofrontalis has two bellies joined by a flat sheet of tendon over the top of the skull, the galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis). The frontal belly, over the forehead, inserts into the skin of the eyebrows; when it contracts it raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The occipital belly at the back anchors the aponeurosis and pulls the scalp backward.
notes: The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids. Pick it if the question asked which muscle produces a blink or a squint.
The occipital belly lies over the back of the skull and pulls the scalp backward. It would be the answer for the part of the occipitofrontalis attached to the occipital bone.

The procerus is a small muscle over the bridge of the nose that pulls the skin between the eyebrows downward, wrinkling the bridge of the nose as in a frown. It works against the frontal belly, not with it.
Correct. The frontal belly lifts the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which chewing muscle elevates the mandible and can be felt bulging at the angle of the jaw when you clench your teeth?
options: Lateral pterygoid
Temporalis
Buccinator
Masseter
questions.why: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch down to the angle and lateral surface of the ramus of the mandible. It is the prime mover for closing the jaw and one of the strongest muscles for its size. Because it lies just under the skin at the back of the cheek, you can feel it harden at the angle of the jaw when you clench your teeth.
notes: The lateral pterygoid is a deep chewing muscle that pulls the mandible forward and moves it side to side, and it cannot be felt from the surface. Choose it for a question about protracting the jaw.

The temporalis also elevates the mandible, but it is a fan-shaped muscle over the side of the skull that you feel at the temple, not at the angle of the jaw. Pick it if the question described the muscle at the temple.
The buccinator is the thin cheek muscle that presses the cheek against the teeth and helps blow out air. It is not one of the chewing muscles that close the jaw.
Correct. The masseter closes the jaw and bulges at its angle when you clench.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which fan-shaped muscle over the temporal bone elevates and retracts the mandible?
options: Masseter
Zygomaticus major
Temporalis
Medial pterygoid
questions.why: The temporalis has a broad, fan-shaped origin on the temporal fossa on the side of the skull, and its fascicles converge onto the coronoid process of the mandible. It elevates the mandible to close the jaw, and its posterior fibers retract it (pull it backward). Its name comes from its location over the temporal bone.
notes: The masseter also elevates the mandible, but it runs from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the jaw and is not fan-shaped. Pick it for the muscle that bulges at the jaw angle when clenching.
The zygomaticus major is a muscle of facial expression that pulls the corner of the mouth up to smile; it does not move the mandible. It would be the answer for the smiling muscle.
Correct. The temporalis fans over the temple and closes and retracts the jaw.

The medial pterygoid lies deep, on the inner side of the ramus, and helps elevate the mandible and move it side to side. It is not over the temporal bone, so choose it for a question about the deep grinding muscles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which deep muscles of mastication move the mandible from side to side for grinding food?
options: Buccinator and orbicularis oris
Sternohyoid and omohyoid
Medial and lateral pterygoids
Masseter and temporalis
questions.why: The medial and lateral pterygoids lie deep to the ramus of the mandible and arise mainly from the sphenoid bone. When the pterygoids on one side contract, they pull the mandible toward the opposite side, and alternating sides produces the side-to-side grinding motion of chewing. The lateral pterygoids also pull the jaw forward.
notes: These are muscles of facial expression around the mouth; the buccinator keeps food between the teeth and the orbicularis oris closes the lips. They do not move the mandible.
The sternohyoid and omohyoid are infrahyoid neck muscles that pull the hyoid bone down. Choose them for a question about the strap muscles in front of the neck.
Correct. The pterygoids produce the side-to-side grinding movement of the jaw.

The masseter and temporalis are the superficial chewing muscles, and their main job is elevating the mandible to close the jaw. Pick them for a question about which muscles harden when you clench your teeth.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: When you clench your teeth, you can feel one muscle harden over the back of your cheek and another over your temple. Which two muscles are these?
options: Buccinator and frontal belly
Medial and lateral pterygoids
Masseter and temporalis
Masseter and sternocleidomastoid
questions.why: The masseter and the temporalis are the two superficial muscles of mastication, and both elevate the mandible to close the jaw. The masseter lies over the back of the cheek near the angle of the jaw, and the temporalis fans over the side of the skull at the temple. Because both are close to the surface, clenching makes both easy to feel.
notes: The buccinator is the thin cheek muscle, and the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis raises the eyebrows. Neither closes the jaw, so neither hardens strongly when you clench.
The pterygoids are deep chewing muscles hidden behind the ramus of the mandible, so they cannot be felt through the skin. Pick them for a question about grinding the jaw from side to side.
Correct. The masseter and temporalis both close the jaw and lie just under the skin.

The masseter is right, but the sternocleidomastoid is a neck muscle running from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. It flexes the neck and turns the head, so it is not the muscle felt at the temple.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process, flexing the neck and turning the head?
options: Platysma
Sternohyoid
Trapezius
Sternocleidomastoid
questions.why: The sternocleidomastoid is named for its attachments: the sternum, the clavicle (cleido), and the mastoid process of the temporal bone. When both sides contract together, they flex the neck, bringing the chin toward the chest. When one side contracts alone, it turns the face toward the opposite side.
notes: The platysma is a thin sheet of muscle in the superficial fascia of the anterior neck, extending from the upper chest to the mandible. It tenses the skin of the neck rather than turning the head; choose it for the thin muscle that stands out as cords when you grimace.

The sternohyoid runs from the sternum up to the hyoid bone and pulls the hyoid down during swallowing and speech. It shares a sternal origin, which causes the mix-up, but it does not reach the mastoid process.

The trapezius is the large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and back of the neck, running from the occipital bone and spinous processes to the clavicle and scapula. Pick it for a question about elevating or retracting the scapula.
Correct. The name of the sternocleidomastoid lists its attachments.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: When the right sternocleidomastoid contracts alone, which way does the face turn?
options: Down toward the chest
Up toward the ceiling
Toward the left side
Toward the right side
questions.why: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the sternum and clavicle in front up to the mastoid process behind the ear. When the right muscle shortens, it pulls the right mastoid process down and forward, which rotates the head so the face turns toward the left, the opposite side. You can see and feel the right muscle stand out when you turn your face to the left.
notes: Bringing the chin down toward the chest is flexion of the neck, which happens when both sternocleidomastoids contract together. Pick this if the question asked what the two muscles do at the same time.
Tilting the head back to look up is extension, done mainly by muscles at the back of the neck. A single sternocleidomastoid contracting alone rotates the head rather than tipping it back.
Correct. One sternocleidomastoid turns the face toward the opposite side.
This is the side of the muscle that contracted, not the direction the face turns. Because the muscle attaches behind the ear, pulling that point forward swings the chin to the opposite side.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: How many extraocular muscles move each eyeball?
options: Seven: four recti, two obliques, and a levator
Eight: four recti and four obliques
Four: the four recti only
Six: four recti and two obliques
questions.why: Six extraocular muscles attach to each eyeball and move it: the superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti, and the superior and inferior obliques. The recti pull the eye up, down, in, and out, while the obliques help with rotation and diagonal movements. The levator palpebrae superioris sits in the orbit too, but it raises the upper eyelid rather than moving the eyeball.
notes: Seven counts the levator palpebrae superioris, which lies in the orbit with the eye muscles but inserts into the upper eyelid. Pick seven only if the question asked for all the muscles in the orbit listed on the lab structure list.
There are only two obliques, superior and inferior, not four. This choice assumes the obliques come in the same four-way set as the recti.
The four recti do move the eye, but this leaves out the two obliques. Without the superior and inferior obliques, the eye could not make its rotating and diagonal movements.
Correct. Four recti and two obliques move each eye.
questions.answerText: Six: four recti and two obliques
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which extraocular muscle turns the eye laterally, away from the nose?
options: Inferior rectus
Superior rectus
Medial rectus
Lateral rectus
questions.why: The lateral rectus attaches to the lateral side of the eyeball, so when it contracts it pulls the front of the eye outward, away from the nose. This movement is called abduction of the eye. Its partner on the opposite side of the eyeball, the medial rectus, pulls the eye toward the nose.
notes: The inferior rectus attaches to the bottom of the eyeball and mainly depresses the eye, turning the gaze downward. Choose it for looking down.
The superior rectus attaches to the top of the eyeball and mainly elevates the eye, turning the gaze upward. It would be the answer for looking up.
The medial rectus attaches to the side of the eye nearest the nose and turns the eye medially, the opposite movement. Pick it if the question asked which muscle turns the eye toward the nose.
Correct. The lateral rectus abducts the eye, turning it outward.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Two muscles of facial expression are named orbicularis because their fascicles form rings. Which pair is it, and what does each ring surround?
options: Orbicularis oculi around the mouth; orbicularis oris around the eye
Orbicularis oculi around the eye; orbicularis oris around the mouth
Orbicularis oris around the mouth; buccinator around the cheek
Orbicularis oculi around the eye; platysma around the neck
questions.why: Orbicularis is a shape term for a circular muscle, and both orbicularis muscles have fascicles in concentric rings around an opening. Orbicularis oculi rings the eye and closes the eyelids, as in blinking and squinting. Orbicularis oris rings the mouth and closes and purses the lips.
notes: Both names are right, but the openings are swapped. Oculi goes with the eye and oris with the mouth.
Correct. Oculi rings the eye and oris rings the mouth.
The buccinator lies in the cheek and presses it against the teeth. It inserts into the orbicularis oris but is not a ring muscle itself.
The platysma is a broad sheet over the neck, from the fascia of the upper chest to the mandible and the corner of the mouth. It does not form a ring.
questions.answerText: Orbicularis oculi around the eye; orbicularis oris around the mouth
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares zygomaticus major and zygomaticus minor?
options: Both start on the maxilla; major elevates the upper lip, minor draws the mouth corner up and out.
Both start on the zygomatic bone; major elevates the upper lip, minor draws the mouth corner up and out.
Both start on the zygomatic bone; major draws the mouth corner up and out, minor elevates the upper lip.
Major starts on the zygomatic bone and minor on the mandible; both pull the mouth corner down.
questions.why: Both zygomaticus muscles start on the zygomatic bone. Zygomaticus major inserts on the angle of the mouth and draws the corner up and out, as in smiling. Zygomaticus minor inserts on the upper lip and elevates it.
notes: Both start on the zygomatic bone, as their names say, not the maxilla, and the two actions are swapped.
The origin is right, but the actions are swapped. Major inserts on the angle of the mouth and minor on the upper lip.
Correct. Major pulls the corner of the mouth into a smile, and minor lifts the upper lip.
Neither zygomaticus starts on the mandible or pulls the mouth down. Pulling the corner down is the job of the depressor anguli oris.
questions.answerText: Both start on the zygomatic bone; major draws the mouth corner up and out, minor elevates the upper lip.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: The buccinator and the masseter both lie in the cheek region. Which statement correctly classifies them?
options: The buccinator is a muscle of mastication; the masseter is a muscle of facial expression.
The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression; the masseter is a muscle of mastication.
Both are muscles of mastication, and both elevate the mandible to close the jaw.
Both are muscles of facial expression, and both press the cheek against the teeth.
questions.why: The buccinator runs from the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible to the orbicularis oris at the angle of the mouth, and it presses the cheek against the teeth. It is grouped with the muscles of facial expression. The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch to the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible and is the prime mover for closing the jaw, so it is a muscle of mastication.
notes: This swaps the two groups. The masseter moves the mandible, which makes it a chewing muscle, and the buccinator is grouped with facial expression.
Correct. The buccinator works on the cheek, and the masseter closes the jaw.
The masseter elevates the mandible, but the buccinator does not move the jaw. It keeps food between the teeth by pressing the cheek inward.
The buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth, but the masseter pulls on the mandible to close the jaw. That makes it a muscle of mastication.
questions.answerText: The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression; the masseter is a muscle of mastication.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: After a cheek injury, a patient can still bite and chew, but food keeps collecting between the cheek and the teeth on that side. Which muscle is most likely weakened, and why does that fit?
options: Masseter, which elevates the mandible for chewing
Orbicularis oris, which closes and purses the lips
Buccinator, which presses the cheek against the teeth
Zygomaticus major, which draws the mouth corner up
questions.why: The buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth, which keeps food between the teeth while chewing. If it is weak, the cheek is not held in and food slips into the space beside the teeth. Biting and chewing still work because the muscles of mastication that move the jaw are not affected.
notes: The masseter closes the jaw, and the patient can still bite and chew. A weak masseter would make closing the jaw weak, not let food collect in the cheek.
The orbicularis oris closes and purses the lips. It rings the mouth and does not hold the cheek against the teeth.
Correct. A weak buccinator lets food slip out from between the teeth.
The zygomaticus major draws the corner of the mouth up and out in smiling. It does not hold the cheek against the teeth.
questions.answerText: Buccinator, which presses the cheek against the teeth
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: On a head model, a thin muscle over the forehead raises the eyebrows, and its upper edge ends in a broad flat sheet over the top of the skull. What is that sheet, and which muscle do you reach by following it to the back of the head?
options: The galea aponeurotica, leading to the temporalis
The ligamentum nuchae, leading to the trapezius
The galea aponeurotica, leading to the orbicularis oculi
The galea aponeurotica, leading to the occipital belly
questions.why: The muscle over the forehead is the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis, which starts on the galea aponeurotica, also called the epicranial aponeurosis. The galea is the broad flat sheet over the top of the skull. Its back edge receives the occipital belly, which starts on the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone and pulls the scalp backward.
notes: The temporalis fans over the temporal fossa on the side of the skull and inserts on the coronoid process of the mandible. It is a chewing muscle and does not attach to the galea.
The ligamentum nuchae runs down the back of the neck and gives origin to the trapezius. It is not the sheet over the top of the skull.
The orbicularis oculi rings the eye, in front of and below the frontal belly. Following the galea backward leads away from it.
Correct. The galea joins the frontal belly in front to the occipital belly behind.
questions.answerText: The galea aponeurotica, leading to the occipital belly
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: A muscle on a model starts on the fascia over the upper pectoralis major and deltoid and ends on the lower border of the mandible and the skin at the corner of the mouth. Which muscle is it, and what does it do?
options: Sternocleidomastoid; it flexes the neck and turns the face.
Platysma; it elevates the mandible to close the jaw.
Depressor anguli oris; it pulls the mouth corner down.
Platysma; it tenses the neck skin and pulls the mouth corner down.
questions.why: A thin sheet that rises from the fascia of the upper chest and shoulder to the mandible and the corner of the mouth is the platysma. It is a muscle of facial expression even though most of it lies over the neck. It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the lower lip and the corner of the mouth down.
notes: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the manubrium and medial clavicle to the mastoid process. It does not reach the mandible or the skin of the mouth.
The muscle is the platysma, but it pulls the lip and mouth corner down rather than closing the jaw. Elevating the mandible is done by the muscles of mastication.
The depressor anguli oris does pull the corner of the mouth down, but it starts on the body of the mandible, not on fascia over the chest and shoulder.
Correct. Those attachments belong to the platysma, which tenses the neck skin and pulls the mouth down.
questions.answerText: Platysma; it tenses the neck skin and pulls the mouth corner down.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle of mastication attaches to the disc of the temporomandibular joint?
options: Medial pterygoid
Masseter
Lateral pterygoid
Temporalis
questions.why: The lateral pterygoid inserts on the neck of the mandible and the disc of the temporomandibular joint. It starts on the greater wing of the sphenoid and the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate. It protrudes the mandible and opens the jaw.
notes: The medial pterygoid inserts on the medial surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible, not the joint disc.
The masseter inserts on the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible, below the joint.
Correct. The lateral pterygoid inserts on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc.
The temporalis inserts on the coronoid process of the mandible, in front of the joint, not on its disc.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which two muscles of mastication sandwich the ramus of the mandible, one attached to its lateral surface and one to its medial surface?
options: Masseter and medial pterygoid
Temporalis and lateral pterygoid
Masseter and temporalis
Medial and lateral pterygoids
questions.why: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch to the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible. The medial pterygoid runs from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate to the medial surface of the ramus and angle. They hold the ramus between them from outside and inside, and both elevate the mandible.
notes: Correct. The masseter covers the outer ramus and the medial pterygoid the inner ramus.
The temporalis inserts on the coronoid process and the lateral pterygoid on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc. Neither attaches along the flat surfaces of the ramus.
The masseter does cover the lateral ramus, but the temporalis inserts on the coronoid process, not the medial surface of the ramus.
The medial pterygoid does attach to the inner ramus, but the lateral pterygoid inserts on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc, not the outer ramus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which two muscles of mastication both protrude the mandible, pushing the lower jaw forward?
options: Masseter and temporalis
Temporalis and lateral pterygoid
Medial and lateral pterygoids
Masseter and medial pterygoid
questions.why: The medial pterygoid elevates and protrudes the mandible, and the lateral pterygoid protrudes it and opens the jaw. Both start on the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid and both help with side to side grinding. The temporalis does the opposite of protrusion, retracting the mandible.
notes: Both of these elevate the mandible to close the jaw, and the temporalis also retracts it, pulling it back. Neither pushes the jaw forward.
The lateral pterygoid does protrude the mandible, but the temporalis retracts it, the opposite movement.
Correct. Both pterygoids protrude the mandible.
The medial pterygoid protrudes the mandible, but the masseter only elevates it. These two are the pair that holds the ramus between them.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: A fracture of the zygomatic arch tears the origin of the chewing muscle that starts there and ends on the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible. Which jaw movement is weakened most?
options: Opening the jaw, since the lateral pterygoid starts there
Closing the jaw, since the masseter is its prime mover
Side to side grinding, since the medial pterygoid starts there
Pulling the jaw back, since the temporalis starts there
questions.why: The muscle from the zygomatic arch to the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible is the masseter. The masseter elevates the mandible and is the prime mover for closing the jaw. Tearing its origin weakens that movement most, even though the temporalis and the medial pterygoid also help close the jaw.
notes: The lateral pterygoid starts on the greater wing of the sphenoid and the lateral pterygoid plate, not the zygomatic arch.
Correct. The masseter starts on the zygomatic arch and is the prime mover for closing the jaw.
The medial pterygoid starts on the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, deep to the ramus, not on the zygomatic arch.
The temporalis starts in the temporal fossa of the skull, above the zygomatic arch, and inserts on the coronoid process.
questions.answerText: Closing the jaw, since the masseter is its prime mover
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: After a deep jaw injury, a patient can still clench the teeth firmly, but opening the mouth wide is weak. Which muscle of mastication is most likely weakened, and where does it insert?
options: Masseter, on the lateral ramus and angle of the mandible
Temporalis, on the coronoid process of the mandible
Lateral pterygoid, on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc
Medial pterygoid, on the medial ramus and angle of the mandible
questions.why: Of the four muscles of mastication, only the lateral pterygoid helps open the jaw; it also protrudes the mandible. It runs from the greater wing of the sphenoid and the lateral pterygoid plate to the neck of the mandible and the disc of the temporomandibular joint. Clenching still works because the masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid all close the jaw.
notes: The masseter is the prime mover for closing the jaw, and the patient can still clench. It does not help open the mouth.
The temporalis elevates and retracts the mandible, so it closes the jaw rather than opening it.
Correct. The lateral pterygoid helps open the jaw and inserts on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc.
The medial pterygoid elevates and protrudes the mandible, so it helps close the jaw. It does not help open the mouth.
questions.answerText: Lateral pterygoid, on the neck of the mandible and the joint disc

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: On a deep model, one jaw muscle starts on the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, and another starts on the lateral surface of the same plate. Which statement identifies the two and their main difference in action?
options: Medial pterygoid helps open the jaw; lateral pterygoid elevates it.
Medial pterygoid retracts the jaw; lateral pterygoid elevates it.
Both pterygoids elevate the jaw, and neither helps to open it.
Medial pterygoid elevates the jaw; lateral pterygoid helps open it.
questions.why: The muscle from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate is the medial pterygoid, which elevates and protrudes the mandible. The muscle from the lateral surface of the plate and the greater wing of the sphenoid is the lateral pterygoid, which protrudes the mandible and opens the jaw. Both help with side to side grinding, but only the lateral pterygoid helps open the jaw.
notes: The two muscles are named correctly by their surfaces, but their actions are swapped. The medial pterygoid elevates the mandible, and the lateral pterygoid helps open it.
Neither pterygoid retracts the mandible; both protrude it. Retraction is done by the temporalis.
The medial pterygoid does elevate the jaw, but the lateral pterygoid opens it. It is the one muscle of mastication that is not a jaw closer.
Correct. The medial pterygoid closes the jaw and the lateral pterygoid helps open it.
questions.answerText: Medial pterygoid elevates the jaw; lateral pterygoid helps open it.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which suprahyoid muscle forms the floor of the mouth?
options: Geniohyoid
Stylohyoid
Mylohyoid
Thyrohyoid
questions.why: The mylohyoid runs from the mylohyoid line on the inside of the mandible to the body of the hyoid. It elevates the hyoid and forms the floor of the mouth. Like the other suprahyoid muscles, it sits above the hyoid bone.
notes: The geniohyoid runs from the inner surface of the mandible at the chin to the hyoid and pulls the hyoid up and forward. The muscle named as the floor of the mouth is the mylohyoid.
The stylohyoid runs from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the hyoid and elevates and retracts the hyoid. It runs from behind, not across the floor of the mouth.
Correct. The mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth.
The thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that runs from the thyroid cartilage up to the hyoid, below the hyoid in the front of the neck. It is not part of the floor of the mouth.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: The scalene muscles run from the cervical vertebrae down to which ribs?
options: Ribs 3 to 5
Ribs 7 to 12
Ribs 1 and 2
Rib 12 only
questions.why: The scalenes start on the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae. The anterior and middle scalenes insert on rib 1, and the posterior scalene inserts on rib 2. That is why the scalenes elevate ribs 1 and 2.
notes: Ribs 3 to 5 give origin to the pectoralis minor in the muscle charts, not the scalenes.
The inner surfaces of ribs 7 to 12 give origin to the diaphragm. The scalenes stop at the first two ribs.
Correct. The anterior and middle scalenes reach rib 1, and the posterior scalene reaches rib 2.
Rib 12 is an attachment of the quadratus lumborum, low on the back. The scalenes reach only the first two ribs.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which neck muscle has a belly that starts on the superior border of the scapula?
options: Sternohyoid
Omohyoid
Sternothyroid
Thyrohyoid
questions.why: The omohyoid starts on the superior border of the scapula and reaches the body of the hyoid. It has two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon. It is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid.
notes: The sternohyoid starts on the manubrium and the medial clavicle, not the scapula.
Correct. The omohyoid runs from the superior border of the scapula to the hyoid.
The sternothyroid starts on the posterior surface of the manubrium and ends on the thyroid cartilage.
The thyrohyoid starts on the thyroid cartilage and ends on the body and greater horn of the hyoid.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which list contains only suprahyoid muscles?
options: Sternohyoid, omohyoid, thyrohyoid, sternothyroid
Digastric, sternohyoid, mylohyoid, omohyoid
Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, stylohyoid, geniohyoid
Digastric, mylohyoid, stylohyoid, geniohyoid
questions.why: The hyoid bone sorts the anterior neck muscles. Suprahyoid muscles sit above it and elevate it: the digastric, mylohyoid, stylohyoid, and geniohyoid. Infrahyoid muscles sit below it and depress it: the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid, and thyrohyoid.
notes: These are the four infrahyoid muscles. They sit below the hyoid and depress it or the larynx.
The digastric and mylohyoid are suprahyoid, but the sternohyoid and omohyoid are infrahyoid. This list mixes the two groups.
The stylohyoid and geniohyoid are suprahyoid, but the sternocleidomastoid and the scalenes do not attach to the hyoid at all.
Correct. All four sit above the hyoid and elevate it.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the sternohyoid and the sternothyroid?
options: Both start on the manubrium; the sternohyoid ends on the thyroid cartilage and the sternothyroid on the hyoid.
Both end on the body of the hyoid; the sternohyoid elevates it and the sternothyroid depresses it.
Both start on the superior border of the scapula and end together on the body of the hyoid.
Both start on the manubrium; the sternohyoid ends on the hyoid and the sternothyroid on the thyroid cartilage.
questions.why: The sternohyoid starts on the manubrium and the medial clavicle and ends on the body of the hyoid, which it depresses. The sternothyroid starts on the posterior surface of the manubrium and ends on the thyroid cartilage, and it depresses the larynx. Each name gives its two attachments.
notes: Both start on the manubrium, but the endings are swapped. The second half of each name tells you where it ends.
Only the sternohyoid ends on the hyoid, and it depresses it. Both are infrahyoid muscles, so neither elevates the hyoid.
The superior border of the scapula is the origin of the omohyoid. The sternohyoid and sternothyroid both start on the manubrium.
Correct. Each name gives its attachments: sterno to hyoid, and sterno to thyroid.
questions.answerText: Both start on the manubrium; the sternohyoid ends on the hyoid and the sternothyroid on the thyroid cartilage.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: On a model, a muscle has two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon that is held to the hyoid by a fibrous loop. One belly runs to the mandible near the midline and the other to the mastoid notch. Which muscle is it, and what does it do?
options: Digastric; it elevates the hyoid and depresses the mandible.
Omohyoid; it depresses the hyoid toward the scapula.
Digastric; it depresses the hyoid and elevates the mandible.
Mylohyoid; it elevates the hyoid and forms the mouth floor.
questions.why: Two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon describe both the digastric and the omohyoid, so the attachments decide it. This muscle runs to the mandible and the mastoid notch, above the hyoid, which makes it the suprahyoid digastric rather than the omohyoid, which runs down to the scapula. The digastric elevates the hyoid and depresses the mandible.
notes: Correct. Bellies to the mandible and mastoid notch mark the digastric, which raises the hyoid and lowers the mandible.
The omohyoid also has two bellies on an intermediate tendon, but it runs from the superior border of the scapula, below the hyoid, not to the mandible and mastoid notch.
The muscle is the digastric, but its actions are reversed. As a suprahyoid muscle it elevates the hyoid, and it depresses the mandible.
The mylohyoid runs from the mylohyoid line inside the mandible to the body of the hyoid. It has no intermediate tendon and does not reach the mastoid notch.
questions.answerText: Digastric; it elevates the hyoid and depresses the mandible.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: During a hard breath in, a student feels muscles tighten on the side of the neck that run from the cervical transverse processes down to the first two ribs. Which muscles are these, and what are they doing to the ribs?
options: The scalenes, elevating ribs 1 and 2
The sternocleidomastoids, flexing the neck
The scalenes, depressing ribs 1 and 2
The infrahyoids, depressing the larynx
questions.why: Muscles from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae to rib 1 and rib 2 are the scalenes. They elevate ribs 1 and 2 and also flex the neck to the same side. Lifting the first two ribs is the movement the student feels during the deep breath in.
notes: Correct. The scalenes run from the cervical transverse processes to ribs 1 and 2 and elevate them.
The sternocleidomastoid runs from the manubrium and medial clavicle to the mastoid process. It does not attach to the cervical transverse processes or the first two ribs.
The muscles are the scalenes, but they elevate ribs 1 and 2. Depressing the ribs is the job of muscles such as the internal intercostals.
The infrahyoid muscles run between the sternum, scapula, thyroid cartilage, and hyoid. They do not attach to the cervical transverse processes or the ribs.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: The thyrohyoid runs from the thyroid cartilage up to the body and greater horn of the hyoid. If the suprahyoid muscles hold the hyoid still, what does the thyrohyoid move when it contracts?
options: It lowers the hyoid down toward the thyroid cartilage.
It raises the thyroid cartilage, elevating the larynx.
It lowers the thyroid cartilage, depressing the larynx.
It raises the mandible, closing the jaw against the teeth.
questions.why: A muscle pulls its two attachments toward each other, and whichever bone is held still stays put. The thyrohyoid depresses the hyoid when the larynx is the steady end, but with the hyoid held fixed by the suprahyoid muscles, its pull lifts the thyroid cartilage toward the hyoid instead. That is how the thyrohyoid elevates the larynx.
notes: Lowering the hyoid is the thyrohyoid's action when the larynx is the steady end. Here the hyoid is held still, so the thyroid cartilage moves instead.
Correct. With the hyoid fixed, the thyrohyoid lifts the thyroid cartilage and the larynx.
Depressing the larynx is the job of the sternothyroid, which pulls the thyroid cartilage down toward the manubrium. The thyrohyoid pulls it up.
The thyrohyoid does not reach the mandible. Closing the jaw is done by the muscles of mastication.
questions.answerText: It raises the thyroid cartilage, elevating the larynx.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: What is the trochlea of the orbit?
options: A tendon ring at the back of the orbit where the four recti start
A pulley on the frontal bone for the superior oblique tendon
A small muscle in the orbit that raises the upper eyelid
A bony ridge on the maxilla where the inferior oblique starts
questions.why: The trochlea is a pulley on the frontal bone. The tendon of the superior oblique passes through it on its way to the superior lateral surface of the eyeball, behind its middle. The superior oblique moves the eye down and laterally.
notes: That describes the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit, where the four rectus muscles start.
Correct. The trochlea is the pulley that the superior oblique tendon runs through.
That describes the levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the upper eyelid.
The inferior oblique starts on the floor of the orbit at the front, on the maxilla. The trochlea is on the frontal bone and serves the superior oblique.
questions.answerText: A pulley on the frontal bone for the superior oblique tendon

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which muscle in the orbit raises the upper eyelid?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris
Superior rectus
Superior oblique
Orbicularis oculi
questions.why: The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid. It is learned with the extraocular muscles because it lies in the orbit, but it moves the eyelid, not the eyeball. Levator is an action term, the same one used for muscles that elevate a structure.
notes: Correct. The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid.
The superior rectus moves the eyeball up and toward the midline. It does not lift the eyelid.
The superior oblique moves the eyeball down and laterally. It does not lift the eyelid.
The orbicularis oculi is a muscle of facial expression that closes the eye, the opposite of raising the lid.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which four extraocular muscles share an origin at the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit?
options: Superior and inferior recti, plus both obliques
Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti
Medial and lateral recti, plus both obliques
Both obliques, plus the medial and superior recti
questions.why: All four rectus muscles start on the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit and run forward to attach to the eyeball. The obliques start elsewhere. The superior oblique starts on the body of the sphenoid above and medial to the optic canal, and the inferior oblique starts on the floor of the orbit at the front, on the maxilla.
notes: The superior and inferior recti do start on the ring, but the obliques do not. The superior oblique starts on the sphenoid and the inferior oblique on the maxilla.
Correct. The common tendinous ring is the origin of all four recti.
The medial and lateral recti do start on the ring, but the two obliques start elsewhere in the orbit.
The medial and superior recti start on the ring, but neither oblique does. The inferior oblique starts at the front of the orbit floor.
questions.answerText: Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which pair of extraocular muscles moves the eye in opposite directions, one toward the nose and one away from it?
options: Superior rectus and inferior rectus
Superior oblique and inferior oblique
Medial rectus and lateral rectus
Lateral rectus and superior oblique
questions.why: The medial rectus attaches to the medial surface of the eyeball and adducts the eye, moving it toward the nose. The lateral rectus attaches to the lateral surface and abducts the eye, moving it away from the nose. They form an opposing pair.
notes: The superior and inferior recti move the eye up and down, both toward the midline. They oppose each other vertically, not toward and away from the nose.
The superior oblique moves the eye down and laterally, and the inferior oblique moves it up and laterally. Both move it away from the nose.
Correct. The medial rectus adducts and the lateral rectus abducts.
The lateral rectus and superior oblique both move the eye laterally, away from the nose. They do not pull in opposite directions.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the superior rectus and the superior oblique?
options: Both move the eye upward, because both attach on the top of the eyeball.
The superior rectus moves the eye down and laterally; the superior oblique moves it up and toward the midline.
Both start on the common tendinous ring and move the eye up and toward the midline.
The superior rectus moves the eye up and toward the midline; the superior oblique moves it down and laterally.
questions.why: The superior rectus starts on the common tendinous ring and attaches to the superior surface of the eyeball, moving it up and toward the midline. The superior oblique starts on the body of the sphenoid, runs its tendon through the trochlea, and attaches to the superior lateral surface behind the middle of the eyeball. It moves the eye down and laterally, even though it attaches near the top.
notes: Both attach near the top, but the superior oblique moves the eye down and laterally. Only the superior rectus moves it up.
This swaps the two actions. The superior rectus moves the eye up and toward the midline, and the superior oblique moves it down and laterally.
Only the superior rectus starts on the common tendinous ring. The superior oblique starts on the body of the sphenoid and moves the eye down and laterally.
Correct. The superior rectus lifts the eye, and the superior oblique turns it down and out.
questions.answerText: The superior rectus moves the eye up and toward the midline; the superior oblique moves it down and laterally.

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: On an orbit model, a muscle starts on the sphenoid above and medial to the optic canal, and its tendon turns through a pulley on the frontal bone before attaching to the superior lateral eyeball behind its middle. Which muscle is it, and which way does it move the eye?
options: Superior rectus, moving the eye up and toward the midline
Superior oblique, moving the eye up and laterally
Inferior oblique, moving the eye up and laterally
Superior oblique, moving the eye down and laterally
questions.why: A tendon that passes through the trochlea, the pulley on the frontal bone, belongs to the superior oblique. Its origin on the body of the sphenoid, above and medial to the optic canal, and its insertion on the superior lateral surface behind the middle of the eyeball confirm it. The superior oblique moves the eye down and laterally.
notes: The superior rectus starts on the common tendinous ring and runs straight to the top of the eyeball. It has no pulley in its path.
The muscle is the superior oblique, but it moves the eye down and laterally. Up and laterally is the action of the inferior oblique.
The inferior oblique starts on the floor of the orbit at the front, on the maxilla, and has no pulley in its path. It moves the eye up and laterally.
Correct. The pulley identifies the superior oblique, which moves the eye down and laterally.
questions.answerText: Superior oblique, moving the eye down and laterally

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: At rest, a patient's right eye drifts toward the nose, and the patient cannot turn that eye outward. The other eye muscles test normally. Which muscle is weak, and why does the eye drift inward?
options: The lateral rectus, so the medial rectus pulls the eye inward unopposed
The medial rectus, so the lateral rectus pulls the eye inward unopposed
The inferior oblique, so the superior oblique pulls the eye inward
The lateral rectus, so the superior rectus pulls the eye inward unopposed
questions.why: The lateral rectus abducts the eye, turning it away from the nose, and the medial rectus adducts it, turning it toward the nose. They are an opposing pair. If the lateral rectus is weak, the eye cannot turn outward, and the normal medial rectus pulls it toward the nose with nothing to balance it.
notes: Correct. A weak lateral rectus leaves the medial rectus unopposed.
The medial rectus pulls the eye toward the nose, and the lateral rectus pulls it away. A weak medial rectus would let the eye drift outward, not inward.
Both obliques move the eye laterally, not toward the nose, so neither explains an inward drift. The patient's problem is turning the eye outward.
The weak muscle is right, but the direct opponent of the lateral rectus is the medial rectus. The superior rectus mainly moves the eye up.
questions.answerText: The lateral rectus, so the medial rectus pulls the eye inward unopposed

questions.topic: Muscles of the head and neck
questions.q: A patient's upper eyelid droops, but the eye itself moves normally up, down, toward the nose, and away from it. Which muscle is most likely affected?
options: Superior rectus
Levator palpebrae superioris
Orbicularis oculi
Superior oblique
questions.why: Normal movement in every direction means the four recti and the two obliques are working. The muscle in the orbit that raises the upper eyelid is the levator palpebrae superioris, so a drooping lid with normal eye movement points to it.
notes: The superior rectus moves the eyeball up and toward the midline, and the eye moves up normally here. It does not lift the lid.
Correct. The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid, and the eye movers are normal.
The orbicularis oculi closes the eye. A drooping lid points to the muscle that raises the lid, not the one that closes it.
The superior oblique moves the eye down and laterally, and those movements are normal here. It does not lift the lid.

questions.q: Which list names the four paired muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall?
options: Rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, quadratus lumborum
Rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
Rectus femoris, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
Rectus abdominis, external oblique, serratus anterior, transversus abdominis
questions.why: The anterolateral abdominal wall has four paired muscles. The rectus abdominis runs vertically on each side of the midline, and three flat muscles layer the sides: the external oblique on the surface, the internal oblique beneath it, and the transversus abdominis deepest. Together they support and protect the abdominal organs and move the trunk.
notes: The quadratus lumborum lies in the posterior abdominal wall, between the iliac crest and the last rib. It would be the answer for a muscle of the back wall of the abdomen.
Correct. These are the four paired muscles of the front and sides of the abdomen.
The rectus femoris is a quadriceps muscle on the front of the thigh. Students pick it because its name looks like rectus abdominis, but it belongs to the thigh.
The serratus anterior is a chest wall muscle on the side of the ribs that holds the scapula against the thorax. It fits a question about the thorax and shoulder, not the abdominal wall.
questions.answerText: Rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis

questions.q: Which abdominal wall muscle has fibers that run vertically from the pubis up to the lower ribs and sternum?
options: Transversus abdominis
Rectus abdominis
External oblique
Internal oblique
questions.why: Rectus means straight, and the rectus abdominis runs straight up the front of the abdomen on each side of the midline, from the pubis to the xiphoid process and the lower costal cartilages. Because its fibers run vertically, its main action is to flex the trunk, pulling the rib cage toward the pelvis as in a sit-up.
notes: The transversus abdominis is the deepest flat muscle, and its fibers run horizontally across the abdomen like a belt. It is the answer for the muscle whose fibers run transversely.
Correct. The rectus abdominis is the vertical, straight muscle of the abdomen.
The external oblique is the most superficial flat muscle on the side of the abdomen, and its fibers run downward and toward the midline. Pick it for the outer diagonal layer.

The internal oblique lies just deep to the external oblique, and its fibers run upward and toward the midline, roughly at right angles to the external oblique. It is the answer for the middle diagonal layer.

questions.q: The linea alba is a fibrous band running down the midline of the abdomen. What forms it?
options: Costal cartilages of the lower ribs fused together
The falciform ligament fused to the parietal peritoneum
Tendinous intersections crossing the rectus abdominis
Aponeuroses of both sides meeting at the midline
questions.why: An aponeurosis is a flat, sheet-like tendon. The three flat abdominal muscles on each side end in aponeuroses that wrap the rectus abdominis and then meet their partners from the other side in the midline. Where they interweave from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, they form a tough white line, the linea alba (white line).
notes: The costal cartilages connect the ribs to the sternum and sit above the abdomen. They are the answer for the cartilage that forms the edges of the rib cage, not a midline band of the abdominal wall.

The falciform ligament is a fold of peritoneum inside the abdomen that attaches the liver to the anterior wall. It lies deep to the abdominal muscles, so it is the answer for a liver question, not the linea alba.
Tendinous intersections are the horizontal fibrous bands that cross the rectus abdominis and create the separate bulges of a six-pack. They run across the muscle rather than down the midline.
Correct. The linea alba is where the aponeuroses of both sides meet in the midline.
questions.answerText: Aponeuroses of both sides meeting at the midline

questions.q: Which sequence lists the three flat abdominal muscles from superficial to deep?
options: External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
Transversus abdominis, internal oblique, external oblique
External oblique, transversus abdominis, internal oblique
Internal oblique, external oblique, transversus abdominis
questions.why: The external oblique is the outermost flat muscle, with fibers running down and toward the midline. Beneath it the internal oblique runs roughly at right angles to it, and deepest of all the transversus abdominis runs horizontally. Because the fibers of the three layers run in different directions, like the layers of plywood, together they make a strong wall from three thin sheets.
notes: Correct. External oblique, then internal oblique, then transversus abdominis.
This is the correct sequence read from deep to superficial. Pick it only if a question asks you to start next to the peritoneum and work outward.
This places the transversus abdominis in the middle, but it is the deepest of the three, lying just outside the peritoneum. The internal oblique is the middle layer.
This puts the internal oblique on the surface, but external means outer, so the external oblique must come first. The names tell you the order of the two oblique muscles.
questions.answerText: External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis

questions.q: A fit athlete has a visible six-pack, the rectus abdominis crossed by bands. Which vertical band separates the left half of the six-pack from the right?
options: Tendinous intersections
Inguinal ligament
Linea semilunaris
Linea alba
questions.why: The two rectus abdominis muscles lie side by side, one on each side of the midline. Between them runs the linea alba, the white line formed where the aponeuroses of the left and right abdominal muscles meet. On a lean athlete it shows as the vertical groove down the center of the six-pack.
notes: Tendinous intersections are the horizontal fibrous bands across each rectus abdominis that divide it into the separate blocks of the six-pack. They are the answer for the horizontal lines, not the vertical one.
The inguinal ligament is the lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It marks the crease between the abdomen and thigh.
The linea semilunaris is a curved line along the lateral edge of each rectus abdominis, where it meets the flat muscles. It marks the outer border of the six-pack rather than the midline.
Correct. The linea alba is the vertical midline band between the two rectus muscles.

questions.q: Which abdominal wall muscle is named for fascicles that run horizontally across the abdomen?
options: Transversus abdominis
Rectus abdominis
External abdominal oblique
Internal abdominal oblique
questions.why: Transversus means across, so the transversus abdominis has fascicles running horizontally around the abdomen. It is the deepest of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall, lying under the external and internal obliques.
notes: Correct. Transversus means across, so its fascicles run horizontally.
Rectus means straight. The rectus abdominis fascicles run vertically, from the pubic crest up to the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages.
Oblique means at an angle, so the external oblique runs diagonally, not horizontally. It is the most superficial of the three flat muscles.
The internal oblique is also named for fascicles that run at an angle, not across. It is the middle layer of the three flat muscles.

questions.q: On a cadaver, you cut and fold back the external oblique and then the internal oblique on the side of the abdomen. Which muscle is now exposed, and which way do its fascicles run?
options: Transversus abdominis, running horizontally
Rectus abdominis, running vertically
Transversus abdominis, running vertically
Rectus abdominis, running horizontally
questions.why: The three flat muscles on the side of the abdomen are layered from superficial to deep as the external oblique, the internal oblique, and the transversus abdominis. Once both obliques are folded back, the transversus abdominis is exposed. Its name means across, so its fascicles run horizontally, a third direction that adds strength the way the layers of plywood do.
notes: Correct. The transversus abdominis is the deepest flat muscle, and its fascicles run across.
The rectus abdominis does run vertically, but it lies at the front of the abdomen beside the linea alba, not deep to the obliques on the side.
The muscle is right, but transversus means across, so its fascicles run horizontally. Vertical fascicles belong to the rectus abdominis.
The rectus abdominis lies at the front beside the linea alba, and its name means straight, for vertical fascicles. Neither part fits the deep muscle on the side.

questions.q: Both rectus abdominis muscles are traced on a cadaver from the pubic crest up to the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7. If the pelvis is held still, what does contracting both muscles do?
options: Extends the trunk, pulling the rib cage backward
Rotates the trunk, turning the chest toward one side
Flexes the trunk, pulling the rib cage toward the pelvis
Elevates the ribs, lifting the front of the chest
questions.why: The rectus abdominis runs from the pubic crest and symphysis below to the xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5 to 7 above. With the pelvis held still, the muscle pulls the rib cage and sternum down toward the pubis. That bends the trunk forward, which is trunk flexion, and it also compresses the abdomen.
notes: The rectus abdominis lies on the front of the trunk, so it pulls the trunk forward. Extending the vertebral column is the job of back muscles such as the erector spinae.
Rotating the spine is an action of the external and internal obliques, whose fascicles run at an angle. The vertical rectus abdominis flexes the trunk.
Correct. Pulling the rib cage toward the pubis flexes the trunk.
Elevating the ribs is done by muscles such as the external intercostals and the scalenes. The rectus abdominis pulls the rib cage down, not up.
questions.answerText: Flexes the trunk, pulling the rib cage toward the pelvis
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a pelvis model viewed from above, a thin muscular sheet runs from the pubis and the ischial spine back to the coccyx and the perineal body, forming most of the pelvic floor. Which muscle is it, and what does it do?
options: Transversus abdominis; it compresses the abdomen.
Levator ani; it flexes the trunk toward the pelvis.
Rectus abdominis; it holds up the pelvic organs.
Levator ani; it holds up the pelvic organs.
questions.why: A sheet running from the pubis and the ischial spine to the coccyx and the perineal body is the levator ani. Together with the coccygeus it forms the pelvic diaphragm, the muscular floor of the pelvis. It holds up the pelvic organs and resists the downward pressure when you cough or strain.
notes: The transversus abdominis is the deepest flat muscle of the abdominal wall. It does compress the abdomen, but it ends on the linea alba and pubic crest, not the coccyx and perineal body.
