questions.why: More pumps clear Ca2+ from the cytosol more quickly, so troponin empties sooner and the crossbridges shut down earlier, giving a briefer twitch. Fast twitch fibers really do have a higher density of SERCA than slow fibers for this reason. Pumping does consume ATP, but not at a rate that starves the crossbridges in a single twitch, and the number of pumps does not shorten excitation contraction coupling or raise the amount of Ca2+ released per impulse.
questions.answerText: Relaxation is faster, because cytosolic Ca2+ falls sooner

questions.q: A person is exposed to an irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Trace the sequence from the enzyme failure to the weakness that follows the initial twitching.
options: Acetylcholine accumulates, the end plate stays depolarized, and Na+ channels remain inactivated
Acetylcholine accumulates, the terminal runs out of vesicles, and release stops
Acetylcholine accumulates, SERCA is inhibited directly, and Ca2+ can no longer be cleared
Acetylcholine accumulates, the receptors are internalized within seconds, and the end plate potential vanishes
questions.why: The chain runs from the cleft into the muscle membrane. With no enzyme, transmitter stays bound, the end plate holds a maintained depolarization, and voltage gated Na+ channels in the neighboring sarcolemma pass into their inactivated state, from which they cannot recover until the membrane repolarizes. The result is a depolarizing block, weakness caused by too much transmitter. Vesicle depletion and receptor internalization are much slower processes, and the poison does not act on SERCA.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine accumulates, the end plate stays depolarized, and Na+ channels remain inactivated

questions.q: A patient has a partial SERCA deficiency. After vigorous exercise, muscles tighten and are slow to loosen, yet strength and the speed of onset of contraction are normal. Explain the pattern.
options: The deficiency slows acetylcholine clearance, so the fibers keep firing after exercise
Contraction depends on Ca2+ removal and relaxation depends on Ca2+ release, so the deficit appears only at rest
Both contraction and relaxation depend on SERCA, so the normal strength must be due to a compensating pump
Contraction depends on Ca2+ release, which is intact, while relaxation depends on Ca2+ removal, which is limited
questions.why: Separating the two halves of the Ca2+ cycle explains the whole picture. Release through the ryanodine receptor is untouched, so each contraction starts on time and reaches normal force, but a weak pump clears Ca2+ slowly, and during rapid repeated activation the cytosol accumulates Ca2+ faster than it can be removed, so the muscle stays partly activated. The deficit therefore worsens with exercise rather than appearing at rest, and the lesion is inside the fiber, not at the junction.
questions.answerText: Contraction depends on Ca2+ release, which is intact, while relaxation depends on Ca2+ removal, which is limited

questions.q: Two fibers both relax abnormally slowly. In fiber A the end plate potential lasts 40 ms instead of 3 ms. In fiber B the end plate potential is normal but the Ca2+ transient decays slowly. Assign the defects.
options: Fiber A has impaired SERCA function, fiber B has impaired acetylcholine clearance
Fiber A has impaired acetylcholine clearance, fiber B has impaired SERCA function
Both have impaired SERCA function, since both relax slowly
Both have impaired acetylcholine clearance, since both start with a synaptic event
questions.why: Each measurement isolates one termination mechanism. A prolonged end plate potential means transmitter is not being cleared from the cleft, which is an acetylcholinesterase problem, and the slow relaxation follows from repeated firing. A normal end plate potential with a slowly decaying Ca2+ signal means the electrical events are fine and the pump inside the fiber is the limiting step. Slow relaxation alone cannot distinguish them, which is exactly why the two extra measurements are given.
questions.answerText: Fiber A has impaired acetylcholine clearance, fiber B has impaired SERCA function

questions.q: During sustained intense exercise, both the acetylcholine system and the Ca2+ system are stressed. Which single change would most directly slow relaxation without changing how quickly force develops?
options: A fall in the rate of Ca2+ uptake by SERCA
A fall in the number of nicotinic receptors at the end plate
A rise in the amount of Ca2+ released per action potential
A fall in acetylcholine release per nerve impulse
questions.why: Force development is driven by how fast Ca2+ rises and crossbridges attach, while relaxation is set by how fast Ca2+ is pumped away, so slowing the pump lengthens the falling phase and leaves the rising phase alone. Less transmitter release or fewer receptors would cause some fibers to drop out entirely, reducing force rather than slowing relaxation. More Ca2+ released per impulse would raise force and could lengthen the transient, but it acts on the release side rather than on the removal step the question asks about.
questions.answerText: A fall in the rate of Ca2+ uptake by SERCA

questions.q: What is a muscle twitch?
options: The electrical response of a fiber to a single nerve impulse
A sustained contraction produced by repeated stimulation
The smallest force a whole muscle can produce
The mechanical response of a fiber to a single action potential
questions.why: A twitch is one contraction and relaxation cycle following one action potential, and it is the basic mechanical unit from which all larger responses are built. The electrical event is the action potential itself, which is a separate and much briefer signal. A sustained response to repeated stimulation is tetanus, and the smallest force a whole muscle can produce depends on how many motor units are recruited, not on the twitch of a single fiber.
questions.answerText: The mechanical response of a fiber to a single action potential

questions.q: On a twitch tracing, what defines the latent period?
options: The interval between the stimulus and the first measurable rise in tension
The interval between peak tension and the return to baseline
The interval during which the action potential is still propagating along the axon
The interval between two successive stimuli
questions.why: The latent period is the delay you can see on the tracing before force starts to rise, and in skeletal muscle it lasts only a few milliseconds. The fall from peak back to baseline is the relaxation phase. Axonal conduction is not what the tracing shows, since the latent period is measured on the muscle itself, and the interval between stimuli is a property of the stimulator rather than of the twitch.
questions.answerText: The interval between the stimulus and the first measurable rise in tension

questions.q: What is happening inside the fiber during the latent period of a twitch?
options: Acetylcholine is still being synthesized in the nerve terminal
Crossbridges are cycling but the force has not yet been measured
Excitation contraction coupling, up to Ca2+ binding troponin
SERCA is pumping Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: Nothing mechanical can happen until the action potential has run down the T tubules, opened the release channels, raised cytosolic Ca2+, and moved tropomyosin, and those steps take the few milliseconds the latent period occupies. Some slack in the series elastic elements is also taken up at the very start. Crossbridge cycling marks the beginning of the contraction phase rather than the latent period, and Ca2+ reuptake belongs to relaxation.
questions.answerText: Excitation contraction coupling, up to Ca2+ binding troponin

questions.q: What limits how fast tension rises during the contraction phase of a twitch?
options: The rate at which acetylcholine is cleared from the synaptic cleft
The rate at which crossbridges attach and stretch the elastic elements
The rate at which SERCA removes Ca2+ from the cytosol
The conduction velocity of the motor axon
questions.why: Once Ca2+ has uncovered the binding sites, the rise of force reflects how quickly heads attach and how quickly the tendons and other elastic structures in series with the fibers are pulled taut. Ca2+ removal governs the falling phase, not the rising one. Transmitter clearance and axonal conduction are over long before tension peaks and affect timing only through the latent period.
questions.answerText: The rate at which crossbridges attach and stretch the elastic elements

questions.q: What limits the duration of the relaxation phase of a twitch?
options: How quickly the action potential repolarizes
How quickly ATP is resynthesized by the mitochondria of the fiber
How quickly SERCA lowers cytosolic Ca2+ so troponin releases it
How quickly acetylcholinesterase clears the cleft
questions.why: Crossbridges keep cycling as long as troponin is occupied, so relaxation waits on the pump that drags cytosolic Ca2+ back down, which is the slowest step in the whole sequence. Transmitter clearance and repolarization finish within a few milliseconds, far too early to set the length of a relaxation phase lasting tens of milliseconds. Mitochondrial ATP production is not a limiting factor for a single twitch in a rested muscle.
questions.answerText: How quickly SERCA lowers cytosolic Ca2+ so troponin releases it

questions.q: Which phase of a twitch is normally the longest?
options: The relaxation phase
All three are of equal duration
The latent period
The contraction phase
questions.why: The latent period runs only a few milliseconds, the contraction phase takes a few tens of milliseconds, and relaxation typically takes longer still, because pumping Ca2+ uphill against a steep gradient is slower than releasing it through an open channel. That asymmetry between fast release and slow removal is what makes the twitch tracing look lopsided, and it is also what allows summation.

questions.q: How does the duration of a skeletal muscle action potential compare with the duration of the twitch it produces?
options: They are about the same duration, since one causes the other
The action potential is far briefer, a few ms against tens of ms for the twitch
The action potential lasts longer, and the twitch is over before it ends
The action potential lasts about half as long as the twitch
questions.why: The electrical event is over in roughly two to five milliseconds while the mechanical response can last from about twenty to over a hundred milliseconds depending on fiber type. That mismatch matters, because the membrane is ready to fire again long before the mechanical response has finished, which is the reason mechanical responses can summate while action potentials cannot.
questions.answerText: The action potential is far briefer, a few ms against tens of ms for the twitch

questions.q: In what order do the phases of a twitch occur after a stimulus?
options: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase
Relaxation phase, latent period, contraction phase
Contraction phase, latent period, relaxation phase
Latent period, relaxation phase, contraction phase
questions.why: The stimulus is followed by a silent interval while excitation contraction coupling runs, then tension rises as crossbridges attach, then tension falls as Ca2+ is pumped away. No force can fall before it has risen, so any order that puts relaxation before contraction is impossible, and the latent period must come first because it is defined as the delay after the stimulus.
questions.answerText: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase

questions.q: A fiber is cooled so that SERCA works at half speed. Which phase of the twitch lengthens most?
options: The relaxation phase
None, because temperature does not affect a single twitch
The latent period
The contraction phase
questions.why: Relaxation waits on the removal of Ca2+ from the cytosol, so halving the pump rate stretches that phase noticeably. The latent period depends on release rather than removal, and the rise of tension depends mainly on crossbridge attachment, so both change much less. Cooling does slow every protein somewhat, but the pump dependent phase is where the effect shows up most clearly.

questions.q: A muscle is attached to a recording lever with slack in the connection. What happens to the twitch tracing?
options: The relaxation phase appears longer, because the lever falls slowly
Peak tension appears higher, because the muscle shortens farther
The latent period appears longer, because the slack must be taken up first
The latent period appears shorter, because the muscle can shorten freely
questions.why: Part of the measured latent period is mechanical rather than chemical: crossbridges have to pull the elastic and slack elements in series with the fiber taut before any force reaches the transducer. Extra slack adds to that delay. Free shortening does not speed excitation contraction coupling, the falling phase still tracks Ca2+ removal, and slack reduces measured tension rather than increasing it.
questions.answerText: The latent period appears longer, because the slack must be taken up first

questions.q: A drug prolongs the opening of ryanodine receptors so Ca2+ release lasts longer. Which change to the twitch do you predict?
options: A longer contraction phase and a higher peak tension
A shorter relaxation phase and an unchanged peak tension
No change, because the amount of Ca2+ released is unchanged
A longer latent period and a lower peak tension
questions.why: Keeping the release channel open longer keeps troponin occupied longer, so crossbridges continue to attach and tension keeps climbing before Ca2+ removal takes over. Peak force in a single twitch is normally submaximal precisely because Ca2+ is withdrawn before all binding sites are engaged, so extending release raises it. The latent period depends on how quickly release begins, not on how long it lasts, and relaxation gets longer rather than shorter when there is more Ca2+ to clear.
questions.answerText: A longer contraction phase and a higher peak tension

questions.q: A fast glycolytic fiber and a slow oxidative fiber are stimulated once each. How do their twitches compare?
options: The fast fiber has a longer twitch, because it generates more force in each fiber
The two twitches have the same duration but different peak forces
The slow fiber has a briefer twitch, because it uses less ATP per cycle
The fast fiber has a briefer twitch, because it handles Ca2+ faster and cycles faster
questions.why: Twitch duration is set by how long cytosolic Ca2+ stays elevated and how fast the myosin isoform cycles, and fast fibers are built for speed on both counts, with a denser sarcoplasmic reticulum and more SERCA. Slow fibers hold Ca2+ up longer and cycle more slowly, giving twitches several times longer. Force per fiber and ATP economy are real differences between the types but they are not what sets twitch duration.
questions.answerText: The fast fiber has a briefer twitch, because it handles Ca2+ faster and cycles faster

questions.q: Why is the peak tension of a single twitch lower than the tension the same fiber can reach during a maintained contraction?
options: A single action potential produces a smaller depolarization than repeated ones
Only some myofibrils in the fiber respond to a single action potential
The myosin heads run out of ATP within a single twitch
Ca2+ is pumped away before every binding site is engaged
questions.why: One Ca2+ transient is brief, so troponin is only partly and briefly saturated and the elastic structures in series with the fibers never get fully taut before force starts to fall. Repeated stimulation keeps Ca2+ elevated and lets both processes go to completion. Action potentials are all or none and do not grow with repetition, the whole fiber responds to each one, and ATP is not depleted by a single twitch.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ is pumped away before every binding site is engaged

questions.q: An experiment slows conduction of the action potential into the T tubules without changing anything else. Which part of the twitch changes?
options: The relaxation phase lengthens
The latent period lengthens
Peak tension rises
The contraction phase shortens
questions.why: Everything that happens between the stimulus and the first rise in tension belongs to the latent period, and T tubule conduction is one of those steps, so delaying it pushes the start of force later. Relaxation is governed by Ca2+ removal and is untouched. Slower delivery of the signal does not increase force, and the contraction phase reflects crossbridge attachment rather than how the signal arrived.

questions.q: A twitch tracing shows a latent period of 3 ms, a contraction phase of 25 ms, and a relaxation phase of 55 ms. Roughly how long after the stimulus does tension peak?
options: About 25 ms
About 28 ms
About 55 ms
About 83 ms
questions.why: Tension peaks at the end of the contraction phase, so you add the latent period to the contraction phase, giving 3 plus 25, or 28 ms. Using 25 alone ignores the delay before force begins. The value of 55 is the relaxation phase alone, and 83 ms is the end of the whole twitch, when tension has returned to baseline.

questions.q: Two fibers produce identical peak tension, but fiber A returns to baseline in 30 ms while fiber B takes 90 ms. Which difference best explains this, and what does it predict about their fusion frequencies?
options: Fiber A releases less Ca2+ per action potential, so it needs a lower frequency to fuse
Fiber A has more myosin heads, so its fusion frequency is unaffected by Ca2+ handling
Fiber A has faster Ca2+ removal, so it needs a higher stimulus frequency to fuse
Fiber A has faster Ca2+ removal, so it fuses at a lower stimulus frequency
questions.why: Equal peak tension tells you activation was equally complete, so the difference lies in how quickly Ca2+ is cleared, which is what shapes the falling phase. A fiber that relaxes in 30 ms has fully recovered before a fiber relaxing in 90 ms has, so stimuli must arrive closer together, at a higher frequency, to catch it before relaxation is complete. Less Ca2+ released would have shown up as lower peak tension, and head number does not change the time course of the transient.
questions.answerText: Fiber A has faster Ca2+ removal, so it needs a higher stimulus frequency to fuse

questions.q: A fiber is treated so that its Ca2+ transient is normal but its myosin heads attach and detach at half the usual rate. Predict the effect on the latent period and on the contraction phase.
options: Both the latent period and the contraction phase are roughly doubled
The latent period is longer and the contraction phase is unchanged
Both are unchanged, since the Ca2+ transient is normal
The latent period is roughly unchanged and the contraction phase is slower
questions.why: The latent period covers the steps before force appears, and those are electrical and chemical, not mechanical, so a slower myosin barely touches it. The rise of tension, in contrast, is exactly the process of heads attaching and pulling, so halving the attachment rate stretches that phase out. Saying nothing changes ignores that force development is a crossbridge process even when the Ca2+ signal is intact.
questions.answerText: The latent period is roughly unchanged and the contraction phase is slower

questions.q: On a twitch tracing, a manipulation leaves the latent period and the peak tension unchanged but doubles the time from peak back to baseline. Which single change is most consistent with this result?
options: Reduced ryanodine receptor opening
Reduced SERCA activity
Reduced acetylcholine release at the junction
Reduced number of functioning myosin heads
questions.why: The tracing pins the change to the falling phase alone. Since latent period and peak tension are normal, release, coupling, and the number of available crossbridges must all be intact, which leaves the removal of Ca2+ as the only step that could be selectively slowed. Reduced release or fewer heads would lower peak tension, and reduced transmitter release would either do nothing at all or fail to trigger the fiber, since transmission is all or none for a single fiber.

questions.q: A muscle is stimulated once at 37 C and again after being warmed slightly, which speeds both Ca2+ release and Ca2+ reuptake. Predict the effect on twitch duration and on the frequency needed for the twitches to fuse.
options: Twitch duration lengthens and a higher frequency is needed for fusion
Twitch duration is unchanged but fusion occurs at a lower frequency
Twitch duration shortens and a higher frequency is needed for fusion
Twitch duration shortens and a lower frequency is needed for fusion
questions.why: Speeding both halves of the Ca2+ cycle compresses the whole mechanical response, so each twitch begins and ends sooner. Fusion requires the next stimulus to arrive before the previous response has decayed, so a briefer twitch leaves a shorter window and the stimuli have to come faster. This is the same principle that makes fast fibers require higher frequencies to reach fused tetanus than slow fibers do.
questions.answerText: Twitch duration shortens and a higher frequency is needed for fusion

questions.q: What is wave summation?
options: The addition of tension when a stimulus arrives before relaxation is complete
The addition of two action potentials to make one larger action potential
The activation of additional motor units as stimulus strength rises
The gradual increase in twitch force during the first few contractions of warm up
questions.why: Summation is mechanical: the second contraction starts from a baseline that is still elevated, so the tensions add and the fiber reaches a higher force than a single twitch. Action potentials cannot summate, because the refractory period keeps them separate and all or none. Adding motor units is recruitment, a different way of grading whole muscle force, and the warm up increase is treppe.
questions.answerText: The addition of tension when a stimulus arrives before relaxation is complete

questions.q: What is unfused tetanus?
options: A contraction in which only some motor units are active
A smooth maximal contraction with no fluctuation in tension
A high tension response with visible dips between stimuli
A single twitch of unusually large amplitude and duration
questions.why: In unfused, or incomplete, tetanus the stimuli come fast enough that the fiber cannot relax fully between them, so tension builds but the tracing still oscillates. When the frequency rises further and no relaxation at all is possible, the oscillations disappear and the response is fused. A single twitch has one peak, and partial activation of a muscle is a question of recruitment rather than of stimulus frequency.
questions.answerText: A high tension response with visible dips between stimuli

questions.q: What distinguishes fused tetanus from unfused tetanus on a tracing?
options: Fused tetanus shows a return to baseline between each stimulus
Fused tetanus shows a slow decline in tension from the first stimulus onward
Fused tetanus shows larger oscillations at a lower frequency
Fused tetanus shows a smooth plateau with no relaxation between stimuli
questions.why: Fusion means the stimuli arrive so close together that relaxation never begins, so individual twitches are no longer distinguishable and the tracing is a flat maximal plateau. Oscillations are the signature of unfused tetanus, and a full return to baseline between stimuli means the stimuli are too far apart for summation at all. A steady decline from the first stimulus describes fatigue rather than fusion.
questions.answerText: Fused tetanus shows a smooth plateau with no relaxation between stimuli

questions.q: What accumulates in the cytosol during a high frequency train of stimuli and explains why tetanic tension exceeds twitch tension?
options: Ca2+
ATP
Na+
K+
questions.why: Each action potential releases another load of Ca2+, and at high frequency the pump cannot clear it between stimuli, so cytosolic Ca2+ climbs and stays high enough to keep nearly every troponin site occupied. That sustained activation is what a single brief twitch never achieves. Na+ and K+ do shift slightly during repeated firing but they are not what activates the thin filament, and ATP is consumed rather than accumulated during activity.

questions.q: Why can twitches summate while action potentials cannot?
options: Action potentials travel too quickly to overlap with each other in time
Twitches use Ca2+ while action potentials use Na+
Action potentials are graded while twitches are all or none
The refractory period is far shorter than the twitch that follows it
questions.why: A second action potential cannot begin until the membrane has recovered from the first, so the electrical events remain separate and identical in size. The mechanical response, however, lasts far longer than that refractory period, so a new contraction can begin while the previous one is still in progress and the tensions add. The gradedness is on the mechanical side, not the electrical side, and both events involve their own ion movements without that being the reason for the difference.
questions.answerText: The refractory period is far shorter than the twitch that follows it

questions.q: What does the term fusion frequency mean?
options: The frequency at which two motor units begin to contract together
The stimulus frequency at which twitches merge into a smooth contraction
The maximum frequency at which a motor axon can conduct action potentials
The frequency at which a fatigued muscle can no longer respond
questions.why: Fusion frequency is a property of the mechanical response, the rate of stimulation at which relaxation no longer has time to begin, and it varies with fiber type because it depends on twitch duration. It is not about motor units acting together, which is recruitment, and it is well below the maximum firing rate an axon can support. Failure in a fatigued muscle is a separate phenomenon.
questions.answerText: The stimulus frequency at which twitches merge into a smooth contraction

questions.q: Roughly how does the tension of a fused tetanic contraction compare with the tension of a single twitch in the same fiber?
options: About the same
Slightly less
Several times greater
About a hundred times greater
questions.why: Tetanic tension typically runs about three to five times twitch tension, because a maintained high Ca2+ level saturates troponin and the series elastic elements are fully stretched, neither of which a brief single transient accomplishes. Equal tension would mean a single twitch already activates the fiber fully. A hundredfold difference is far too large, since a twitch already recruits a substantial fraction of the available crossbridges.

questions.q: How does treppe differ from wave summation?
options: In treppe the muscle relaxes fully between stimuli yet grows stronger
In treppe the twitches merge into a smooth plateau
In treppe additional motor units are recruited with each stimulus
In treppe the action potentials themselves grow larger
questions.why: Treppe, or the staircase effect, appears at low stimulation rates where each twitch ends completely before the next begins, so it cannot be summation. The rising force comes from warming and from Ca2+ handling becoming more efficient in the first few contractions. Merging into a plateau is tetanus, recruitment is a whole muscle phenomenon rather than a single fiber one, and action potentials never grow larger.
questions.answerText: In treppe the muscle relaxes fully between stimuli yet grows stronger

questions.q: A fiber whose twitch lasts 100 ms is stimulated every 200 ms. What does the tracing show?
options: Separate twitches with a full return to baseline
Unfused tetanus with oscillating tension
Fused tetanus with a smooth plateau
A single twitch, because the later stimuli fall in the refractory period
questions.why: An interval of 200 ms is twice the twitch duration, so each contraction is completely over before the next stimulus arrives and there is nothing left to add to. Summation requires the stimulus interval to be shorter than the twitch, not longer. The membrane refractory period is only a few milliseconds, far shorter than any of these intervals, so every stimulus produces its own twitch.
questions.answerText: Separate twitches with a full return to baseline

questions.q: The same fiber, with a twitch lasting 100 ms, is now stimulated at 50 Hz. Predict the response.
options: No response, because the fiber cannot fire that quickly
Separate twitches, because 50 Hz is below the fusion frequency
Fused tetanus, because a stimulus arrives every 20 ms and relaxation never begins
Unfused tetanus, because the stimuli fall exactly at the point of peak tension
questions.why: At 50 Hz the interval between stimuli is 20 ms, only a fifth of the twitch duration, so each new activation arrives while tension is still rising and Ca2+ never has a chance to fall, producing a smooth plateau. Separate twitches would require intervals longer than the twitch. A muscle fiber can certainly fire at 50 Hz, since its refractory period is a few milliseconds.
questions.answerText: Fused tetanus, because a stimulus arrives every 20 ms and relaxation never begins

questions.q: Two fibers are stimulated at the same frequency. Fiber A has faster SERCA and a briefer twitch. Which is more likely to show fused tetanus?
options: Fiber B, because its longer twitch leaves less time to relax
Both fuse identically, because fusion depends only on stimulus frequency
Neither fuses, because fusion depends on recruiting more motor units
Fiber A, because faster Ca2+ handling means Ca2+ accumulates sooner
questions.why: Fusion depends on the relationship between the stimulus interval and the twitch duration, so at any given frequency the fiber with the longer twitch fuses first. Fiber A clears Ca2+ quickly and relaxes between stimuli, which is why fast fibers need higher frequencies to fuse. Fusion is not set by frequency alone, and recruitment is a separate mechanism operating at the level of the whole muscle.
questions.answerText: Fiber B, because its longer twitch leaves less time to relax

questions.q: A SERCA inhibitor is applied to a muscle fiber. What happens to the frequency needed to produce fused tetanus?
options: It rises, because more stimuli are needed to raise cytosolic Ca2+
It falls, because each twitch now lasts longer
It is unchanged, because fusion depends on the action potential frequency
It rises, because the fiber becomes less sensitive to Ca2+
questions.why: Slowing Ca2+ removal prolongs the mechanical response, so relaxation takes longer to begin and stimuli spaced farther apart are still close enough to summate. Fewer stimuli per second are therefore needed to reach a smooth plateau. Fusion is set by the time course of the mechanical response rather than by the electrical events, and this drug does not change the sensitivity of troponin to Ca2+.
questions.answerText: It falls, because each twitch now lasts longer

questions.q: In a lab preparation, increasing the stimulus voltage delivered to a whole nerve raises muscle force, and increasing the stimulus frequency also raises force. Which mechanism is which?
options: Both recruit more motor units, by different routes
Both produce summation, by different routes
Higher voltage produces summation within units, higher frequency recruits more motor units
Higher voltage recruits more motor units, higher frequency produces summation within units
questions.why: A stronger stimulus reaches the thresholds of more axons in the nerve, so more motor units join in, which is recruitment. A faster stimulus does not activate any new units but drives the ones already active to summate their twitches. Keeping these two mechanisms distinct is the key to interpreting almost every whole muscle tracing in the lab.
questions.answerText: Higher voltage recruits more motor units, higher frequency produces summation within units

questions.q: Why does cytosolic Ca2+ rise during a train of stimuli rather than returning to baseline each time?
options: Ca2+ enters from the extracellular fluid during repeated stimulation
Each action potential adds Ca2+ before SERCA has cleared the previous load
Each action potential releases progressively more Ca2+ than the one before
SERCA is switched off by the second action potential in any train
questions.why: Release is fast and removal is slow, so at high frequency the two processes fall out of balance and Ca2+ accumulates in the cytosol. The amount released per action potential does not grow, at least not early in a train, and the pump is not switched off, it is simply outpaced. Skeletal muscle contraction does not depend on Ca2+ entering from outside the cell, which is a cardiac rather than a skeletal feature.
questions.answerText: Each action potential adds Ca2+ before SERCA has cleared the previous load

questions.q: A fiber has a twitch lasting 40 ms. Approximately what is the lowest stimulus frequency that will produce any wave summation?
options: About 5 Hz
About 25 Hz
About 100 Hz
About 400 Hz
questions.why: Summation begins when the interval between stimuli becomes shorter than the twitch duration, and an interval of 40 ms corresponds to 25 stimuli per second. At 5 Hz the interval is 200 ms and each twitch is long finished. Higher frequencies such as 100 Hz will certainly summate and probably fuse, but the question asks for the lowest frequency at which summation appears at all.

questions.q: A fiber with an 80 ms twitch is stimulated three ways: every 100 ms, every 30 ms, and every 10 ms. Match the three tracings.
options: Unfused tetanus, separate twitches, fused tetanus
Separate twitches, unfused tetanus, fused tetanus
Fused tetanus, unfused tetanus, separate twitches
Separate twitches, fused tetanus, unfused tetanus
questions.why: Compare each interval with the 80 ms twitch. At 100 ms the twitch has ended before the next stimulus, so the responses are separate. At 30 ms the fiber has started to relax but not finished, so tension builds with visible dips, which is unfused tetanus. At 10 ms there is no time for any relaxation at all, so the tracing is a smooth plateau. Ordering these correctly is just a matter of holding the twitch duration next to each interval.
questions.answerText: Separate twitches, unfused tetanus, fused tetanus

questions.q: Give the two linked reasons a fused tetanic contraction produces several times the tension of a single twitch in the same fiber.
options: The myosin heads cycle faster, and each power stroke moves the filament farther
More Ca2+ enters from the extracellular fluid, and the sarcomeres shorten past their optimal length
Sustained high Ca2+ keeps nearly all binding sites exposed, and the elastic elements are fully stretched
More motor units are recruited, and each action potential becomes larger
questions.why: Two things limit a single twitch, and tetanus removes both. Ca2+ is pumped away before troponin is fully occupied, and the tendons and other elastic structures in series with the fibers absorb part of the early force. Maintaining the stimulus keeps Ca2+ high and gives the elastic elements time to be pulled taut, so the tension the crossbridges generate actually reaches the tendon. Recruitment involves other motor units and cannot explain the behavior of one fiber, action potentials do not grow, and stroke size is fixed.
questions.answerText: Sustained high Ca2+ keeps nearly all binding sites exposed, and the elastic elements are fully stretched

questions.q: A fiber fuses at 40 Hz at 37 C. After cooling, it fuses at 25 Hz. Explain the shift.
options: Cooling reduces the refractory period, allowing the membrane to fire at lower frequencies
Cooling recruits additional motor units within the fiber
Cooling slows Ca2+ removal and lengthens the twitch, so relaxation is delayed
Cooling speeds Ca2+ removal, shortening the twitch, so fewer stimuli are needed
questions.why: Fusion frequency is the reciprocal of twitch duration in practical terms, so anything that lengthens the twitch lowers the frequency needed to fuse. Cold slows SERCA, the Ca2+ transient lasts longer, and relaxation is delayed, so a 40 ms gap between stimuli that used to allow partial relaxation no longer does. Cooling does not speed the pump, refractory period is not what sets fusion, and a single fiber belongs to one motor unit and cannot recruit within itself.
questions.answerText: Cooling slows Ca2+ removal and lengthens the twitch, so relaxation is delayed

questions.q: In a whole muscle experiment, force rises when either stimulus strength or stimulus frequency is increased. At maximal stimulus strength, force still rises when frequency is raised further. What does this tell you?
options: The muscle fibers are generating larger action potentials at the higher frequency
The extra force comes from fibers that were previously fatigued and have now recovered
Some motor units remain unrecruited, and higher frequency recruits them
All motor units are already recruited, so the rest comes from summation
questions.why: Once the stimulus is strong enough to bring every axon in the nerve to threshold, no further recruitment is possible, so any additional force must come from the other grading mechanism. Raising frequency keeps cytosolic Ca2+ elevated in the units already firing and moves them from twitches toward tetanus. Frequency never recruits units, action potentials are all or none, and recovery from fatigue would not track stimulus frequency.
questions.answerText: All motor units are already recruited, so the rest comes from summation

questions.q: What is a motor unit?
options: One motor neuron and all of the muscle fibers it innervates
One muscle fiber and all of the motor neurons that innervate it
All of the motor neurons that supply a single muscle
One sarcomere and the portion of the sarcoplasmic reticulum around it
questions.why: A motor unit is the smallest part of a muscle the nervous system can control, because every fiber in the unit is reached by the same axon and contracts whenever that neuron fires. A skeletal muscle fiber is normally innervated by exactly one motor neuron, so the reverse definition does not describe anything real. The full set of neurons supplying a muscle is called the motor neuron pool, and the sarcomere is a structural unit rather than a functional one.
questions.answerText: One motor neuron and all of the muscle fibers it innervates

questions.q: What does innervation ratio mean?
options: The number of muscle fibers controlled by a single motor neuron
The ratio of fast to slow fibers within one muscle
The proportion of motor units active during a contraction
The number of motor neurons supplying a single muscle
questions.why: Innervation ratio counts fibers per neuron, so a low ratio means a small motor unit and finer control while a high ratio means a large unit and coarser but more powerful steps of force. The number of neurons supplying a muscle describes the size of the motor neuron pool. Fiber type composition and the fraction of units currently active are both important properties of a muscle, but neither is what this term names.
questions.answerText: The number of muscle fibers controlled by a single motor neuron

questions.q: Which muscle would you expect to have the smallest motor units?
options: The gluteus maximus of the hip
The gastrocnemius of the calf
The quadriceps of the thigh
The extraocular muscles of the eye
questions.why: Muscles that make small, precisely graded movements have very low innervation ratios, sometimes only a handful of fibers per neuron, so each additional unit adds only a tiny increment of force. The eye muscles are the classic example, along with the small muscles of the hand and the larynx. The large limb and hip muscles are built for force rather than precision and have hundreds to over a thousand fibers per neuron.
questions.answerText: The extraocular muscles of the eye

questions.q: What does the size principle state?
options: Motor units are recruited from smallest to largest as more force is required
Larger muscles are recruited before smaller muscles in any movement
Larger motor units generate less force per fiber than smaller ones
Motor units are recruited from largest to smallest as more force is required
questions.why: Small motor neurons have a higher input resistance, so a given synaptic current depolarizes them more and brings them to threshold first, which means the small, fatigue resistant units are always used first and the large powerful ones join only when they are needed. This ordering is automatic and gives fine control at low forces. Recruiting the largest units first would make delicate movements impossible, and force per fiber is broadly similar across unit types.
questions.answerText: Motor units are recruited from smallest to largest as more force is required

questions.q: What is meant by recruitment in a skeletal muscle?
options: Increasing the amount of Ca2+ released per action potential
Increasing the firing rate of the motor units already active
Activating additional motor units to increase whole muscle force
Adding new muscle fibers to a motor unit through training
questions.why: Recruitment adds units, and it is one of the two ways the nervous system grades force, the other being the firing rate of the units already active. Raising the firing rate is rate coding and produces summation within a unit. Training changes fiber size rather than adding fibers to existing units, and the Ca2+ released per action potential is not under moment to moment neural control.
questions.answerText: Activating additional motor units to increase whole muscle force

questions.q: When a motor neuron fires, how many of the fibers in its motor unit contract?
options: About half, depending on the strength of the action potential
Only the fibers nearest the axon branch point
A number that varies with how much Ca2+ is available
All of them, because every fiber in the unit receives the same signal
questions.why: The axon branches to reach every fiber in its unit, transmission at each junction has a large safety factor, and the action potential is all or none, so one impulse contracts the entire unit. That is why the motor unit is the smallest controllable element of a muscle. Action potentials do not vary in strength, distance from the branch point does not matter, and Ca2+ supply is not a limiting factor in a rested fiber.
questions.answerText: All of them, because every fiber in the unit receives the same signal

questions.q: What kind of fibers are typically found in the small motor units recruited first?
options: Fast glycolytic fibers that fatigue quickly
Slow oxidative fibers that resist fatigue
Fibers that lack a sarcoplasmic reticulum
Fibers that contract without an action potential
questions.why: Small motor neurons supply small numbers of slow, highly oxidative fibers with many mitochondria and a rich capillary supply, which is exactly what postural work demands, since these units are active almost continuously. The large units recruited last contain fast glycolytic fibers that produce a great deal of force briefly and then fatigue. Every skeletal fiber has a sarcoplasmic reticulum and every one requires an action potential to contract.
questions.answerText: Slow oxidative fibers that resist fatigue

questions.q: What are the two mechanisms the nervous system uses to grade the force of a whole muscle?
options: Recruitment of more motor units and increasing the amount of acetylcholine per vesicle
Recruitment of more motor units and increasing the firing rate of active units
Increasing action potential amplitude and increasing action potential duration
Increasing the number of fibers per motor unit and lengthening the sarcomeres
questions.why: Force is graded by how many units are switched on and by how fast each one is driven, and together these give smooth control from the lightest to the heaviest effort. Action potentials are all or none and their size cannot be adjusted. Innervation ratios are fixed on the timescale of a movement, and the quantity of transmitter per vesicle is not a variable the nervous system uses to grade force.
questions.answerText: Recruitment of more motor units and increasing the firing rate of active units

questions.q: A person picks up a pencil and then a heavy suitcase using the same muscles. How does the pattern of motor unit activity differ?
options: The suitcase requires the same small units plus additional larger ones firing faster
The suitcase requires the large units instead of the small ones, which switch off
The suitcase requires the same units firing at the same rate but with larger action potentials
The two tasks use different muscles entirely rather than different motor units
questions.why: Recruitment is additive and ordered, so the small units used for the pencil keep working and larger units are layered on top as the demand grows, with firing rates rising at the same time. Small units are not switched off to make room for large ones, which would produce a jump in force rather than a smooth increase. Action potentials cannot get larger, and the same muscles are doing both jobs.
questions.answerText: The suitcase requires the same small units plus additional larger ones firing faster

questions.q: Which motor units are active while a person simply stands still for several minutes?
options: No units at all, since standing requires no muscle activity
Large, fast, fatigable units
Small, slow, fatigue resistant units
All units in the muscle, firing at a low rate
questions.why: Quiet standing is a low force task that must be sustained for a long time, which is exactly the job description of the small units recruited first by the size principle. Their oxidative metabolism lets them work for hours without fatiguing. Large fatigable units would exhaust themselves within a minute and are held in reserve for high force efforts, and posture certainly does require continuous low level contraction.

questions.q: A muscle has 200 motor neurons and 200000 fibers. Another has 1000 motor neurons and 50000 fibers. Which produces more finely graded force, and why?
options: The second, because 50 fibers per neuron makes each step smaller
The first, because it has more fibers in total
The second, because it has fewer fibers in total
The first, because its 1000 fibers per neuron give each step more power
questions.why: Divide fibers by neurons: the first muscle has 1000 fibers per unit and the second has 50, so each unit added in the second muscle contributes a twentieth as much force and the increments are far finer. Precision depends on the size of the step, not on the total number of fibers or on the raw power of each unit. A large innervation ratio buys force at the cost of fine control.
questions.answerText: The second, because 50 fibers per neuron makes each step smaller

questions.q: A single motor axon is stimulated with progressively stronger shocks. Once the axon is firing, further increases in stimulus strength do not increase force. Why?
options: The axon begins to conduct in the reverse direction
The extra current is absorbed by the surrounding connective tissue
The unit already contracts all of its fibers, and there are no others
The stronger stimulus causes some fibers to fatigue immediately
questions.why: Motor unit behavior is all or none: once the axon reaches threshold, every fiber it supplies contracts, and there is no further force to be had by stimulating harder. Grading force in a whole muscle requires access to other axons, which is why whole nerve stimulation shows graded responses and single axon stimulation does not. Fatigue does not appear instantly, and neither reverse conduction nor current absorption explains the plateau.
questions.answerText: The unit already contracts all of its fibers, and there are no others

questions.q: A whole nerve is stimulated with gradually increasing voltage while force is recorded from the muscle. What shape does the force curve take and why?
options: Force rises and then falls, because high voltage inhibits the larger axons
Force rises smoothly without limit as voltage increases
Force rises in steps and then plateaus as axons reach threshold in order
Force stays at zero and then jumps to maximum at a single threshold voltage
questions.why: Different axons have different thresholds, so each increment in voltage brings a few more into play and adds their units to the total, giving a stepwise rise. Once every axon is firing, the muscle is maximally recruited and further voltage adds nothing, hence the plateau. A single jump to maximum would require all axons to share one threshold, and stimulation does not inhibit large axons.
questions.answerText: Force rises in steps and then plateaus as axons reach threshold in order

questions.q: After a motor neuron is lost to injury, surviving axons in the muscle sprout and adopt the orphaned fibers. What is the functional consequence?
options: Innervation ratios fall, so control becomes finer than before
The muscle loses the ability to contract at all
Each surviving fiber generates less force than before
Innervation ratios rise, so force is graded in larger, coarser steps
questions.why: Reinnervation rescues fibers that would otherwise atrophy, so total force is largely preserved, but the surviving units are now much larger and every recruitment step adds more force at once. The practical result is a muscle that works but is clumsy at low force levels, which is why tremor and poor fine control are typical after such injuries. Ratios go up rather than down, and the individual fibers themselves contract normally.
questions.answerText: Innervation ratios rise, so force is graded in larger, coarser steps

questions.q: During a sustained submaximal contraction held for several minutes, force stays constant while the electrical activity of individual motor units comes and goes. What is happening?
options: All units are firing continuously and the recording is unreliable
The muscle is switching from recruitment to rate coding within each unit
Fibers are being transferred from one motor unit to another
Units are taking turns, with some resting while others carry the load
questions.why: At submaximal force the nervous system can rotate through the available units, letting some recover while others contract, which extends how long the task can be sustained. This is only possible when more units are available than the task requires. Continuous firing by all units would make the alternation invisible, rate coding changes firing frequency rather than which units are on, and fibers do not move between units on this timescale.
questions.answerText: Units are taking turns, with some resting while others carry the load

questions.q: A person gradually increases the force of an elbow flexion from very light to maximal. Describe how recruitment and rate coding contribute across that range.
options: Rate coding dominates at low force and recruitment takes over near maximum, when the largest units are added last
Recruitment dominates at low and moderate force, and rising firing rates carry the rest
Recruitment alone accounts for the entire range, since firing rate is fixed by the axon
Rate coding alone accounts for the entire range, since all units are recruited from the start
questions.why: The two mechanisms overlap but their relative importance shifts. Early in the range the nervous system adds units in order of size, which gives fine steps and low fatigue. Once the pool is largely recruited there are no more units to add, so further force comes from driving the active units toward tetanus by raising their firing rates. Neither mechanism works alone, and rate coding does not lead at low forces, where fine gradation matters most.
questions.answerText: Recruitment dominates at low and moderate force, and rising firing rates carry the rest

questions.q: Two muscles produce the same maximum force. Muscle A has 100 motor units, muscle B has 1000. Predict how each performs when a task requires exactly five percent of maximum force.
options: Muscle A can match the target more closely, because it has fewer units to coordinate
Muscle B, because each of its units contributes a tenth as much force
Both match the target equally, since their maximum forces are the same
Neither can produce five percent of maximum, since motor units are all or none
questions.why: With equal maximum force, muscle A grades in steps of about one percent of maximum per unit while muscle B grades in steps of about one tenth of a percent, so B can land much nearer any given low target. Having fewer units to coordinate makes control coarser, not easier. Individual units are indeed all or none, but the muscle as a whole is graded precisely because it can activate any number of them.
questions.answerText: Muscle B, because each of its units contributes a tenth as much force

questions.q: A whole muscle is stimulated through its nerve at maximal voltage but only 1 Hz, and the recorded force is far below what the person can produce voluntarily. Explain the gap.
options: Voluntary contraction recruits fibers that electrical stimulation cannot reach
All units are recruited but each produces only single twitches
Only the small units are recruited at 1 Hz, so the large units contribute nothing
The stimulation is fatiguing the muscle, so force declines from the start
questions.why: Maximal voltage guarantees full recruitment, so the missing ingredient is the other grading mechanism. At 1 Hz each unit relaxes completely between stimuli and delivers a twitch, which is only a fraction of the tension the same unit reaches in fused tetanus, and voluntary effort drives units at rates high enough to fuse. Stimulus strength determines which units fire, not frequency, and 1 Hz is far too slow to fatigue a muscle.
questions.answerText: All units are recruited but each produces only single twitches

questions.q: A person lifting a very heavy object can hold it only briefly, while the same person can hold a light object for many minutes. Explain the difference in terms of motor unit properties.
options: Heavy loads deplete extracellular Ca2+, which light loads do not
Heavy loads recruit units in reverse order, starting with the most fatigable and ending with the least
Heavy loads need the large fatigable units, while light loads use only the fatigue resistant ones
Heavy loads use fewer units, so each one has to work harder and tires sooner
questions.why: The size principle links the amount of force required to the type of unit doing the work. A light load stays within the small oxidative units, which are built for endurance and can even take turns, whereas a heavy load necessarily brings in the large glycolytic units whose anaerobic metabolism runs down within seconds to a minute or two. Heavy loads use more units rather than fewer, skeletal contraction does not draw on extracellular Ca2+, and recruitment order does not reverse with load.
questions.answerText: Heavy loads need the large fatigable units, while light loads use only the fatigue resistant ones

questions.q: In the length tension relationship, what sets the amount of active tension a sarcomere can generate at a given length?
options: The number of myosin heads that can reach binding sites on actin
The amount of ATP stored inside the sarcomere
The resting membrane potential of the muscle fiber
The length of the thick filament itself
questions.why: Active tension tracks the overlap between thick and thin filaments, because overlap decides how many crossbridges can form, and each crossbridge adds a fixed increment of force. Stored ATP is not limiting in a rested fiber, so it does not shape the curve. Resting membrane potential decides whether the fiber fires at all, not how much force one contraction produces. Thick filament length is fixed near 1.6 micrometers and does not change when the sarcomere is stretched.
questions.answerText: The number of myosin heads that can reach binding sites on actin

questions.q: At about what sarcomere length does a skeletal muscle fiber generate its maximal active tension?
options: About 1.2 to 1.4 micrometers
About 3.0 to 3.2 micrometers
About 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers
About 3.6 to 3.8 micrometers
questions.why: Optimal length sits near 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers, where every myosin head in the crossbridge bearing region lies opposite a thin filament. At 1.2 to 1.4 micrometers the thick filaments are already jammed against the Z discs. At 3.0 to 3.2 micrometers overlap is partial and tension is on the descending limb. At 3.6 micrometers and beyond the filaments have pulled apart completely and active tension is zero.

questions.q: Passive tension in a stretched skeletal muscle comes mainly from which source?
options: Titin and the connective tissue surrounding the fibers
Crossbridges cycling slowly without Ca2+
Ca2+ still bound to troponin C
The Na+/K+ ATPase holding the fiber polarized
questions.why: Passive tension is elastic recoil, and it comes from titin inside the sarcomere plus the collagen of endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium outside it. It appears in a relaxed, unstimulated muscle, so cycling crossbridges cannot be the source. Ca2+ bound to troponin would produce active tension, not passive. The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains ion gradients and has no mechanical role in resisting stretch.
questions.answerText: Titin and the connective tissue surrounding the fibers

questions.q: On the descending limb of the length tension curve, what has changed compared with the plateau?
options: Thick filaments have buckled against the Z discs
Thin filaments from the two ends now overlap each other
Overlap between thick and thin filaments has decreased
Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum has stopped
questions.why: Pulling the sarcomere past optimal length slides the thin filaments away from the myosin heads, so fewer crossbridges can form and tension falls in direct proportion to the lost overlap. Buckling of thick filaments against the Z discs and double overlap of thin filaments both happen at short lengths, on the ascending limb, not the descending limb. Ca2+ release is unchanged; the deficit is mechanical, not a failure of excitation contraction coupling.
questions.answerText: Overlap between thick and thin filaments has decreased

questions.q: Total tension recorded from a muscle at a given length is the sum of which two components?
options: Isometric tension plus isotonic tension
Active tension plus passive tension
Twitch tension plus tetanic tension
Series elastic tension minus parallel elastic tension
questions.why: Total tension is what the transducer reads, and it combines the crossbridge derived active tension with the elastic passive tension already present before stimulation. Isometric and isotonic name conditions of contraction, not components that add together. Twitch and tetanic tension are two ways of stimulating the same muscle, so they are alternatives rather than addends. Series and parallel elastic elements both contribute to passive tension, and they are not subtracted from one another.

questions.q: At very short sarcomere lengths, what physically limits the tension a fiber can produce?
options: Thick and thin filaments have lost all overlap
Titin has been stretched past its elastic limit
Thick filaments hit the Z discs and thin filaments overlap each other
Troponin can no longer bind the Ca2+ released during the twitch
questions.why: Squeezing the sarcomere below about 2.0 micrometers forces the thin filaments from opposite ends past each other and drives the rigid thick filaments into the Z discs, both of which oppose further shortening. Complete loss of overlap is the opposite problem and belongs at very long lengths. Titin is slack at short lengths, not overstretched. Troponin binds Ca2+ normally, so the loss of force is mechanical rather than a signaling failure.
questions.answerText: Thick filaments hit the Z discs and thin filaments overlap each other

questions.q: What structural feature of the thick filament explains the flat plateau at the top of the length tension curve?
options: The central bare zone carries no myosin heads
The Z discs stretch elastically over a short range
Titin unfolds at constant tension over that range
The T tubules reach their widest diameter over that range
questions.why: Across the plateau the thin filaments slide over the bare zone, a stretch of thick filament with no heads on it, so the number of crossbridges that can form does not change and tension stays flat. Z discs are anchoring structures and do not stretch enough to flatten the curve. Titin does unfold under load, but that shapes passive tension at long lengths rather than the active plateau. T tubule diameter has no bearing on filament overlap.
questions.answerText: The central bare zone carries no myosin heads

questions.q: Where on the length tension curve does an intact skeletal muscle normally rest in the body?
options: Far out on the descending limb
Well down the ascending limb
At or very close to optimal length
Past the point where active tension reaches zero
questions.why: Tendon attachments and joint anatomy hold most skeletal muscles near optimal length at rest, so ordinary movements start close to peak force. Sitting far out on the descending limb would waste most of the muscle's force capacity. Sitting well down the ascending limb would do the same at the other extreme. No intact muscle rests past the point of zero overlap, since the joint would have to be dislocated to get there.
questions.answerText: At or very close to optimal length

questions.q: A single sarcomere is stretched to 3.7 micrometers, beyond the point where thick and thin filaments overlap at all, and then stimulated. Predict its active tension.
options: About half of maximum, because half the heads still reach actin
Maximal, because the filaments are fully extended
Essentially zero, because no crossbridges can form
Above maximal, because elastic recoil adds to crossbridge force
questions.why: Active tension is proportional to overlap, and at 3.7 micrometers the thin filaments have slid clear of every myosin head, so no crossbridge can attach and active tension collapses to zero. Half maximal tension would require partial overlap, which is what you see closer to 3.0 micrometers. Stretch does not improve crossbridge access; it removes it. Elastic recoil at this length is real and large, but it is passive tension, and passive tension is measured separately from active tension.
questions.answerText: Essentially zero, because no crossbridges can form

questions.q: A fiber is held at a sarcomere length of 1.6 micrometers and stimulated. Compared with the same fiber at 2.1 micrometers, what happens to active tension and why?
options: Lower, because thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
Lower, because thick filaments are compressed against the Z discs
Higher, because more crossbridges can form at short lengths
Unchanged, because the number of crossbridges is fixed
questions.why: At 1.6 micrometers the sarcomere is on the ascending limb, where the thick filaments run into the Z discs and the thin filaments interfere with each other, so force is well below the value at 2.1 micrometers. Loss of overlap is the right idea for the wrong limb; that explains the fall at long lengths. Shortening does not add crossbridges, because the extra sliding happens over the bare zone. Crossbridge number is exactly what changes with length, which is the whole point of the curve.
questions.answerText: Lower, because thick filaments are compressed against the Z discs

questions.q: A relaxed muscle is stretched progressively beyond its optimal length. Predict what happens to passive tension.
options: It falls toward zero as the filaments separate
It stays flat until active tension reaches zero
It rises steeply as the muscle is stretched further
It rises briefly and then returns to zero
questions.why: Titin and the surrounding connective tissue behave like nonlinear springs, so passive tension is near zero around resting length and then climbs steeply the further the muscle is stretched. It cannot fall as the muscle lengthens, since that is the direction that loads the elastic elements. It does not wait for active tension to disappear before rising; the two curves overlap across a wide range of lengths. And elastic recoil does not release on its own while the stretch is maintained.
questions.answerText: It rises steeply as the muscle is stretched further

questions.q: A person holds the wrist in full flexion, which shortens the finger flexor muscles. Predict the effect on maximum grip force and the reason for it.
options: Grip force rises, because the muscle is already partly shortened
Grip force is unchanged, because force depends only on motor unit recruitment
Grip force falls, because the flexor sarcomeres now sit below optimal length
Grip force falls, because filament overlap is completely lost
questions.why: Flexing the wrist slackens the finger flexors onto the ascending limb, where thick filaments crowd the Z discs, so the same maximal effort produces less force. A partly shortened muscle is weaker, not stronger, once it passes optimal length. Recruitment does set force, but the force each recruited fiber can make still depends on its length. Total loss of overlap describes the far end of the descending limb, which is the opposite of what wrist flexion does.
questions.answerText: Grip force falls, because the flexor sarcomeres now sit below optimal length

questions.q: Two sarcomeres in the same fiber are compared, one at 2.2 micrometers and one at 2.8 micrometers. Which generates more active tension, and why?
options: The 2.8 micrometer sarcomere, because it has more distance available to shorten
The 2.8 micrometer sarcomere, because passive tension adds to crossbridge force
They are equal, because both lie on the plateau of the curve
The 2.2 micrometer sarcomere, because more myosin heads lie opposite thin filaments
questions.why: At 2.2 micrometers the sarcomere is at the top of the plateau, while 2.8 micrometers is out on the descending limb with reduced overlap, so the shorter one forms more crossbridges and makes more active force. Available shortening distance does not determine peak tension, which is measured isometrically. Passive tension is a separate component and is not counted as active tension. The plateau ends near 2.2 micrometers, so the two lengths are not equivalent.
questions.answerText: The 2.2 micrometer sarcomere, because more myosin heads lie opposite thin filaments

questions.q: Why does shortening a sarcomere from 2.2 to 2.0 micrometers fail to increase active tension?
options: The extra sliding crosses the bare zone, which has no myosin heads
Ca2+ release falls as the sarcomere shortens
Titin begins to resist any further shortening
Thin filaments begin to detach from the Z discs at very short lengths
questions.why: Between roughly 2.0 and 2.2 micrometers the thin filaments advance over the head free bare zone, so no new crossbridges are gained and tension holds flat. Ca2+ release is set by the action potential, not by length over this range. Titin is slack rather than resistive at lengths at or below optimal. Thin filaments stay anchored to the Z discs throughout, which is what allows them to transmit force at all.
questions.answerText: The extra sliding crosses the bare zone, which has no myosin heads

questions.q: A whole muscle stretched well beyond optimal length shows a higher total tension than at optimal length, even though its active tension is lower. What explains this?
options: Passive tension from titin and connective tissue is large at long lengths
Crossbridge cycling speeds up when the muscle is stretched
The muscle recruits extra motor units when it is stretched
Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum increases with stretch
questions.why: Total tension is active plus passive, and at long lengths the steeply rising passive component more than makes up for the crossbridges lost to poor overlap. Crossbridge cycling rate sets shortening velocity, not the height of an isometric plateau, and stretch does not speed it. Recruitment is a nervous system decision and is not triggered by passively stretching the muscle. Ca2+ release is essentially unchanged, which is why active tension falls rather than rises.
questions.answerText: Passive tension from titin and connective tissue is large at long lengths

questions.q: A muscle is tested isometrically at four lengths. Length A: total tension 100, passive 0. Length B: total 110, passive 20. Length C: total 120, passive 60. Length D: total 70, passive 0. Which length is closest to the optimal length for active tension?
options: Length B
Length C
Length D
Length A
questions.why: Subtract passive from total to get active tension: A gives 100, B gives 90, C gives 60, and D gives 70, so A produces the most crossbridge force and sits closest to optimal length. Length C is the trap, because its total tension is the highest recorded, but most of that is elastic recoil rather than crossbridge force. Length B is already onto the descending limb, with passive tension starting to appear. Length D has no passive tension at all, which marks it as a short length on the ascending limb.

questions.q: An elbow is immobilized in a flexed cast for eight weeks. The biceps adapts by removing sarcomeres in series so that its remaining sarcomeres sit near optimal length in the flexed position. Predict what happens when the cast is removed and the elbow is straightened.
options: Active tension rises and passive tension falls, because the muscle is now closer to optimal length
Active tension falls and passive tension falls, because the sarcomeres are compressed against the Z discs
Active tension falls and passive tension rises, because the shortened muscle is pulled onto its descending limb
Active and passive tension are both unchanged, because sarcomere number does not affect force
questions.why: With fewer sarcomeres spanning the same tendon to tendon distance, each remaining sarcomere must stretch further to allow full extension, which pushes it past optimal overlap and loads titin heavily. The muscle is worse off at extension, not better, since optimal length has been reset to the flexed position. Compression against the Z discs is an ascending limb event, and it would not raise passive tension. Sarcomere number in series is precisely what sets the joint angle at which peak force occurs.
questions.answerText: Active tension falls and passive tension rises, because the shortened muscle is pulled onto its descending limb

questions.q: Grip force is measured at three wrist positions: 20 kg with the wrist fully flexed, 45 kg with the wrist slightly extended, and 30 kg with the wrist fully extended. What best accounts for the pattern?
options: The finger flexors are beyond optimal length in wrist flexion and below optimal length in full extension
The finger flexors are below optimal length in wrist flexion and beyond optimal length in full extension
Motor unit recruitment is maximal only in slight extension and submaximal at the two extremes
Passive tension in the finger flexors subtracts from grip force at both extremes of wrist position
questions.why: Wrist flexion slackens the finger flexors onto the ascending limb and full wrist extension stretches them onto the descending limb, so both extremes lose crossbridge overlap and peak force appears in between. The reversed version has the limbs backward: flexing a wrist shortens its flexors, it does not lengthen them. Recruitment is under voluntary control and a motivated subject recruits fully at every position tested. Passive tension adds to recorded tension rather than subtracting from it.
questions.answerText: The finger flexors are below optimal length in wrist flexion and beyond optimal length in full extension

questions.q: A stimulated muscle fiber produces 45 units of passive tension and no active tension at all, and the fiber is confirmed to depolarize and release Ca2+ normally. What can you conclude about its sarcomere length?
options: It is compressed below roughly 1.3 micrometers, so the thick filaments are crushed against the Z discs
It is stretched past roughly 3.6 micrometers, so thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
It is at optimal length, but the crossbridges have run out of ATP
It is on the plateau, but the Ca2+ signal is too brief to activate troponin
questions.why: Normal excitation and Ca2+ release rule out a signaling problem, and the large passive tension tells you the elastic elements are heavily loaded, which only happens at long lengths, so the fiber must be stretched past the point of zero overlap. A crushed short sarcomere would give little or no passive tension, since titin is slack there. Running out of ATP would cause rigor and stiffness, not a clean loss of active force with normal Ca2+ handling. The stem states Ca2+ release is normal, so a defective Ca2+ signal is excluded.
questions.answerText: It is stretched past roughly 3.6 micrometers, so thick and thin filaments no longer overlap

questions.q: What defines an isometric contraction?
options: The muscle shortens while tension stays constant
The muscle lengthens while tension stays constant
The muscle changes length without developing tension
The muscle develops tension but its length does not change
questions.why: Isometric means same length: crossbridges cycle and tension climbs, but the load is too large to move, so the muscle holds its length. Shortening at constant tension is a concentric isotonic contraction. Lengthening at constant tension is an eccentric contraction. A length change without tension is not a contraction at all; it is passive stretch or recoil.
questions.answerText: The muscle develops tension but its length does not change

questions.q: What is happening to the muscle during a concentric contraction?
options: It lengthens while generating force
It holds a fixed length while generating force
It shortens without generating force
It shortens while generating force
questions.why: Concentric contraction is the familiar case in which crossbridge force exceeds the load, so the muscle shortens and does positive work on the load. Lengthening under load is eccentric. Holding a fixed length is isometric. Shortening with no force generation is elastic recoil, not contraction.

questions.q: What is happening to the muscle during an eccentric contraction?
options: It shortens while still generating force
It holds a fixed length while generating force
It lengthens while still generating force
It lengthens after all crossbridges have detached
questions.why: In an eccentric contraction the external load exceeds the force the muscle can produce, so the muscle is pulled longer even though crossbridges are attached and resisting, which is how you lower a heavy object under control. Shortening under load is concentric. Holding length is isometric. If every crossbridge detached the muscle would be relaxed, and the lengthening would be uncontrolled.
questions.answerText: It lengthens while still generating force

questions.q: In the load velocity relationship for skeletal muscle, what happens to shortening velocity as the load on the muscle increases?
options: Shortening velocity decreases
Shortening velocity increases
Shortening velocity is unchanged until the load exceeds maximal tension
Shortening velocity increases and then plateaus
questions.why: Heavier loads mean each crossbridge spends more of its cycle bearing force, so the filaments slide more slowly and the load velocity curve falls steadily from left to right. Velocity cannot rise with load, since more work must be done per unit distance. It also does not stay flat, because even a small load slows shortening measurably. A plateau would imply that load stops mattering, which the curve does not show.

questions.q: At what load does a muscle reach its maximum shortening velocity, usually written Vmax?
options: At the load that produces maximum power
At zero load
At the load equal to maximal isometric tension
At the load that is just above maximal isometric tension
questions.why: With nothing to lift, crossbridges cycle as fast as their myosin ATPase allows, so Vmax is measured at zero external load. Maximum power occurs near a third of maximal load, where force and velocity are both moderate. At a load equal to maximal isometric tension the muscle cannot shorten at all, so velocity is zero. Above that load the muscle is stretched, which is eccentric rather than shortening.

questions.q: What does the term isotonic contraction describe?
options: A contraction in which the muscle length is held constant
A contraction in which the muscle changes length against a constant load
A contraction in which tension rises continuously to a peak
A contraction in which the muscle is stimulated at a constant frequency
questions.why: Isotonic means same tension: once tension matches the load, the muscle changes length while the force it exerts stays fixed at the load value. Constant length is isometric, the opposite condition. Continuously rising tension describes the early, isometric phase before movement begins. Constant stimulus frequency is a property of the stimulator, not of the mechanics of the contraction.
questions.answerText: A contraction in which the muscle changes length against a constant load

questions.q: Which type of contraction produces the greatest tension in a maximally activated muscle?
options: Eccentric
Concentric
Isometric
Concentric at very low load
questions.why: Eccentric contractions generate the highest tension, roughly 1.2 to 1.8 times maximal isometric force, because stretching an attached crossbridge adds mechanical strain to the force it already produces. Isometric force is the next highest and is the usual reference point. Concentric force is lower than isometric at every velocity, because attached crossbridges are detaching to allow sliding. Concentric contraction at very low load produces the least force of all, since the load itself sets the tension.

questions.q: In an isotonic twitch against a load, what is happening during the delay between the stimulus and the start of shortening?
options: The action potential is still traveling along the motor nerve
Ca2+ is being pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The muscle is contracting isometrically until its tension matches the load
The tendon is being stretched by the falling load
questions.why: Nothing can move until muscle tension equals the load, so every isotonic contraction begins with an isometric phase, and the heavier the load, the longer that phase lasts. Nerve conduction is over in a few milliseconds and does not account for the load dependence of the delay. Ca2+ reuptake happens during relaxation, at the end of the twitch. The load is held stationary by a support before the contraction, so it is not stretching the tendon.
questions.answerText: The muscle is contracting isometrically until its tension matches the load

questions.q: A student holds a heavy textbook motionless in an outstretched hand. How would you classify the activity of the elbow flexors?
options: Concentric, because the flexors are actively shortening to hold the book
Isometric, because tension is high and muscle length is constant
Eccentric, because gravity is pulling the forearm down
Isotonic, because the load on the muscle stays constant
