questions.why: The book is not moving, so the elbow angle and therefore the muscle length are fixed while the flexors generate force, which is the definition of isometric. Concentric requires visible shortening, which is not happening. Gravity pulls downward but the arm is not descending, so no lengthening occurs and it is not eccentric. The load is indeed constant, but isotonic requires a length change, which this contraction does not have.
questions.answerText: Isometric, because tension is high and muscle length is constant

questions.q: A lifter slowly lowers a dumbbell from a fully flexed elbow to a straight arm, keeping control the whole way. How would you classify the biceps activity?
options: Eccentric, because the biceps lengthens while producing force
Concentric, because the biceps is actively producing force
Isometric, because the biceps controls the speed of descent
Passive lengthening, because the biceps is relaxed during lowering
questions.why: The elbow is extending, so the biceps is getting longer, and it is still generating force to keep the descent slow, which makes this eccentric. Producing force alone does not make a contraction concentric; the direction of length change decides that. Controlling speed does not make it isometric, since the length is clearly changing. If the biceps were relaxed the dumbbell would drop, so passive lengthening is ruled out by the controlled descent.
questions.answerText: Eccentric, because the biceps lengthens while producing force

questions.q: A person rises from a chair to a standing position. How would you classify the quadriceps activity during the rise?
options: Eccentric, because the quadriceps resists gravity throughout
Isometric, because the knee is loaded through the whole movement
Concentric, because the quadriceps shortens as the knee extends
Eccentric, because body weight exceeds the force the quadriceps can produce
questions.why: Standing up extends the knee, which shortens the quadriceps while it lifts body weight, so this is a concentric contraction doing positive work. Resisting gravity does not by itself make a contraction eccentric; sitting back down would be the eccentric half of the same movement. The knee angle changes markedly, so nothing about this is isometric. If body weight exceeded quadriceps force the person would not rise at all.
questions.answerText: Concentric, because the quadriceps shortens as the knee extends

questions.q: A muscle shortening against a 2 kg load is then asked to shorten against a 6 kg load. Predict what happens to its shortening velocity and to the tension it develops.
options: Velocity rises and tension falls
Velocity falls and tension also falls
Velocity is unchanged and tension rises
Velocity falls and tension rises
questions.why: In an isotonic contraction the tension the muscle develops equals the load it moves, so a heavier load means higher tension, and the load velocity curve says the higher the tension, the slower the shortening. Velocity cannot rise with load, since more force per crossbridge means slower cycling. Tension cannot fall while the load rises, because the muscle must at least match the load to move it. And velocity is strongly load dependent, so it does not stay fixed.

questions.q: A muscle is stimulated maximally while attached to a load heavier than its maximal isometric tension. Predict what the muscle does.
options: It shortens very slowly against the load
It lengthens rapidly because the crossbridges cannot attach
It develops tension without shortening, so the contraction remains isometric
It shortens at Vmax because maximal stimulation overrides the load
questions.why: Shortening requires muscle tension to exceed the load, and here it cannot, so tension rises to its maximum and the length never changes, which is an isometric contraction by definition. Slow shortening happens only for loads below maximal isometric tension. The crossbridges do attach, which is exactly why the muscle can hold the load rather than being pulled out rapidly. Vmax is the zero load velocity and is the opposite extreme from this situation.
questions.answerText: It develops tension without shortening, so the contraction remains isometric

questions.q: Which type of contraction is most strongly associated with delayed onset muscle soreness one or two days after unfamiliar exercise?
options: Concentric contractions
Isometric contractions held at short muscle length
Low load concentric contractions at high velocity
Eccentric contractions
questions.why: Eccentric work loads a small number of attached crossbridges with high force per bridge, which produces microscopic damage to the sarcomeres and the inflammatory response felt a day or two later. Concentric contractions distribute lower force across the working bridges and cause much less damage. Isometric holds at short lengths produce lower tension still, and short lengths are the least damaging. Fast, light concentric work generates the lowest tension of any of these options.

questions.q: A hiker walks steadily downhill. What is the quadriceps doing at each step as the leading knee bends under body weight?
options: Contracting concentrically to drive the knee forward
Contracting eccentrically to control knee flexion
Contracting isometrically to lock the knee in place
Relaxing completely while the ligaments absorb the load
questions.why: Body weight bends the loaded knee, which lengthens the quadriceps while it keeps generating force to slow the descent, the textbook eccentric contraction and the reason downhill walking causes soreness. Concentric quadriceps work extends the knee, which is what happens going uphill. The knee is flexing rather than holding a fixed angle, so it is not isometric. If the quadriceps relaxed the knee would buckle.
questions.answerText: Contracting eccentrically to control knee flexion

questions.q: A muscle with a maximal isometric tension of 60 N is tested at three loads. At 10 N it shortens at 40 mm/s, at 30 N at 18 mm/s, and at 50 N at 4 mm/s. At which of these loads does the muscle generate the most mechanical power?
options: 10 N, because shortening velocity is highest there
50 N, because force is highest there
30 N, because the product of force and velocity is highest there
All three are equal, because power depends only on maximal isometric tension
questions.why: Power is force times velocity, so the products are 400, 540, and 200 in these units, and the intermediate load wins because it trades a moderate amount of force for a moderate amount of speed. The lightest load gives high velocity but almost no force, and the heaviest gives high force but almost no movement, so both produce less power. Maximal isometric tension is measured at zero velocity, where power is zero by definition.
questions.answerText: 30 N, because the product of force and velocity is highest there

questions.q: In an isotonic twitch experiment, the load is increased from 5 g to 20 g. Predict how the tracing changes in two respects: the delay before shortening begins and the distance the muscle shortens.
options: The delay shortens and the shortening distance decreases
The delay lengthens and the shortening distance decreases
The delay lengthens and the shortening distance increases
The delay is unchanged and the shortening distance decreases
questions.why: A heavier load takes longer for the isometric phase to build tension up to the load value, so the delay grows, and less of the twitch remains for shortening, so the muscle lifts the load a shorter distance before relaxation begins. The delay cannot shorten with a heavier load, since more tension must be developed first. Shortening distance falls rather than rises, because both force and available time are working against the muscle. And the delay is load dependent, so it does not stay fixed.
questions.answerText: The delay lengthens and the shortening distance decreases

questions.q: A lifter cannot curl a 30 kg dumbbell but can lower the same dumbbell slowly and under full control. Which sequence of statements explains this?
options: Eccentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds concentric force at any shortening velocity
Concentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds eccentric force
Isometric force exceeds both eccentric and concentric force
Eccentric and concentric force are equal, and the difference is entirely motor unit recruitment
questions.why: Stretching attached crossbridges adds strain to the force they already generate, so a maximally activated muscle can resist more load while lengthening than it can lift while shortening, which is why the lowering succeeds when the lift fails. Concentric force is the smallest of the three, so ranking it highest reverses the relationship. Isometric force sits between the other two rather than above both. Recruitment is maximal in both attempts here, so the difference comes from crossbridge mechanics rather than from how many motor units are active.
questions.answerText: Eccentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds concentric force at any shortening velocity

questions.q: A muscle is stimulated maximally while an experimenter slowly pulls it longer against the contraction, then repeats the test while allowing it to shorten at 20 mm/s. Compared with a maximal isometric contraction of the same muscle, what tensions would you predict?
options: Lower than isometric during the pull and higher than isometric during the shortening
Higher than isometric in both tests, because the muscle is maximally stimulated
Higher than isometric during the pull and lower than isometric during the shortening
Equal to isometric in both tests, because stimulation rather than velocity sets tension
questions.why: Forced lengthening is eccentric and raises tension above the isometric value by straining attached crossbridges, while shortening is concentric and drops tension below isometric because bridges must detach to permit sliding. The reversed answer swaps the two limbs of the force velocity curve. Maximal stimulation sets how many fibers are active but does not exempt the muscle from the velocity dependence of force. That same dependence is why tension is not simply equal in all three conditions.
questions.answerText: Higher than isometric during the pull and lower than isometric during the shortening

questions.q: Which skeletal muscle fiber type contains the highest density of mitochondria?
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic
All three carry the same mitochondrial density
questions.why: Slow oxidative fibers are built for sustained aerobic work, so they are packed with mitochondria to keep oxidative phosphorylation supplying ATP for hours. Fast glycolytic fibers sit at the other extreme, with few mitochondria and a reliance on stored glycogen. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate, with a substantial but smaller mitochondrial complement than slow oxidative fibers. The three types differ sharply on this measure, which is one of the main ways they are told apart.

questions.q: High myoglobin content, which gives a muscle its red appearance, is characteristic of which fiber type?
options: Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic only
Slow oxidative
Fibers with the largest diameter
questions.why: Myoglobin stores oxygen inside the fiber and speeds its diffusion to the mitochondria, so the fibers that depend most on oxygen carry the most, and slow oxidative fibers are the reddest. Fast glycolytic fibers have little myoglobin and appear pale or white. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers do contain myoglobin, but less than slow oxidative fibers, so naming them alone is wrong. Diameter tracks with force capacity, and the largest fibers are actually the palest.

questions.q: Fast glycolytic fibers depend mainly on which source of ATP during activity?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis using stored glycogen
Oxidative phosphorylation using fatty acids
Oxidative phosphorylation using blood glucose
Creatine phosphate alone for the entire contraction
questions.why: Fast glycolytic fibers have few mitochondria and a poor capillary supply, so they break down their large glycogen stores anaerobically to lactate, which supplies ATP quickly but only briefly. Fatty acid oxidation requires abundant mitochondria and oxygen, which describes slow oxidative fibers. Oxidative use of blood glucose has the same requirement and the same problem. Creatine phosphate is used by all fiber types, but it lasts only seconds and cannot carry a contraction on its own.

questions.q: Which fiber type fatigues most rapidly during repeated maximal contractions?
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
All three fatigue at the same rate
questions.why: Fast glycolytic fibers burn through glycogen quickly and accumulate the metabolic byproducts of anaerobic work, so their force falls within a minute or less. Slow oxidative fibers resist fatigue for hours because oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP as fast as it is used. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate, holding force for minutes rather than seconds. Fatigue resistance is one of the main axes on which the three types differ.

questions.q: Differences in myosin ATPase activity between fiber types most directly determine what?
options: How fast the fiber shortens
How much force one crossbridge produces
How resistant the fiber is to fatigue
How many capillaries surround the fiber
questions.why: Myosin ATPase splits ATP at the crossbridge, and the speed of that step sets the speed of the cycle, which is what makes fast fibers fast and slow fibers slow. Force per crossbridge is nearly the same in all fiber types; whole fiber force differences come from fiber diameter and the number of myofibrils. Fatigue resistance is set by metabolic machinery, not by the ATPase rate. Capillary supply is a property of the surrounding tissue, established by the fiber's oxidative demand.

questions.q: Capillary density around the fiber is greatest in which type?
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Whichever type has the largest cross sectional area
questions.why: Slow oxidative fibers must be supplied with oxygen and fuel continuously, so they are surrounded by the richest capillary network of the three. Fast glycolytic fibers work anaerobically for short bursts and have the sparsest capillary supply. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers fall between the two. Large diameter actually works against oxygen delivery, because it lengthens the diffusion distance from capillary to the center of the fiber.

questions.q: Which fiber type stores the most glycogen?
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Fibers with the highest myoglobin content
questions.why: Fast glycolytic fibers rely on anaerobic glycolysis, and glycogen is the substrate for that pathway, so they hold the largest intracellular stores. Slow oxidative fibers store less glycogen and lean more on fatty acids and blood borne fuel delivered continuously by their capillaries. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers store an intermediate amount. High myoglobin marks the oxidative end of the spectrum, which is the low glycogen end.

questions.q: Which fiber type has the largest diameter and generates the greatest force per fiber?
options: Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Fast glycolytic
Fiber diameter is the same in all three types
questions.why: Fast glycolytic fibers pack in the most myofibrils, so they are the widest and produce the most force per fiber, which suits them to brief powerful efforts. Slow oxidative fibers are the smallest, a design that keeps oxygen diffusion distances short. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate in diameter as in most other properties. Diameter differs substantially among the types and is one reason motor unit force output varies so widely.

questions.q: The soleus muscle works continuously at low force to keep a standing person from falling forward. Which fiber type would you expect to predominate?
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic
An even mix of fast glycolytic and slow oxidative
questions.why: A postural task demands low force sustained for hours, which is exactly what fatigue resistant, oxygen dependent slow oxidative fibers deliver. Fast glycolytic fibers would fatigue within a minute and are wasteful for a low force job. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers hold up better than fast glycolytic but still fatigue faster than the task requires. A mix weighted toward fast fibers would not match the continuous demand.

questions.q: A biopsy from a competitive sprinter's gastrocnemius shows large pale fibers with abundant glycogen and few mitochondria. Which type are they, and what does that predict about fatigue?
options: Fast oxidative glycolytic, and they resist fatigue for many minutes
Slow oxidative, and they resist fatigue for hours
Fast glycolytic, and they fatigue within about a minute of maximal work
Fast glycolytic, and they resist fatigue because glycogen stores are large
questions.why: Pale color means low myoglobin, few mitochondria means little oxidative capacity, and abundant glycogen means anaerobic fuel, so these are fast glycolytic fibers, which fatigue rapidly. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers would show many more mitochondria and a redder appearance. Slow oxidative fibers would be small, red, and mitochondria rich, the opposite of what is described. Large glycogen stores do not confer fatigue resistance, because the byproducts of anaerobic glycolysis accumulate long before the glycogen runs out.
questions.answerText: Fast glycolytic, and they fatigue within about a minute of maximal work

questions.q: A biopsy shows fibers with a fast myosin ATPase, a high mitochondrial density, and moderate glycogen. Which fiber type is this?
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
A denervated fiber reverting to an immature type
Fast oxidative glycolytic
questions.why: Fast ATPase with strong oxidative machinery is the signature of the intermediate type, which contracts quickly yet resists fatigue reasonably well. Slow oxidative fibers would have the oxidative machinery but a slow ATPase. Fast glycolytic fibers would have the fast ATPase but very few mitochondria. Denervated fibers atrophy rather than adopt a distinct hybrid profile, and nothing in the description points to denervation.

questions.q: As a person gradually increases force from a light to a maximal effort, which motor units are recruited first, and why?
options: Fast glycolytic units, because they generate the most force per fiber
Fast oxidative glycolytic units, because they balance speed with endurance capacity
Slow oxidative units, because their motor neurons reach threshold first
All units at once, because recruitment follows the all or none law
questions.why: The size principle says smaller motor neurons depolarize to threshold at lower synaptic current, and those neurons innervate slow oxidative fibers, so light efforts use the fatigue resistant units first and save the powerful ones for later. Fast glycolytic units do produce the most force, which is precisely why they are held in reserve until high force is needed. Fast oxidative glycolytic units are recruited in the middle of the range, not at the start. The all or none law applies to a single fiber's action potential, not to how many motor units a muscle activates.
questions.answerText: Slow oxidative units, because their motor neurons reach threshold first

questions.q: A fiber is found to have very few mitochondria, sparse capillaries, and a large glycogen store. Predict how long it can sustain maximal force.
options: Under a minute, because anaerobic glycolysis cannot sustain the ATP demand
Several hours, because its glycogen store is large
About ten to fifteen minutes, because it can shift to fatty acid oxidation
Indefinitely, as long as blood glucose remains normal
questions.why: Without mitochondria and capillaries the fiber must make ATP anaerobically, and that pathway produces byproducts and drains glycogen fast enough that force falls within seconds to a minute. Glycogen size does not rescue it, because fatigue arrives well before the store is exhausted. Fatty acid oxidation requires mitochondria and oxygen, which this fiber lacks. Blood glucose cannot help much either, since sparse capillaries limit delivery and anaerobic yield per glucose is tiny.
questions.answerText: Under a minute, because anaerobic glycolysis cannot sustain the ATP demand

questions.q: A muscle sample looks distinctly pale rather than red. What does that predict about its dominant fiber type and its fatigue resistance?
options: Mostly slow oxidative fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
Mostly fast oxidative glycolytic fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with poor fatigue resistance
Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
questions.why: Color comes from myoglobin and from the density of capillaries, both of which track oxidative capacity, so a pale muscle is dominated by fast glycolytic fibers that tire quickly. Slow oxidative fibers would make the muscle look dark red. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers also carry myoglobin, so they would not produce a pale sample. Correctly naming the fiber type but pairing it with good fatigue resistance misses the tradeoff that defines the type.
questions.answerText: Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with poor fatigue resistance

questions.q: Compare the fiber recruitment demanded by a two hour marathon pace and by a single maximal deadlift. Which comparison is correct?
options: The marathon relies chiefly on fast glycolytic fibers, while the deadlift relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers
Both rely chiefly on fast oxidative glycolytic fibers, because both require substantial force
The marathon relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers, while the deadlift recruits fast glycolytic fibers as well
Both recruit all fiber types equally, because recruitment does not depend on the force required
questions.why: Long, low force work is exactly the job of fatigue resistant slow oxidative fibers, while a brief maximal lift needs so much force that recruitment proceeds up the size principle to include fast glycolytic units. Reversing the two ignores that fast glycolytic fibers cannot sustain two hours of work. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers contribute to both tasks, but they do not dominate either one. Recruitment is graded by required force, so equal recruitment in both tasks is not what happens.
questions.answerText: The marathon relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers, while the deadlift recruits fast glycolytic fibers as well

questions.q: Three fiber samples are measured. Sample X: slow myosin ATPase, very high mitochondrial density, dense capillaries. Sample Y: fast ATPase, high mitochondrial density, moderate capillaries. Sample Z: fast ATPase, low mitochondrial density, sparse capillaries. Which sample would you expect to dominate the calf muscle of a middle distance runner during a hard four minute race?
options: Sample X, because any event lasting several minutes is entirely aerobic in nature
Sample Y, because a four minute effort needs both speed and oxidative capacity
Sample Z, because the effort is described as hard rather than easy
Sample X, because slow fibers are recruited first in every contraction
questions.why: Sample Y is fast oxidative glycolytic, and a four minute maximal effort sits exactly in its niche: fast enough to need a rapid ATPase, long enough to need mitochondria. Sample X is slow oxidative and contributes, but its slow ATPase limits the pace of a race effort. Sample Z is fast glycolytic and would fatigue in well under a minute. Slow fibers are indeed recruited first, but by four minutes at race pace the recruitment has moved well past them.
questions.answerText: Sample Y, because a four minute effort needs both speed and oxidative capacity

questions.q: A single motor unit is stimulated repeatedly in an isolated muscle. Its twitches are brief, it produces high force, and its force falls by more than half within 45 seconds. Classify the unit and name the metabolic feature that explains the force decline.
options: Fast oxidative glycolytic, because its intermediate mitochondrial content limits sustained work
Fast glycolytic, because its few mitochondria force it to depend on anaerobic glycolysis
Slow oxidative, because its small fibers exhaust their glycogen quickly
Fast glycolytic, because its myosin ATPase runs out of ATP binding sites
questions.why: Brief twitches point to a fast ATPase, high force points to large fibers, and rapid fatigue points to little oxidative capacity, which together define a fast glycolytic unit dependent on anaerobic glycolysis. A fast oxidative glycolytic unit would hold force much longer than 45 seconds. Slow oxidative units produce low force with long twitches and resist fatigue, so they do not match the tracing. Myosin does not run out of binding sites; fatigue arises from metabolic changes inside the fiber, not from a shortage of sites.
questions.answerText: Fast glycolytic, because its few mitochondria force it to depend on anaerobic glycolysis

questions.q: In a classic cross innervation experiment, the nerve normally supplying a fast muscle is surgically redirected to a slow muscle and allowed to reinnervate it. Over weeks the slow muscle's contraction speed increases and its myosin isoform shifts. What does this result show?
options: Fiber type is fixed at birth and the observed change must be an artifact of surgery
Fiber type is determined only by the blood supply reaching the muscle
The pattern of neural activity the motor neuron delivers can drive a change in fiber type
The muscle changed type because its capillary density changed first
questions.why: Reinnervation by a nerve with a different firing pattern converts the muscle toward the properties of the donor nerve's usual target, which shows that chronic activity pattern regulates myosin isoform expression and metabolic profile. Fiber type is clearly not fixed, since the change is measurable and reproducible. Blood supply matters for oxidative capacity but was not the variable manipulated here. Capillary density adapts to activity as well, so it is a consequence of the new activity pattern, not the cause of the myosin switch.
questions.answerText: The pattern of neural activity the motor neuron delivers can drive a change in fiber type

questions.q: A subject squeezes a handgrip at 15 percent of maximum for two minutes, then jumps to 90 percent of maximum. Predict what happens to the fiber types in use and to the rate of lactate production.
options: Recruitment shifts from fast glycolytic back to slow oxidative units, and lactate production falls
Recruitment stays limited to slow oxidative units, and lactate production is unchanged
Recruitment extends from slow oxidative to fast glycolytic units, and lactate production rises sharply
Recruitment extends to fast glycolytic units, but lactate production falls because more motor units share the work
questions.why: Raising force recruits progressively larger motor units, so the fast glycolytic units added at 90 percent bring their anaerobic metabolism with them and blood lactate climbs. Recruitment never runs backward down the size principle when force is increasing. Staying limited to slow oxidative units could not generate 90 percent of maximal force. Adding motor units increases total ATP turnover rather than spreading a fixed demand, so lactate production rises rather than falls.
questions.answerText: Recruitment extends from slow oxidative to fast glycolytic units, and lactate production rises sharply

questions.q: Which ATP source supplies the working muscle fastest at the very start of a contraction?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Fatty acid oxidation
Creatine phosphate
questions.why: Creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate to ADP in a single enzymatic step, so it regenerates ATP faster than any other route, though the store is small. Anaerobic glycolysis is next fastest but takes several reactions to get going. Oxidative phosphorylation is the slowest to respond, since it depends on delivering oxygen and on many mitochondrial steps. Fatty acid oxidation is the slowest of all, because the fatty acids must first be mobilized and transported into mitochondria.

questions.q: Which enzyme transfers a phosphate group from creatine phosphate to ADP in a working muscle fiber?
options: Myosin ATPase
Phosphofructokinase
Creatine kinase
ATP synthase
questions.why: Creatine kinase catalyzes the reversible transfer that rebuilds ATP from ADP and creatine phosphate, which is why it is the enzyme of the first few seconds of effort. Myosin ATPase splits ATP at the crossbridge rather than regenerating it. Phosphofructokinase is the rate limiting enzyme of glycolysis, a different pathway. ATP synthase makes ATP in mitochondria using the proton gradient, not using creatine phosphate.

questions.q: For roughly how long can stored creatine phosphate sustain maximal muscle activity?
options: About 1 to 2 seconds
About 2 to 3 minutes
About 10 to 15 seconds
About 20 to 30 minutes
questions.why: Creatine phosphate stores cover the first 10 to 15 seconds of maximal effort, roughly the length of a short sprint, before glycolysis has to take over. One to two seconds is closer to the amount of preformed ATP already sitting in the fiber. Two to three minutes is the range covered by anaerobic glycolysis. Twenty to thirty minutes and beyond belongs to oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: What is the end product of anaerobic glycolysis in a working muscle fiber?
options: Pyruvate entering the mitochondrion
Carbon dioxide and water
Lactate
Acetyl CoA
questions.why: When oxygen supply lags behind demand, pyruvate is reduced to lactate so that NAD+ is regenerated and glycolysis can keep running. Pyruvate entering the mitochondrion is what happens when oxygen is adequate, which makes the pathway aerobic rather than anaerobic. Carbon dioxide and water are the end products of complete oxidation. Acetyl CoA is formed from pyruvate inside the mitochondrion, again an aerobic step.

questions.q: What is the net ATP yield per glucose molecule from anaerobic glycolysis?
options: 2 ATP
4 ATP
18 ATP
30 to 32 ATP
questions.why: Glycolysis generates four ATP but spends two in its early steps, so the net yield is two ATP per glucose when the pathway ends at lactate. Four is the gross figure before the investment is subtracted. Eighteen does not correspond to any standard figure in this pathway. Thirty to thirty two is the yield when glucose is fully oxidized aerobically.

questions.q: Approximately how much ATP does complete oxidative metabolism of one glucose molecule yield?
options: About 2 ATP
About 12 ATP
About 100 ATP
About 30 to 32 ATP
questions.why: Full oxidation through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, about fifteen times the anaerobic yield. Two ATP is the anaerobic figure. Twelve does not match either pathway. About 100 ATP per glucose overstates the yield by a wide margin, although a single long chain fatty acid can approach that range.

questions.q: Which ATP source can sustain muscle activity for hours as long as fuel and oxygen keep arriving?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Creatine phosphate
The preformed ATP already in the fiber
questions.why: Oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP at a modest rate but can do so indefinitely, which is why endurance work depends on it. Anaerobic glycolysis is limited to a couple of minutes at high intensity by byproduct accumulation and glycogen depletion. Creatine phosphate lasts seconds. Preformed ATP is the smallest store of all and would be exhausted in a second or two without regeneration.

questions.q: Which of these ATP sources requires oxygen delivery to the muscle fiber?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Transfer of phosphate from creatine phosphate
Hydrolysis of preformed ATP by myosin
Oxidative phosphorylation
questions.why: Only oxidative phosphorylation uses oxygen, as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, which is why its rate is limited by blood flow and oxygen delivery. Anaerobic glycolysis is defined by proceeding without oxygen. The creatine kinase reaction is a single phosphate transfer with no oxygen requirement. Myosin splits ATP mechanically and chemically, again with no oxygen involved.

questions.q: An athlete performs an all out 8 second effort from rest. Which ATP source supplies most of the energy?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Fatty acid oxidation
Creatine phosphate
questions.why: Eight seconds falls inside the creatine phosphate window, since that system responds instantly and covers roughly the first 10 to 15 seconds of maximal work. Anaerobic glycolysis is contributing by then but has not yet become the main supplier. Oxidative phosphorylation takes tens of seconds to ramp up and cannot match the ATP demand of an all out sprint. Fatty acid oxidation is slower still and dominates only during prolonged low intensity work.

questions.q: A runner sprints as hard as possible for 60 seconds. Which ATP source dominates over most of that effort, and what accumulates as a result?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation, with carbon dioxide accumulating in muscle and blood
Anaerobic glycolysis, with lactate accumulating in muscle and blood
Creatine phosphate, with creatine accumulating in the fiber
Fatty acid oxidation, with ketone bodies accumulating in blood
questions.why: A 60 second maximal effort outruns both the creatine phosphate store and the rate of oxidative ATP supply, so anaerobic glycolysis carries the bulk of the load and lactate builds up. Oxidative phosphorylation contributes but cannot meet the demand at that intensity. Creatine phosphate is largely spent within the first 15 seconds. Fatty acid oxidation is far too slow to matter in a maximal effort of this length.
questions.answerText: Anaerobic glycolysis, with lactate accumulating in muscle and blood

questions.q: A person jogs at a comfortable pace for 30 minutes. Which ATP source supplies most of the energy?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis for the first half and creatine phosphate for the second
Oxidative phosphorylation
questions.why: At a submaximal pace, oxygen delivery keeps up with demand, so mitochondria supply nearly all the ATP and the effort can continue for a long time. Anaerobic glycolysis would flood the muscle with lactate long before 30 minutes elapsed. Creatine phosphate lasts seconds and only covers the first few strides. The final option reverses the physiology entirely, since creatine phosphate is a starting system rather than an ending one.

questions.q: Predict what happens to blood lactate during a maximal 400 meter run lasting about 50 seconds.
options: It falls, because lactate is consumed as fuel during intense exercise
It stays flat, because oxidative phosphorylation covers the whole demand
It rises only after the run ends, because lactate cannot leave muscle during contraction
It rises substantially, because anaerobic glycolysis is supplying a large share of the ATP
questions.why: A 50 second maximal effort demands ATP far faster than oxidative phosphorylation can deliver, so glycolysis runs at high rate and lactate accumulates in muscle and spills into blood. Lactate is used as fuel by heart and by other muscle fibers, but at this intensity production far exceeds consumption. Oxidative metabolism cannot cover a maximal effort of this length. Lactate does leave the fiber on monocarboxylate transporters during the run, so the rise is not delayed to the recovery period.
questions.answerText: It rises substantially, because anaerobic glycolysis is supplying a large share of the ATP

questions.q: An experimental agent blocks creatine kinase in a muscle fiber. Predict the effect on ATP availability during the first five seconds of maximal contraction.
options: ATP falls faster than normal, because the creatine phosphate buffer cannot be tapped
ATP is unaffected, because glycolysis compensates within milliseconds
ATP rises, because creatine phosphate accumulates unused
ATP falls only after 30 seconds, when glycogen stores are depleted
questions.why: Creatine kinase is the only route from creatine phosphate to ATP, so blocking it removes the buffer that normally holds ATP nearly constant through the first seconds of effort. Glycolysis needs several seconds to reach a high rate and cannot fill the gap instantly. Accumulating unused creatine phosphate does not help, because its phosphate can no longer be transferred. Glycogen depletion is a much later event and is not what makes the first five seconds fail.
questions.answerText: ATP falls faster than normal, because the creatine phosphate buffer cannot be tapped

questions.q: Anaerobic glycolysis yields 2 ATP per glucose and complete oxidation yields about 32. About how many times more glucose per minute must a muscle consume to make the same ATP anaerobically?
options: About 2 times more
About 16 times more
About 8 times more
About 32 times more
questions.why: Dividing 32 by 2 gives 16, so an anaerobic fiber must run through roughly sixteen glucose molecules to match the ATP from one oxidized aerobically, which is why glycogen empties so fast during intense work. Two is the anaerobic yield itself rather than the ratio. Eight would be the ratio if aerobic yield were 16 ATP. Thirty two is the aerobic yield, not the ratio between the pathways.

questions.q: Blood flow to a working muscle is partially occluded so that oxygen delivery falls. Predict the shift in how the fiber makes ATP and the immediate consequence.
options: A shift toward oxidative phosphorylation, with faster fatty acid use
A shift toward creatine phosphate, which can now sustain the contraction indefinitely
A shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, with faster glycogen use and lactate accumulation
No shift, because ATP production rate is set by contraction frequency rather than oxygen supply
questions.why: Reduced oxygen limits the electron transport chain, so the fiber leans on the pathway that does not need oxygen, burning glycogen quickly and generating lactate. Oxidative phosphorylation cannot increase when its oxygen supply has been cut. Creatine phosphate does buffer briefly, but the store is small and cannot sustain anything indefinitely. Contraction frequency sets ATP demand, while oxygen availability constrains which pathway can meet it.
questions.answerText: A shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, with faster glycogen use and lactate accumulation

questions.q: Two athletes are tested. Athlete A shows blood lactate of 12 mmol/L and a respiratory exchange ratio near 1.0 at the end of the test. Athlete B shows blood lactate of 2 mmol/L and a ratio near 0.85 at the end of a longer test. Which conclusion about the dominant ATP pathway in each is best supported?
options: Athlete A relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation, while athlete B relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis
Both relied chiefly on creatine phosphate, since both completed the tests successfully
Neither conclusion can be drawn, because lactate reflects only liver metabolism
Athlete A relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, while athlete B relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation
questions.why: High lactate with a ratio near 1.0 marks heavy carbohydrate use and a large anaerobic contribution, while low lactate with a ratio near 0.85 indicates a substantial contribution from fat oxidation and an aerobic effort. Reversing the two ignores what a rising lactate concentration signifies. Creatine phosphate could not sustain either test, since both lasted far longer than 15 seconds. Muscle is a major lactate source during exercise, so the measurement does bear on muscle metabolism.
questions.answerText: Athlete A relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, while athlete B relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: A patient with a deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase cannot break down muscle glycogen. During an ischemic forearm exercise test, predict the blood lactate response and the reason.
options: Lactate rises higher than normal, because oxidative metabolism is also blocked
Lactate fails to rise, because glycogen cannot be fed into glycolysis
Lactate rises normally, because blood glucose substitutes fully for muscle glycogen
Lactate falls below baseline, because the muscle switches entirely to creatine phosphate
questions.why: Anaerobic glycolysis in working muscle runs mostly on glycogen, so if glycogen cannot be mobilized, the pathway has little substrate and the usual exercise induced lactate rise is absent. Oxidative metabolism is not blocked by this enzyme deficiency, so there is no reason for lactate to overshoot. Blood glucose uptake continues but is far too slow under ischemia to replace glycogen. Creatine phosphate contributes for seconds only and does not lower baseline lactate.
questions.answerText: Lactate fails to rise, because glycogen cannot be fed into glycolysis

questions.q: At the start of moderate intensity exercise, oxygen uptake takes about two minutes to reach a steady value, yet the muscle produces the required ATP from the first second. Which combination best explains the gap?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation is already at steady state and the delay in oxygen uptake is purely a measurement artifact
Fatty acid oxidation covers the first two minutes and is then replaced by carbohydrate oxidation
Stored ATP alone covers the first two minutes, after which oxidative phosphorylation begins
Creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis bridges until oxidative supply reaches steady state
questions.why: The lag in oxygen uptake creates an oxygen deficit that is filled by the two systems that do not depend on oxygen, so creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis carries the load until mitochondrial ATP output catches up. The lag is a real physiological delay in delivery and mitochondrial activation, not an artifact. Fatty acid oxidation is a slow system and cannot cover the onset of exercise. Stored ATP would last a second or two at most, nowhere near two minutes.
questions.answerText: Creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis bridges until oxidative supply reaches steady state

questions.q: A muscle needs 5 mmol of ATP per minute during a task. Creatine phosphate stores can supply about 1 mmol total, anaerobic glycolysis can supply up to 8 mmol per minute for about two minutes, and oxidative phosphorylation can supply 4 mmol per minute indefinitely. Predict what limits performance if the task must continue for 10 minutes.
options: Performance fails after a few minutes, because oxidative supply alone falls short of the 5 mmol per minute demand
Performance continues indefinitely, because oxidative phosphorylation alone can meet the demand
Performance fails within 15 seconds, because creatine phosphate is the only usable source for this task
Performance continues indefinitely, because anaerobic glycolysis can be sustained for the full 10 minutes
questions.why: Oxidative supply of 4 mmol per minute leaves a 1 mmol per minute shortfall that glycolysis must cover, and glycolysis can only do so for about two minutes, after which the deficit forces the effort to slow or stop. Oxidative supply alone is not enough, since 4 is less than 5. Creatine phosphate is only 1 mmol total and is not the only source available. Glycolysis is explicitly limited to about two minutes at high rate, so it cannot cover the full task.
questions.answerText: Performance fails after a few minutes, because oxidative supply alone falls short of the 5 mmol per minute demand

questions.q: What defines central fatigue?
options: A decline in force caused by reduced drive from the central nervous system to the motor neurons
A decline in force caused by depletion of ATP within the muscle fiber
A decline in force caused by failure of transmission at the neuromuscular junction
A decline in force caused by accumulation of inorganic phosphate in the sarcoplasm
questions.why: Central fatigue lives above the motor neuron: the brain sends fewer or slower commands, so fewer motor units fire even though the muscle itself could still produce force. ATP depletion and phosphate accumulation are events inside the fiber and belong to peripheral fatigue. Neuromuscular junction failure is also peripheral, since it occurs downstream of the central nervous system.
questions.answerText: A decline in force caused by reduced drive from the central nervous system to the motor neurons

questions.q: Peripheral fatigue is located where in the pathway from brain to force?
options: In the motor cortex and descending motor pathways
At or beyond the neuromuscular junction, within the muscle fiber itself
In the sensory pathways carrying pain signals to the brain
In the cardiovascular centers of the medulla
questions.why: Peripheral fatigue covers everything from the neuromuscular junction outward, including excitation contraction coupling and the crossbridge machinery inside the fiber. Motor cortex and descending pathways are the site of central fatigue. Sensory pain pathways can contribute to the central component but are not the peripheral site. Medullary cardiovascular centers control blood pressure and heart rate rather than force production.
questions.answerText: At or beyond the neuromuscular junction, within the muscle fiber itself

questions.q: What does excess post exercise oxygen consumption describe?
options: Oxygen consumption that stays above resting level after exercise has ended
The oxygen deficit that builds during the first minutes of exercise
The maximal rate of oxygen consumption a person can achieve
The difference between arterial and venous oxygen content during exercise
questions.why: After exercise stops, oxygen uptake falls only gradually, and that elevated consumption is used to restore the systems that ran ahead of oxygen delivery during the effort. The oxygen deficit is the mirror image and occurs at the start of exercise. Maximal oxygen consumption is a capacity measure, not a recovery phenomenon. The arteriovenous oxygen difference describes extraction by tissue rather than what happens after exercise.
questions.answerText: Oxygen consumption that stays above resting level after exercise has ended

questions.q: Accumulation of which ion in the T tubule lumen contributes to peripheral fatigue by reducing the size of the action potential?
options: Ca2+
K+
Cl-
HCO3-
questions.why: Repeated action potentials pump K+ out of the fiber into the narrow T tubule lumen, where it accumulates, depolarizes the membrane, and inactivates Na+ channels so later action potentials are smaller. Ca2+ accumulates in the sarcoplasm rather than in the T tubule and its problem is impaired release, not impaired excitation. Cl- movement stabilizes the membrane rather than accumulating to a fatiguing level. HCO3- is a buffer and plays no role in T tubule excitation.

questions.q: Accumulating inorganic phosphate inside a fatiguing muscle fiber reduces force mainly by what mechanism?
options: It lowers Ca2+ release and reduces crossbridge force
It blocks the myosin binding site on actin directly
It prevents the action potential from spreading into the T tubules
It prevents ATP from binding to the myosin head
questions.why: Inorganic phosphate rises as ATP and creatine phosphate are broken down, and it both precipitates with Ca2+ inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum and shifts crossbridge kinetics toward lower force. It does not sit on the actin binding site; that is the job of tropomyosin under resting conditions. Action potential conduction into the T tubules is affected by K+ rather than by phosphate. ATP still binds myosin during fatigue, which is why the muscle relaxes rather than going into rigor.
questions.answerText: It lowers Ca2+ release and reduces crossbridge force

questions.q: During intense exercise, what happens to intracellular pH in a working muscle fiber?
options: It rises, because lactate consumes H+ as it forms
It stays constant, because muscle has no significant buffering capacity
It rises, because carbon dioxide is exhaled faster during exercise
It falls, because H+ accumulates alongside high rates of glycolysis
questions.why: High rates of ATP turnover and glycolysis release H+ faster than the fiber can buffer or export it, so intracellular pH drops during intense work. Lactate formation actually consumes some H+, but the net effect of the whole pathway during intense exercise is acidification. Muscle does have substantial buffering, which slows but does not prevent the fall. Increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide from blood but cannot keep pace with intramuscular H+ production during maximal work.
questions.answerText: It falls, because H+ accumulates alongside high rates of glycolysis

questions.q: Which of these processes consumes oxygen during the recovery period after exercise?
options: Anaerobic conversion of pyruvate to lactate
Rebuilding creatine phosphate stores in muscle
Transfer of phosphate from creatine phosphate to ADP
Diffusion of oxygen from alveolus to capillary
questions.why: Restoring creatine phosphate requires ATP made oxidatively, which is a major reason oxygen uptake stays elevated after exercise ends. Converting pyruvate to lactate is by definition an anaerobic step and consumes no oxygen. The creatine kinase reaction that spends creatine phosphate uses no oxygen either; it is the rebuilding that costs. Diffusion across the alveolar membrane is a transport step, not a process that consumes oxygen.
questions.answerText: Rebuilding creatine phosphate stores in muscle

questions.q: Which experimental maneuver is used to separate central from peripheral fatigue in a voluntarily contracting muscle?
options: Measuring blood lactate immediately after the effort
Delivering an electrical stimulus to the motor nerve during a maximal voluntary effort
Recording the resting membrane potential of a single fiber
Measuring the muscle's cross sectional area before and after the effort
questions.why: A stimulus superimposed on a maximal voluntary contraction adds force only if the nervous system was failing to activate every motor unit, so any extra force is a direct measure of the central component. Blood lactate reports metabolic activity but says nothing about how completely the nervous system is driving the muscle. Resting membrane potential of one fiber does not distinguish the two sites either. Cross sectional area changes over weeks of training, not over a single fatiguing contraction.
questions.answerText: Delivering an electrical stimulus to the motor nerve during a maximal voluntary effort

questions.q: A subject's maximal voluntary grip force has fallen by 30 percent after a sustained effort. An electrical stimulus applied to the nerve adds a large extra increment of force. What does this indicate?
options: A purely peripheral component, because the muscle can still respond to stimulation
A substantial central component, because the nervous system is no longer fully activating the muscle
Complete neuromuscular junction failure, because extra force required artificial stimulation
A measurement error, because stimulation cannot add force to a maximal contraction
questions.why: If the muscle can produce more force when stimulated than the subject can produce voluntarily, the missing force was never commanded, which is the definition of central fatigue. The muscle responding to stimulation is exactly what rules out a purely peripheral explanation. Junction failure would prevent the stimulus from producing extra force at all. Stimulation adding force to a supposedly maximal effort is the expected finding in central fatigue, not an artifact.
questions.answerText: A substantial central component, because the nervous system is no longer fully activating the muscle

questions.q: After a sustained contraction, voluntary force has fallen by 40 percent and an electrical stimulus to the nerve adds essentially no extra force. Where does the fatigue lie?
options: Peripherally, within the muscle fiber and its excitation contraction coupling
Centrally, in descending drive from the motor cortex
Centrally, in the motivation of the subject
In the sensory nerves reporting muscle tension to the brain
questions.why: When maximal stimulation cannot recover the lost force, the deficit must lie in the muscle itself, so the fatigue is peripheral. Reduced central drive would leave force in reserve that stimulation could recruit, which is not what happened. Motivation is a central explanation and fails for the same reason. Sensory feedback can influence central drive, but the test result already shows the muscle cannot produce more force even when maximally driven.
questions.answerText: Peripherally, within the muscle fiber and its excitation contraction coupling

questions.q: Inorganic phosphate concentration inside a fatiguing fiber rises sharply. Predict the effect on Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and on peak tension.
options: Ca2+ release falls and peak tension falls
Ca2+ release rises and peak tension rises
Ca2+ release falls but peak tension is preserved by increased Ca2+ sensitivity
Ca2+ release is unchanged and peak tension falls only because ATP is depleted
questions.why: Phosphate entering the sarcoplasmic reticulum precipitates with Ca2+ there, so less Ca2+ is available for release, and less Ca2+ in the sarcoplasm means fewer active crossbridges and lower tension. Neither release nor tension increases with phosphate. Ca2+ sensitivity actually falls during fatigue rather than rising to compensate. ATP concentration is defended fairly well during fatigue, so it is not the main cause of the tension loss.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ release falls and peak tension falls

questions.q: A sprinter finishes a 200 meter race and then stands still, breathing hard for several minutes. Why does oxygen consumption remain elevated?
options: Oxygen is being stored in muscle for the next race
Oxygen is being used to rebuild creatine phosphate, reload myoglobin and hemoglobin, and clear lactate
Oxygen consumption tracks heart rate, which is slow to fall for purely mechanical reasons
Oxygen is being consumed by anaerobic glycolysis continuing in the leg muscles
questions.why: Recovery costs are real work: creatine phosphate must be resynthesized, oxygen stores on myoglobin and hemoglobin must be refilled, lactate must be converted back to pyruvate or glucose, and elevated body temperature and catecholamines keep metabolic rate high. Oxygen cannot be stockpiled beyond the small myoglobin and hemoglobin stores. Heart rate stays elevated because metabolic demand is elevated, not the other way round. Anaerobic glycolysis by definition does not consume oxygen.
questions.answerText: Oxygen is being used to rebuild creatine phosphate, reload myoglobin and hemoglobin, and clear lactate

questions.q: During a sustained maximal contraction, which fiber type would you predict to lose force first?
options: Slow oxidative, because it is recruited first and therefore works longest
Fast oxidative glycolytic, because it has the highest ATP demand of the three
Fast glycolytic, because it depends on anaerobic metabolism
All types together, because fatigue is a whole muscle rather than a fiber level event
questions.why: Fast glycolytic fibers have the least oxidative capacity and the fastest byproduct accumulation, so their force falls within seconds to a minute of maximal work. Slow oxidative fibers are recruited first but are the most fatigue resistant, so they hold force longest. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers fall between the two rather than leading. Fatigue develops at the level of individual fibers and differs measurably between them, which is why whole muscle force decays in stages.
questions.answerText: Fast glycolytic, because it depends on anaerobic metabolism

questions.q: During a sustained submaximal effort a subject's force is falling. A researcher shouts encouragement and force immediately rises. What does that tell you about the fatigue present?
options: At least part of it is central, since increased drive recovered force instantly
It is entirely peripheral, since the muscle was able to produce more force
It reflects rapid resynthesis of creatine phosphate during the shout
It shows that lactate was cleared from the fiber within seconds
questions.why: Force that can be recovered by motivation alone was being withheld by the nervous system, so the deficit was central rather than a failure of the muscle. If the fatigue were entirely peripheral, no amount of encouragement could raise force. Creatine phosphate resynthesis takes minutes and requires oxygen, not seconds of shouting. Lactate clearance is likewise far too slow to explain an instant change in force.
questions.answerText: At least part of it is central, since increased drive recovered force instantly

questions.q: A subject produces 300 N in a maximal voluntary contraction when rested, and a superimposed nerve stimulus adds 0 N. After two minutes of sustained effort, voluntary force is 180 N and the superimposed stimulus adds 40 N. How much of the 120 N loss is central and how much is peripheral?
options: 120 N central and 0 N peripheral
40 N central and 80 N peripheral
0 N central and 120 N peripheral
80 N central and 40 N peripheral
questions.why: The stimulus reveals 40 N the nervous system failed to command, so that is the central share, and the muscle's own maximal capacity has fallen from 300 N to 220 N, an 80 N peripheral loss. Calling the whole 120 N central would require the stimulated muscle to still reach 300 N, which it does not. Calling it all peripheral ignores the 40 N that stimulation recovered. Reversing the two numbers misreads which value the superimposed twitch measures.

questions.q: A sprinter's oxygen consumption after a 100 meter race falls steeply for the first two minutes and then declines slowly over the next 30 minutes. Which explanation best fits the two phases?
options: The fast phase reflects clearance of lactate from the blood, while the slow phase refills the creatine phosphate stores
The fast phase refills creatine phosphate and oxygen stores, and the slow phase reflects lactate handling and raised temperature
Both phases reflect continued anaerobic glycolysis in the leg muscles
The fast phase reflects the oxygen deficit incurred at the start of the race, while the slow phase is a measurement drift
questions.why: Creatine phosphate resynthesis and the reloading of myoglobin and hemoglobin are quick, so they dominate the steep early fall, while lactate conversion, elevated body temperature, and lingering hormonal effects keep metabolic rate slightly high for much longer. Swapping the phases misjudges the timescales, since creatine phosphate recovers in minutes, not half an hour. Anaerobic glycolysis consumes no oxygen, so it cannot account for either phase. The oxygen deficit describes the beginning of exercise and is repaid across both phases rather than only the first.
questions.answerText: The fast phase refills creatine phosphate and oxygen stores, and the slow phase reflects lactate handling and raised temperature

questions.q: A patient reports profound exercise fatigue. During testing, maximal voluntary force is low, but supramaximal stimulation of the motor nerve produces normal force, and the force decays no faster than normal with repeated stimulation. Where does the problem lie?
options: At the neuromuscular junction, since voluntary force is reduced
In excitation contraction coupling, since the patient reports fatigue with exertion
In the mitochondria of the muscle fibers, since exercise tolerance is poor
Above the motor neuron, since the muscle performs normally when driven artificially
questions.why: Normal stimulated force and a normal rate of decline show that the nerve terminal, the fiber membrane, the coupling machinery, and the crossbridges are all working, so the deficit must be in the drive reaching the motor neurons. A junction problem would show reduced or rapidly declining stimulated force. A coupling defect would depress stimulated force from the first stimulus. A mitochondrial defect would make stimulated force fall abnormally fast during repeated stimulation, which the test excludes.
questions.answerText: Above the motor neuron, since the muscle performs normally when driven artificially

questions.q: A blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure on the upper arm while the subject performs repeated handgrip contractions. Compared with the same test without the cuff, predict the rate of force loss and the mechanism.
options: Force falls faster, because the cuff blocks motor nerve conduction within seconds
Force falls more slowly, because trapped blood keeps oxygen available to the muscle
Force falls at the same rate, because muscle fatigue is determined centrally
Force falls faster, because oxygen delivery is cut and the fiber must rely on anaerobic metabolism
questions.why: Occluding arterial inflow starves the mitochondria, forces a shift to anaerobic glycolysis, and lets H+, phosphate, and K+ accumulate without washout, so peripheral fatigue develops much faster than usual. Nerve conduction does eventually fail under prolonged compression, but that takes many minutes, far longer than the force decline in this test. Trapped blood is quickly stripped of its oxygen and cannot sustain the muscle. Fatigue in this setting is dominated by the peripheral consequences of ischemia rather than by central drive.
questions.answerText: Force falls faster, because oxygen delivery is cut and the fiber must rely on anaerobic metabolism

questions.q: What is the principal change in a muscle fiber produced by months of heavy resistance training?
options: An increase in fiber diameter from added myofibrils
An increase in the number of fibers from cell division
An increase in mitochondrial density within each fiber
An increase in the number of sarcomeres in series along the fiber
questions.why: Resistance training drives synthesis of new actin and myosin, which are assembled into additional myofibrils, so the fiber grows thicker and produces more force. Mature skeletal muscle fibers do not divide, so the fiber count changes very little. Mitochondrial density is the hallmark of endurance training and often falls slightly with hypertrophy because the fiber grows around the existing mitochondria. Adding sarcomeres in series lengthens a fiber and follows chronic stretch rather than heavy loading.
questions.answerText: An increase in fiber diameter from added myofibrils

questions.q: What are the two most characteristic adaptations to months of endurance training within the trained muscle?
options: Larger fiber diameter and greater glycogen storage
More motor units and larger motor neurons
More mitochondria and a denser capillary network
More sarcomeres in series and a longer resting length
questions.why: Endurance training improves the muscle's ability to make ATP aerobically, so mitochondrial content and capillary supply both rise, which raises oxygen delivery and oxidative enzyme capacity together. Fiber diameter changes little with endurance work and is the resistance training adaptation. Motor unit number is fixed by the number of motor neurons and does not increase with training. Sarcomere number in series changes with chronic length rather than with endurance activity.
questions.answerText: More mitochondria and a denser capillary network

questions.q: What is the difference between hypertrophy and hyperplasia in skeletal muscle?
options: Hypertrophy is an increase in fiber number, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber size
Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of existing fibers, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber number
Hypertrophy is growth in length, and hyperplasia is growth in diameter
Hypertrophy occurs only with endurance training, and hyperplasia only with resistance training
questions.why: Hypertrophy means bigger cells, and it is the dominant response of human skeletal muscle to resistance training, while hyperplasia means more cells and contributes little in humans. Reversing the definitions inverts both terms. Neither term specifies length versus diameter; both describe how mass is added. Hypertrophy is chiefly a resistance training response rather than an endurance one, and hyperplasia is not the endurance response either.
questions.answerText: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of existing fibers, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber number

questions.q: What is the main structural change in a muscle immobilized in a cast for several weeks?
options: Fiber diameter decreases as protein breakdown exceeds synthesis
Fiber number decreases as unused fibers are removed
Fiber diameter increases as connective tissue is deposited inside the fiber
Mitochondrial density increases to compensate for the reduced workload
questions.why: Disuse tips the balance toward protein degradation, so myofibrillar protein is lost and the fibers become thinner, which is why a limb looks smaller when the cast comes off. Fibers atrophy rather than disappear, so the count is roughly preserved. Connective tissue does increase around the muscle with prolonged disuse, but that occurs outside the fibers and does not make them wider. Mitochondrial density falls with disuse rather than rising, because the demand that maintains it is gone.
questions.answerText: Fiber diameter decreases as protein breakdown exceeds synthesis

questions.q: What happens to fiber diameter with several months of pure endurance training?
options: It increases markedly, similar to resistance training
It changes little and may decrease slightly
It doubles, because oxidative fibers grow fastest
It increases in fast fibers only and is unchanged in slow fibers
questions.why: Endurance training improves the aerobic machinery rather than the contractile mass, and a slightly smaller fiber actually shortens the oxygen diffusion path, so diameter stays flat or drops a little. Marked growth in diameter is the resistance training signature. Doubling of diameter does not happen with any training program in that timeframe. Endurance work does not selectively enlarge fast fibers; if anything it shifts them toward a more oxidative profile.
questions.answerText: It changes little and may decrease slightly

questions.q: What role do satellite cells play in skeletal muscle adaptation?
options: They are immune cells that clear damaged proteins from the fiber
They are the cells that form new capillaries around the fiber
They are sensory receptors that report muscle length back to the spinal cord
They are muscle stem cells that fuse with fibers and add nuclei
questions.why: Satellite cells sit under the basal lamina of the fiber, and when the fiber is loaded or injured they proliferate and fuse into it, supplying the extra nuclei that a larger fiber needs to sustain protein synthesis. Clearing damaged protein is the job of macrophages and the fiber's own proteasomes. New capillaries are formed by endothelial cells. Muscle length is reported by muscle spindles, which are specialized fibers with sensory endings rather than satellite cells.
questions.answerText: They are muscle stem cells that fuse with fibers and add nuclei

questions.q: Which training program raises the oxidative enzyme activity of a muscle the most?
options: Heavy resistance training
Endurance training
A single maximal effort repeated once a week
Complete rest, which conserves enzyme protein
questions.why: Repeated prolonged submaximal activity signals the fiber to build more mitochondria and more of the enzymes inside them, which is the core endurance adaptation. Heavy resistance training builds contractile protein rather than oxidative capacity. A single weekly maximal effort provides too little total aerobic work to drive mitochondrial biogenesis. Rest lowers oxidative enzyme activity rather than conserving it, because the stimulus that maintains the machinery is removed.

questions.q: How does atrophy after cutting the motor nerve compare with atrophy from immobilizing a limb with an intact nerve?
options: Denervation atrophy is slower and milder
Denervation atrophy is faster and more severe
The two produce identical rates and degrees of atrophy
Denervation causes hypertrophy rather than atrophy
questions.why: A denervated muscle loses both mechanical loading and the trophic influence of its motor neuron, so it wastes faster and further than a muscle that is merely unloaded but still innervated. Losing two influences cannot be milder than losing one. The two situations are therefore not equivalent, which is why nerve injury carries a worse prognosis for muscle mass. Denervation never produces growth; the fibers shrink and, over long periods, can be replaced by connective tissue and fat.
questions.answerText: Denervation atrophy is faster and more severe

questions.q: After twelve weeks of heavy resistance training, fiber cross sectional area has risen by 25 percent while the number of capillaries per fiber is unchanged. Predict what happens to capillary density expressed per unit of fiber area.
options: It falls, because the same number of capillaries now serves a larger fiber
It rises, because larger fibers always attract new capillaries
It is unchanged, because capillary number and fiber size always change together
It falls, because resistance training destroys capillaries
questions.why: Density is a ratio, so holding the numerator fixed while the denominator grows by a quarter must lower the value, which is one reason pure strength training does not improve endurance. Capillary growth does occur with some programs, but the stem states capillary number per fiber did not change. Capillary number and fiber size are regulated by different signals and often move independently. Nothing in resistance training destroys capillaries; the ratio falls purely because the fibers grew.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the same number of capillaries now serves a larger fiber

questions.q: A leg is immobilized in a cast for six weeks. Predict what happens to fiber cross sectional area and to mitochondrial content.
options: Both decrease
Cross sectional area decreases and mitochondrial content increases
Cross sectional area increases and mitochondrial content decreases
Both are unchanged, because the nerve supply remains intact
questions.why: Disuse removes both the mechanical load that maintains contractile protein and the metabolic demand that maintains mitochondria, so the fiber loses on both fronts. Mitochondria do not increase when demand disappears. Cross sectional area cannot grow without loading, so the third option has the direction backward. An intact nerve slows the loss compared with denervation, but it does not prevent it.

questions.q: A previously sedentary person trains for a marathon over six months. Predict the change in mitochondrial content and in maximal oxygen consumption.
options: Mitochondrial content increases and maximal oxygen consumption is unchanged
Both increase
Mitochondrial content is unchanged and maximal oxygen consumption increases
Both decrease as the fibers become smaller and more efficient
questions.why: Endurance training raises mitochondrial content in the trained muscle and improves cardiac output and oxygen extraction, so both the local and the whole body measures rise together. Mitochondrial gains without any change in maximal oxygen consumption would be unusual in a previously sedentary person, since central adaptations occur as well. Maximal oxygen consumption rarely improves without the peripheral changes that let muscle use the delivered oxygen. Neither measure falls with training, even though fiber diameter may drop slightly.

questions.q: Two programs are compared over twelve weeks: heavy low repetition lifting and long slow distance running. Which program produces the larger increase in maximal voluntary force?
options: The running program, because it improves oxygen delivery to the fibers
The running program, because slow fibers generate the most force per unit area
The lifting program, because it drives hypertrophy and improved neural drive
Neither, because maximal force is fixed by fiber type and cannot be trained
questions.why: Maximal force scales with contractile protein and with how completely the nervous system can recruit and drive the motor units, and heavy lifting improves both. Better oxygen delivery raises endurance rather than peak force. Slow fibers do not produce more force per unit area than fast fibers, and they are the smaller fibers besides. Maximal force is highly trainable, which is why strength programs work in the first place.
questions.answerText: The lifting program, because it drives hypertrophy and improved neural drive

questions.q: A patient is on strict bed rest for four weeks. Predict the change in fatigue resistance when normal activity resumes.
options: Fatigue resistance is improved, because the muscle has been fully rested
Fatigue resistance is unchanged, because it depends only on fiber type
Fatigue resistance is reduced, because the number of motor units has fallen
Fatigue resistance is reduced, because mitochondrial content and capillary supply have fallen
questions.why: Bed rest removes the activity that maintains oxidative capacity, so mitochondria and capillaries regress and the muscle tires quickly on return to activity. Rest of this length is deconditioning rather than recovery. Fiber type composition is only part of the picture, and the oxidative machinery within a given fiber type is itself trainable. Motor unit number is set by the number of motor neurons, which bed rest does not reduce.
questions.answerText: Fatigue resistance is reduced, because mitochondrial content and capillary supply have fallen

questions.q: Predict the fiber type shift produced by several months of endurance training.
options: A shift from slow oxidative toward fast glycolytic properties
A shift from fast oxidative glycolytic toward fast glycolytic properties
A shift from fast glycolytic toward fast oxidative glycolytic properties
No shift at all, because fiber type is fixed by genetics
questions.why: Chronic aerobic activity pushes fibers toward the oxidative end of the spectrum, so fast glycolytic fibers acquire more mitochondria and capillaries and take on fast oxidative glycolytic properties. Shifting toward the glycolytic end is what disuse and sprint style training encourage, not endurance work. Fiber type has a strong genetic component but is clearly modifiable by chronic activity pattern, as cross innervation and training studies both show.
questions.answerText: A shift from fast glycolytic toward fast oxidative glycolytic properties

questions.q: Biopsies before and after a twelve week program show fiber cross sectional area up 22 percent, capillaries per fiber unchanged, and mitochondrial volume density down 8 percent. Which program was most likely performed?
options: Endurance cycling five days a week
Heavy resistance training
Six weeks of limb immobilization followed by six weeks of walking
Complete bed rest
questions.why: Growth in fiber area with no capillary gain and a diluted mitochondrial density is the classic hypertrophy signature, since new myofibrillar protein expands the fiber around a fixed complement of mitochondria and capillaries. Endurance cycling would raise mitochondrial density and capillary number while leaving area roughly flat. Immobilization followed by walking would at best return the fiber to baseline, not add 22 percent. Bed rest would shrink the fiber.

questions.q: An astronaut spends six months in microgravity with limited exercise. Predict what happens to postural muscle fiber size, capillary supply, and oxidative capacity, and name the main driver.
options: Fiber size decreases while capillary supply and oxidative capacity increase, driven by fluid shifts
All three increase, driven by the exercise countermeasures used in flight
All three are unchanged, because muscle adapts only to gravity over years rather than months
All three decrease, driven by the loss of chronic mechanical loading and activity
questions.why: Antigravity muscles such as the soleus lose their principal stimulus in microgravity, so contractile protein, capillary supply, and mitochondrial content all regress, much as they do with bed rest on Earth. Capillary and oxidative gains would require increased activity, which is exactly what is missing. Countermeasure exercise slows the loss but does not reverse it into net gain in this scenario. Detectable atrophy appears within weeks, not years.
questions.answerText: All three decrease, driven by the loss of chronic mechanical loading and activity

questions.q: A coach must choose between two twelve week programs for a client whose goals are a higher one repetition maximum squat and a faster 5 kilometer run time. Which prediction about the two programs is best supported by muscle plasticity?
options: Endurance running will improve both, because aerobic fitness is the foundation of every kind of performance
Heavy lifting will improve both, because a stronger muscle is automatically more fatigue resistant
Either program will improve both equally, because all training raises total muscle protein
Lifting raises the squat more and running lowers the run time more, since the adaptations are separate
questions.why: Hypertrophy and neural adaptations drive maximal force, while mitochondrial and capillary adaptations drive endurance, and each is produced mainly by its own kind of loading, so goals that pull in different directions need different programs. Aerobic training does not build the contractile mass a heavy squat requires. A larger fiber is not automatically more fatigue resistant, because hypertrophy dilutes mitochondrial density. Training adaptations are specific to the stimulus rather than a generic increase in protein.
questions.answerText: Lifting raises the squat more and running lowers the run time more, since the adaptations are separate

questions.q: A trained endurance athlete stops training entirely. Mitochondrial content falls measurably within about two weeks, while maximal oxygen consumption declines more slowly over several weeks. What does this difference in time course indicate?
options: Central cardiovascular adaptations regress faster than the local adaptations inside the muscle
Local muscle adaptations regress faster than central cardiovascular ones
Mitochondrial content and maximal oxygen consumption are unrelated measurements
The measurements conflict, so one of them must be in error
questions.why: Mitochondrial protein turns over quickly and depends on frequent activity to be maintained, while blood volume, cardiac dimensions, and capillary structure change more slowly, so the peripheral machinery is lost first during detraining. The reverse ordering does not match the observed timescales. The two measures are tightly linked, since delivered oxygen must be used by mitochondria to appear in the whole body value. Different rates of change in linked variables are ordinary physiology rather than a measurement error.
questions.answerText: Local muscle adaptations regress faster than central cardiovascular ones

questions.q: What does a surface electromyogram record?
options: The force the muscle is producing at the tendon
