The action potentials traveling down the motor nerve to the muscle
The concentration of Ca2+ released inside the fibers
The summed electrical activity of the fibers under the electrodes
questions.why: Surface EMG picks up the electrical field created by many muscle fiber action potentials occurring under the skin electrodes, which is why its amplitude reflects how much muscle is electrically active. Force is measured separately by a dynamometer, and the relationship between the two signals is exactly what the lab examines. Motor nerve action potentials are far too small and too deep to register on surface electrodes. Intracellular Ca2+ cannot be detected from the skin surface at all.
questions.answerText: The summed electrical activity of the fibers under the electrodes

questions.q: What does a hand dynamometer measure in the grip fatigue lab?
options: The electrical activity of the forearm flexors
The force the hand exerts during a grip
The rate of ATP use in the forearm muscles
The number of motor units recruited in the forearm
questions.why: A dynamometer is a force transducer, so it reports how hard the hand squeezes, usually in kilograms or newtons. Electrical activity is what the EMG electrodes report, and pairing the two signals is the point of the experiment. ATP use is not measured directly in this lab. Motor unit number can only be inferred, and then only indirectly, from the EMG signal rather than from the force record.
questions.answerText: The force the hand exerts during a grip

questions.q: Surface EMG amplitude increases mainly because of which two changes in the muscle?
options: The fibers shorten faster and the tendon stretches further
More motor units are recruited and active units fire faster
More Ca2+ is released per action potential and troponin binds more of it
The muscle warms up and its electrical resistance falls
questions.why: EMG amplitude is a summed electrical signal, so it grows when more fibers are firing and when each active unit fires more often, which are the same two mechanisms the nervous system uses to increase force. Shortening velocity and tendon stretch are mechanical events and do not add electrical signal. Ca2+ release and troponin binding occur after the action potential and are not detected by the electrodes. Warming does change tissue impedance slightly, but that is a minor effect compared with recruitment and rate coding.
questions.answerText: More motor units are recruited and active units fire faster

questions.q: Grip force in this lab is most commonly reported in which units?
options: Kilograms or newtons
Millivolts or microvolts
Milliseconds
Hertz
questions.why: Force is force, so the dynamometer reads in kilograms of force or in newtons. Millivolts and microvolts are the units of the EMG voltage signal, which is recorded on a separate channel. Milliseconds measure the duration of events such as the latent period. Hertz measures stimulus or firing frequency rather than force.

questions.q: Why are surface EMG electrodes placed over the belly of the muscle rather than over the tendon?
options: The tendon carries a larger signal that would saturate the amplifier
The tendon is where the motor nerve enters the muscle
The belly contains the contractile fibers that generate the electrical signal
Skin over the tendon has a lower electrical resistance
questions.why: Only muscle fibers generate action potentials, and they are concentrated in the belly, so that is where the recorded signal is largest and most representative. Tendon is collagen and is electrically silent, so it produces a smaller signal, not a larger one. The motor nerve typically enters near the middle of the muscle belly, not at the tendon. Skin impedance depends on preparation of the skin rather than on what lies beneath it.
questions.answerText: The belly contains the contractile fibers that generate the electrical signal

questions.q: What is a maximal voluntary contraction, usually abbreviated MVC?
options: The force produced when the motor nerve is stimulated supramaximally
The greatest force a subject can produce voluntarily against the transducer
The force at which the EMG signal first becomes detectable
The force a subject can hold for at least five minutes
questions.why: MVC is a voluntary measure and serves as the reference against which submaximal target forces such as 30 percent or 60 percent are set. Force from supramaximal nerve stimulation is an evoked measure and can exceed MVC when central fatigue is present. The point where EMG first appears is closer to a threshold of activation than to a maximum. A force sustainable for five minutes is an endurance measure, far below MVC.
questions.answerText: The greatest force a subject can produce voluntarily against the transducer

questions.q: Why is a raw surface EMG signal usually rectified and then integrated or averaged before analysis?
options: Rectification converts the electrical signal into units of force
The raw signal swings above and below zero, so a plain average would cancel to near zero
Integration removes the contribution of deeper motor units
Rectification eliminates the electromechanical delay between the EMG signal and the force record
questions.why: Motor unit potentials are biphasic, so the raw trace has positive and negative excursions that cancel; taking absolute values first, then smoothing, gives an amplitude measure that tracks activation. Rectification does not convert volts to newtons, and the two signals stay on separate calibrated channels. Integration smooths the signal without selecting for depth. The electromechanical delay between EMG and force is a physiological interval and is not removed by processing.
questions.answerText: The raw signal swings above and below zero, so a plain average would cancel to near zero

questions.q: During a sustained fatiguing contraction, how does the median frequency of the EMG power spectrum change?
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
It stays constant while amplitude falls
It becomes undetectable once fatigue begins
questions.why: Fatigue slows muscle fiber conduction velocity, which stretches out each motor unit action potential and shifts the power spectrum toward lower frequencies, making the downward shift a standard objective marker of peripheral fatigue. An upward shift is what you would see with faster conduction, the opposite condition. Median frequency changes reliably during fatigue rather than staying fixed. The signal remains perfectly detectable, which is why the shift can be measured at all.

questions.q: A subject holds a steady 30 percent of maximum grip force for three minutes. Force stays on target, but EMG amplitude climbs throughout. What explains this?
options: The fatiguing fibers generate larger action potentials as they tire
The dynamometer is drifting out of calibration during the hold
The skin impedance under the electrodes falls steadily as the subject sweats during the hold
More motor units are recruited and firing rates rise to replace fatiguing units
questions.why: As early recruited units fatigue and contribute less force, the nervous system must recruit more units and drive them faster to keep force on target, and all that extra electrical activity shows up as rising EMG amplitude. Individual fiber action potentials actually get slower and smaller with fatigue, not larger. A drifting transducer would show as a drifting force record, which the stem says is steady. Falling skin impedance from sweat can add a small amount, but it cannot account for a progressive rise across three minutes of constant force.
questions.answerText: More motor units are recruited and firing rates rise to replace fatiguing units

questions.q: A subject squeezes at maximum effort continuously for 60 seconds. Force falls steadily and EMG amplitude also falls. How should this be interpreted?
options: The muscle is relaxing voluntarily, since a fall in EMG can only mean the subject stopped trying
The electrodes have detached, since a fatiguing muscle always shows rising EMG
Nothing is left in reserve, so fatigue lowers force and activation together
Force and EMG always fall together, so the recording contains no information about fatigue
questions.why: During a maximal effort everything is already recruited from the start, so there is no reserve to call on, and as fibers fatigue and central drive wanes both the force and the electrical signal decline together. Falling EMG during a maximal effort is expected and does not by itself prove the subject stopped trying. Rising EMG is the signature of a submaximal hold, not of every fatiguing contraction, so detached electrodes are not the only explanation. The joint decline is exactly the informative finding that distinguishes a maximal protocol from a submaximal one.
questions.answerText: Nothing is left in reserve, so fatigue lowers force and activation together

questions.q: Two subjects produce identical grip force, but one has considerably more subcutaneous fat over the forearm. Predict the effect on recorded surface EMG amplitude.
options: The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a smaller recorded amplitude for the same force
The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a larger recorded amplitude for the same force
The amplitudes are identical, because EMG amplitude depends only on the force produced
The amplitudes are identical, because rectification corrects for tissue thickness
questions.why: Fat is a poor conductor and increases the distance from the active fibers to the electrodes, so the recorded signal is attenuated even though the muscle is working just as hard. Extra tissue between source and electrode cannot amplify a signal. Amplitude therefore depends on recording conditions as well as on force, which is why EMG values are compared within a subject rather than between subjects. Rectification changes the shape of the signal but does not restore lost amplitude.
questions.answerText: The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a smaller recorded amplitude for the same force

questions.q: A subject holds 60 percent of maximum grip force in one trial and 30 percent in another, each to the point of failure. Predict the relative endurance times and the reason.
options: The 60 percent hold lasts longer, because higher force recruits more fatigue resistant fibers
The two holds last about the same time, because both end in complete fatigue
The 30 percent hold lasts longer, because low force contractions use no ATP
The 30 percent hold lasts much longer, because fewer motor units are needed and blood flow is less obstructed
questions.why: Lower target force calls on fewer and mostly oxidative motor units and compresses the vessels within the muscle less, so oxygen keeps arriving and the hold can be sustained far longer. Higher force recruits fast fatigable units, not fatigue resistant ones, so it shortens endurance. Endurance time is steeply and inversely related to target force, so the two trials are not equivalent. Low force contractions certainly use ATP, just at a lower rate that oxidative metabolism can match.
questions.answerText: The 30 percent hold lasts much longer, because fewer motor units are needed and blood flow is less obstructed

questions.q: An EMG trace shows large, slow, irregular deflections that appear each time the subject shifts position in the chair, even when grip force is zero. What is the most likely source?
options: Recruitment of additional motor units in the resting forearm
Cardiac electrical activity conducted to the forearm electrodes
The downward shift in median frequency that accompanies fatigue
Movement artifact from the electrodes and cables shifting on the skin
questions.why: Signals that are time locked to body movement rather than to force, and that persist when the muscle is at rest, are almost always mechanical artifact at the skin electrode interface. Motor unit recruitment would produce force, and the stem states force is zero. Cardiac signal appears as a small regular deflection at heart rate rather than as irregular movement locked deflections. A median frequency shift is a change in the spectrum of a genuine EMG signal and does not create deflections during rest.
questions.answerText: Movement artifact from the electrodes and cables shifting on the skin

questions.q: A subject doubles grip force from 20 percent to 40 percent of maximum. Predict what happens to the rectified EMG amplitude.
options: It stays the same, because the same muscle is being used
It decreases, because higher force requires fewer but larger motor units
It increases substantially, because both recruitment and firing rate rise
It doubles exactly, because EMG amplitude and force are linearly proportional
questions.why: Producing more force requires activating more motor units and driving them at higher rates, and both changes add electrical activity, so amplitude rises clearly with force. Using the same muscle does not mean using the same amount of it. Higher force recruits additional large units on top of the small ones, rather than fewer units. The relationship is monotonic but not exactly proportional, since it depends on fiber depth, cancellation between overlapping potentials, and recording conditions.
questions.answerText: It increases substantially, because both recruitment and firing rate rise

questions.q: A right handed subject records a higher maximal grip force in the right hand than the left. What is the most reasonable physiological interpretation?
options: The dominant forearm has slightly more muscle and better practiced neural drive
The dominant forearm has a different fiber type composition determined at birth
The dominant forearm has more motor units, since motor units are added with use
The difference must be a calibration error, since both hands share the same nervous system
questions.why: Habitual use of the dominant hand produces modest hypertrophy and more effective recruitment, which together explain the usual difference of roughly 10 percent. Fiber type composition does differ between people, but it does not differ systematically between a person's two arms because of handedness. Motor unit number is fixed by the number of motor neurons and does not increase with use. A consistent, reproducible difference in the expected direction is a real finding rather than an artifact.
questions.answerText: The dominant forearm has slightly more muscle and better practiced neural drive

questions.q: During a two minute hold at 40 percent of maximum, grip force stays on target for 60 seconds while EMG amplitude rises 25 percent, and then force falls 30 percent over the next 60 seconds while EMG amplitude falls back toward its starting value. What is the best two step interpretation?
options: The muscle grew stronger for the first minute and then weaker for the second
The electrodes gradually detached, which explains both the rise and the later fall in amplitude
The subject increased effort for the first minute and then deliberately relaxed
Compensatory recruitment held force early, and once the reserve was gone both fell
questions.why: The rising EMG at constant force in the first minute is the nervous system recruiting extra units to replace fatiguing ones, and when no reserve remains, further fatigue plus declining central drive drop force and electrical activity together. Muscle cannot gain strength within a minute, so the first option misreads the rising signal. Detaching electrodes would produce a monotonic loss of signal, not a rise followed by a fall. Deliberate relaxation is possible but is not the physiologically expected pattern in a standardized hold to failure.
questions.answerText: Compensatory recruitment held force early, and once the reserve was gone both fell

questions.q: After a fatiguing grip protocol and two minutes of rest, a subject's maximal force has recovered to 85 percent of the prefatigue value, but the EMG median frequency is still well below baseline. What does this combination indicate?
options: Recovery is complete and the residual frequency shift is an artifact of the rest period
Central fatigue has persisted while the peripheral component has fully resolved during the rest
Force recovery outpaces recovery of the fiber, so peripheral fatigue persists
The muscle has adapted to the protocol within two minutes, raising its fatigue resistance
questions.why: Median frequency tracks fiber conduction velocity, which depends on the ionic and metabolic state inside the fiber, and those take longer than two minutes to normalize even as gross force largely returns. A reproducible spectral shift is a measurement of a real state rather than an artifact. Persisting central fatigue would show as a force deficit recoverable by stimulation, and it would not explain a spectral shift, which is a peripheral marker. Training adaptations take weeks, not two minutes.
questions.answerText: Force recovery outpaces recovery of the fiber, so peripheral fatigue persists

questions.q: A blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure on the upper arm and the subject then performs repeated grip contractions at 30 percent of maximum. Compared with the same protocol with free circulation, predict the force decline and the EMG amplitude behavior.
options: Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude falls immediately because the nerve is compressed
Force is maintained longer, because occlusion traps oxygenated blood in the forearm
Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude rises steeply as the nervous system recruits harder to compensate
Force and EMG behave exactly as they do with free circulation, since 30 percent of maximum is a low target
questions.why: Cutting off arterial supply forces the working fibers into anaerobic metabolism and traps the byproducts, so peripheral fatigue develops rapidly, and the nervous system compensates by recruiting more units, which drives EMG amplitude up steeply. Nerve compression under a cuff takes many minutes and does not explain a fast force decline. Trapped blood is stripped of oxygen within seconds and cannot sustain the muscle. Low target forces are normally sustainable for minutes precisely because circulation keeps up, which is what the cuff removes.
questions.answerText: Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude rises steeply as the nervous system recruits harder to compensate

questions.q: Two subjects hold 50 percent of their own maximum to failure. Subject 1 lasts 45 seconds with a rapid force decay; subject 2 lasts 140 seconds with a gradual decay. Assuming similar effort and technique, what does this suggest about their forearm muscle composition?
options: Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of fast glycolytic fibers
Subject 1 likely has more total motor units, allowing faster recruitment
The difference must reflect maximal strength, since a stronger subject always fatigues faster
Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of oxidative fibers and a denser capillary supply
questions.why: Endurance at a fixed percentage of each subject's own maximum reflects the fatigue resistance of the fibers doing the work, so the longer holding subject probably carries more slow oxidative fibers with a better capillary supply. Fast glycolytic fibers fatigue quickly and would shorten the hold, not lengthen it. Motor unit number does not vary in a way that would explain a threefold endurance difference. Because each target is set as a percentage of the subject's own maximum, absolute strength has largely been normalized out.
questions.answerText: Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of oxidative fibers and a denser capillary supply

questions.q: In a muscle stimulation experiment, what is the threshold stimulus?
options: The smallest stimulus voltage that activates every motor unit in the muscle
The stimulus frequency at which individual twitches begin to fuse
The stimulus voltage above which further increases damage the muscle
The smallest stimulus voltage that produces a measurable contraction
questions.why: Threshold is the voltage at which the first and most excitable motor units reach their firing threshold, so it is the lowest voltage that produces any tension at all. The voltage that activates every motor unit is the maximal stimulus, which is much higher. The frequency at which twitches begin to fuse is a frequency phenomenon, not a voltage one. Damaging voltages are a practical concern in a real preparation but are not what threshold means.
questions.answerText: The smallest stimulus voltage that produces a measurable contraction

questions.q: What is the maximal stimulus in a muscle stimulation experiment?
options: The highest voltage the stimulator can deliver
The lowest voltage that produces any detectable contraction in the muscle at all
The voltage that produces complete tetanus in a single stimulus
The lowest voltage that activates every motor unit, so force stops rising
questions.why: As voltage rises, progressively less excitable motor units are recruited, and once the last one is included, further voltage adds nothing, which defines the maximal stimulus. The stimulator's ceiling is a property of the equipment rather than of the muscle. The lowest voltage producing any contraction is threshold, at the other end of the recruitment range. Tetanus depends on stimulus frequency, and no single stimulus can produce it at any voltage.
questions.answerText: The lowest voltage that activates every motor unit, so force stops rising

questions.q: What are the three phases of a single muscle twitch as recorded on a tracing?
options: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase
Threshold, summation, tetanus
Depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization
Recruitment, treppe, fatigue
questions.why: A twitch tracing starts with a latent period in which tension has not yet appeared, then a contraction phase as tension rises to peak, then a relaxation phase as tension returns to baseline. Threshold, summation, and tetanus describe how twitches respond to stimulus intensity and frequency rather than the shape of one twitch. Depolarization and repolarization are phases of the action potential, an electrical event that precedes the mechanical one. Recruitment, treppe, and fatigue are separate phenomena of repeated stimulation.
questions.answerText: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase

questions.q: What is happening during the latent period of a muscle twitch?
options: Ca2+ is being pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The muscle is relaxing from the tension developed during the previous stimulus
Excitation contraction coupling is underway, but tension has not yet appeared
The stimulator is charging before it delivers the pulse
questions.why: During the latent period the action potential spreads, the T tubules signal the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ is released, and the series elastic elements begin to take up slack, all before measurable tension appears. Ca2+ reuptake happens later, during the relaxation phase. In a single twitch from rest there is no previous stimulus to relax from. The latent period is a property of the muscle, not of the stimulator's electronics.
questions.answerText: Excitation contraction coupling is underway, but tension has not yet appeared

questions.q: What is treppe, sometimes called the staircase effect?
options: A progressive rise in twitch force over the first several identical stimuli
The fusion of successive twitches into a smooth tetanus
The progressive fall in force during a sustained tetanus
The stepwise increase in whole muscle force as the stimulus voltage is raised
questions.why: When a rested muscle is stimulated repeatedly at a low frequency, the first several twitches get stronger even though the stimulus is unchanged, mainly because Ca2+ accumulates in the sarcoplasm and enzyme activity rises with warming. Fusion of twitches is summation leading to tetanus, which is a different phenomenon. Force falling during a sustained tetanus is fatigue. Stepwise increases with rising voltage are multiple motor unit recruitment.
questions.answerText: A progressive rise in twitch force over the first several identical stimuli

questions.q: What produces incomplete or unfused tetanus?
options: Stimuli arriving before full relaxation, so twitches summate but tension still ripples
Stimuli arriving after the muscle has fully relaxed, producing a train of separate twitches
A stimulus voltage between threshold and maximal, producing partial recruitment
Stimuli continuing after the muscle has begun to fatigue
questions.why: If the next stimulus arrives while some tension remains, the new twitch adds on top of it, and force climbs to a level higher than a single twitch while still showing a visible ripple. Stimuli spaced beyond full relaxation give a train of separate twitches, not tetanus. A submaximal voltage changes how many motor units contribute, not whether their twitches fuse. Fatigue causes force to fall during a stimulus train rather than producing the fused or unfused pattern.
questions.answerText: Stimuli arriving before full relaxation, so twitches summate but tension still ripples

questions.q: What defines complete or fused tetanus on a tracing?
options: A smooth sustained plateau with no relaxation between stimuli
A tension record showing distinct peaks separated by periods of partial relaxation
The maximal tension a single twitch can produce
A tension record that falls steadily throughout the stimulus train
questions.why: At high enough stimulus frequency there is no time for any relaxation between stimuli, so Ca2+ stays elevated and tension holds a smooth maximal plateau. Distinct peaks with partial relaxation describe unfused tetanus, one step below. A single twitch produces far less tension than tetanus, typically a third to a fifth as much. Steadily falling tension during a train is fatigue, not fusion.
questions.answerText: A smooth sustained plateau with no relaxation between stimuli

questions.q: Between threshold and maximal voltage, why does whole muscle force increase as stimulus voltage is raised?
options: Progressively more motor units are brought to threshold and contribute to the total force
Each activated fiber produces a larger action potential at higher voltage
The frequency of stimulation rises with voltage
Ca2+ release per action potential rises with voltage
questions.why: Motor units differ in excitability, so raising voltage recruits additional units, and their individual contributions add up, which is called multiple motor unit summation. A muscle fiber action potential is all or none, so it does not get larger with a stronger stimulus. Voltage and frequency are set independently on the stimulator. The Ca2+ released per action potential is likewise fixed for a given fiber and does not scale with stimulus strength.
questions.answerText: Progressively more motor units are brought to threshold and contribute to the total force

questions.q: A simulated muscle reaches its maximal stimulus at 4.0 V. Predict what happens to twitch force when the voltage is raised from 4.0 V to 8.0 V.
options: Force doubles, because voltage doubled
Force rises modestly, because the remaining fibers fire more strongly
Force falls, because the higher voltage inactivates some fibers
Force stays the same, because every motor unit is already recruited
questions.why: Once the maximal stimulus is reached, there are no unrecruited motor units left to add, so extra voltage produces no extra force, which is exactly how the maximal stimulus is identified in the simulation. Force does not scale with voltage; it scales with how many units the voltage recruits. Fibers already firing cannot fire more strongly, because the action potential is all or none. Excess voltage would damage a real preparation, but in the simulation force simply plateaus.
questions.answerText: Force stays the same, because every motor unit is already recruited

questions.q: A muscle is stimulated at a maximal voltage, and the frequency is raised from 5 Hz to 20 Hz. Predict what happens to the tracing.
options: Individual twitches begin to summate, so peak tension rises above single twitch tension
The tracing shows the same twitch height but four times as many twitches
Peak tension falls, because the muscle has less time to recover between stimuli
The muscle enters complete fused tetanus immediately at 20 Hz
questions.why: At 5 Hz the stimuli are 200 ms apart, long enough for full relaxation, but at 20 Hz they are 50 ms apart, so a new twitch begins before the previous one has decayed and the tensions add. Simply seeing more twitches of unchanged height would require the interval to still exceed the twitch duration. Tension rises rather than falls, since fatigue is not the dominant effect at this frequency early in a train. Complete fusion usually requires a higher frequency, so 20 Hz commonly gives unfused tetanus.
questions.answerText: Individual twitches begin to summate, so peak tension rises above single twitch tension

questions.q: In a simulation, the stimulus interval is set shorter than the muscle's relaxation time but long enough that a small dip in tension still occurs between stimuli. What will the tracing look like?
options: A series of identical separate twitches each returning fully to baseline
A perfectly smooth plateau with no oscillation
An oscillating ripple riding on an elevated plateau, or unfused tetanus
A single twitch followed by a flat baseline
questions.why: Partial relaxation between stimuli produces the characteristic ripple of unfused tetanus, with average tension well above single twitch level. Separate twitches returning to baseline require intervals longer than the twitch duration. A perfectly smooth plateau is complete tetanus, which needs a shorter interval than described. A single twitch would mean the stimulator delivered only one pulse.
questions.answerText: An oscillating ripple riding on an elevated plateau, or unfused tetanus

questions.q: A stimulus of 0.2 V is delivered to a simulated muscle whose threshold is 0.8 V. Predict the result.
options: A small contraction, since some fibers always respond to any stimulus
A normal sized twitch, since muscle contraction is all or none
A delayed contraction, since subthreshold stimuli take longer to act
No contraction, because no motor unit reaches threshold
questions.why: Below threshold no motor axon is brought to firing level, so no fiber contracts and the tracing stays flat. Fibers do not respond partially to a subthreshold stimulus, since the axon either fires or it does not. The all or none rule applies to individual fibers, not to a whole muscle, and it does not mean any stimulus produces a full twitch. Subthreshold stimuli do not eventually produce a delayed contraction; they produce none at all.
questions.answerText: No contraction, because no motor unit reaches threshold

questions.q: What intracellular condition must be maintained for a muscle to hold complete fused tetanus?
options: Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must return to its resting level between successive stimuli
The fiber must remain depolarized continuously without repolarizing
ATP must be depleted so that crossbridges stay attached
Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must stay elevated between successive stimuli
questions.why: Rapid stimulation releases Ca2+ faster than the sarcoplasmic reticulum can reclaim it, so troponin stays saturated, crossbridges keep cycling, and tension holds a smooth plateau. If Ca2+ returned to resting level between stimuli the muscle would relax and the tetanus would break up. The fiber does repolarize between action potentials; it is the mechanical response, not the electrical one, that fuses. Depleted ATP would produce rigor and a failure to relax, which is not what tetanus is.
questions.answerText: Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must stay elevated between successive stimuli

questions.q: A simulated muscle produces 10 g of tension in a single maximal twitch. What tension would you expect during complete tetanus of the same muscle?
options: About 10 g, since all motor units are already recruited in the maximal twitch
About 15 g, since summation adds only a small increment
About 200 g, since each stimulus in the train adds a full twitch of tension
About 30 to 50 g
questions.why: Tetanic tension typically runs three to five times single twitch tension, because sustained high Ca2+ keeps far more crossbridges attached than the brief Ca2+ transient of a single twitch allows. Recruitment is indeed maximal in both cases, which is exactly why the extra force must come from frequency rather than from more motor units. A 50 percent increase understates summation considerably. Tension does not accumulate without limit across a train; it plateaus once every available crossbridge is engaged.

questions.q: A simulated twitch lasts about 100 ms from stimulus to full relaxation. Roughly what minimum stimulus frequency is needed before twitches begin to summate?
options: Just above 1 Hz, since any repeated stimulus summates
Just above 100 Hz, since frequency must exceed the twitch duration in milliseconds
Just above 50 Hz, since fusion always requires 50 Hz or more
Just above 10 Hz, since a 100 ms twitch means stimuli must be closer than 100 ms apart
questions.why: A 100 ms twitch means one stimulus every 100 ms, or 10 Hz, lands just as the previous twitch ends, so anything faster than 10 Hz makes the twitches overlap and summate. At 1 Hz the stimuli are a full second apart, leaving 900 ms of quiet baseline between them. Treating 100 ms as 100 Hz confuses the interval with the frequency; those are reciprocals, not the same number. Around 50 Hz would give complete fusion in this muscle, which is well above the frequency at which summation merely begins.
questions.answerText: Just above 10 Hz, since a 100 ms twitch means stimuli must be closer than 100 ms apart

questions.q: A voltage series is run on a simulated muscle: 0.2 V gives 0 g, 0.4 V gives 0 g, 0.6 V gives 3 g, 1.5 V gives 12 g, 3.0 V gives 21 g, 4.5 V gives 24 g, 6.0 V gives 24 g. What are the threshold and maximal stimulus voltages?
options: Threshold 0.2 V and maximal stimulus 6.0 V
Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 4.5 V
Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 6.0 V
Threshold 0.4 V and maximal stimulus 3.0 V
questions.why: Threshold is the lowest voltage that produces any tension, which is 0.6 V here, and the maximal stimulus is the lowest voltage at which force stops rising, which is 4.5 V because 6.0 V adds nothing. Choosing 0.2 V as threshold ignores that it produced no contraction at all. Calling 6.0 V maximal misses that the plateau had already been reached one step earlier, and the maximal stimulus is defined as the lowest such voltage. At 3.0 V force is still climbing, so recruitment is incomplete there.
questions.answerText: Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 4.5 V

questions.q: A maximal voltage is held constant while frequency is stepped through 4 Hz, 12 Hz, 25 Hz, and 60 Hz. The tracings show separate twitches, small ripples on a raised baseline, larger ripples on a much higher baseline, and a smooth plateau. Which explanation of the progression is correct?
options: Rising frequency recruits progressively more motor units until every unit is active
Rising frequency increases the Ca2+ released per action potential until saturation
Rising frequency shortens the latent period until the twitches merge
Less time for Ca2+ reuptake at high frequency, so twitches summate until tension fuses
questions.why: With voltage held at maximal, every motor unit is already firing, so the only variable left is how often, and closer spacing keeps sarcoplasmic Ca2+ high and lets mechanical responses add until the record fuses. Recruitment cannot explain the change, since the constant maximal voltage means recruitment is already complete. Ca2+ released per action potential is fixed for a given fiber and does not grow with frequency. The latent period is essentially constant and far too brief to account for fusion.
questions.answerText: Less time for Ca2+ reuptake at high frequency, so twitches summate until tension fuses

questions.q: A rested simulated muscle is stimulated at 1 Hz with an unchanging maximal voltage. Twitch force rises from 8 g to 11 g over the first ten stimuli, holds near 11 g for two minutes, and then declines to 6 g. Which pair of mechanisms accounts for the rise and the later fall?
options: Recruitment of additional motor units, followed by loss of motor units from the stimulus train
Treppe from accumulating Ca2+ and warming, followed by metabolic fatigue
Increasing stimulus voltage delivered by the stimulator, followed by voltage decay
Progressive summation of twitches, followed by complete tetanus and then relaxation
questions.why: The early rise at fixed stimulus strength is treppe, driven by Ca2+ that has not been fully cleared between stimuli and by rising enzyme activity as the muscle warms, and the later decline is ordinary fatigue as byproducts build up. Recruitment cannot change, because the voltage is maximal and unchanging, and motor units are not lost during a stimulus train. The stem specifies that voltage is constant, so a drifting stimulator is excluded. At 1 Hz the twitches are a full second apart and never summate, so this is not a fusion phenomenon.
questions.answerText: Treppe from accumulating Ca2+ and warming, followed by metabolic fatigue

questions.q: A simulation parameter is changed so that the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ pump works at half its normal rate, which roughly doubles the relaxation time of each twitch. Predict the effect on the stimulus frequency needed to produce complete tetanus.
options: A higher frequency is now needed, because each twitch produces less tension
The fusion frequency is unchanged, because it depends only on stimulus voltage
Complete tetanus becomes impossible, because Ca2+ can no longer reach the required level
A lower frequency now produces complete tetanus, because each twitch takes longer to decay
questions.why: Fusion occurs when the next stimulus arrives before the previous twitch has relaxed, so a longer relaxation phase means the stimuli can be further apart and still overlap, which lowers the fusion frequency. A slower pump does not reduce peak twitch tension in a way that would demand faster stimulation. Fusion frequency depends on twitch duration, not on voltage, which controls recruitment instead. Slowing reuptake actually makes Ca2+ easier to keep elevated, so tetanus becomes easier rather than impossible.
questions.answerText: A lower frequency now produces complete tetanus, because each twitch takes longer to decay

questions.q: In smooth muscle, which protein does calcium bind to in order to start contraction?
options: Calmodulin
Tropomyosin
Actin
Troponin C
questions.why: Smooth muscle has no troponin, so the Ca2+ receptor is calmodulin, a soluble protein floating in the cytosol rather than sitting on the thin filament. Four Ca2+ bind calmodulin, and that complex is what switches on the next enzyme in the pathway. Troponin C is the Ca2+ receptor in skeletal and cardiac muscle, which is the single most useful contrast to carry out of this chapter. Tropomyosin blocks myosin binding sites in striated muscle but does not bind the activating Ca2+, and actin is the thin filament itself.

questions.q: What does the Ca2+ calmodulin complex activate in smooth muscle?
options: Phospholipase C
Myosin light chain phosphatase
Protein kinase A
Myosin light chain kinase
questions.why: Ca2+ calmodulin binds and activates myosin light chain kinase, the enzyme that turns a Ca2+ signal into a working cross bridge. Myosin light chain phosphatase does the opposite job and is not Ca2+ activated, so it runs steadily in the background and drives relaxation when the kinase quiets down. Protein kinase A is activated by cAMP, not by Ca2+ calmodulin, and in smooth muscle it tends to promote relaxation. Phospholipase C sits upstream: it makes IP3 that raises Ca2+ in the first place.

questions.q: Once activated, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates what?
options: The troponin I subunit on the thin filament
A serine on the tropomyosin strand
The regulatory light chain on the myosin head
The actin monomer at the myosin binding site
questions.why: The target is a small regulatory light chain sitting on the neck of the myosin head, and phosphorylating it lets that head bind actin and cycle. Because the switch is on myosin, smooth muscle regulation is called thick filament regulation, in contrast to the thin filament regulation of striated muscle. Troponin I is not present in smooth muscle at all. Tropomyosin is present but is not the phosphorylation target, and actin itself is never phosphorylated to turn contraction on.
questions.answerText: The regulatory light chain on the myosin head

questions.q: Where does most of the Ca2+ that activates smooth muscle contraction come from?
options: Ca2+ pried off troponin when the cell depolarizes
The extracellular fluid, through plasma membrane Ca2+ channels
The sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is very extensive in this tissue
Mitochondrial stores dumped at the start of contraction
questions.why: Smooth muscle has only a sparse sarcoplasmic reticulum, so it leans on Ca2+ entering from outside through voltage gated and ligand gated channels, with a smaller contribution released from the SR. That dependence is why smooth muscle tone collapses quickly in a low Ca2+ bath and why Ca2+ channel blockers relax blood vessels. The SR answer describes skeletal muscle, where the store is large and self sufficient. Mitochondria buffer Ca2+ rather than supply it, and there is no troponin in smooth muscle to hold Ca2+.
questions.answerText: The extracellular fluid, through plasma membrane Ca2+ channels

questions.q: Which enzyme dephosphorylates the myosin light chain and allows smooth muscle to relax?
options: Phospholipase C
Myosin light chain phosphatase
Adenylyl cyclase
Myosin light chain kinase
questions.why: Relaxation is not simply the absence of Ca2+; a phosphatase has to strip the phosphate off the myosin light chain before the head stops cycling. Myosin light chain kinase adds that phosphate, so it is the on switch, not the off switch. Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, which promotes relaxation indirectly by reducing kinase activity, but it does not touch the light chain. Phospholipase C acts upstream to raise Ca2+, which pushes the cell toward contraction rather than relaxation.

questions.q: Which intracellular messenger releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of smooth muscle?
options: IP3
cGMP
Diacylglycerol
cAMP
questions.why: IP3 is made when a Gq coupled receptor activates phospholipase C, and it opens IP3 receptor channels on the SR to let stored Ca2+ into the cytosol. cAMP and cGMP both favor relaxation in smooth muscle rather than Ca2+ release; cGMP is the messenger nitric oxide works through. Diacylglycerol is the other product of phospholipase C, but it stays in the membrane and activates protein kinase C instead of releasing Ca2+.

questions.q: What is the latch state in smooth muscle?
options: The rigor condition that appears when cellular ATP is exhausted
A burst of extra force produced as Ca2+ first enters the cell
A refractory period after contraction when the cell cannot be restimulated
Sustained tension held by slowly cycling cross bridges at low ATP cost
questions.why: In the latch state, dephosphorylated myosin heads stay attached to actin and detach only very slowly, so tension holds while ATP use per second drops. This is the reason a sphincter or an arteriole can maintain tone for hours without exhausting the cell. It is not a refractory period, since smooth muscle can be restimulated during it. Rigor is a pathological state from lack of ATP, and unlike latch it cannot be reversed by the cell.
questions.answerText: Sustained tension held by slowly cycling cross bridges at low ATP cost

questions.q: How does the ATPase activity of smooth muscle myosin compare with that of skeletal muscle myosin?
options: About the same, with speed set only by Ca2+ removal
Somewhat faster, offset by having fewer cross bridges
Far slower, which is why shortening velocity is low
Far faster, but limited by the small sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: Smooth muscle myosin splits ATP roughly ten to several hundred times more slowly than skeletal myosin, so each cross bridge cycle takes longer and the muscle shortens slowly. That same slow cycling is what makes smooth muscle economical, because a head spends most of its cycle attached and bearing load. Slow Ca2+ removal does prolong relaxation, but it is not the reason shortening itself is slow. Nothing about smooth muscle myosin is faster than skeletal myosin.
questions.answerText: Far slower, which is why shortening velocity is low

questions.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane of an arteriole. What happens to myosin light chain kinase activity and to vessel tone?
options: MLCK activity is unchanged because its Ca2+ comes from the SR
MLCK activity falls but tone stays the same
MLCK activity falls and the vessel dilates
MLCK activity rises and the vessel constricts
questions.why: Blocking the channel cuts Ca2+ entry, less Ca2+ calmodulin forms, MLCK activity drops, and with the phosphatase still working the light chains are dephosphorylated and the vessel dilates. Tone cannot stay the same, because in smooth muscle tension tracks the fraction of phosphorylated light chains. The SR answer would be closer to the truth in skeletal muscle, where the store supplies nearly all the activator Ca2+ and channel blockers barely change force. Nothing in this pathway increases kinase activity.
questions.answerText: MLCK activity falls and the vessel dilates

questions.q: A signaling pathway inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase while cytosolic Ca2+ stays constant. What happens to tension?
options: Tension briefly rises and then returns to baseline
Tension rises at that same Ca2+ level
Tension falls because the kinase is inhibited as well
Tension is unchanged because Ca2+ alone sets tension
questions.why: Tension follows the balance between the kinase adding phosphate and the phosphatase removing it, so slowing the phosphatase lets phosphorylated myosin accumulate even with no extra Ca2+. Physiologists call this Ca2+ sensitization, and it is how several vasoconstrictors work. The Ca2+ only answer is the common misreading: Ca2+ sets kinase activity, not tension directly. Nothing here touches the kinase, and the shift persists as long as the phosphatase is inhibited.
questions.answerText: Tension rises at that same Ca2+ level

questions.q: A smooth muscle strip and a skeletal muscle fiber are moved into a Ca2+ free bath and stimulated repeatedly. Which one fails first, and why?
options: The smooth muscle, because its activator Ca2+ comes from outside the cell
Both fail at about the same time, since both depend on Ca2+ entry
Neither fails, since both release their Ca2+ from the internal stores
The skeletal fiber, because it has no internal store of Ca2+ to draw on
questions.why: Smooth muscle depends on Ca2+ crossing the plasma membrane, so removing extracellular Ca2+ takes away most of its trigger within seconds to minutes. Skeletal muscle keeps twitching because the voltage sensor in the T tubule opens the SR release channel mechanically, with no Ca2+ influx required. Saying both fail together ignores that difference in Ca2+ source. Skeletal muscle does store Ca2+, in a large and well loaded sarcoplasmic reticulum.
questions.answerText: The smooth muscle, because its activator Ca2+ comes from outside the cell

questions.q: Why does smooth muscle take much longer to reach peak tension than skeletal muscle after cytosolic Ca2+ rises?
options: The action potential in smooth muscle is much longer than the twitch
Ca2+ must diffuse the length of a long T tubule network first
Troponin in smooth muscle binds Ca2+ more slowly than elsewhere
An enzyme must phosphorylate myosin before cross bridges can cycle
questions.why: Skeletal muscle goes almost directly from Ca2+ binding troponin to cross bridge cycling, while smooth muscle inserts an enzymatic step: Ca2+ calmodulin must activate MLCK and MLCK must phosphorylate each myosin head. Add the slow myosin ATPase and peak tension can take a second or more instead of tens of milliseconds. Smooth muscle has no T tubules, using surface caveolae instead, and it has no troponin at all. The action potential length is not what sets the delay here.
questions.answerText: An enzyme must phosphorylate myosin before cross bridges can cycle

questions.q: A vascular smooth muscle cell holds a steady contraction for an hour. Compared with the first few seconds, what happens to ATP consumption per unit of tension?
options: It stays constant, since tension and ATP use are proportional
It falls only because tension itself is fading
It rises steadily as more cross bridges are recruited
It falls sharply as cross bridges settle into the latch state
questions.why: Once tension is established, many heads are dephosphorylated while still attached, and they detach so slowly that ATP splitting per second drops far below what the same tension costs in skeletal muscle. Tension is maintained, so the last option has the cause backwards. ATP use and tension are proportional only if cycling rate is fixed, and the whole point of latch is that the cycling rate changes. Smooth muscle also has no motor units to recruit.
questions.answerText: It falls sharply as cross bridges settle into the latch state

questions.q: A drug prevents Ca2+ from binding calmodulin. A smooth muscle cell is then stimulated and cytosolic Ca2+ rises normally. What tension develops?
options: Normal tension, since Ca2+ itself activates the myosin head
Reduced tension, because Ca2+ binds troponin more slowly
Little or none, because MLCK is never activated
Increased tension, because free Ca2+ stays elevated longer
questions.why: Ca2+ has no direct effect on smooth muscle myosin; it works only through calmodulin, which activates MLCK, which phosphorylates the light chain. Break the calmodulin step and a normal Ca2+ signal produces nothing. Troponin is not in this tissue, so a slowed troponin response cannot be the answer. Higher free Ca2+ does not help either, because with calmodulin blocked there is no route from Ca2+ to a cycling cross bridge.
questions.answerText: Little or none, because MLCK is never activated

questions.q: Norepinephrine binds an alpha1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle and the cell contracts without firing a full action potential. Which pathway explains this?
options: Gs raises cAMP, which activates protein kinase A
Gq activates phospholipase C, and IP3 releases SR Ca2+
Nitric oxide raises cGMP, which activates protein kinase G
The receptor opens voltage gated Na+ channels directly
questions.why: Alpha1 receptors couple to Gq, so phospholipase C makes IP3, IP3 empties SR Ca2+ into the cytosol, and tension develops with no change in membrane potential. Physiologists call this pharmacomechanical coupling, and it is why smooth muscle can grade tone without spikes. The Gs and cAMP route is what beta2 receptors use, and in smooth muscle it favors relaxation. The cGMP route is the nitric oxide relaxation pathway. Receptors do not gate voltage dependent Na+ channels directly.
questions.answerText: Gq activates phospholipase C, and IP3 releases SR Ca2+

questions.q: In an artery preparation, agonist A doubles cytosolic Ca2+ and doubles tension. Agonist B doubles tension with no measurable change in Ca2+. What best explains agonist B?
options: It inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase, so phosphorylated myosin builds up
It binds troponin C directly and bypasses the calmodulin pathway
It speeds the uptake of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during contraction
It opens more L-type Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane than A does
questions.why: Tension reflects the fraction of myosin light chains carrying a phosphate, and that fraction depends on kinase activity and phosphatase activity together. If tension doubles while Ca2+ is flat, the kinase side is unchanged, so the phosphatase side must have slowed. Opening more Ca2+ channels would have shown up as a Ca2+ rise, which is exactly what was not seen. There is no troponin in smooth muscle to bind. Faster SR uptake would lower Ca2+ and reduce tension, not raise it.
questions.answerText: It inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase, so phosphorylated myosin builds up

questions.q: A smooth muscle strip is stimulated and holds steady tension for twenty minutes. During that time cytosolic Ca2+ falls back toward baseline and the fraction of phosphorylated myosin light chains falls, yet tension barely changes. What accounts for the maintained tension?
options: Dephosphorylated cross bridges remain attached and detach very slowly
Troponin continues to hold the thin filament in its activated position
The muscle has entered rigor because ATP has been depleted
A second wave of Ca2+ entry keeps the kinase fully active
questions.why: This is the latch state: heads that were phosphorylated earlier stay bound to actin after losing their phosphate, and because their detachment rate is very low the tension they carry persists. That is the mechanical basis of the economy of smooth muscle tone. A second Ca2+ wave is ruled out by the measurement, since Ca2+ was falling. Troponin is absent from smooth muscle. Rigor would be irreversible and would follow ATP depletion, which does not happen during ordinary sustained tone.
questions.answerText: Dephosphorylated cross bridges remain attached and detach very slowly

questions.q: A toxin selectively blocks IP3 receptors on the smooth muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. The tissue is then tested with a Gq coupled agonist and, separately, with a high K+ solution that depolarizes the membrane. What is the expected result?
options: The high K+ response is abolished while the agonist response stays normal
Both responses are normal, since IP3 acts only during relaxation
Both responses are abolished, since all of the activator Ca2+ is SR derived
The agonist response is much reduced, while the high K+ response is preserved
questions.why: The Gq agonist works largely by making IP3 and emptying the SR, so blocking IP3 receptors takes most of that route away. High K+ depolarizes the membrane and opens voltage gated Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane, a path that does not require IP3 at all, so that response survives. The first option would be right in skeletal muscle, where essentially all activator Ca2+ is SR derived. IP3 raises Ca2+ and promotes contraction, so it is not a relaxation signal.
questions.answerText: The agonist response is much reduced, while the high K+ response is preserved

questions.q: An internal anal sphincter and a skeletal muscle are each asked to hold the same tension for ten minutes. How does ATP use compare, and why?
options: The two use similar ATP, since tension and ATP cost are fixed together
The skeletal muscle uses less, because motor units can be rotated
The smooth muscle uses far less, because its cross bridges cycle slowly
The smooth muscle uses more, because it must keep MLCK active throughout
questions.why: Each ATP is spent on one cross bridge cycle, so the cost of holding tension depends on how often bridges detach and reattach, not on tension alone. Smooth muscle myosin cycles slowly and latch bridges hold on longer still, so the same force costs a fraction of the ATP. Rotating motor units spreads fatigue in skeletal muscle but does not lower the total ATP needed for a given tension. Keeping some MLCK activity is cheap compared with the cost of fast cycling cross bridges.
questions.answerText: The smooth muscle uses far less, because its cross bridges cycle slowly

questions.q: Smooth muscle joined by many gap junctions contracts as one coordinated sheet. Which type is built this way, and where is it found?
options: Multi unit smooth muscle, as in the iris of the eye
Single unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine
Multi unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine
Single unit smooth muscle, as in the iris of the eye
questions.why: Single unit, also called visceral, smooth muscle is electrically coupled, so current spreads cell to cell through gap junctions and the layer behaves as a functional syncytium. The gut, ureter, uterus, and small blood vessels are built this way because a coordinated squeeze is the point. The iris is the standard example of the opposite arrangement, multi unit muscle, whose fibers are largely uncoupled. Pairing multi unit with the intestine or single unit with the iris swaps the two designs and their jobs.
questions.answerText: Single unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine

questions.q: In the iris and the arrector pili muscles, fibers are largely uncoupled and each has its own autonomic ending. What does that arrangement make possible?
options: Coordinated contraction of the whole sheet from one stimulus
Precise graded control of small numbers of fibers at a time
Spontaneous rhythmic contraction with no nerve input at all
Much faster conduction of excitation across the tissue
questions.why: Because the fibers are not electrically tied together, the nervous system can activate a few at a time and grade the response finely, which is what setting pupil size or lens shape demands. Contraction of the whole sheet from a single stimulus is the single unit design, and it depends on gap junctions this tissue mostly lacks. Spontaneous rhythm also comes from coupled pacemaker activity, so multi unit muscle is largely quiet without its nerves. Losing coupling slows the spread of excitation rather than speeding it.
questions.answerText: Precise graded control of small numbers of fibers at a time

questions.q: What are slow waves in single unit smooth muscle?
options: Spontaneous rhythmic swings in membrane potential from pacemaker cells
Long action potentials carried by a slow inward Ca2+ plateau current
Slowly spreading waves of Ca2+ released from the internal stores
Sustained depolarizations produced by continuous stretch of the wall
questions.why: Slow waves are subthreshold oscillations of the resting potential, set up by pacemaker cells such as the interstitial cells of Cajal and spread through gap junctions. When a wave crests above threshold it triggers a burst of spikes and a contraction, which is why gut motility has an underlying rhythm. A plateau bearing action potential describes cardiac muscle and some smooth muscle spikes, but it is not the pacemaker rhythm itself. Ca2+ waves are intracellular events, and stretch produces depolarization but not the intrinsic rhythm.
questions.answerText: Spontaneous rhythmic swings in membrane potential from pacemaker cells

questions.q: How does an autonomic axon deliver its transmitter to smooth muscle?
options: By direct current flow through gap junctions with the axon
Through capillaries after the transmitter enters the blood
Through a single tightly organized motor end plate per fiber
From varicosities along the axon into the surrounding space
questions.why: Autonomic axons run past smooth muscle cells and release transmitter from swellings called varicosities into a diffuse junction, so one axon can influence many cells and the transmitter reaches receptors across a wider gap. That diffuse arrangement is part of why smooth muscle responses are slower and more graded than a skeletal twitch. The tight motor end plate belongs to skeletal muscle. Neurons do not couple to smooth muscle electrically, and local transmitter is not delivered by way of the bloodstream, which is how hormones act.
questions.answerText: From varicosities along the axon into the surrounding space

questions.q: What is the myogenic response of smooth muscle?
options: Loss of tone when the muscle is held at a fixed length
Relaxation of the muscle when it is stretched
Contraction of the muscle in response to being stretched
Contraction triggered by sympathetic nerve traffic
questions.why: Stretch opens mechanically sensitive channels, the cell depolarizes, voltage gated Ca2+ channels open, and the muscle contracts. In an arteriole this is the basis of autoregulation, since a rise in pressure meets a rise in resistance. Relaxation to stretch is the opposite of what is observed and would let a vessel balloon. Sympathetic constriction is a neural stimulus, not the myogenic one, and the myogenic response is defined by a change in length, not by holding one.
questions.answerText: Contraction of the muscle in response to being stretched

questions.q: Which set of local changes in an actively metabolizing tissue relaxes nearby arteriolar smooth muscle?
options: Rising O2 with rising H+ and falling K+
Rising O2 with falling CO2 and falling adenosine
Falling O2 with rising CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine
Falling K+ with rising pH and rising O2
questions.why: Working tissue consumes O2 and produces CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine, and each of those changes relaxes the arteriolar smooth muscle upstream, so blood flow rises to meet demand. This is active hyperemia, and it is local: no nerve or hormone is required. The options built around rising O2 describe a tissue that is less active, which would allow tone to increase instead. Rising pH with falling K+ also points away from active metabolism.
questions.answerText: Falling O2 with rising CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine

questions.q: Which signal released by vascular endothelium relaxes the smooth muscle underneath it?
options: Angiotensin II
Nitric oxide
Thromboxane A2
Endothelin
questions.why: Nitric oxide diffuses from endothelium into the smooth muscle, raises cGMP, activates protein kinase G, and lowers cytosolic Ca2+ while promoting dephosphorylation of the myosin light chain, so the vessel dilates. Endothelin also comes from endothelium but is one of the strongest constrictors known. Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor rather than a local endothelial one. Thromboxane A2 comes mainly from platelets and constricts as well.

questions.q: What is meant by smooth muscle tone?
options: A steady partial contraction maintained at rest
The maximum tension the muscle can generate
The passive stiffness of the connective tissue in the wall
The rate at which the muscle can be stretched
questions.why: Smooth muscle sits partly contracted most of the time, so a stimulus can raise tone or lower it from that baseline, giving a two way control range. Arterioles rely on this: without resting tone there would be no way to dilate. Maximum tension is a separate measurement made under full activation. Passive stiffness comes from elastin and collagen and persists in dead tissue, while tone requires living, Ca2+ handling muscle. Rate of stretch is a property of the load, not a state of the muscle.
questions.answerText: A steady partial contraction maintained at rest

questions.q: A drug uncouples the gap junctions in the wall of the small intestine. What happens to peristalsis?
options: Nothing changes, since each fiber is separately innervated
The muscle becomes unable to contract at all
Contractions become stronger and better synchronized
Coordinated waves are lost and contraction becomes patchy
questions.why: Intestinal smooth muscle is single unit, so a pacemaker depolarization has to travel cell to cell through gap junctions to make a whole segment contract in sequence. Cut those connections and individual cells still contract, but not together, so propulsion fails. Separate innervation of every fiber describes multi unit muscle, not the gut. The cells retain their contractile machinery, so a complete loss of contraction is too strong a prediction.
questions.answerText: Coordinated waves are lost and contraction becomes patchy

questions.q: The ciliary muscle adjusts lens shape in small graded steps under autonomic control. Which classification does this behavior indicate?
options: Single unit smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Skeletal muscle under voluntary control
Multi unit smooth muscle
questions.why: Fine grading requires that the nervous system be able to activate some fibers and not others, which is only possible when the fibers are not electrically coupled. That uncoupled, individually innervated design is the definition of multi unit smooth muscle. Single unit muscle would move as one sheet and could not focus a lens smoothly. Cardiac muscle contracts as a whole by design, and the ciliary muscle is not under voluntary control, which rules out skeletal muscle.

questions.q: As the bladder fills, the smooth muscle in its wall is stretched. What is the immediate effect on membrane potential and on contraction?
options: The membrane potential is unchanged but Ca2+ still rises
The membrane depolarizes while contraction is suppressed
The membrane depolarizes and the muscle contracts
The membrane hyperpolarizes and the muscle relaxes
questions.why: Stretch opens mechanically gated cation channels, the cell depolarizes toward threshold, voltage gated Ca2+ channels open, and tension develops. Hyperpolarization would move the cell away from threshold and is the response to relaxing signals such as nitric oxide. Ca2+ can rise without a potential change when a Gq agonist acts, but stretch works through the membrane. Depolarization with suppressed contraction does not occur, because in smooth muscle depolarization is a route to Ca2+ entry.
questions.answerText: The membrane depolarizes and the muscle contracts

questions.q: Perfusion pressure to an arteriole rises abruptly while tissue metabolism stays constant. What does the myogenic response predict for vessel radius and for flow?
options: The vessel dilates, so flow rises in proportion to pressure
The vessel constricts, so flow rises much less than pressure did
The vessel is unchanged, so flow rises in proportion to pressure
The vessel constricts so hard that flow falls below baseline
questions.why: Higher pressure stretches the wall, the muscle depolarizes and contracts, and the smaller radius raises resistance, which blunts the rise in flow. That is autoregulation, and it protects downstream capillaries from a pressure surge. A dilating vessel would amplify the flow change rather than buffer it. An unchanged vessel would let flow track pressure directly. Autoregulation blunts the change, it does not overshoot into ischemia.
questions.answerText: The vessel constricts, so flow rises much less than pressure did

questions.q: A skeletal muscle goes from rest to heavy exercise and its metabolic rate rises sharply. What happens to the arterioles feeding it, and by what mechanism?
options: They dilate, because local metabolites accumulate and relax the muscle
They dilate, because circulating epinephrine reaches them first
They are unchanged, because flow is set entirely by blood pressure
They constrict, because sympathetic tone rises during exercise
questions.why: Adenosine, K+, CO2, and H+ build up faster than they are washed out, and each relaxes the arteriolar smooth muscle, so resistance falls and flow rises to match demand. This local control happens even in a denervated muscle, which is the classic evidence for it. Sympathetic tone does rise in exercise, but in working muscle the local metabolic signal overrides it. Epinephrine contributes at beta2 receptors, but the local metabolite effect is the dominant and faster mechanism, and flow is not set by pressure alone since resistance can change.
questions.answerText: They dilate, because local metabolites accumulate and relax the muscle

questions.q: Mast cells release histamine into an injured patch of skin. What is the effect on the local arteriolar smooth muscle and on the appearance of the skin?
options: The muscle relaxes, so the arterioles dilate and the skin reddens
The muscle is unaffected, since histamine acts only on capillaries
The muscle relaxes but skin color is unchanged, since flow is fixed
The muscle contracts, so the arterioles narrow and the skin pales
questions.why: Histamine is a local chemical signal that relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, and the resulting rise in local blood flow produces the redness and warmth of an inflamed area. Pallor would follow a constrictor such as norepinephrine acting on alpha1 receptors. Histamine also acts on venules to increase permeability and cause swelling, but it clearly acts on arteriolar muscle as well. Since resistance falls, flow is not fixed and the color change follows.
questions.answerText: The muscle relaxes, so the arterioles dilate and the skin reddens

questions.q: In one artery ring the endothelium has been rubbed away; in a matching ring it is intact. Acetylcholine is added to both. The intact ring relaxes and the denuded ring constricts slightly. What explains the difference?
options: Acetylcholine is broken down much faster when the endothelium is missing
The denuded ring lost its gap junctions, so the relaxation cannot spread through the wall
Rubbing the vessel damaged the underlying smooth muscle so it cannot relax
Acetylcholine releases nitric oxide from endothelium; without it, it acts on the muscle
questions.why: Acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors on endothelial cells, which raise nitric oxide, and nitric oxide raises cGMP in the smooth muscle and relaxes it. Strip the endothelium and acetylcholine reaches muscarinic receptors on the muscle itself, which raise Ca2+ and produce mild constriction. Mechanical damage to the muscle would abolish contraction as well as relaxation, and the denuded ring still contracts. Faster breakdown would produce no response rather than an opposite one, and gap junction loss would not reverse the sign of the response.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine releases nitric oxide from endothelium; without it, it acts on the muscle

questions.q: Near the end of pregnancy, hormonal changes increase the number of gap junctions between uterine smooth muscle cells. Predict how the uterus behaves during labor and why.
options: The muscle loses its stretch sensitivity as coupling increases
Each cell becomes independently innervated, allowing graded contractions
Excitation spreads farther, so contractions become coordinated and forceful
Contractions weaken, because current leaks away from each cell
questions.why: More gap junctions mean stronger electrical coupling, so a depolarization started anywhere in the wall spreads through a large mass of muscle and many cells contract together. A coordinated squeeze generates far more useful pressure than the scattered contractions of the uncoupled organ earlier in pregnancy. Adding gap junctions pushes the tissue further toward single unit behavior, not toward multi unit independent innervation. Coupling recruits neighbors rather than wasting current, and stretch sensitivity is retained, which matters as the uterus is distended.
questions.answerText: Excitation spreads farther, so contractions become coordinated and forceful

questions.q: Two smooth muscle preparations are studied. In preparation A, cutting the nerve supply abolishes all contraction. In preparation B, rhythmic contractions continue after the nerve is cut and a stimulus at one edge makes the whole strip contract. What are A and B?
options: A is single unit and B is multi unit
A is multi unit and B is single unit
Both are single unit, differing only in innervation density
A is smooth muscle and B is cardiac muscle
questions.why: Preparation A depends entirely on its nerves and shows no spread of excitation, which is the signature of multi unit muscle with individually innervated, uncoupled fibers. Preparation B has intrinsic pacemaker activity and propagates excitation through gap junctions, so it is single unit. Reversing the two ignores that spontaneous rhythm and spread both require coupling. If both were single unit, cutting the nerve would not silence A. Cardiac muscle would be a fair guess from B alone, but the preparation was stated to be smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: A is multi unit and B is single unit

questions.q: Blood pressure to a resting muscle bed rises by 20 percent. Flow jumps at first, then returns nearly to its original value within a minute even though pressure stays elevated. Which combination best explains the return?
options: Falling cardiac output that lowers flow back to baseline
Myogenic constriction plus washout of vasodilator metabolites
Sympathetic reflex dilation triggered by the higher pressure
A rise in blood viscosity produced by the faster flow
questions.why: Two local mechanisms push in the same direction here. Stretch of the arteriolar wall triggers myogenic contraction, and the initial surge in flow washes out adenosine and other dilator metabolites, so tone rises from both sides and resistance climbs until flow is close to where it started. Pressure was stated to stay elevated, so a fall in cardiac output is not the explanation. A sympathetic reflex to high pressure would reduce constrictor tone rather than dilate actively, and it is not needed since autoregulation persists in a denervated bed. Viscosity does not change appreciably over a minute.
questions.answerText: Myogenic constriction plus washout of vasodilator metabolites

questions.q: Which component of the intercalated disc lets current pass directly from one cardiac cell to the next?
options: Gap junctions
The fascia adherens
Tight junctions
Desmosomes
questions.why: Gap junctions are pores built from connexon proteins that link the cytoplasm of neighboring myocytes, so ions carrying a depolarization flow straight into the next cell with no synapse in between. That low resistance path is what turns millions of separate cells into one conducting mass. Desmosomes and the fascia adherens are the mechanical halves of the disc: they hold cells together and transmit force. Tight junctions seal spaces between epithelial cells and are not a feature of the intercalated disc.

questions.q: Which part of the intercalated disc keeps cardiac cells from being pulled apart during a forceful contraction?
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal cisternae
The gap junctions
The T tubules at the Z line
The desmosomes and fascia adherens
questions.why: Desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments between cells and the fascia adherens ties the thin filaments of one cell to those of the next, so tension generated in one myocyte is handed mechanically to its neighbor. Without them the electrical connection would tear apart under load. Gap junctions handle the electrical job and are far too small to carry much force. T tubules bring the action potential into the interior of a cell, and terminal cisternae store Ca2+; neither joins cell to cell.

questions.q: Which ion current is chiefly responsible for the plateau phase of the ventricular action potential?
options: K+ leaving through delayed rectifier channels
Cl- entering through anion channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type Ca2+ channels
Na+ entering through fast Na+ channels
questions.why: During the plateau, slow L-type Ca2+ channels stay open and the inward Ca2+ current roughly balances the outward K+ current, holding the membrane depolarized for a couple hundred milliseconds. That Ca2+ does double duty, since it also triggers Ca2+ release from the SR. Fast Na+ channels drive the upstroke and then inactivate within a few milliseconds. Delayed rectifier K+ current is present but is what finally ends the plateau when it grows, and Cl- current is not the main plateau carrier.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ entering through L-type Ca2+ channels

questions.q: About how long does a ventricular action potential last?
options: Roughly 2 ms
Roughly 25 ms
Roughly 250 ms
Roughly 2500 ms
questions.why: A ventricular action potential lasts on the order of 200 to 300 ms, most of it plateau, which is comparable to the duration of the contraction it produces. That match is the reason the heart cannot summate twitches. Roughly 2 ms is the skeletal muscle value, and comparing the two numbers is the fastest way to see why one tissue tetanizes and the other does not. 2500 ms would be longer than an entire cardiac cycle at rest.

questions.q: What is the absolute refractory period?
options: The interval when only a stronger than normal stimulus can trigger a response
The interval during which no stimulus of any strength can trigger a response
The interval when the cell is repolarized but still mechanically contracted
The interval between the action potential and the start of tension
questions.why: During the absolute refractory period the fast Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot be reopened at any voltage, so the cell simply will not fire again. In ventricular muscle it covers nearly the whole plateau and much of repolarization. The option about needing a stronger stimulus defines the relative refractory period that follows it, when some Na+ channels have recovered. The other choices describe mechanical timing, which is a separate matter from excitability.
questions.answerText: The interval during which no stimulus of any strength can trigger a response

questions.q: What does it mean to say the myocardium behaves as a functional syncytium?
options: The cells stay separate but are coupled enough to respond as one unit
The cells contract independently and their forces add up in the wall
The cells share one nerve supply that reaches every fiber directly
The cells fuse into one giant multinucleated cell during development
questions.why: Each myocyte keeps its own membrane and nucleus, but gap junctions couple them electrically so an impulse anywhere spreads through the whole mass and the chamber contracts all or none. That is what functional means here, as opposed to the true structural fusion seen in skeletal muscle fibers. Independent contraction is exactly what the coupling prevents, and it would make the chamber a poor pump. Cardiac cells are influenced by autonomic nerves, but the coordinated contraction does not depend on neural distribution.
questions.answerText: The cells stay separate but are coupled enough to respond as one unit

questions.q: What is calcium induced calcium release in cardiac muscle?
options: Ca2+ leaving the SR then triggers Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane
Ca2+ binding calmodulin activates a kinase that opens the SR channels
Ca2+ pumped into the SR triggers a release of Ca2+ from mitochondria
Ca2+ entering from outside opens SR ryanodine receptors to release more
questions.why: A modest trigger of Ca2+ crossing the sarcolemma through L-type channels opens ryanodine receptors on the neighboring SR, and the SR supplies most of the Ca2+ that actually binds troponin. Because the trigger comes from outside, the size of the beat depends on extracellular Ca2+, unlike skeletal muscle. The reversed version has the sequence backwards. The calmodulin and kinase route is smooth muscle regulation, and mitochondria buffer Ca2+ rather than release activator Ca2+.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ entering from outside opens SR ryanodine receptors to release more

questions.q: What keeps the atrial syncytium electrically separate from the ventricular syncytium?
options: The coronary vessels running in the AV groove
The pericardium wrapped around each chamber
The interventricular septum, which has no gap junctions
The fibrous skeleton, which conducts only at the AV node
questions.why: Nonconducting connective tissue rings sit between atria and ventricles, so excitation cannot cross directly and must funnel through the AV node. The delay that funnel imposes is what lets atria finish filling the ventricles before the ventricles contract. The pericardium surrounds the whole heart and plays no role in conduction.
