The interventricular septum is muscle and conducts well. Coronary vessels supply blood, not insulation.
questions.answerText: The fibrous skeleton, which conducts only at the AV node

questions.q: Why can skeletal muscle be tetanized while cardiac muscle cannot?
options: Cardiac muscle relaxes faster than skeletal muscle, preventing summation
Cardiac muscle lacks the sarcoplasmic reticulum needed for summation
Cardiac cells are refractory almost as long as the contraction lasts
Cardiac muscle cannot be stimulated more than once per second
questions.why: In skeletal muscle a 2 ms action potential is long over before the twitch peaks, so a second stimulus can arrive while tension is still present and the twitches add. In cardiac muscle the long plateau keeps the cell refractory through nearly the entire contraction, so by the time another beat can be triggered the muscle has relaxed. Cardiac muscle has a working sarcoplasmic reticulum. It can be driven at three or four beats per second, just never fast enough to summate. Cardiac relaxation is slower, not faster, than skeletal.
questions.answerText: Cardiac cells are refractory almost as long as the contraction lasts

questions.q: A drug shortens the ventricular action potential from about 250 ms to about 10 ms without changing anything else. What becomes possible, and what is the consequence for the heart?
options: Conduction between cells would stop, since gap junctions need the plateau
Twitches could summate into tetanus, and the heart could not fill
Contraction would become weaker but the rhythm would be safer
The heart would beat more slowly but pump more per beat
questions.why: The long refractory period exists because of the plateau, so shortening the action potential shortens the refractory period and lets a second stimulus arrive while tension is still developing. A tetanized ventricle stays contracted, never relaxes, and therefore never fills, so output falls to nothing. This is a rhythm hazard, not a safety feature. Stroke volume depends on filling, which is precisely what is lost, and gap junctions conduct current regardless of action potential shape.
questions.answerText: Twitches could summate into tetanus, and the heart could not fill

questions.q: A blocker of cardiac gap junctions is applied to a sheet of ventricular myocytes, then one cell is stimulated. What is observed?
options: Only that cell and its immediate neighbors contract
The whole sheet contracts, but more slowly than before
No cell contracts, since excitation requires cell to cell coupling
The whole sheet contracts as usual, since each cell is separately innervated
questions.why: Excitation spreads through the myocardium by current flowing through gap junctions, so blocking them isolates cells and the impulse dies out near where it started. This is why uncoupling produces slow, fragmented conduction rather than a slower whole heart beat. Cardiac muscle is not innervated fiber by fiber the way multi unit smooth muscle is. The stimulated cell itself still has intact channels and contracts normally, so a complete absence of contraction is wrong.
questions.answerText: Only that cell and its immediate neighbors contract

questions.q: A second stimulus is delivered to a ventricular myocyte 100 ms after the first, during the plateau. What happens?
options: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory
The plateau is cut short and the cell repolarizes early
A second, smaller action potential is triggered
A full second action potential is triggered and tension adds
questions.why: At 100 ms the cell is still in the plateau with its fast Na+ channels inactivated, so no stimulus strength will produce another upstroke. That protection is what prevents summation of cardiac twitches. A smaller response would be possible only later, in the relative refractory period, once some Na+ channels have recovered. Tension cannot add during absolute refractoriness, and an ordinary stimulus does not truncate the plateau.
questions.answerText: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory

questions.q: A stimulus is delivered late in repolarization, during the relative refractory period. How does the response compare with a normal beat?
options: A normal action potential is produced with a stimulus of normal size
A normal action potential is produced but the tension is doubled
No response occurs at any stimulus strength at all
A weaker action potential, and only a stronger stimulus triggers it
questions.why: By late repolarization some fast Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation but many have not, so a larger than normal stimulus can trigger an upstroke, and that upstroke rises more slowly and conducts more slowly than usual. That premature beat is also weaker mechanically because SR Ca2+ has not fully recovered. Total unresponsiveness describes the absolute refractory period that came just before. A fully normal response requires waiting until the cell has repolarized completely.
questions.answerText: A weaker action potential, and only a stronger stimulus triggers it

questions.q: Since cardiac muscle can neither recruit more fibers nor summate twitches, how does the heart increase the force of a beat?
options: By shortening the refractory period so more cross bridges can attach
By recruiting the reserve myocytes that stayed silent on the previous beat
By raising Ca2+ per beat and by stretching the fibers before contraction
By firing action potentials at a higher frequency until twitches fuse
questions.why: Every beat already activates every cell, so the two available levers are how much Ca2+ reaches troponin, which sympathetic stimulation increases, and how much the fibers are stretched by filling, which is the length tension relationship. There is no reserve pool of silent myocytes to recruit; that idea belongs to motor unit recruitment in skeletal muscle. Fusion of twitches is exactly what refractoriness prevents. A shorter refractory period would threaten rhythm without adding cross bridges to a single beat.
questions.answerText: By raising Ca2+ per beat and by stretching the fibers before contraction

questions.q: An L-type Ca2+ channel blocker is applied to a ventricular myocyte. Predict the effect on the strength of contraction and give the reason.
options: Contraction is unchanged, because troponin is already saturated with Ca2+
Contraction weakens, because less trigger Ca2+ enters and the SR releases less
Contraction strengthens, because Ca2+ stays in the SR for the next beat
Contraction is unchanged, because activator Ca2+ is entirely SR derived
questions.why: Cardiac contraction depends on calcium induced calcium release, so the amount of Ca2+ crossing the sarcolemma sets how much the SR adds, and blocking the L-type channel scales the whole beat down. The same drug barely changes skeletal muscle force, which is the comparison worth remembering. Retaining Ca2+ in the SR does not help if there is no trigger to release it. Troponin is far from saturated during a normal beat, which is why beat strength can be graded at all.
questions.answerText: Contraction weakens, because less trigger Ca2+ enters and the SR releases less

questions.q: In a region of ischemic myocardium, connexons close and the cells uncouple electrically. Trace the consequences for conduction through that region and for the pumping of the chamber.
options: Conduction speeds up locally, and the chamber contracts more forcefully
Conduction slows or fails there, and the chamber contracts unevenly and pumps less
Conduction is unaffected, since impulses travel through the interstitial fluid
Conduction stops everywhere in the heart, since one syncytium is lost
questions.why: Current spreading from cell to cell needs open gap junctions, so uncoupling raises the resistance of the path and the impulse crawls or blocks. Muscle that is excited late, or not at all, contracts out of step with the rest of the wall, so some regions are still shortening while others are already relaxing and less pressure is developed. Uncoupling can never speed conduction. Impulses do not travel usefully through interstitial fluid between cells. The rest of the syncytium remains coupled, so the whole heart does not stop.
questions.answerText: Conduction slows or fails there, and the chamber contracts unevenly and pumps less

questions.q: A ventricular strip is stimulated, then a test stimulus is applied at varying delays. At 150 ms there is no response at any strength; at 250 ms a strong stimulus gives a small beat; at 400 ms a normal stimulus gives a full beat. What do these results show?
options: Absolute refractoriness ends between 150 and 250 ms, full recovery near 400 ms
The muscle was fatigued at 150 ms and had recovered its ATP by 400 ms
The tissue was briefly tetanized at 250 ms, producing that small extra beat
The action potential lasts only 150 ms, since a response appeared after that
questions.why: Failure at any strength marks absolute refractoriness, a response only to a strong stimulus marks the relative refractory period, and a normal response to a normal stimulus means the cell has fully recovered. Reading the three delays in order gives the timing of recovery directly. The 150 ms result puts a lower bound on refractoriness, not the exact action potential duration. Fatigue would not resolve on this timescale and would not depend on stimulus strength. A single small beat is a premature response, not tetanus.
questions.answerText: Absolute refractoriness ends between 150 and 250 ms, full recovery near 400 ms

questions.q: A drug lengthens the ventricular action potential by 100 ms. Predict its effects on the refractory period and on the highest heart rate the ventricle can follow.
options: The refractory period lengthens but maximum rate is set by the SA node alone
The refractory period shortens, since repolarization is spread over more time
Neither changes, because refractoriness depends only on Na+ channel number
The refractory period lengthens and the maximum followable rate falls
questions.why: The refractory period is tied to the action potential, since Na+ channels recover from inactivation only as the membrane repolarizes, so a longer plateau means a longer wait before the next beat is possible. If beats cannot be triggered more often than about once per refractory period, the ceiling on ventricular rate drops. The SA node sets the rate it tries to impose, but the ventricle can only follow what its own refractoriness allows. A longer action potential cannot shorten refractoriness, and refractory timing depends on the voltage course, not on channel number alone.
questions.answerText: The refractory period lengthens and the maximum followable rate falls

questions.q: Two muscle preparations are stimulated at 50 Hz. Preparation X fuses into a smooth sustained contraction; preparation Y produces separate beats at the same rate the stimulator allows and never fuses. Which is cardiac, and what single property explains the difference?
options: X is cardiac, because only cardiac muscle can maintain sustained tension
X is cardiac, because its cells are electrically coupled and contract together
Y is cardiac, because its refractory period covers nearly the whole contraction
Y is cardiac, because it lacks a sarcoplasmic reticulum to sustain Ca2+
questions.why: Fusion requires that a second stimulus arrive while tension from the first is still present, and cardiac muscle stays refractory for nearly the entire twitch, so it simply cannot be restimulated in that window. Preparation X, which fuses, must be skeletal. Electrical coupling explains why cardiac cells beat together, but coupling has nothing to do with whether twitches summate. Cardiac muscle does have a sarcoplasmic reticulum. Sustained tetanic tension is a skeletal capability, and for a pump it would be a disaster, since a ventricle that never relaxes never fills.
questions.answerText: Y is cardiac, because its refractory period covers nearly the whole contraction

questions.q: In which muscle types does Ca2+ start contraction by binding troponin C on the thin filament?
options: All three muscle types
Skeletal muscle only
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
questions.why: Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated and both use the troponin tropomyosin complex, so Ca2+ binding troponin C swings tropomyosin off the myosin binding sites. Smooth muscle has no troponin at all, which is why it cannot be on this list, and it is the single most useful fact for telling the three tissues apart mechanistically. Answering skeletal only forgets that cardiac thin filaments carry the same regulatory proteins. Grouping cardiac with smooth mixes a thin filament system with a thick filament one.

questions.q: In which muscle type is the Ca2+ binding regulatory protein a soluble cytosolic protein rather than part of the thin filament?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac and skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Smooth muscle uses calmodulin, which floats free in the cytosol and, once it has bound Ca2+, activates myosin light chain kinase. Because the switch ends up on the myosin head, smooth muscle regulation is called thick filament regulation. Skeletal and cardiac muscle both attach the Ca2+ sensor to the thin filament as troponin C, so the switch sits on actin rather than on myosin. That difference in where the switch lives predicts almost everything else about the three tissues.

questions.q: How much of the activator Ca2+ for a skeletal muscle twitch comes from outside the cell?
options: Essentially none of it
None during a twitch, but all during tetanus
Essentially all of it
About half of it
questions.why: In skeletal muscle the voltage sensor in the T tubule membrane opens the SR release channel by direct mechanical coupling, so no Ca2+ needs to cross the plasma membrane for a twitch to occur. That self sufficiency is why a skeletal fiber keeps twitching in a Ca2+ free bath and why Ca2+ channel blockers do not weaken it. Cardiac and smooth muscle are the tissues that depend on Ca2+ entry. Tetanus is repeated activation of the same mechanism, so the Ca2+ source does not change.

questions.q: Which muscle types require Ca2+ to cross the plasma membrane for each contraction?
options: Skeletal and smooth muscle
All three types equally
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
questions.why: Cardiac muscle needs a trigger of entering Ca2+ to open ryanodine receptors, and smooth muscle relies on entering Ca2+ for most of its activator supply, so both tissues are sensitive to extracellular Ca2+ and to Ca2+ channel blockers. Skeletal muscle is the exception, since its T tubule voltage sensor opens the SR channel mechanically. Any option that includes skeletal muscle in the entry dependent group misses that mechanical coupling. The three are not equal here, and this is exactly the difference that experiments in low Ca2+ solutions expose.

questions.q: In which muscle type does the Ca2+ regulated switch sit on the myosin head rather than on actin?
options: Skeletal muscle
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
questions.why: In smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates a regulatory light chain on the myosin head, so the thick filament carries the on switch. In skeletal and cardiac muscle the switch is on the thin filament, where troponin and tropomyosin control access to the myosin binding sites. Because a kinase has to act before a smooth muscle cross bridge can cycle, contraction there begins more slowly than in either striated tissue. Recognizing which filament holds the switch tells you which drugs and which second messengers can change tension.

questions.q: Which muscle type grades the force of contraction by recruiting more motor units?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
questions.why: Only skeletal muscle is organized into motor units, each a somatic motor neuron and the fibers it controls, so the nervous system can add units to add force. Cardiac muscle is a syncytium and activates every cell on every beat, leaving nothing to recruit, so it grades force through Ca2+ per beat and fiber length instead. Smooth muscle grades force through the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated. Recruitment requires separate control of separate fibers, which the coupled tissues do not have.

questions.q: Which muscle type takes the longest to reach peak tension and can hold that tension the longest?
options: Slow twitch skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Fast twitch skeletal muscle
questions.why: Smooth muscle can take a second or more to reach peak tension, because a kinase must phosphorylate myosin and the myosin ATPase is very slow, and the same slow cycling lets it hold tension for hours at low ATP cost. Cardiac muscle contracts in a couple hundred milliseconds and must relax to allow filling, so long holding is not an option. Fast twitch skeletal fibers peak in tens of milliseconds and fatigue quickly. Slow twitch fibers are more fatigue resistant than fast ones but are still far faster and more expensive than smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which muscle types can generate their own rhythmic excitation without any input from a nerve?
options: Cardiac and single unit smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle
Multi unit smooth muscle only
Skeletal muscle alone
questions.why: Pacemaker activity requires cells with unstable resting potentials plus gap junctions to spread the rhythm, and both the heart and single unit smooth muscle have them, which is why a denervated heart still beats and an isolated loop of intestine still shows waves. Skeletal muscle is quiet without its motor neuron, so any option containing it is wrong. Multi unit smooth muscle is largely uncoupled and depends on its nerves, which is what makes its control precise rather than rhythmic.
questions.answerText: Cardiac and single unit smooth muscle

questions.q: A cardiac myocyte and a skeletal fiber are moved into a Ca2+ free solution and stimulated. Which stops contracting first, and why?
options: The cardiac myocyte, because it needs entering Ca2+ to trigger SR release
They stop together, since both depend on the same SR store of Ca2+
Neither stops, since both release all of their Ca2+ from the SR
The skeletal fiber, because it holds a smaller store of Ca2+ in its SR
questions.why: Cardiac contraction depends on calcium induced calcium release, so within a few beats there is no trigger Ca2+ and the SR stops releasing, even though the store itself is still there. Skeletal muscle opens its SR channel mechanically from the T tubule voltage sensor, so it keeps twitching until the store runs down. The skeletal SR is the larger, better loaded store, not the smaller one. The two tissues do not behave alike here, and this experiment is the cleanest demonstration of that difference in Ca2+ source.
questions.answerText: The cardiac myocyte, because it needs entering Ca2+ to trigger SR release

questions.q: A drug binds troponin C and prevents Ca2+ from binding it. Which tissues lose the ability to contract?
options: Cardiac and smooth muscle, with skeletal muscle unaffected
All three muscle types
Smooth muscle only
Skeletal and cardiac muscle, with smooth muscle unaffected
questions.why: The drug can only work where its target exists, and troponin is a thin filament protein of striated muscle. Smooth muscle has no troponin and routes Ca2+ through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase instead, so it goes on contracting. Saying all three assumes a shared mechanism that the tissues do not share. The options that spare skeletal muscle or hit smooth muscle alone reverse which tissues carry troponin, which is the fact this card is asking you to reason from.
questions.answerText: Skeletal and cardiac muscle, with smooth muscle unaffected

questions.q: A drug inhibits calmodulin. Which muscle tissue loses the ability to contract, and why?
options: Cardiac muscle, because calmodulin triggers Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release
All three, because calmodulin is the universal Ca2+ sensor
Smooth muscle, because Ca2+ reaches myosin only through calmodulin there
Skeletal muscle, because calmodulin activates its SR release channel
questions.why: In smooth muscle, Ca2+ has no direct effect on the contractile machinery; it must bind calmodulin, and Ca2+ calmodulin must activate myosin light chain kinase. Remove calmodulin from that chain and a normal Ca2+ signal produces no tension. Skeletal and cardiac muscle route Ca2+ through troponin C, so their twitch is intact. Calmodulin is present in nearly all cells and does many jobs, but it is not the trigger for striated muscle contraction, so it is not universal in that sense.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle, because Ca2+ reaches myosin only through calmodulin there

questions.q: A patient takes a Ca2+ channel blocker that relaxes arteries and reduces the force of cardiac contraction. Why is skeletal muscle strength essentially unchanged?
options: Skeletal muscle uses a different regulatory protein, so channel blockers cannot bind
Skeletal muscle does not need Ca2+ entry, since its SR release is triggered mechanically
Skeletal muscle contracts too quickly for the drug to take effect
Skeletal muscle receives less blood flow, so the drug concentration is lower
questions.why: The drug lowers Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane, and only tissues that depend on entry feel it. In skeletal muscle the T tubule voltage sensor opens the SR release channel by physical coupling, so entering Ca2+ is not part of the pathway and force is preserved. The regulatory protein difference is real but is not what saves skeletal muscle here, since the drug acts on channels rather than on troponin. Speed of contraction and blood flow do not determine whether a pathway needs Ca2+ entry.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle does not need Ca2+ entry, since its SR release is triggered mechanically

questions.q: An unlabeled muscle strip develops peak tension slowly over about a second and then holds that tension for many minutes at very low ATP cost. From that behavior alone, which regulatory system is it most likely using?
options: Troponin and tropomyosin on the thin filament, with a fast myosin ATPase
Calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase acting on the myosin head
Troponin regulation combined with a long plateau action potential
Direct Ca2+ binding to myosin with no regulatory protein involved
questions.why: Slow onset points to an enzymatic step between the Ca2+ signal and the cross bridge, and cheap maintained tension points to slowly cycling latch bridges, and both are hallmarks of the calmodulin and MLCK system with its slow myosin. Troponin regulation with a fast ATPase would give a twitch in tens of milliseconds and would cost far more ATP to hold. Troponin plus a long plateau describes cardiac muscle, which contracts in a few hundred milliseconds and must relax to refill. No vertebrate muscle activates by Ca2+ binding myosin without a regulatory protein.
questions.answerText: Calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase acting on the myosin head

questions.q: A single stimulus produces an all or none twitch in a skeletal fiber, but graded tension in a smooth muscle cell. What accounts for the graded response in smooth muscle?
options: Tension tracks the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated
Smooth muscle recruits more cells as the stimulus grows stronger
Smooth muscle action potentials vary in amplitude with stimulus strength
Only some sarcomeres in the smooth muscle cell are activated at a time
questions.why: The amount of Ca2+ in a smooth muscle cell sets how much MLCK activity there is, that sets what fraction of myosin heads carry a phosphate, and tension follows that fraction, so intermediate levels of activation give intermediate tension. In a skeletal fiber a single action potential dumps enough SR Ca2+ to saturate troponin, so the twitch is all or none. Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres to activate selectively. Recruiting more cells grades the tissue response but not the response of one cell, and action potentials are all or none wherever they occur.
questions.answerText: Tension tracks the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated

questions.q: Cytosolic Ca2+ falls at a similar rate in a smooth muscle cell and a skeletal fiber after stimulation, yet the smooth muscle stays contracted much longer. Why?
options: Smooth muscle has no mechanism at all for pumping Ca2+ back out
Smooth muscle myosin binds actin irreversibly once tension develops
Smooth muscle Ca2+ stays bound to troponin after cytosolic Ca2+ falls
A phosphatase must strip phosphate from each myosin light chain first
questions.why: In skeletal muscle, relaxation follows Ca2+ removal almost immediately because Ca2+ simply leaves troponin. In smooth muscle the Ca2+ signal has already been converted into phosphorylated myosin, and that phosphate has to be removed by myosin light chain phosphatase before the heads stop cycling, which adds a further delay. Troponin is not present in smooth muscle. Smooth muscle does have Ca2+ pumps in the SR and the plasma membrane. Attachment is reversible, or the muscle could never relax at all.
questions.answerText: A phosphatase must strip phosphate from each myosin light chain first

questions.q: An unlabeled tissue contracts when it is stretched, shows no striations, holds tension for long periods with little ATP use, and is completely unaffected by a drug that blocks Ca2+ binding to troponin. Which tissue is it, and which two facts identify it?
options: Cardiac muscle, identified by its long plateau and its syncytial coupling
Slow twitch skeletal muscle, identified by fatigue resistance and troponin
Smooth muscle, identified by calmodulin regulation and slow economical cycling
Multi unit smooth muscle, identified by the absence of any Ca2+ requirement
questions.why: Insensitivity to a troponin drug rules out both striated tissues at once, since only smooth muscle regulates through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase. Long cheap tension is the latch behavior that follows from the very slow smooth muscle myosin ATPase, and stretch induced contraction is the myogenic response. Cardiac muscle would have been silenced by the troponin drug and cannot hold tension without failing as a pump. Slow twitch skeletal fibers still use troponin. Smooth muscle certainly requires Ca2+; it simply routes it differently.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle, identified by calmodulin regulation and slow economical cycling

questions.q: An unlabeled tissue has action potentials lasting about 250 ms, cannot be tetanized, loses much of its force when extracellular Ca2+ is halved, and is silenced by a drug that blocks Ca2+ binding to troponin. Which tissue is it, and which two findings separate it from skeletal muscle?
options: Cardiac muscle, separated by its use of calmodulin rather than troponin
Smooth muscle, separated by its slow contraction and its calmodulin based regulation
Cardiac muscle, separated by dependence on entering Ca2+ and a long refractory period
Skeletal muscle, separated only by the presence of gap junctions between cells
questions.why: The troponin drug works, so the tissue is striated, which leaves skeletal or cardiac. Two findings then point to cardiac: force falls when extracellular Ca2+ drops, which fits calcium induced calcium release rather than the self sufficient skeletal SR, and the long action potential makes the refractory period cover the contraction so tetanus is impossible. Smooth muscle is excluded by its sensitivity to the troponin drug. Calling it cardiac because of calmodulin contradicts the same finding, since cardiac muscle regulates through troponin.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle, separated by dependence on entering Ca2+ and a long refractory period

questions.q: A toxin blocks ryanodine receptors. Predict its effect on a skeletal fiber and on a smooth muscle cell, and explain the difference.
options: Both are abolished, since both tissues release all activator Ca2+ through ryanodine receptors
The skeletal twitch is nearly abolished while smooth muscle contracts on, using entering Ca2+ and IP3 receptors
Smooth muscle contraction is abolished while skeletal muscle is unaffected, since only smooth muscle has an SR
Neither tissue is affected, since ryanodine receptors are found only in cardiac muscle cells
questions.why: Skeletal muscle sends essentially all of its activator Ca2+ through the ryanodine receptor, opened mechanically by the T tubule voltage sensor, so blocking that channel takes the twitch away. Smooth muscle draws most of its Ca2+ across the plasma membrane and releases the rest through IP3 receptors, so it has routes the toxin does not touch. Skeletal muscle has by far the more developed SR, so the third option has the tissues backwards. Ryanodine receptors are present in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle, not in the heart alone.
questions.answerText: The skeletal twitch is nearly abolished while smooth muscle contracts on, using entering Ca2+ and IP3 receptors

questions.q: Two strips reach the same peak tension. Strip 1 gets there in about 50 ms and burns ATP rapidly; strip 2 takes about 1.5 s and then holds tension with very little further ATP use. Explain the difference in terms of the regulatory protein and the myosin.
options: Strip 1 uses troponin with a fast myosin ATPase, while strip 2 uses MLCK and cycles slowly
Strip 1 stores more Ca2+, so it can afford to spend ATP faster
Strip 2 has a longer action potential, which spreads the same ATP cost over more time
Strip 2 simply has more cross bridges, so each one works less hard
questions.why: Speed of onset is set by how directly the Ca2+ signal reaches the cross bridge, and Ca2+ binding troponin is immediate while an MLCK phosphorylation step is not. ATP cost per unit tension is set by cycling rate, and the slow smooth muscle myosin, with latch bridges that hang on after dephosphorylation, holds force for a fraction of the ATP. More cross bridges would not reduce the ATP each cycle costs. Ca2+ storage does not change the price of a cross bridge cycle, and action potential duration does not set the rate of ATP hydrolysis by myosin.
questions.answerText: Strip 1 uses troponin with a fast myosin ATPase, while strip 2 uses MLCK and cycles slowly
